# First.

...understood universally: because they are such that Man by nature—once the meaning of the words they contain is understood—immediately, aided by the intellect, clearly knows their truth. As for example: when it is said that **the Whole is greater than the Part**: once the meaning of these two words, "Whole" and "Part," is known, then and there one knows, without any other help, that such a position is so true that if someone wanted to make you believe otherwise, their words would not be trusted, and they would be considered a madman.

**CLAV.** Truly, anyone who wanted to persuade me of the contrary would labor in vain.

**GIOS.** This principle is called "Common" because it serves in various Sciences. Thus, in Geometry, the Geometer applies it to measurable quantities; in Arithmetic, the Arithmetician accommodates it to countable quantities; and in Music, the Musician uses it and adapts it to **Intervals**, or rather, to **Sonorous Quantities**. These common principles or propositions are called **Maxims** <term>Maxim<gloss>original: "Dignità"; in logic, these are axioms or self-evident truths that serve as the foundation of a system</gloss></term>; and because of the excellent knowledge they hold, they are assumed as the most well-known and primary principles of every Science. But other principles and other propositions are of a different nature: for some of them are found which, although not naturally known by the one who wants to learn a Science, must nevertheless be granted as true. One must not seek any other demonstration for them in that Science, for there is nothing more known above them there. And such propositions are of two kinds. One is that which, affirming or denying something, is called a **Definition**: which declares many terms necessary to that Science. Such Definitions are accepted as true without any other proof. For instance, when dealing with the Spheres, circles, and other such terms in Astronomy <note>original: "Astrologia"; in the 16th century, this term was often used interchangeably with astronomy to describe the mathematical study of the heavens</note>, it is assumed above all things that the nature of the celestial Circle consists of a circular figure, comprised of a single line, having a point in the middle from which all lines drawn to its circumference are equal.

**DESI.** The same can also be said of the Sphere, and of every other term necessary in such a Science.

**GIOS.** That is so. Hence, Astronomers, by means of such definitions, prove the properties of celestial bodies, which are truly their **Subject**.

**FRAN.** This same thing could also be said in Music regarding **Sonorous Bodies** which contain the interval, such as **Strings**: for dividing or measuring a straight line—placed in the stead of a string stretched over a space—is a very suitable means for the Musician to prove the conclusions of his Subject.

**GIOS.** You understand it very well; however, we shall move on to speak of the other kinds of propositions which are Maxims. These occur when, in a Science, certain things are assumed which contain an affirmation or negation; and they should be called and esteemed as propositions. And even if they are not manifest by their nature, they must nonetheless be assumed in the Sciences as known. These are of two manners.

**CLAV.** I pray you, do not fail to provide examples.

**GIOS.** I shall do so; just listen to me. The first manner is when the person who has to learn that Science, upon hearing such propositions, easily assents to them, not having been previously disposed more to accept them as true than to deny them as false. To give you an example: if I said that he who wishes to learn and understand Music must assume that all **Octaves** <term>Octave<gloss>original: "Diapason"; the fundamental interval in music that sounds like the "same" note at a higher or lower pitch</gloss></term> are equal in proportion; and you, hearing this, believed it—not having previously held an opinion yourself that they were more equal than unequal—these Positions are called **Suppositions** <term>Suppositions<gloss>also known as postulates; things taken for granted so that the lesson can proceed</gloss></term>.

**ADRI.** I understand very well; therefore, you may continue.

**GIOS.** The second manner of these Positions are those where, on the contrary, the one who has to learn the Science, hearing the Positions proposed to him for belief, assents to them because he is told he must do so—but not because he knows or it seems to him that it is so, having truly held the opposite view beforehand. To come to an example, I will say: if to you, who desire to learn the matters of Music, it were proposed that one must assume the **Unison** <term>Unison<gloss>original: "Unisono"; two sounds of the exact same pitch</gloss></term> is that which has no interval: at which Position you would perhaps marvel. It would seem strange to you, if you had no knowledge of this Science, that one could find something that is not dissonant and yet has no interval.

**ADRI.** Therefore, having understood everything well, we can say that all Positions, Maxims, Definitions, Suppositions, and also **Petitions** <term>Petitions<gloss>original: "Petitioni" or "Dimande"; logical demands or postulates that a student must grant the teacher</gloss></term> or Demands, are to be esteemed as the principles of that Science in which they are placed.

**GIOS.** It is truly so. But take note further: that even if any of the named Petitions and Suppositions could be demonstrated in another Science, nevertheless

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous discussion on the foundations of logic and science. # Reasoning

*...within that faculty <note>The word "faculty" here refers to a specific branch of knowledge or science, such as geometry or music.</note> in which a principle is established, one could not find any way to demonstrate it; for if one wished to demonstrate it, other principles would be required, so that such Suppositions and Postulates would cease to be principles. But by taking them as known and noted, the conclusions belonging to that faculty are then demonstrated from them, as from sufficient premises. Therefore, if in any particular science—such as Music, Astrology, or any other—someone wishes to deny any principle, they will not be permitted to dispute within that science, nor will they be in any way fit to learn it.*

<margin>
Aristotle, *Physics*,
Book 1,
Chapter 2.
</margin>
ADRI. *So far I have learned many and beautiful things; however, if you have anything else to say, I pray you to continue.* GIOS. *Regarding this part, I do not wish to say anything more; but believe me, Sir, now the good part begins.* ADRI. *God be praised then; continue, and say what you wish, for we are prepared to listen to you.* GIOS. *I want you to know that every Proposal put forward for demonstration can be of two kinds: either it leads us toward Contemplation, or it leads us to act. That which leads us to contemplation is called a **Theorem** <note>original: Θεώρημα (*Theorema*)</note>; but the other is called a **Problem** <note>original: Πρόβλημα (*Problema*)</note>. It is called by this name because from it we learn the way to divide, compose, describe, design, and form every quality of surface figure, with all those accidents that may occur in many arts—such as painting, perspective, chorography <note>The art of mapping a particular region or district.</note>, cosmography, geography, sculpture, architecture, and other similar arts. Beyond this, I want to tell you that every Theorem or Problem that is complete in its parts must have six things within it:* 

*The first is the **Proposal**, which the Greeks call **Protasis** <note>original: Πρότασις (*Protasis*)</note>; in this is contained the **Given** and the **Sought**, which are the two things that compose every perfect Proposal. The office of this part is to teach what is being sought from the Given. The second is called the **Exposition**, or the **Explanation of the Given**, called **Ekthesis** <note>original: Ἔκθεσις (*Ekthesis*)</note>; its office is to receive the Given into itself and prepare it for the Question.* CLAV. *Tell me, please, what each of these two things is.* GIOS. *I will make you understand with an example. If I were to say: "One can, upon a **given string**, place a **Tone** <note>A musical interval.</note> according to its proportion," the "given string" is truly called the **Given**, and the "placing of the Tone" is the **Sought**.* CLAV. *I understand perfectly; continue your speaking, and forgive me if I sometimes cause you disturbance.* GIOS. *On the contrary, you give me pleasure. But to return to our subject, I say: the third part is named **Determination** <note>original: Διορισμὸς (*Diorismos*)</note>; that is, the Determination of the Sought, whose office is to set apart what the Sought is. The fourth is called **Construction**, called by the Greeks **Kataskeue** <note>original: Κατασκευὴ (*Kataskeue*)</note>; this is the part that, in order to find the Sought, adds those things that are missing from the Given. To these is added the fifth, called **Demonstration** <note>original: Ἀπόδειξις (*Apodeixis*)</note>; that is, the scientific proof that gives us the point through the means of the things granted and presupposed. Lastly, there is the sixth, called the **Conclusion**, or we may say the **Epilogue** <note>original: Συμπέρασμα (*Symperasma*)</note>; which turns back once more to the proposal, confirming what has been demonstrated.* ADRI. *Are all these things found in every Theorem or Problem?* GIOS. *No, Sir; but in each one the Proposal, the Demonstration, and the Conclusion are necessarily found. For it is necessary first to know the Sought—that is, what is proposed in the question—and then to demonstrate it with the proper means, and after it is demonstrated, to conclude it. Thus, none of these three things can be missing. In some places, the others are often used, and in many they are set aside, as can be seen in the 10th [proposition] of the 4th [book] of Euclid, which says: "We can construct a triangle of two equal sides <note>An isosceles triangle.</note> that has each of the angles at the base double the other angles." Here, the Determination and the Exposition are missing, especially when the Explanation of the Given is sufficient so that no other addition is needed to demonstrate what is proposed. But the Construction is frequently not found in many Theorems. And when there is no Given in the Proposal, then the Exposition will be missing. However, the proposal will most often have the Given and the Sought, though not always; for sometimes it will have only the Sought, which it is necessary to know, or to do, or to bring to effect, as is seen in the aforementioned Problem or Proposal; for it does not say: "From which Given it is necessary to construct the triangle of two equal sides—"*

# First Book.
<sig>B 3</sig>

...equal: that has one of its equal sides double the other side; but it is only proposed that such a triangle to be made be Isosceles <note>A triangle with at least two equal sides.</note>. When the Proposition truly possesses both of these, then the Determination and the Exposition will be found. But when the Given <note>The "Given" (Latin: *datum*) refers to the starting information or objects provided at the beginning of a geometric problem.</note> is not present, all these things will also be missing: because the Exposition and the Determination are elements that belong to the Given. DESI. Truly, the knowledge of these things is very necessary if one wishes to have full understanding of the Demonstration; but perhaps some of these Gentlemen are still not satisfied, as they might wish for a specific example of the Six Things named above. FRAN. You have hit the mark; this is exactly what I was about to ask. Therefore, please do not find it tedious to help us understand these things through an example. GIOS. I thought that my long speaking would surely tire you, but from what I see, it is quite the opposite. Now, since it pleases you so, listen to me. Let the foundation for what I am about to tell you be the First Proposition of the 1st Book of Euclid's *Elements* <note>Euclid's *Elements* was the standard textbook for geometry for over 2,000 years.</note>, as it is the easiest, the shortest, and contains all these Six Things. It says: ***On a given finite straight line, we can construct an equilateral triangle.*** This entire statement is called the Proposition; and it is divided into two parts: namely, the Given, which is the finite straight line; and the Goal <note>original: *Quesito* (the "Sought")</note>, which is the equilateral triangle. Now, if I want to demonstrate this thing to you, I will begin first with the **Exposition** of the Given, and I will say: *Let the given finite line be **ab**.* Afterward, I will come to the exposition of the Goal, saying: *It is necessary to construct an equilateral triangle upon this straight line **ab**.* Having done this, I will come to the **Construction**,

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the construction of an equilateral triangle as described in Euclid's Elements, Book I, Proposition 1. It consists of two intersecting circles of equal radius. The circle on the left is centered at point 'a', with its circumference passing through point 'b' and labeled 'bgc'. The circle on the right is centered at point 'b', with its circumference passing through point 'a' and labeled 'agd'. The intersection of the two circles at the top is labeled 'g'. A triangle is formed by connecting points 'a', 'b', and 'g'.</image-desc>

and I will say: *With center **a** and the length of the line **ab**, I will describe the circle **bgc**. Similarly, with center **b** and the length of the same line **ab**, I will describe the circle **agd**. Having done this, I will draw the lines **ag** and **gb**.* Now I pronounce the result of the Construction, saying: *I say that the triangle **agb** is equilateral.* Having finished this, I come to the **Demonstration**, and I say: *In every circle, the lines drawn straight from the center to the circumference are equal. The figure **bgc** is a circle, and its center is **a**; therefore, **ag** is equal to **ab**.* And to prove each of the assumed premises, and to show that the syllogism <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> is not defective in its matter—for as to its form, it belongs to the First Figure <note>In Aristotelian logic, the "First Figure" is the most direct and perfect form of a syllogism.</note> and contains no defect—I say that the major premise is the Definition of the circle, and the minor premise is known from the construction. I say further: *In every circle, the straight lines that go from the center to the circumference are equal. The figure **agd** is a circle, and its center is **b**; therefore, the line **gb** is equal to **ba**.* And to prove this second syllogism, I do what I did in the first: I say that the major premise is the definition of the circle contained in the Principles, and the minor is manifest from the Construction. I come now to a third syllogism and say: *Those things that are equal to another thing are also equal to each other. Each of the straight lines **ag** and **gb** is found to be equal to the straight line **ab**; therefore, the straight line **ag** is equal to the straight line **gb**.* And I prove this syllogism by saying: *The major premise is a Common Notion <note>Also known as an Axiom; a self-evident truth that requires no proof.</note>, and the first part of the Minor is the conclusion of the first syllogism, and the part that follows is the conclusion of the second.* Now I come to the fourth syllogism and say: *Every Triangle contained by three equal straight lines is an equilateral Triangle. The triangle **agb** is contained by three equal straight lines; therefore, the Triangle **agb** is equilateral.* The proof of this syllogism is as follows: the major...

# Reasoning.

*...the major premise is the definition of the Triangle: and the minor is the conclusion of the third syllogism <note>A syllogism is a form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises.</note>. And thus the entire demonstration is finished. Once this is done, I add the Conclusion, and I say: The Triangle **a g b** is equilateral, and it is placed upon the given line **a b**. Therefore, upon the given finite straight line, an equilateral triangle has been constructed; just as it was required to be done <note>This mirrors the classical "Quod erat faciendum" (which was to be done) found at the end of geometric proofs.</note>. And so the whole thing is complete, as you can see. But I wanted to give you this long discourse before I come to demonstrate the matters of Music for this purpose: so that I do not have to repeat anything to you in every future demonstration. Therefore, keep in memory what I have told you thus far.*

FRAN. *I have understood and considered it all very well, so that I will have no further reason to make you repeat these things.*

ADRI. *See, I pray you, what a beautiful order is kept in demonstrating, and how sensibly everything is understood.*

DESI. *This is the nature of the Sciences that demonstrate: once the demonstration of a thing is made, the Master understands it as much as the Disciple, and the Disciple as much as the Master.*

GIOS. *Many more things could truly be said, but because I understand that you are very well instructed in those things of which I have spoken so far, I assume (these being the most difficult and most necessary to know) that the others will not be difficult for you when I place them before you, as they are matters of little importance. Therefore, I wish to have said enough for now. Consequently, we shall move further ahead and come to our principal intention; because these things I have discussed with you until now are not what I intend to say, but rather a preparation for those discourses that will follow.*

DESI. *This discourse you have made, Master Gioseffo, has truly been very useful and very necessary. Since our dear friends here do not usually attend to these matters—even though we have heard them discussed many times—it was necessary to show them how well and conveniently they apply to what you wish to say. Therefore, proceed ahead whenever you please, for it seems to me that we have had a good lesson thus far.*

GIOS. *Wishing then to give a beginning to the demonstrations, it is necessary first to show the principles of this science, so that by means of them we can come to the conclusions, demonstrating those things that seem necessary to us. These principles, I believe, will not be denied by you if you wish for me to proceed to the act of demonstrating. But to follow the order held by our predecessors, and by modern Mathematicians as well, I will first set down the Definitions in order; then the Axioms <note>Zarlino uses "Dignità" (Dignities), a common Renaissance term for axioms or self-evident truths.</note>, or Maxims, or truly "Common Notions" as we might call them; and lastly the Postulates <note>Original: "Dimande" (Demands/Requests), the standard term for Euclidean postulates.</note>, without which I could demonstrate little—indeed, nothing at all.*

ADRI. *None of us would ever have such boldness as to deny you anything, as we know all too well that you would not propose anything false to us. But tell us, I pray you: for what reason do you place the Definitions before everything else?*

GIOS. *A truly beautiful question, and it seems to me a necessary one—not out of place, and of great use to know. Know then, that although I told you above that I do it to follow the Ancients, nonetheless that cannot be your only good reason. Rather, the true reason is that Definitions are what give us to understand what the things are that must be treated. For all reason requires that one first knows what the thing is that one wishes to treat—at least as far as the name—before it is treated, so that one does not proceed using unknown terms. Beyond this: because the Definition is (as the Philosophers hold, and as I have said further back) the middle <note>In Aristotelian logic, the "middle term" is the link that connects the subjects of a syllogism to produce a proof.</note> of the Demonstration. From this, you can see for what reason I have been moved to want to place the Definitions before everything else.*

ADRI. *I am satisfied; therefore, begin where and when you please.*

GIOS. *I shall then give a beginning, in the name of the Lord, to the first Definition, which shall be this.*

# D E F I N I T I O N
## F I R S T.

->Sound is the pitching of a voice suitable for modulation, occurring under a single extension.<-

<margin>Boethius, *Fundamentals of Music*, Book 1, Chapter 3.</margin>
DESI. *For what reason, Master Gioseffo, do you define Sound before anything else?* GIOS. *Because the Sound which I have defined is the principle of consonance <note>Consonance refers to a combination of notes that sound pleasant or "stable" together.</note> and of every other interval in Music, whatever it may be: just as the Point is the principle of quantity in Geometry, which is born from it and depends upon it. DESI. This answer of yours satisfies me well enough; but tell me, in good faith: is not the definition of Sound given by Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), a Roman philosopher whose works on music were foundational for centuries.</note> a good one? He says that it is the striking of air that reaches the sense of hearing. GIOS. In truth, his definition does not suit our purpose, because the Musician considers Sound in a different manner than Boethius defines it. He defines Sound as a natural and universal thing; the Musician defines it in a particular way. The Musician considers it as the principle of Consonance and of every other musical interval when he says: "Sound is the pitching of a voice suitable for modulation <note>Modulation here refers to the movement of the voice from one pitch to another in melody.</note>, occurring under a single extension," meaning by such "extension" the dwelling and the state of the voice. For when the voice is seen to remain in one extension, then we say that Sound is the voice—as if ordained for modulation. DESI. If Sound is the pitching of the voice, such a pitching cannot happen without movement; since movement is not found without time, nor time without quantity (given that length and brevity are attributed to it according to different respects), it follows, as it seems to me, that one cannot say Sound is the principle of Consonance like the Point is the principle of the line. Rather, it would be a quantity, like the line itself, which can be divided infinitely because it has its parts joined at a common boundary, which is the Instant. GIOS. You argue very well, Signor Desiderio, and truly your argument would be conclusive if the Musician considered the defined Sound—which the Greeks call* <term>phthongos</term> <note>original: "φθόγγος"; a technical term for a musical sound of a fixed pitch.</note> *—in its length. But it is not so: for he considers it with another respect, as I will tell you further on. You must know that three things happen regarding Sound: the first is Place; the second is Time; and the third is Color, so to speak. As for the first: the Place of the Sound is considered insofar as we make it lower or higher. For those Sounds that are gathered in the same place—that is, in the same point—the Musician calls Unisons; they are without any interval between them and under the same extension. But when they are higher or lower than one another—that is, when some depart from the said point and go elsewhere—they are in different places, and have intervals and different extensions between them, and receive many divisions among themselves, in the manner I have declared in many places in the *Institutions*. Thus, such extension changes, and different Sounds are born from the varying extension of the string. For low sounds are born when a string, stretched under any extension, is loosened; and high sounds are born when such a string is tightened further. And the more the said string is loosened, the lower the sound it renders; and conversely, the more it is tightened, the more it renders a higher sound. Therefore, when the Musician considers the voice or the Sound according to different extensions, it does not fall under time, but under the quality of low and high, even though such a change cannot be made without time. And that single extension is placed indivisibly in the manner of a point; while different extensions are like different lines that go in different directions and can be divided. We can therefore say that although the first Sounds are divisible by duration as far as length is concerned, they are nonetheless indivisible as far as the distance between low and high is concerned, since they have no...*

<summary>This page defines Sound as the fundamental unit of music, comparing its role to the geometric point. Zarlino distinguishes between the physical definition of sound and the musical definition, which focuses on fixed pitch (extension) rather than duration.</summary>
<keywords>Sound, Consonance, Modulation, Unisons, Boethius, Gioseffo Zarlino, Music Theory, Geometry, pitch, phthongos</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Desiderio and Gioseffo Zarlino regarding the definition of Sound as the foundational "point" of music. Gioseffo is defending his definition against Desiderio’s skepticism about the physical duration of sound versus its theoretical indivisibility.</meta>

# Reasoning

...any width. Since they are considered as if in a point, and the point being indivisible, it follows also that sounds are indivisible; for they have no actual distance between them, just like a point, even if they possess it potentially. But just as when such a point moves, a **Line** is created, so too when a **Sound** is moved toward the low <note>original: *grave*</note> or toward the high <note>original: *acuto*</note>, an **Interval** is created, which is divisible in its width. Sound, then, taken in this first sense, cannot be divided, as I have said; and being indivisible (since divisibility is contrary to being a "principle" or starting point), it remains that without any contradiction, this Sound is indeed a principle.

DESI. *How then? Does Sound perhaps not last through time? And if it lasts, does it not have length, being measured by time, whether long or short? And if this is so, how can it not be divided? For which reason I say to you again: being divisible, it is contradictory for it to be a principle.*

GIOS. I have already told you that although Sound has length in terms of its duration, the Musician does not consider it from that perspective. The Musician does not focus on that small detail that Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, the primary authority on music theory in the Middle Ages.</note> puts in his definition of Sound: *That which reaches the hearing*. The Musician knows well enough that it must be so if it is to be heard; but he considers it solely as the **pitching of the voice** <note>original: *cadimento di voce*</note>, and he adds, *at a single extension*. For when a Sound is born, it is seen as if "falling" in a certain way from the sonorous body from which it derives; but one hears no change in the sound from low to high, or vice versa. If it did, it would have more than one "extension," as can be understood from what I have said. Instead, it has only one quality and is of a single character; such a Sound is called **continuous** as long as it remains in this extension. 

And you know that the continuous voice—since it creates no consonance nor any harmony—is not considered by the Musician. Rather, he considers the **discrete** voice <note>Discrete voice refers to sounds with distinct, stable pitches, like notes on a keyboard, rather than the sliding pitches of speech.</note>. Even though our familiar speech (as you might say) has a certain something of high and low, nevertheless, in the Sound we have defined, one sees no addition of these qualities that would prove the contrary of what has been said. 

I do not want you to think, however, that the Musician holds these Sounds or Voices in little account regarding their duration; since they fall under the sense of Hearing, they certainly belong to his field. For this reason, note the second thing that occurs concerning Sound, which is **Time**. Time is considered as that which encompasses **Number** or **Rhythm** <note>original: *Rithmo*</note>. Thus, from this perspective, Sound is considered secondarily according to its duration, in the pronunciation <note>original: *prolatione*</note> of long or short syllables contained in Prose or in Verse.

DESI. *I am very well satisfied by your explanation of what I doubted; but do not forget to mention the third thing that follows Sound: which is **Color**.*

GIOS. I have not forgotten. I tell you that **Color** is that by which voices and sounds are made different from one another, as in songs <note>original: *cantilene*</note>. These consist of voices or sounds which are all under different extensions and are (I shall put it this way) winding and bent, now one way and now the other; that is, now toward the high and now toward the low. This is the opposite of what **Unisons** do, which from their beginning through their whole duration until the end are under a single extension, a single quality, and a single character—much like a straight line, which lies evenly between its points and is found to be without any width.

DESI. *You have come to confess, then, that your defined Sound has duration, which consists of length.*

GIOS. What does that matter, provided that in the way the Musician considers it—as a principle—it is indivisible? But I want to tell you one more thing and then end the discussion on this principle. Do you not know that when Music is considered and brought to its ultimate purpose, it is truly an **active** thing, put into action by means of things that belong to the category of things that succeed one another? Such is Sound. It does not consist of things that are durable and permanent. How then would you have it be put into action if sounds did not remain and make themselves heard for some space of time? This time has no part that is indivisible, except for the **Instant**. But in truth, a thing is one way regarding its existence, and another way regarding how it is considered; just as we see with **Mathematical Quantities**, which, although they cannot exist apart from matter, are nevertheless considered as being separate from it.

DESI. *In fact, it is just as you have said, and you are right; therefore, continue with whatever pleases you most.*

GIOS. I shall do so.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 20, where Gioseffo Zarlino is explaining the fundamental nature of sound. Having established sound as a "principle" or point in music, he now transitions into how music is classified as an art and moves toward the definition of an "Interval."</meta>

# First.

CLAUDIO. You have placed Music in the **Active Genus** and have said that sounds fall under the **category of things that succeed one another**: please make yourself a bit better understood; and then you may proceed as you please.

GIOSEFFO. Take note, then, that the Arts are found to be of four kinds. For one is called by our ancestors <note>original: "Θεωρ.τικὴ" (Theōrētikē)</note> **Contemplative**: which has its end in speculation, such as Arithmetic, Astronomy, and other similar ones. The second is called <note>original: "πρακτικὴ" (Praktikē)</note> **Active**, or **Practical**, as we might say: such as the art of Dancing, of playing the Cittern <note>A wire-strung instrument similar to a lute, popular in the Renaissance.</note>, and of Singing. The third is named <note>original: "ποιητικὴ" (Poiētikē)</note> **Productive** <note>original: "Fattiua"</note>: such as the art of the Blacksmith, Painting, Sculpture, and other similar ones. But the fourth is called <note>original: "Κτητικὴ" (Ktētikē)</note> **Investigative**, or **Searching**: such as the art of fishing and that of Hunting. 

Thus, some Arts *make* things: such as the art of the Weaver, the Shoemaker, and others. Some *preserve* things already made: such as the art of steering a ship. And others do *both*: such as the Art of building. And although Music, from the speculative side, is called **Theoretical**; nevertheless, because it puts things into action and achieves its purpose through them, it is called **Active**, or **Practical**. 

But the things put into action in Music do not always remain, except for as long as they are being performed: for the Dance lasts only as long as the one performing it moves. And the Cittern is heard only as long as the strings are moved by the one who strikes them. Similarly, the song <note>original: "cantilena"</note> is heard only as long as the singer sends forth the voice. And because all the movements made in these acts are "violent" <note>In the Aristotelian sense, "violent" motion is forced rather than natural, and thus temporary.</note>, they are not durable. Therefore, once one has passed, another must necessarily succeed it, if the thing is to remain in action. Or indeed, once such movements have reached their end, they must necessarily be renewed from the start. This is why I said that Music is an active thing, and that the things it employs are not among those that remain—like those of the blacksmith's art—but have their place among those things that succeed one another.

CLAUDIO. I do not regret having made you discuss these few words, because in truth it has been a good lesson. Therefore, I pray you to give us such "good food" often; which you will do by following what you have begun, as it becomes convenient for you.

GIOSEFFO. I am ready to do so. But because when a Sound extends toward the **low** <note>original: "graue"</note> or toward the **high** <note>original: "acuto"</note>, an **Interval** is immediately generated—which is the first thing considered by the Musician in a certain way, and not simply. For the Musician, simply and before any other thing, considers **Consonance**, from which he intends to compose his song. Therefore, without wasting any time, I will define the **Interval** in this manner.

---

### DEFINITION II.

->An **Interval** is that which is comprised of two sounds differing in<-
->low and high pitch: which arise from sounding bodies or quantities.<-

<margin>Part 2, Chapter 15.</margin>
I will not stay now to repeat what I said in the *Institutions* <note>Zarlino's own *Le Istitutioni harmoniche* (1558), his most famous work.</note> regarding the interval, nor will I tell you its species, for I believe you remember them. But I will tell you only that this definition is for the **Interval** properly speaking, and not as it is commonly used. And if you hold in memory what I said above, know that it is necessary for these sounds to be different in extension; for if they all had the same extension, no interval would be created, since these sounds would seem to be, and would indeed be, in the same place. So, the difference or distance found between the low sound and the high sound—beyond the high and the low themselves—is called an **Interval**.

ADRIANO. This is clear and understood very well; it needs no further comment.

GIOSEFFO. And although I believe you know what a **Sounding Body** is, I nevertheless wish to define it anew, so that you may have a more certain and firm knowledge of it. Therefore, I shall say that according to the Musician...

### DEFINITION III.

->A sonorous body is that which, when struck in any manner,<-
->emits a sound.<-

<margin>Part 2, Chapter 20.</margin>
*LAVINIO. Therefore, a sonorous body will be any string of every musical instrument. The interval in which the larger sonorous quantity contains the smaller once, plus several parts of it—which are called **non-aliquot parts** <note>In Renaissance mathematics, an "aliquot part" is a unit fraction like 1/2 or 1/3 that divides the whole exactly. The other numbers, such as **Even**, **Odd**, **Evenly-even**, **Prime and incomposite**, **Composite**, **Squares**, **Cubes**, and **Perfect numbers**—are they not all simple numbers, without any relation <note>original: "relatione" — referring to the ratio between two numbers rather than the properties of a single number.</note>? GIO S. That is so, Sir; and you show very well that you have studied my *Institutions* <note>Referring to Zarlino's own famous work, *Le Istitutioni Harmoniche*.</note>. But let us move on to another definition.

### DEFINITION XI.

<margin>4 3 2</margin> When three sonorous quantities are placed one after the other in such a way that the **difference** found between the greater and the middle one is equal to the difference between the middle and the lesser; and where the greater proportion is found between the lesser terms, and the lesser proportion between the greater terms; then they shall be said to be arranged and ordered in **Arithmetic progression**.

So that you may understand me more easily, I tell you: that mathematicians call **Difference** that by which a larger quantity exceeds a smaller one, as is evident from the fourth definition of Book 7 of Euclid, according to the translation of Campanus <note>Johannes Campanus of Novara, whose 13th-century Latin translation of Euclid’s *Elements* was the standard version used during the Renaissance.</note>. Now I give you an example of what I said in the definition. Let us suppose that *a*, *b*, and *c* are the named quantities; and that *d* is the difference found between *a* and *b*, and *e*

Between the ends of 'c' and 'b' is a small segment 'e' (length 1), and between 'b' and 'a' is a small segment 'd' (length 1), showing the equal differences between the terms.</image-desc>

is the difference between *b* and *c*. I say that since these two differences are equal to each other—and since a greater proportion is found between the lesser terms 3 and 2 <note>The ratio 3:2 is a "Sesquialter" or a perfect fifth.</note> than between the greater terms 4 and 3 <note>The ratio 4:3 is a "Sesquitertia" or a perfect fourth.</note>—these quantities are said to be ordered according to **Arithmetic progression**. ADRI. We have understood this easily; therefore, continue with the rest. GIO S. I shall come then to the next definition and say:

### DEFINITION XII.

Three sonorous quantities shall be called proportional to one another, or ordered according to **Geometric proportionality**, when the proportions found between the greater and the middle, and

## DEFINITION XIII.

When three <term>sonorous quantities</term> <note>Values representing musical pitches or string lengths.</note> are placed in order, and between the greater and the middle there is a **greater proportion** than that which is between the middle and the lesser: and also that which is found between the differences of the greater quantity to the middle, and of this to the lesser, is equal to that which is placed between the extremes: then such an order shall be said to be made according to <term>Harmonic proportionality</term> or <term>mediocrity</term>.

LAV. Here a little commentary is needed. GIOS. Let **a**, **b**, and **c** then be three quantities: and let **f** be the difference of **a** and **b**: and **g** be that of **b** and **c**. I say that the said quantities will be called arranged in Harmonic Proportionality, or Mediocrity:

| a (6) | b (4) | c (3) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| | f (2) | g (1) |

<note>In this Harmonic example, the ratio 6:4 (3:2, a Perfect Fifth) is larger than 4:3 (a Perfect Fourth). The ratio of the differences (2:1) equals the ratio of the outer terms (6:3, which is 2:1).</note>

since the proportion found between **a** and **b** is greater than that which is between **b** and **c**: as is the property of this Mediocrity. DESI. What follows then? GIOS. It follows, that:

## DEFINITION XIIII.

If there are three sonorous quantities ordered one after the other in such a way that between the **two smaller ones** there is a **greater proportion** than that which is contained between the **two larger ones**: and that which is found between the two extremes is similar to that which is placed between the differences (which are between the greater and the middle, and between this and the lesser): such an order shall be said to be made according to <term>Contra-harmonic proportionality</term>.

### DIGNITY III.

**Unity is a part of any number: named by that same number.**

And this is taken directly from the Seventh Book of Euclid <note>Euclid's *Elements*, a foundational Greek mathematical text.</note>. The example is taken from **Unity** <note>The number one, considered the building block of all numbers.</note>: which, being one of the parts of the *Binary* <note>The number two.</note>, such a part is called the Half. But let us move a little further.

### DIGNITY VI.

**That which measures the part taken away and the remainder of a quantity: also measures the Whole of it.**

And this is made clear to anyone of sound judgment: for if we take 18 from 24: 6 will remain. Therefore I say, if 3 numbers, or measures, the 18 (which is the part taken from 24) and the 6 (which is the remainder): in the same way it will also measure, or number, the Whole, which is 24. And it is true: because 3 numbers 6 twice; 18 six times; and 24 eight times. **CLA.** <note>Claudio Merulo, a famed organist and composer of the late Renaissance.</note>

*They are rightly called Common Opinions, or Maxims, or indeed Dignities <note>original: "Dignità"; in Renaissance logic, these are axioms—self-evident mathematical truths that form the foundation of a demonstration.</note>, whatever we wish to call them: for I cannot imagine who would be so foolish as to want to hold the contrary. ### DIGNITY VII.

**Those Intervals are similar and equal which are contained by similar terms: or rather, they have their Denominations from one same Denominator. <margin>Part 1, Chapter 25.</margin>
*The first part of this Dignity is manifest in itself: when similarity and equality are taken from the perspective of the form and not the matter; for the rest, we have the proof in hand. ### DIGNITY VIII.

**That is the Greater interval which is denominated by a greater Denominator: and that is the lesser which is denominated by a lesser.**

*And this is manifest: because the Sesquialtera interval <note>3:2 or 1.5</note> is greater than the Sesquiterza <note>The ratio 4:3, or approximately 1.33, which creates the musical interval of a Perfect Fourth.</note>; just as the Denominator of the first (1 1/2) is greater than 1 1/3, which is the Denominator of the second.* **DESI.** *This is quite manifest: and therefore it is well that this principle be numbered among the Dignities.* **GIOS.** *I wish also to add to you that, similarly:*

### DIGNITY IX.

**Of Numbers and of Intervals, that part is greater which has the greater Denominator: and that is lesser which has the lesser.**

*Even though it appears that this and the preceding one are almost the same thing, and that this one should be placed before that one; nevertheless, I wanted its place to be here: since the Whole always precedes the Parts. And because that part which is the half of...*

...; however, I will not stand here to repeat anything further to you, but I will come to the **Demonstration**. Let *a-b* and *c-d* be the **lowest terms** <term>minimi termini: the smallest whole numbers that can express a specific musical ratio</term> of any two intervals you wish, differing in proportion: that is, *a* and *b* of one, and *c* and *d* of the other, which we wish to multiply together. I first multiply *a* by *c* and by *d*, and then *b* by *d*: from which result *e*, *f*, and *g*. I say now that *e*, *f*, and *g* contain the interval *a-b* and the interval *c-d*: that is, *e-f* contains the first, and *f-g* the second. And because, by the **Fifth Axiom** <note>original: "Quinta dignità." In the mathematical tradition of Zarlino's time, "dignity" refers to a self-evident axiom or common notion, likely referring here to the Euclidean principle that multiplying terms by the same number preserves their ratio.</note>, any number multiplied by the terms of any proportion produces the same proportion: therefore, since *e* and *f* arise from the multiplication of *a* by the terms *c* and *d*, I say that *e* and *f* are of the same proportion as *c* and *d*. Similarly, I say that since *f* and *g* result from the multiplication of *d* by *a* and *b*: by the same Axiom, *f-g* contains the same proportion as *a* and *b*, according to our purpose. Therefore, if the proportion of *e* and *f* is the same as *c* and *d*, and that of *f* and *g* <note>The text says "f & e", but the logic of the proof dictates f and g.</note> is the same as *a* and *b*, it follows that between these terms *e*, *f*, and *g* we have continued two different intervals of proportion, one after the other, as the proposal stated, and as I was meant to demonstrate to you. But because *e*, *f*, and *g* are three **Composite Numbers** among themselves <term>Numeri composti: numbers that share a common divisor other than 1</term>, which, by the Tenth Definition, can be numbered by a number other than Unity: therefore, as Chapter 43 of the First Part of the *Istitutioni* <note>Zarlino is referring to his own seminal work, *Le Istitutioni harmoniche* (1558).</note> teaches us, we will find a number, or term—the largest that can be found—that measures each of the three named numbers individually and together. This will be *h*. Thus, dividing *e*, *f*, and *g* by *h*, there will arise *x*, *l*, and *m*. These, I say, by the Ninth Definition, are **Relatively Prime** <term>Contraseprimi: numbers that have no common divisor other than 1; they represent the ratio in its simplest form.</term> numbers, and consequently the lowest terms and **radicals** of these two intervals. By the already mentioned Fifth Axiom, they contain those same proportions that are contained between *e*, *f*, and *g*, because every number that divides the terms of any proportion produces the same proportion. And this is all that, according to the proposal, I was meant to demonstrate to you. Note also that if you wished to add a third interval to these two: by multiplying its larger radical term with *x*, *l*, and *m*, and the smaller term again with *m*, you would achieve your goal. Then, if necessary, reducing the terms to their **Radix** <note>The simplest, irreducible whole-number ratio.</note> if they were composite numbers, following the order shown in the said Chapter 43, one could proceed into infinity. But if by chance you wanted the opposite—that the proportion or interval *c-d* were placed first and *a-b* were added after—then you would have nothing else to do but change the places, putting *a-b* in the place of *c-d* and vice versa, and you would have your goal. *DESI.* <margin>Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, Book 2, commentary 16.</margin> These things are very delightful, for in them one sees an open truth; once demonstrated, they immediately quiet the intellect. And therefore that great Philosopher [Aristotle] said well: that the mathematical disciplines are placed in the first degree of certainty, and that the natural sciences follow them. *GIOS.* This is true; but hear another proposal.

*The first proposition of this discussion of ours: it is divided into two equal parts, such that c is to d as a* **Multiple** <term>Multiple: A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number exactly two or more times without a remainder, such as 2:1 (duple) or 3:1 (triple).</term>, *and d is to e. I also say that the resulting interval c and e is a* **Multiple**. *And because d is a multiple of e: therefore, by the* **Definition of Multiples**, *e measures d exactly more than once. But from the supposition made above: just as d is a multiple with e: so c is a multiple with d. Therefore e measures c exactly many more times. Thus, by the aforementioned Definition, c is a multiple of e: as was required to be demonstrated.* **ADRIANO.** *Tell me, please, and forgive my curiosity: because the ease of this demonstration makes me ask you: if this proposition can be demonstrated in another way.* **GIOSEFFO.** *It truly can, Sir.* **CLAUDIO.** *Then is it possible to make different demonstrations for the same proposition?* **GIOSEFFO.** *You know it well; for there being many means, there are also many demonstrations.* **FRANCESCO.** *Demonstrate it then, by your faith.* **GIOSEFFO.** *I wish to do so, to satisfy you. Let the interval a and b be again a* **Multiple**, *as the proposition proposes; which, by the First [proposition] of this [book], let it be doubled; and let c and e be the double: and the proportion found between c and d, let it also be between d and e. I say the interval c and e is similarly a* **Multiple**. *And that it is so, I demonstrate. The proportion found between a and b, by the* **Seventh Axiom** <note>original: "Settima dignità." In the context of Zarlino’s Euclidean logic, a "dignity" is a self-evident mathematical truth or common notion.</note>, *is that which is found also between c and d, and similarly between d and e. Wherefore each one by itself is half of the doubled [interval] c and e: but the proportion a and b is set as a* **Multiple**: *therefore the proportion c and d is likewise a multiple. The d, therefore, by the* **Fourth Definition**, *measures the c two or more times: and in the same way e measures d just as many times. I say that, similarly, between a and b a middle term can fall. Therefore, I argue by the Eleventh Axiom <term>Dignità: Translated here as Axiom, from the Latin "dignitas," used in Euclidean geometry to mean a self-evident truth.</term> regarding equal proportion: as much as the proportion of d to f, so is that of a to c; and as much as that of f to e, so is that of c to b. In this way, one finds that between a and c there is the same proportion found between d and f; and that which is found between c and b is the same as that placed between f and e. Which, proportionally, comes to fall in the middle of a and b, as was required to be demonstrated.*

# PROPOSITION VIII.

### Any number may be set as the difference between the terms of any proportion.

Let *a* & *b* be the radical terms of any interval: and let *c* be their difference: given that *a* is different from *b* by such an amount. Wishing to set *d* as the

| a | b | c | d |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 3 | 2 | 1 | 2 |
| e | f | g | |
| 6 | 4 | 2 | |

difference of such extremes, one will multiply *d* by *a* and by *b*: and there will come *e* & *f*: which, by the **Fifth Axiom** <note>original: "Quinta dignità"</note>, will likewise be the extremes of the proposed proportion *a* & *b*. But that which is born from *d* multiplied by *a*, is the same as that which is born from *d* multiplied by *b* & *c*. And *d* multiplied by *c* produces *g*: and *d* by *c*, which is **Unity**, produces—by the **Fourth Axiom**—itself, *d*: therefore *g* is set as the difference of *e* & *f*: as I had to demonstrate to you. And this can also be done when one wishes to set another number for such a difference: be it **Ternary** [3], or **Quaternary** [4]. Always multiplying the radical terms, or non-radical terms, of that interval to which one wishes to set such a number as the difference of its extremes. **ADRIANO.** I hope to gain much from these reasonings of yours: and to move beyond mere practice <note>Adriano refers to "prattica," the practical application of music, as opposed to the theoretical and mathematical "science" they are discussing.</note>. ->PROPOSITION IX.<-

# The **Superparticular Interval** does not receive one or more rational middle terms that divide it into two or more proportional parts.

Let $a$ and $c$ be the **Superparticular interval** <note>A superparticular ratio is one where the larger number is equal to the smaller number plus one part of it, such as 3:2 (a Fifth) or 4:3 (a Fourth). This proposition proves that you cannot find a middle whole number that splits these into two equal musical intervals.</note>. Let its extremes, according to the preceding proposition, differ by the **Binary** [the number 2]; thus they are capable of a middle term:

| a | b | c |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 6 | | 4 |

---

| d | e | f |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 3 | | 2 |

---

| g | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 3 | | |

<note>This diagram shows the ratio 6:4 being reduced to its simplest form (radical terms) 3:2. The number 3 represents 'g' in the proof below.</note>

This interval we wish to divide (if possible) into two equal rational parts: that is, into $a:b$ and $b:c$, using certain specific numbers. For this to be true, the ratio $b:c$ must be the same as $a:b$. I reduce $a, b,$ and $c$ to their **Radical Terms** <term>Radical terms: The lowest possible whole numbers that express a ratio, like 3:2 instead of 6:4.</term> according to the method shown in chapters 42 and 43 of the first part of the *Institutions* <note>Zarlino's *Le Istitutioni Harmoniche*.</note>. This results in $d, e, f$, three proportional terms in the same ratio as $a$ and $b$. Because $d:e$ is the same as $a:b$, and $e:f$ is the same as $b:c$, it follows that $d:f$ is proportional to $a:c$. 

But $a:c$ is established as a **Superparticular interval**; therefore $d:f$ is likewise Superparticular. Because $d, e, f$ are the smallest terms of that order, then $d$ and $f$ (the first and last) must be **Numbers prime to each other** <note>original: "Numeri contra se primi". These are numbers that share no common factors other than 1.</note> according to the Ninth Definition. Having shown $d$ and $f$ to be Superparticular, then by the Fifth Definition, $d$ contains $f$ plus an **Aliquot part** <term>Aliquot part: A part that divides a whole number exactly, like 2 is an aliquot part of 6.</term> of it. This part, as I declared in Chapter 23 of the first part of the *Institutions*, measures $f$ itself. 

And if such a part were a whole number: measuring $d$ (according to the Sixth Common Notion), it would also measure itself—which is the part taken out—and the remainder, which is equal to $f$. In this way, $d$ and $f$ would not be **Prime to each other** <note>They would share a common divisor.</note>; however, the opposite has already been shown to be true, which would be impossible. Therefore, that part must necessarily be **Unity** [the number 1].

**DESIDERIO.** This is truly necessary; but what follows from this? 

**GIOSEFFO.** It follows that I add this **Unity** to $f$, resulting in $g$: in such a way that $g$ and $f$ are separated by only **Unity**. I now say, by the Seventh Axiom <note>original: "Settima dignità". In mathematical logic of this era, "dignità" refers to an axiom or self-evident truth.</note>, that the ratio found between $d$ and $f$ is the same as that found between $g$ and $f$. But it was supposed that a single middle term falls between $d$ and $f$; therefore, by the penultimate proposition, a middle number would similarly have to fall between $g$ and $f$, which are numbers differing only by **Unity**. This, according to the First Demand <note>An introductory postulate or principle.</note>, is impossible. We conclude, therefore, that if the **Superparticular interval** cannot receive a single rational middle term to divide it into two proportional parts, it is even less likely to receive...

### PROPOSITION X.

**If an Interval which is not Multiple is doubled: that which results from such doubling will be neither Multiple nor Superparticular.**

And to see that this is true, listen to me. Let the non-Multiple interval be $a$ & $b$: and let the doubled one be $a$ & $c$: in such a way that the same proportion exists between $a$ & $b$ as is found between $b$ & $c$. I say that the interval $a$ & $c$ is neither **Multiple** nor

| a | b | c |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 9 | 6 | 4 |

<note>This diagram illustrates the doubling of the ratio 3:2 (a Perfect Fifth). If you double a Fifth, you get the ratio 9:4 (a Major Ninth). **Superparticular**. Wherefore, if $a$ & $c$ were set as multiple, there is no doubt that by the Sixth proposition, the interval $a$ & $b$ would also be multiple. This being evident, and according to the Preceding [proposition] being impossible: it is also manifest in itself: that if one wishes to double a non-multiple interval, the composed interval cannot be either Multiple, nor even Superparticular: according to our purpose.*

ADRI. *Oh, how marvelously such demonstrations are chained together, so that one comes to offer help to the other, no differently than what **Geometric** demonstrations do. Therefore they are deservedly called **Elements**.* FRAN. *Truly, those who have named them with such a name have spoken well: because (as is clearly seen) one comes to be an element of the other.* <margin>Above, chapter 3.</margin> DESI. *And rightly so: since that of which something is primarily composed is called an **Element** (as has been said at other times). What do you say to this, Master Claudio?* CLAV. *I have always heard it said that the **Mathematics** are Sciences that have something of the divine: and I see it now in effect, to my great satisfaction.* GIOS. *Since until now you have been pleased with everything I have said: it will not grieve me to follow with the rest. Therefore, note what I wish to demonstrate to you in this next proposition.*

### PROPOSITION XI.

## **If an Interval is doubled: and that which results from such doubling is not Multiple: then that interval itself will also not be Multiple.**

ADRI. *This seems to me the reverse of what you have just demonstrated: for in that one, the antecedent of the Parts added together denies the Whole: and in this one, the Parts are denied by the Whole.* <note>Adriano is pointing out that this is the logical converse of Proposition X. In the previous proof, they moved from the properties of the smaller intervals to the result of the sum; here they move from the result back to the components.</note> GIOS. *You say well: therefore I shall continue the undertaking. Let **a** & **c** be the doubled interval, as it was set in the Previous one: and let **a** & **c** not be a multiple interval. I say likewise, that the interval **a** & **b** is not multiple.*

*For if **a** & **b** were a multiple interval: since **a** & **c** arises (by what we have supposed) from the doubling of interval **a** & **b**: by the Third proposition of this discourse, the interval **a** & **c** would also be Multiple. But that which is given is not multiple: therefore, if a non-Multiple interval arises from the doubling of some interval: neither will the interval being doubled be Multiple. And this is what I intended to demonstrate to you.* FRAN. *So far you have proceeded so clearly that I believe nothing remains that is not clear and evident: therefore we pray you to follow the rest just as easily, for we shall listen to you with great pleasure.* GIOS. *I will strive to satisfy you; thus I shall say:*

### PROPOSITION XII.

I say that **a** taken according to the number **c**, from which **e** arises: is equal to **b**, taken according to the...*

## PROPOSITION XIII.

->The larger terms of any proportion, taken according to the number of the smaller ones, are equal to the smaller ones taken according to the number of the larger ones.<-

And here is the example of this, which will serve you not only for the <term>Multiples</term> <note>Ratios like 2:1, 3:1.</note> or <term>Superparticulars</term> <note>Ratios like 3:2, 4:3.</note>, but also for the other genera of proportion. Let **a** and **b**, then, be any proportion: and let **a** be its larger term, and **b** the smaller. I say that **a** taken according to the number **b**, which is smaller, is equal to **b** taken according to the larger number **a**. For it is manifest that what arises from the multiplication of **a** by **b**, which is **c**, is equal to what is produced by the multiplication of **b** by **a**, which is **d**. But that which arises from the multiplication of **a** by **b** is **a** taken according to **b**; and that which arises from the multiplication of **b** by **a** is **b** taken according to **a**, as the preceding proposition demonstrates. Therefore **a** taken according to **b** is equal to **b** taken according to **a**, just as I had to demonstrate. And if you wish for me to descend to particulars, as I did in the preceding one, I will do so willingly, so that you remain satisfied by me.

## PROPOSITION XIV.

### When several of the larger terms of an interval are equal to several of the smaller ones: that same proportion is found between one of the larger & one of the smaller, as is also found between the sum of the smaller ones gathered together and the sum of the larger ones added together.

<margin>ADRIANO</margin> *This seems to me to be the previous one reversed, if I am not mistaken.* <margin>GIOSEFFO</margin> *You are not at all mistaken, Sir: Note then that, by the previous proposition, the smaller numbers gathered together according to the larger number are equal to the larger ones added according to the number of the smaller ones. But the number of the larger is a larger term: Therefore that same proportion is found between one of the larger and one of the smaller, as is also found between the sum of the smaller numbers gathered and the number of the larger ones placed together.* <margin>CLAUDIO</margin> *It seems to me that this thing is very difficult: and perhaps this is because it is not commonly used. Therefore, by your faith, give us a better understanding of this proposal with an example, so that what is so obscure to us may become lucid and clear.* <margin>GIOSEFFO</margin> *These things are truly difficult: but the use of them in the following demonstrations will remove the difficulty for you. Listen, however, to what I want to tell you. We have, from the previous proposition, that in every <term>genus</term> <note>A category of mathematical ratios, such as "multiple" or "superparticular."</note> of proportion: if the larger number is compared to the smaller, the larger taken according to the number of the smaller is equal to the smaller taken according to the number of the larger. Whence we see in the <term>Sesquialtera</term> <note>The ratio 3:2, which forms the interval of a Perfect Fifth.</note>: that two 3s (larger numbers) are equal to three 2s (smaller numbers). Wherefore, in every genus of proportion, the proportion contained in the <term>radical terms</term> <note>original: "termini radicali" — the simplest, lowest whole numbers of a ratio (e.g., 3:2 is radical; 6:4 is not).</note> of any interval is the same as that contained in non-radical terms that are multiplied, or when those radical terms are doubled. And to give you an example in the <term>Superparticulars</term> <note>Ratios where the larger number is the smaller number plus one (e.g., 3:2, 4:3).</note>: I say that when two larger terms are equal to three smaller ones, or four to six, or six to nine, or eight to twelve, the ratio of one of the larger to one of the smaller is a Sesquialtera interval. Then that proportion found between 3 and 2, which is Sesquialtera, is also found between 6 and 4, and between 9 and 6, just as it is found between 12 and 8. And in the <term>Multiples</term> <note>Ratios like 2:1 (double), 3:1 (triple), etc.</note>, when one is equal to two, or two to four, or four to eight, and the larger is double the smaller: then the double proportion between 2 and 1 will be the same as between 4 and 2, and also between 8 and 4, because the larger is double the smaller. The same can be said for the other genera; because it is a clear matter, I do not wish to dwell much longer on it. But in <term>Composite numbers</term> <note>In music theory, these represent compound intervals formed by adding two or more ratios together.</note>, or composite proportions, it should be noted: that when 2 [larger] are equal to 4 1/2, then they will be two conjoined Sesquialteras <note>Two Perfect Fifths (3/2 x 3/2 = 9/4, and 9/4 of 2 is 4.5).</note>. And when 2 are equal to 3 3/8, or they make three: just as there will then be two conjoined <term>Sesquiterzas</term> <note>The ratio 4:3, which forms the interval of a Perfect Fourth.</note> when 3 are equal to 5 1/3; and three [Sesquiterzas] when 3 are equal to 7 1/9; or in other similar cases that arise from their doubling and beyond. But such a thing will be easy for you to understand once you have grasped everything I am about to tell you. Listen then attentively: and keep it in your memory. But before I demonstrate to you in what manner these intervals are composed or multiplied into composite numbers: I want us to see in what manner...*

## PROPOSITION XV.

->One can find any part, whether Aliquot or Non-aliquot, of a given number.<-
<note>An "aliquot" part is a factor that divides a number exactly (like 3 is an aliquot part of 12), whereas a "non-aliquot" part does not (like 5 is a non-aliquot part of 12).</note>

Let this be said regarding the proposition: but I also want to add a Corollary, so that you may have a perfect understanding of the matter; it shall be this:

### COROLLARY.

Whence it happens that the part of any number whatever is numbered by it, and is named by the denominator of that part.

<margin>
Aristotle, Physics, Book 4, Chapter 3.
</margin>
I believe you remember what Aliquot and Non-aliquot parts are; therefore I will not stand here to repeat anything. **FRANC.** We know it; hence there is no need to waste time on this matter. **DESI.** Clear up a doubt for me now, and then continue your speaking: Can <term>Unity</term><note>The number "1," considered the indivisible source of all numbers in classical mathematics.</note> be divided, since among Mathematicians it is considered indivisible? **GIOS.** I said before, while explaining the first Demand, that among the <term>Philosophers</term><note>Meaning natural philosophers or followers of Aristotle.</note> numbers are found to be of two kinds: the first is called <term>Numbering Number</term><note>Latin: *numerus numerans*. Abstract numbers used for counting.</note> and the second is called <term>Numbered Number</term><note>Latin: *numerus numeratus*. Concrete things being counted, like apples or beats of music.</note>. The first are a model and an Idea in our Soul: and their Unity cannot be divided under any condition. But in the second—as are the numbers of movements in natural things; lines, surfaces, bodies, and other similar things in Geometric matters; the numbers of times in Astronomical things; and the number of intervals in Musical things—their Unity (or rather, to put it better, the thing understood as Unity) is divisible into several parts, without any contradiction. **DESI.** I have understood you: that you mean the Numbered Number and its Unity in this proposition. Although you made that discourse during the first Demand, which I remembered quite well, I nevertheless wished to clarify it so that I would not fall into error. **GIOS.** This matter must be understood exactly as I have told you. Whence, returning to my first purpose, I say: Let *a* be any number of which one of the parts named by *b* is sought. Therefore, to satisfy the proposal, I say: that if the part one wishes to extract from the given Number is <term>Non-aliquot</term><note>A "non-aliquot" part is a fraction where the numerator is greater than one (like 2/3), meaning it does not divide the whole number exactly into equal units of 1.</note>, it is necessary that it has a <term>Numerator</term> that is a number other than <term>Unity</term><note>Unity refers to the number 1.</note>. **GIOS.** I wish to satisfy you entirely, if I can, my dear Sir: and so that you may see the whole thing with an example; let the part of the sum of 16 be sought, as I demonstrated above; and let such a part be 1/15. I first multiply 16 and 15 (the denominator of such a part) with one another: and from it comes 240/15: for 16, when resolved into parts, contains that many <term>fifteenths</term>. I then divide 240 by 15: and the result is 16/15: which is the fifteenth part of the whole sum of 240 parts. Whence 16 also comes to be the fifteenth part <note>original: "Quintadecima parte"</note>. But 16/15 contains one Unity and 1/15: therefore the Unity with 1/15 alongside it will be the fifteenth part of the given number 16; which is an Aliquot part. But to have the Non-aliquot part: by multiplying the Aliquot part by the numerator of the Non-aliquot part, we will always have what we seek: as is seen in the example placed in the middle, where having multiplied 4 by 2 (the numerator of the part 2/3), we will have 8/3: that is 2 and 2/3: which will be the sought Non-aliquot part of 4. In such a way that if one wants the part of any proposed number: operating in this manner: one will always have what is sought. But let us come to the other proposal.

And this is what you proposed I should demonstrate to you. Thus, wanting to add yet another, and then another: by keeping this order, one could go on to infinity and achieve the purpose. **FRANCESCO.** What do you think, Master? Does it seem to you that one must know how to use the pen well, and calculate well, if one wants to understand and put these things into practice? **ADRIANO.** I can tell you this: one must not be <note>original: "di ceruello grosso" (thick-brained)</note> dull-witted, for otherwise nothing good would be accomplished. But what will you add to this, Master Gioseffo? **GIOSEFFO.** This: that—

# PROPOSITION XVII.

## The Duple Interval arises from the conjunction of the two greatest
## Superparticulars.

And that this is true, we shall soon see. Let *a, b, c* be the <term>Duple</term><note>A ratio of 2:1, which represents the musical interval of an Octave.</note> interval: and let *a:b* be <term>Sesquialtera</term><note>A ratio of 3:2, representing a Perfect Fifth.</note>, and *b:c* be <term>Sesquiterza</term><note>A ratio of 4:3, representing a Perfect Fourth.</note>. I say that *a:c* arises from the conjunction of *a:b* with *b:c*. And because *a:b* is Sesquialtera; therefore, by the Fifth Definition, *a* contains *b* once and one of its half parts. Therefore, by the Twelfth Proposition, two of *a* are equal to three of *b*. And again: because *b* and *c* is Sesquiterza; therefore by the same Definition, *b* contains *c* once and one of its third parts. Therefore three of *b* are equal to four of *c*: and two of *a* are set as equal to three of *b*: therefore two of *a* are equal to four of *c*. Being, by the <term>Tenth Common Notion</term><note>original: "Decimo parere commune." A reference to the Euclidean principle: "Things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another."</note>, that those things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another. And the number 4, from the lesser terms joined together, is double (according to the Fourteenth Proposition) of the two greater terms placed together—

<header>Discourse.</header>

**GIOSEFFO.** ...therefore, by the same Fourteenth <term>Axiom</term><note>The author uses the term "dignity" (*dignità*) to refer to Euclid's Common Notions or Axioms, which are fundamental mathematical truths.</note>, one *a* will be double one *c*. But because the <term>Sesquialter</term><note>The ratio 3:2, which in music produces the interval of a Perfect Fifth.</note> and the <term>Sesquitertial</term><note>The ratio 4:3, which in music produces the interval of a Perfect Fourth.</note> are—by the Eighth and Ninth Axioms—the two largest among the <term>Superparticulars</term><note>A category of ratios where the larger number is exactly one unit greater than the smaller (e.g., 3:2, 4:3, 5:4). In Renaissance theory, these were considered the most "pure" musical intervals.</note>: I therefore say that the Duple interval is born from the conjunction of the two largest Superparticulars: a thing which I had to demonstrate to you.

**ADRIANO.** This proposition can also be demonstrated, as it seems to me, by another path: and this by means of the Twelfth Axiom; and I have the spirit to know how to demonstrate it.

**GIOSEFFO.** What you say is true, Sir; and when you demonstrate it, you would make it known in fact that you understand very well what I have said until now; therefore, do what pleases you.

**ADRIANO.** I wish to prove it in every way. I say then, that two *a*’s of your proposed example being equal to four *c*’s—as you have concluded—one *a*, by the named Axiom, comes to be equal to two *c*’s. For: of those things of which the Wholes are equal, their parts are also equal. But because two *c*’s are the double of one: therefore one *a* equal to two *c*’s will be the double of one *c*. But *a* and *c* arise from the conjunction of *a:b* and *b:c*—which are (as you have proved) the two largest superparticulars: therefore the Duple interval arises from the conjunction of the two largest superparticulars: as I was to demonstrate to you.

**GIOSEFFO.** You are in fact a great little Sir: and you are like pepper, which is small in quantity, but great in virtue and power <note>A Renaissance idiom suggesting that Adriano's physical stature or junior status is belied by his intellectual strength.</note>. Because you have shown yourself a great disciple in a short time. What do you think, Lord Desiderio, has he not behaved well?

**DESIDERIO.** Well truly: and he has not deceived me at all in what I believed of him: for I have always held Master Adriano to be a man of fine intellect.

**ADRIANO.** I thank your Lordship for this favor: but let us leave these words aside for your sake: and let us wait to see what Master Gioseffo wishes to add: and let us not depart from the established order.

**GIOSEFFO.** What I want to add is this: I wish to demonstrate this same proposal to you by another means, if it does not weary you to listen to me.

**DESIDERIO.** How weary? You could not do us a greater favor, nor bring us greater delight, than to follow what you have begun: for I, for my part, did not believe I would see so many and varied things concerning Music.

**GIOSEFFO.** In the name of God then. Let *a:b* be a Sesquialter interval, and *b:c* a Sesquitertial. I say *a* with *c* is a Duple interval. I first make *a* equal to *b*, and there comes *d*; and *e* remains over. Then I make *b* equal to *c*; and *f* is born; and *g* remains. This done, I say: because *a* is Sesquialter with *b*; *e* comes to be the Third part of *a*, and the half of *b*. Similarly, because *b* is Sesquitertial with *c*, *g* comes to be the Fourth part of *b*, and the Third of *c*. 

---

**a** |————————————— (6)

**b** |————————— (4)
**f** |—————— (3) | **g** |——— (1)

Wherefore, *g* being the Fourth part of *b*, and *e* its half: *g* will be the entire half of *e*. But we have said, *e* is the Third part of *a*: therefore *g* will be its Sixth part. And because *g* is the Third part of *c* and the Sixth of *a*: therefore *a*, by the Fourth definition, will be Double to *c*. But the Sesquialter and the Sesquitertial are named one from the half and the other from the Third part: which are, by the Ninth Axiom, the largest parts of any other whatsoever: Therefore these two intervals are the largest in the Superparticular genus. Wherefore, the Duple interval being born from their conjunction: we can say that it is born from the conjunction of the two largest Superparticulars. And all this is what I was to demonstrate to you according to the proposal.

# COROLLARY.

It is therefore manifest that the <term>Duple</term><note>The ratio 2:1, which in music forms the interval of an Octave.</note> is reintegrated—or, we might say, composed—of the <term>Sesquialter</term> and <term>Sesquitertial</term> proportions, as if from its principal parts.

*And this shall be a Corollary that we will derive from this proposition: which is approved by the Fourth <term>Postulate</term><note>The text uses "dimanda" (demand), a standard term in Renaissance geometry for a postulate.</note>, which states: that the proportion of the extremes of any proportion or interval is said to be composed of its proportional means, as if from its parts.* **DESIDERIO.** *That was truly a beautiful demonstration, and it has pleased me immensely; therefore, continue with whatever is most relevant to your purpose.* **GIOSEFFO.** *It is now convenient for me to demonstrate to you that:*

I say that from the interval **a** and **c** composed in such a manner, <term>Harmonic proportionality</term><note>A type of mathematical progression where the ratio of the differences between the terms is equal to the ratio of the outer terms themselves (e.g., 6, 4, 3).</note> is born. And because between the greater terms **a** and **b**, by the Eighth Axiom, the greater proportion is found, and between the lesser terms **b** and **c** the lesser is found; therefore, by the Thirteenth Definition, I say that between the terms **a**, **b**, and **c**, one finds Harmonic proportionality (or mediation), when the two largest superparticular intervals are joined together: just as I proposed to demonstrate to you.* **ADRIANO.** *Everything fits well.
