<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Gioseffo Zarlino and his students regarding the mathematical nature of musical intervals. The previous page established that the Octave is composed of the Fifth and the Fourth. Now, they distinguish between Harmonic and Arithmetic proportionality based on how these intervals are ordered.</meta>

<page-num>56</page-num>
<header>Discussion</header>

**ADRIANO.** *A <term>Sesquitertial</term><note>A ratio of 4:3, which forms the musical interval of a Fourth.</note> and a <term>Sesquialter</term><note>A ratio of 3:2, which forms the musical interval of a Fifth.</note>, between these terms: 4, 3, 2, or others similar: as I have many times found: can one not perhaps say that such intervals are found ordered in Harmonic proportionality?* **GIOSEPPO.** *One may well say, Sir, that it is an interval composed of the two named intervals; but certainly not that such an order is placed in Harmonic proportionality.* **ADRIANO.** *For what reason? Is it not composed of those intervals that enter into our proposal?* **GIOSEPPO.** *That the <term>Duple</term><note>The 2:1 ratio, or Octave.</note> interval is composed of a Sesquialter and a Sesquitertial simply is not the reason that such an interval contains Harmonic proportionality; rather, it consists in the order. For it is necessary that the proportions be ordered in such a way—beyond the proportions found between the differences and between the extremes, which must be similar—that the greater proportion is found among the larger terms, and the lesser among the smaller. Because (as I declared in Chapter 40 of the first part of the <term>Istitutioni</term><note>Zarlino’s *Le Istitutioni harmoniche* (1558), the definitive music theory text of the Renaissance.</note>, which is worthy of consideration) the musician (if you remember, Sir) goes about making and deriving his ratios from the Whole and from the Parts made of the <term>Sonorous Body</term><note>original: "Corpo sonoro." This refers to the physical object producing sound, usually a string on a monochord.</note>; whether it be a string or whatever other thing suits the purpose; which Body is infinitely divisible. Whence he understands and takes, in whatever order of proportion, the larger number for the Whole of the Sonorous Body divided into so many parts, and not the smaller. For this reason, he always accommodates the larger terms of the intervals to the Whole made into parts, and the others to the remainder, according to the parts he considers, and just as by their nature they ought to be accommodated, according to their degrees in order. Therefore, you see that the terms which you have proposed are placed in reverse: because between the larger numbers the smaller proportion is found, and between the smaller, the larger. Thus, one sees from their differences—which are Units equal to each other—that such terms are ordered in progression, or as you prefer to say, <term>Arithmetic proportionality</term><note>In an arithmetic proportion like 4:3:2, the difference between terms is equal (4-3=1 and 3-2=1). In music, this puts the smaller interval (the Fourth, 4:3) above the larger (the Fifth, 3:2).</note>, and not in the <term>mean</term><note>original: "mediocrità." A Renaissance term for a proportional middle or mean.</note> or Harmonic proportionality, as can be understood from the eleventh definition.* **ADRIANO.** *I understand everything now, since you have brought this Chapter back to my memory; but in truth, I did not remember that far back. And even if you had no other reason to tell me, the Definition you cited was sufficient. But I will no longer forget this thing you have said in effect: that is, that the Terms used by the Musician are parts of the Sonorous Body, and those used by the Arithmetician are things, or multiplied Units, such as those contained in the terms I proposed to you, and not the parts of the named Body.* **GIOSEPPO.** *So it is, truly. Therefore, in the future, when you see me propose a number in practice, you will always take it for as many parts made of the Sonorous Body as that Number denotes. And when you see more than one in another order, you will always take the largest for the Whole of said Body made into so many parts, and the others you will understand as those that follow.* **FRANCESCO.** *This has been another good lesson and very useful; for I too had not understood in what way you applied these Numbers or terms to the said Body.* **CLAUDIO.** *Nor I, certainly; therefore this thing has pleased me immensely.* **DESIDERIO.** *Say no more, for it was a very necessary thing to know. Now Master Gioseppo, if it pleases you, proceed further.* **GIOSEPPO.** *Pay attention then, and do not let what I am demonstrating escape your memory, for it could be a cause of confusion. But coming to the proposal, I say:*

---

## PROPOSITION XIX.

*Between two given terms of any proportion, the middle term can be found: which constitutes Harmonic proportionality; or that which makes the Contra-harmonic, in its radical terms.*

<meta>catchword: Siano (Let... be)</meta>

<summary>Zarlino explains the vital distinction between Harmonic and Arithmetic proportionality in music, noting that musicians view numbers as divisions of a physical string (the sonorous body) rather than abstract units. He establishes that in Harmonic proportion, the larger interval must correspond to the larger numbers (the larger parts of the string).</summary>

## PROPOSITION XXI.

### The <term>Sesquiquarto</term><note>A ratio of 5:4, which forms the interval of a Major Third.</note> interval is divided by a harmonic middle term into a <term>Sesquiottavo</term><note>A ratio of 9:8, known as a Major Tone or whole step.</note> and a <term>Sesquinono</term><note>A ratio of 10:9, known as a Minor Tone.</note>.

**Desiderio.** It occurs to me now that I have never found that the Ancients considered any <term>Harmonic division</term><note>A mathematical way of dividing a musical interval so that the resulting parts are in a specific proportional relationship.</note> other than that of the <term>Dupla</term><note>The 2:1 ratio, which forms the Octave.</note>: thus it seems to me that this could proceed either from ignorance or from too much superstition. **Gioseffo.** Oh, do not say that. I believe the Ancients were more likely superstitious than ignorant—although one may believe that they were not entirely free from ignorance regarding what I have already said, since they did not understand the degrees of the <term>Consonances</term><note>Pleasant-sounding musical intervals. In the Middle Ages, only octaves, fifths, and fourths were considered perfect consonances; Zarlino was instrumental in championing thirds and sixths as consonances.</note>. This all proceeded from their refusal to admit any interval into their system that was smaller than the <term>Diatessaron</term><note>The interval of a Perfect Fourth.</note>. The proof of how much they were mistaken is shown to us every day by the <term>Ditone</term><note>Literally "two tones"; a Major Third.</note> and the <term>Semiditone</term><note>Literally a "half-ditone"; a Minor Third.</note>, which are two parts arising from the proposed and demonstrated division. But let us come to the demonstration. Let **a**, **b**, and **c** be the Sesquiquarto interval, divided according to the nineteenth proposition by the harmonic middle term **b** into two parts:

| a | b | c |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 45 | 40 | 36 |

that is, into **a-b** and **b-c**. I say that from such a division are born the Sesquiottavo and the Sesquinono intervals. For if **a** contains **b** plus an eighth part of itself, there is no doubt—by the definition of <term>Superparticular</term><note>original: "Molteplici"; Zarlino is referring to ratios where the numerator is one greater than the denominator (like 9:8 or 10:9).</note> ratios—that **a** and **b** form a Sesquiottavo interval. In the same way, because **b** contains **c** once plus a ninth part of itself, therefore, by the same definition, **b** and **c** will be a Sesquinono interval. Therefore I say: when the Sesquiquarto interval is divided by a harmonic middle term, as the proposition states, it is divided into a Sesquiottavo and a Sesquinono, as I had to demonstrate to you. To this we shall also add:

Let **a** be the minor term, found through the twenty-fourth [proposition] <note>Original: "p la uẽtesima quarta"; likely referring to a common denominator or base value established in Proposition 24.</note>. Wherefore I say: since **c** results in

When, therefore, you wish to take 1/4 from 1/3, which are parts neighboring one another: first you shall <term>cross-multiply</term><note>A method for finding a common denominator when subtracting or adding fractions.</note> the Numerator of one by the Denominator of the other: which

<image-desc>A mathematical calculation demonstrating the manipulation of fractions. Two large crosses (X) represent cross-multiplication. having been done, will yield 4 and 3: which will be the Numerators of the two parts that will be born, similar to the proposed parts. Then you shall multiply the Denominators of the proposed parts together, and the result will be 12: which will be the Denominator for the two said Numerators. For what I have done until now is nothing other than reducing many parts with different Denominators under a single identical Denominator. Whence from such multiplication will be born 3/12 and 4/12: of which the first corresponds to 1/4 and the second corresponds to 1/3. This being done, you shall subtract the 3/12 from the 4/12: and the result will without fail be 1/12: which, if you add it to 3/12, you will have 4/12. This will be achieved when you cross-multiply the numerators of 1/12 and 1/4 by the Denominators: adding the products together, and also multiplying the Denominators by one another: placing the products of these below a line, and those of the first calculation above: as you see in the example I have formed for you, so that you might understand me more easily. ...similarly, twelve twelfth parts are equal to each other. From this, it follows that 1/2 is equal to 6/12; and 1/4 is equal to 3/12; and 2/3 are also equal to 8/12; and 1/3 is also equal to 4/12. Because, by the <term>Twelfth Axiom</term><note>original: "Duodecima dignità"; referring to the common mathematical notions (axioms) of Euclid. This specific axiom states that if things are equal to the same thing, they are equal to each other, or that halves of equals are equal.</note>: of those things whose Wholes are equal, their Halves are also equal. But 4/12 is 1/3; therefore they are a Third part of the whole <term>Interval</term><note>The distance in pitch between two sounds, here expressed as a mathematical fraction of a string length.</note>: to which twelve twelfths are equal: and they are one and the same thing. However, therefore, 1/4 is a smaller part of the whole interval, which is equal (as has been shown) to 3/12: and 1/12 added to 3/12 restores 1/3, which is the larger part of that interval. Thus 1/4 and 1/12 are equal to a Third, as I have shown you. From which, the remainder of a larger part of whatever interval: from which a smaller one nearest or continuous to it has been taken: added to the second: produces the first. And this is what, according to the proposition, I had to demonstrate to you. And although this demonstration is restricted to a specific case: nevertheless it is verified universally in any two neighboring and Universal <note>Zarlino uses "Universal" to refer to the primary harmonic ratios.</note> parts: such as a Fourth and Fifth part: because adding a Twentieth to the Fifth part results in a whole Fourth. Similarly, adding a Sixth part and a Thirtieth: a Fifth is born: which could also be said of the others: which I leave out for brevity.

We have already said, however, that nine B's are equal to eight A's; therefore eight A's are equal to ten C's and an eighth part of it. Let A, B, C, and D be three joined <term>Sesquioctave</term> intervals, by the first rule of this book: so that A-B is the first, B-C the second, and C-D the third. Because eleven and 3/8 of one and 1/64 contain the eighths one time and more than their third part. Whence it follows that A contains D and more than a third part of it. ->PROPOSITION XXXVI.<-

## If Three terms are placed in order: the proportion found between the extremes will be greater than that of each of them individually with the middle term.

So that you may understand this, which is easy, pay attention. Let *a, b, c* be Three terms placed in order: I say that the proportion found between the extreme terms *a* and *c* is greater than that of the middle term *b* with *a*, or indeed with *c*. Because, according to the Fourth Demand <note>A "Demand" or "Postulate" in a mathematical proof.</note>, the proportion of the extremes *a* and *c* is composed of the proportions *a-b* and *b-c* as its parts: the proportions *a-b* and *b-c* are

| a | b | c |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | 3 | 2 |

parts of *a-c*: and *a-c* is the Whole. But because, by the Final Axiom <note>Referring to the common notion in Euclidean geometry that "the whole is greater than the part."</note>, Every whole is greater than its part: therefore the proportion of *a* and *c* is greater than that of *a* and *b*, or of *b* and *c*, as the proposition says. And this is what I wanted to demonstrate to you. And this manner of argument will serve for every similar proposal. **Adri.** Truly, it is beautiful: and also, as you have said, it is very easy. Whence it pleases me much, because it is intelligible. Continue, then, with the rest. **Gios.** I want us now to demonstrate: that

This is the proposition: and the Demonstration will proceed in this manner. We have already demonstrated in the seventeenth proposition that the <term>Double interval</term> <note>A 2:1 ratio, which defines the musical Octave.</note> is made of the two largest <term>Superparticular</term> <note>A ratio where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator (e.g., 2:1, 3:2, 4:3).</note> intervals: which are the <term>Sesquialter</term> <note>A 3:2 ratio, the Perfect Fifth.</note> and the <term>Sesquiterce</term> <note>A 4:3 ratio, the Perfect Fourth.</note>. # ON THE
# HARMONIC
## DEMONSTRATIONS
### BY THE REVEREND
# MASTER GIOSEFFO ZARLINO
### OF CHIOGGIA, MASTER
### OF THE CHAPEL
### OF THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS SEIGNIORY
### OF VENICE.

#### Second Discussion.

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap letter 'S' featuring an engraved scene with two figures, one standing on the left and another seated on the right, within a landscape or architectural setting.</image-desc>

*Following the order established a little earlier, the following day we returned to the house of Master Adriano <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), the influential Flemish composer and Zarlino's teacher at St. Mark's Basilica.</note> to continue our delightful and useful discussions already begun. Thus, having first discussed various matters spoken of the day before, when the time seemed right to me, with everyone's permission, I began to speak in this manner:* **GIOS.** *I know, my Lords, by many signs—and especially by this: that you have gathered together before the hour appointed yesterday—that our past discussions have pleased you. Which I also recognized yesterday from the patience you had in listening to me; therefore, I plan to tell you things today that will delight you even more. For we are entering into a discussion slightly more specific to the matters of Music, since the discussion held yesterday was about demonstrating many things regarding Numbers and Proportions. But today we shall descend to give a particular knowledge of musical intervals, and to demonstrate to you in what manner the <term>consonants</term><note>Intervals that sound stable and harmonious to the ear.</note> and also <term>dissonants</term><note>Intervals that sound harsh or unstable, requiring a "resolution" to a consonant sound.</note> are born, which serve in the compositions of our songs. I will also make you recognize how much difference is found between those intervals used by the Ancients, which were smaller than the <term>Diatessaron</term><note>original: "Diatessaron"; the interval of a perfect fourth.</note>, and were held by them to be dissonant. Whereby you may afterward realize in what error those people are who, in our day, believe and obstinately affirm that such intervals prohibited by the Ancients belong among the number of our Consonances. Which things I hope to demonstrate so easily and clearly that every one of us may remain satisfied. And if any of us ever held a contrary opinion to what I am about to tell and show you, I am certain he will be brought back to believe what is true—and what in fact cannot be otherwise—and will cease to believe the false.* **FRAN.** *Even until now, the error of such people can be all too well known if one has understood what you have written in the <term>Institutions</term><note>Referring to Zarlino's "Le Istitutioni harmoniche" (1558), his most famous treatise on music theory.</note>, because it appears so manifest that it has no need of other demonstrations.* **CLAV.** *What will you say of this, Master: that some, perhaps to appear to understand the things of Music better than anyone else, when they hear it said that we use the major <term>semitone</term><note>The smallest interval in standard Western music; Zarlino is distinguishing between two different sizes of this interval used in tuning systems.</note> in our compositions and not the minor; similarly, when they hear the diffe-*

...ness of the Major Tone and its decrease: they show wonder at these things: which they still do when they hear it said that the Modes, or Tones, reach the number of Twelve, as if these things were not true: and that they had not been demonstrated excellently by Master Gioseffo: and that the matter was not so clear that anyone of mediocre intellect could be capable of it: but consisted rather in opinion.

**ADRI.** Do not wonder at this, because there are even some who, although they cannot be numbered among the ignorant, can at least be placed among the malicious: who, when they know that a thing is to bring some benefit and some honor to someone, to diminish the praise that is due to them—overcome by a certain passion of theirs—would rather, to their own shame and against their conscience, hide the truth and oppose it, than affirm what they feel in their soul is not false.

**FRAN.** This is a bad breed of men, Monsieur. But what will you say of those others who, not being able to openly blame what they find to be good—because they see that in fact their plan would not succeed—seek to obscure in some part the glory of those who, for some good work done, deserve it, by praising them coldly along with their works? This is much worse than if they openly blamed them. Or at least by extremely praising the works of someone else, even if they know they do not deserve such praise; and they do it all for the purpose of lowering the others, even if they happen to be present. Furthermore, if they know not what else to do, they at least praise the Ancients so much (even though they have no knowledge of their works) that with all their power they seek to take away that little reputation that the Moderns have acquired from their good works.

**ADRI.** To these people belongs that fine saying of Horace, which fits very well this purpose of these rabid, envious, ignorant, and malicious men, when he says:

See how he puts before our eyes this evil generation of men, painting for us their nature: because even he in his time was targeted by similar envious, malicious, and perverse people. But please, let us speak no more of them: for I do not want us to have anything to do with them: and I desire that we return to discussing those things from which we began our reasoning yesterday.

**DESI.** It will be well done, Master Gioseffo: and you shall begin from whatever is most convenient for you.

**GIOS.** Having therefore to discuss those things that lead to the knowledge of Consonances and also of Dissonances: and to demonstrate to you many things that occur around them, according to the truth, and as Science requires: it is necessary first to set before you those principles upon which all our discussions depend: and to declare to you what certain terms mean and the name of certain intervals used in the Science—even though you have acquired knowledge of most of them by means of the *Institutions* <note>Referring to Zarlino's own *Le Istitutioni harmoniche* (1558), his most famous and foundational work on music theory.</note>—so that by chance we do not proceed through unknown things. And this will not be without utility: for I shall not cease to declare to you certain things, and open to you some secrets, which will be of great contentment and benefit to you. And so as not to go on for too long, I will give a beginning to the definition of **Consonance**: which (as I have said elsewhere many times) is primarily considered by the Musician: and then I will say what **Dissonance**, its contrary, is, which is considered in the second place, and by accident. But before we pass further, I want to give you a brief discourse, which will be of great use to you, and perhaps never heard before...

<meta>This page continues the "Second" book or section of the treatise. The previous page featured a dialogue between Adriano (Willaert), Francesco, and others regarding the skepticism surrounding new musical demonstrations. Here, the text shifts toward a formal theoretical lecture on the nature of musical opposition and the definition of consonance.</meta>

Second.

Regarding this matter: it will be useful, in order to resolve certain things I am about to show you. Pay attention first: and then we will come, without delay, to state the Definitions one after the other. I say then, to begin, that Opposition, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, specifically his work on the *Categories*.</note>, is found to be of four kinds (so that you may know for what reason I have said that Dissonance is the contrary of Consonance): that is, Relative; Contrary; Privative; and Contradictory. But because the first and the two last do not serve our purpose, I wish to set them aside and speak only of the Second: which is nothing other than the repugnance of two contraries that do not coexist in one and the same subject: but by their nature, one drives out or destroys the other. 

And these Contraries are of two kinds: for they are either mediate or they are immediate. The first are those that admit certain intermediates between their extremes: just as between Black and White there are many intermediate colors. Thus it is not always necessary that one of the two extremes be in the subject: for the Body can be Red, or Green, or some other color, even if it is not Black or White. But the Second kind are those that admit no intermediate thing of the same genus: such as Health and Infirmity: between which no middle ground is given, according to the Philosophers—although the Physicians hold another opinion. 

The Middle ground in this context is of two sorts: first, by Participation in both extremes, such as intermediate Colors and Flavors; and second, by Negation of both the aforementioned extremes, which occurs when a subject is found that possesses neither extreme. Thus, from what I have said, you can understand that Consonance and Dissonance should be placed as two extremes in the Second species of Opposites: since they admit many middle points between them. And this is true: for, just as a visible Body is not of necessity always white or black, but sometimes red, sometimes green, and sometimes some other color; nor is a Tangible thing always cold or hot, or hard or soft, but at times lukewarm, and now more or now less hot or cold, or of some other intermediate quality; just as the Tastable is not always of necessity sweet or bitter, but tart or sour, or in some other way; so the Audible is not always simply Consonant or Dissonant: but at times participates in an intermediate quality, which holds something of both: more or less, according as it approaches more to one of the named extremes. 

For I do not see, nor can I find a reason, that compels me to say and believe that among the extreme Objects of the other Senses many intermediates can fall, but not in those of Hearing. Therefore, let us say that between Consonance and Dissonance there fall many intermediate intervals: which participate (according as they approach more to one than the other) in these two audible extremes. And these will be those (leaving aside any other distinctions that could be made between them) that arise from any proportion other than those contained in the Multiple and Superparticular Genera <term>Multiple: a ratio where the larger number is an exact multiple of the smaller (e.g., 2:1). Superparticular: a ratio where the larger number contains the smaller plus one part (e.g., 3:2).</term> located among the parts of the number Six <note>The "Senario," or the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, which Zarlino considers the source of all pure musical intervals.</note>. Wherefore we shall divide Consonance into two species: the first of which we shall call Consonance properly so called; and the second, Consonance commonly so called. Wishing to know these, beginning with the first: we shall say.

# DEFINITION.
## FIRST.

Consonance properly so called is a mixture or composition of a low and a high sound: which comes sweetly and uniformly to the Hearing: the form of which is contained by a Multiple or Superparticular proportion: which is found in action among the parts of the first Perfect Number: that is, the Senario <note>The number six.</note>.

Adri. This has removed many doubts I had in my head. In practice, I heard all these things, but I did not know how to explain how the matter stood. Gios. # DEFINITION III.

Dissonance is the distance between a low sound and a high sound which, by their nature, cannot mix or unite with one another; it strikes the hearing harshly and without any pleasure. It arises from proportions whose names are different from those found in action among the parts of the <term>Senario</term> <note>The set of numbers from 1 to 6, which Zarlino considered the foundation of all musical harmony</note> and the <term>Ottonario</term> <note>The set of numbers from 1 to 8, an extension used to include intervals like the sixth</note> numbers.

Lav. *Truly, he who has understood the definition of Consonance can also understand that of Dissonance, unless by chance you wished to make some distinction of it, as you did for Consonance.* <term>GIOSEFFO.</term> *I do not wish to provide any other distinction at present; but I only want to say that, according to the definition of the Philosopher <note>Referring to Aristotle</note>, who defines Consonance as a ratio of numbers, one also finds a certain ratio of numbers in Dissonance. For this reason I added: "Contained by proportions of different names from those found in action among the parts of the grouping of six <note>Senario</note> and the grouping of eight <note>Ottonario</note> numbers," so that you may know that Dissonance is entirely deprived of that "Rationality of Numbers" intended by the Philosopher, as I have declared elsewhere on this subject.*

<meta>This page continues the technical dialogue between the composer Adrian Willaert (ADRI.) and Gioseffo Zarlino (GIOS.). Following the mathematical breakdown of intervals on the previous page, Zarlino now explains why only certain intervals are considered truly "harmonious" based on the "Senario" (the numbers 1 through 6).</meta>

<header>Discourse</header>

ADRI. I was just about to ask you: If every Consonance and every rational Musical Interval is contained under a fixed ratio of number to number—as I have heard you say many times—how can it be that only Consonance is "reason of numbers" <note>original: "ragione di Numeri"</note> and not Dissonance as well? 

GIOS. One cannot deny, Sir, that Dissonance, being contained by a rational ratio from number to number, could be said to have a "reason of numbers," since that ratio is considered and perceived insofar as the greater term contains the lesser once, twice, or more times, along with some Aliquot <note>A part of a number that divides it exactly, like 2 is an aliquot part of 6.</note> or Non-aliquot part of it. However, "having a reason of numbers" or "being a reason of numbers" belongs, by a certain excellence, to the first perfect number, which is the *Senario* <note>The "number of six" (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6). Zarlino believed these first six numbers were the source of all musical perfection.</note>; even though the Ancients attributed such reason to the *Quaternario* <note>The "number of four" (1, 2, 3, 4), which formed the basis of the earlier Pythagorean system of music.</note>, calling it Perfect for several reasons. Therefore, Consonances—which truly take their true forms from the ratios contained between the parts of the *Senario*—are said to have the "reason of numbers," or truly to *be* the reason of numbers. But Dissonances cannot be said to be so, nor to have such reasons, because their ratios are contained among numbers other than those placed between the aforementioned parts. 

ADRI. I am very satisfied; therefore, I pray you to continue with the rest. 

GIOS. Having defined Consonance according to the two methods declared, and Dissonance as well, it is necessary that I define Harmony <note>original: "Harmonia"</note> for you, which is composed of at least two consonances. Thus, you must first know that the distinction I made regarding Consonance must also be made regarding Harmony—referring here to "improper" Harmony, according to the method declared in Chapter 12 of the second part of the *Institutes* <note>Refers to Zarlino's own work, *Le Istitutioni Harmoniche*.</note>—for it too is of two sorts: namely, Harmony "Simply so-called" and Harmony "In a certain manner." Thus, declaring the first, I will say that:

### DEFINITION IV.

->Harmony Simply so-called is the ensemble that arises from at<-
->least two parts joined together, according to the steps of Harmonic<-
->proportionality: which reaches the Hearing pleasantly.<-

Therefore, when two sounds distant from one another by low and high pitch receive a middle sound that divides the interval found between them into two consonances, according to the steps of Harmonic proportionality <note>original: "proportionalità Harmonica"</note>: then this composition is created, which we mean in the definition: which is called Harmony Simply so-called. But to explain to you the second member of "improper" harmony, I say that:

### DEFINITION V.

->Harmony so-called In a certain manner is the chord made by<-
->at least two parts placed together: but not according to the steps of<-
->the Harmonic mean: which does not come to the sense of Hearing<-
->as pleasantly as that which is Simply so-called.<-

<summary>Zarlino explains that while all musical intervals have mathematical ratios, only consonances derived from the first six numbers (the Senario) possess "mathematical reason." *...two consonances joined together, whose ratios are ordered in this way: 6, 4, 3. You will say that these two consonances joined together in this manner create **Harmony simply so-called** <note>original: "Harmonia Semplicemēte detta"</note>: because between them is found the **Harmonic mean** <term>Harmonica mediocrità: a mathematical proportion where the middle term relates to the extremes in a specific ratio, here creating a Perfect Fifth on the bottom (6:4) and a Perfect Fourth on top (4:3)</term>: as yesterday’s fifteenth definition will always make clear. You should say the same of other similar ones; and this is regarding the "simply so-called." But the **So-called in a certain way** <note>original: "Ad un certo modo detta"</note> is made when, between two consonances ordered in the said manner, such a Mean is not found; as one might say: when its ratios are placed between these terms 4, 3, 2. For if you remember yesterday’s thirteenth definition, these are placed in **Arithmetic progression** <term>Arithmetica progressione: where the difference between terms is equal; here 4-3=1 and 3-2=1</term>, or proportionality, however you prefer to say it. The reason is that in the first case, the form of the **Diapente** <term>Diapente: the interval of a Perfect Fifth</term>, or rather the Diapente itself, is placed in the low range and the **Diatessaron** <term>Diatessaron: the interval of a Perfect Fourth</term> in the high range; but in this second case, everything is placed to the contrary: because the Diatessaron holds the lower place, and the Diapente occupies the high. This is something not found among the ratios that are placed in the natural order of the **Harmonic Numbers** <term>Numeri Harmonici: the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, which Zarlino believed were the foundation of all musical beauty</term>. Hence, that which is less sweet to the hearing—as was said in its definition—is not caused by the named intervals (for they are consonant), but rather by the order, which is placed contrary to the first; for this reason, they move the sense of hearing less sweetly.* DESI. *This is a beautiful consideration. And I understand it now; therefore pass to another proposal, if you have nothing else you wish to tell me on this.* GIOS. *I do not wish to tell you anything else. But I want you to know that Consonances, speaking universally, are of two kinds: for some are called Simple, and some Compound. So that you may know both, we shall come to their definition; beginning with the first, we shall say:*

### DEFINITION VI.

Simple Consonances are those that are smaller than the **Diapason** <term>Diapason: the interval of an Octave</term>: such as the Diapente (Fifth), the Diatessaron (Fourth), the **Ditone** <term>Ditone: a Major Third</term>, the **Semiditone** <term>Semiditone: a Minor Third</term>, and the Diapason itself; whose forms are contained between the parts of the number **Senario** <note>The "Number of Six" (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)</note> in the Multiple and Superparticular Genres <term>Generi Molteplice & Superparticolare: classifications of ratios where one number is a multiple of the other (like 2:1) or contains the other plus one part (like 3:2)</term>.

<margin>Part 1, chapters 13 & 16.</margin>
ADRI. *I recall that in the* Institutions <note>Zarlino’s famous 1558 work, "Le Istitutioni Harmoniche"</note> *you also enumerated the two **Hexachords** <term>Hexachordi: here referring to the Major and Minor Sixths</term>: that is, the major and the minor; thus I do not believe you wish to exclude them now.* GIOS. *It is true that I called the Hexachord a simple consonance—yet not "simply," but "in a certain way" and for a certain respect: because it is smaller than the Diapason, and thus the Diapason does not enter into its composition. But here I call "simple" only those consonances that I have named, and not the others.* ADRI. *That is fine; continue then.* GIOS. *So I shall do.*

### DEFINITION VII.

Compound Consonances are all those that are larger than the Diapason: such as the **Diapason-diapente** <term>Diapason-diapente: an Octave plus a Fifth (a compound Twelfth)</term>, the **Disdiapason** <term>Disdiapason: a double Octave (a Fifteenth)</term>, and all others larger than these.

FRAN. *Every interval, whatever it may be, when accompanied by the Diapason, will therefore make an interval that can be called Compound, from what I see.* GIOS. *So it is in fact. But without wasting time, we shall come to the particular definition of each Consonance; beginning with that which is Queen of all others, which is the Diapason.*

### DEFINITION VIII.

->The Diapason <term>Diapason: the interval of an Octave</term> is a consonance contained in its true form by<-
->the Double proportion <term>Proportione Dupla: the mathematical ratio of 2:1</term>.<-

<margin>
Part 1, chapter 13.
Part 2, chapter 48.
</margin>
*This Consonance is the first of all others: for just as among simple numbers no greater proportion is found in the natural order from one number to the next closest than the Double proportion; since every other that is found, if it is smaller, is a part of it, and if it is larger, it is placed between numbers which are not adjacent and is composed of it and one of its parts. Thus, the Diapason holds the first place among other Consonances and intervals, and no other interval is found, whatever it may be, that is greater than it; for if it is smaller, it is a part of it, and if it is larger, it is composed of one of its parts and of its Whole, as I have declared elsewhere. And by the Musician, it is taken as his divisible Whole. But just as no proportion is found that precedes the Double; so no Consonance is found that is prior to the Diapason, since the Double is its true form—the divisible Whole being, without any doubt, prior to its parts, as is known to all intelligent people. Now, having defined the Whole for you, I will come to define its parts; and starting from the larger, I shall speak in this way.*

### DEFINITION X.

->The Diatessaron <term>Diatessaron: the interval of a Perfect Fourth</term> is a consonance that has its true form from<-
->the Sesquiterza proportion <term>Proportione Sesquiterza: the mathematical ratio of 4:3</term>.<-

*ADRIANO. If the Diapente is the larger part of the Diapason, there is no doubt that the Diatessaron will be its smaller part; since these two parts added together make exactly the Diapason. FRANCESCO. GIOSEFFO. You understand it perfectly, for it is so in fact. CLAUDIO. ...and my teacher <term>Jean Mouton: a famous French composer of the Renaissance</term> in many places in their compositions have placed it in the lower part without adding any other interval. **GIOSEFFO:** Sir: If the <term>Diatessaron: the interval of a Fourth</term> were a dissonance, you would not place it in your counterpoints in the way that you do: above the <term>Diapente: the interval of a Fifth</term>, or above the <term>Ditono: a Major Third</term>, or the <term>Semiditono: a Minor Third</term>. Nor would other composers do this. **CLAUDIO:** Nor could any kind of instrument be tuned by means of this interval if it were not consonant; yet many kinds are tuned this way: such as organs, viols, lutes, lyres, and other similar ones, just as well as it is done by means of the Fifth and the <term>Diapason: the interval of an Octave</term>. **GIOSEFFO:** Listen, please, for I want to tell you a reason that has just now occurred to me, which cannot be reasonably contradicted. **ADRIAN:** Please, tell us. **GIOSEFFO:** I want you to hold this as a Maxim: that when one of the extremes <note>The "extremes" are the high and low notes of a musical interval.</note> of any interval is changed—whether it be consonant or dissonant—by making the low note high, or conversely the high note low by an Octave, one obtains a corresponding interval in the high or low range which is of the *same nature* as the first. And so that you understand me, I want to speak practically. Let us suppose we have that interval which we call a Second. This (as is known to everyone) is a most dissonant interval. However, if we transport the lower extreme of this interval to the high range, or its high extreme toward the low by an Octave—while the other terms remain in their places—there is no doubt that we will have an interval corresponding to the Second in the high or low part, which will be of the same nature as that Second; it will be a Seventh, which every one of us knows to be dissonant. The same will also happen by doing the opposite: that is, when the high extreme of the Seventh is transported toward the low, or its low extreme toward the high, the aforementioned Second will be born from it. Therefore, it cannot be denied that both of these two intervals are of the same nature, and are comprised under the same Genre of Dissonance. **FRANCESCO:** In fact, it is so; but I do not see where you want to arrive with this. **GIOSEFFO:** The matter will go but a little further before you see it. I say again: if we again take a Third—which you know is placed among the number of the <term>Imperfect Consonances: intervals like Thirds and Sixths that are harmonious but less stable than Fifths or Octaves</term>—and we do the same: transporting its low extreme to the high by an Octave, or placing its high extreme in the low by a similar interval, the Sixth will immediately result, which is also numbered among the Imperfect Consonances. Therefore, it would also happen that by transporting the extremes of the Sixth in the same way, the Third would result; a thing which truly no one of sound judgment can deny. **FRANCESCO:** It truly cannot be. **GIOSEFFO:** But if, by using such methods of transporting said terms, it is seen that one Dissonance produces another, and an Imperfect Consonance gives another of the same genre, what greater privilege should Dissonances and Imperfect Consonances have over Perfect Consonances? None, certainly; for there is no greater reason for the first two than for these last. We shall say then, by the same logic: that if one reports the low extreme of a Fifth toward the high by an Octave, or the high extreme toward the low by a similar interval, that which results will be a Fourth. Which, for the reasons cited regarding Dissonances and Imperfect Consonances, I say is of the nature of the Fifth, and is subject to the same genre of Consonance. And just as the Fifth, for various respects, is called a Perfect Consonance, so too, for those same respects, the Fourth is called a Perfect Consonance. Because by also reporting the extremes of the Fourth to the high and low, as we did those of the Fifth, that same Fifth is born in the same way. Wherefore we are forced, whether we want to or not, to say: that if the Fourth is dissonant, the Fifth must be dissonant in the same way; or if the latter is consonant, then the former must also be of such a nature. I do not believe this would be denied by men of sound intellect. **ADRIAN:** This reasoning is truly new, and it is one of the beautiful ones that can be brought in confirmation of your arguments. Even if I learned nothing else today but this, I would be quite satisfied. **GIOSEFFO:** I hope to tell you other things, Sir, that will please you; therefore, be cheerful. **FRANCESCO:** I will say, Master Gioseffo, that the logic of the Second and the Seventh works well, because they are both dissonant; similarly that of the Third with the Sixth. But that of the Fifth with the Fourth seems different to me. And I say this so that...

Therefore, I say the Fourth is a consonance and is perfect; but I do not say that it is as consonant or as perfect as the Fifth, nor as the Octave. ### DEFINITION XVI.

## The Double Octave plus a Fifth <note>original: "Disdiapason diapente"; this is an interval spanning 19 diatonic notes.</note> is a consonance whose form is contained by the Sextuple proportion <note>A ratio of 6:1.</note>.

*But as to why it is called a "Compound" consonance more than any other: since the terms of its form are mediated in such a way—6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, or indeed 60, 30, 20, 15, 12, 10—the reason given above should suffice for you. Therefore, we shall proceed to the seventeenth definition.*

### DEFINITION XVII.

## The Major Sixth <note>original: "Hexachordo maggiore"</note> is a consonance whose form is contained by the Superbipartient third proportion <note>original: "proportione Superbipartiente terza"; a ratio of 5:3, where the larger number contains the smaller once, plus two remaining parts.</note>.

*FRANCESCO: It seems to me that we are turning backward, from what I can see. Previously you defined the consonances by starting from the Simple ones and moving to the Compound ones, and you went from the smaller to the larger. Now, you return to the beginning again. By your faith, for what reason do you do this? GIOSEFFO: Those consonances I have defined until now are contained within the Multiple and Superparticular genera <note>Multiple ratios are like 2:1, 3:1; Superparticular ratios are those where the larger number is one greater than the smaller, like 3:2 or 4:3.</note>, which are the simple genera of proportion. Therefore, having finished with those contained under these two genera, I now come to define those contained in the others, so that I may follow a proper order. Nor do I care whether these I am currently defining are larger or smaller, as that is of very little importance. It is enough for you to know that this "superbipartient third" proportion mentioned above is comprised in the third genus of proportion, called the Superpartient <note>In this genus, the larger number contains the smaller once, plus multiple remaining parts (e.g., 5:3 contains 3 once, plus 2 leftovers).</note>, and it is the first of that kind. FRANCESCO: I like the order, and I am satisfied; therefore, continue as you please.*

<margin>Institutions, Part 1, Chapter 16. <note>original: "Institut, 1. part. c. 16."</note></margin>
*GIOSEFFO: Even though the form of the Minor Sixth <note>original: "Hexachordo minore"</note> does not exist "in act" <note>meaning as a direct ratio of the primary numbers 1 through 6</note> among the parts of the <term>Senario: the number six, which Zarlino considers the boundary of perfect harmony</term>, nevertheless, because it exists "in potential" (as I have declared elsewhere) and exists between the first <term>Cube: the number 8, as it is 2 to the third power</term> and the <term>Quinario: the number 5</term> "in act," I do not wish to omit it. Since its form is contained in the aforementioned Genus, I shall give you its definition; thus we shall say:*

### DEFINITION XVIII.

## The Minor Sixth <note>original: "Hexachordo minore"</note> is a consonance which has its form contained by the Supertripartient fifth proportion <note>original: "proportione Supertripartiente quinta"; a ratio of 8:5, where 8 contains 5 once, with 3 remaining.</note>.

*This consonance (as I have said) has its proportion contained in the second place of the named Genus, between these numbers or terms: 8 and 5. But to come to the other two Generi, which are compound: to show you that in every Genus of proportion some consonance is found—if not simple, at least Compound—I will provide, without any delay, the definition of the Octave plus a Major Third <note>original: "Diapason col Ditono"; a compound interval of a tenth.</note> in this manner.*

### DEFINITION XIX.

## The Octave plus a Major Third <note>original: "Diapaſon col Ditono"; a compound interval spanning ten diatonic steps.</note> is a consonance whose true form is contained by the Double Sesquialter proportion <note>A ratio of 5:2, where 5 contains 2 twice, with 1 remaining (which is half of 2).</note>.

*But the terms of this proportion are found located among the parts of the Senario <note>The numbers 1 through 6, which Zarlino considered the foundation of all musical harmony.</note>, specifically between these terms: 5 and 2. ADRIAN: Hold on a moment, please, Master Gioseffo, and let me ask you about a doubt I have. GIOSEFFO: I am happy to. ADRIAN: You say that the Octave plus a Major Third has its form from the Double Sesquialter; nevertheless, this interval is composed of an Octave (which has its form from the Double proportion, 2:1) and a Major Third (which has its form from the Sesquiquarta proportion, 5:4), as you have stated in their definitions. But if the Sesquialter (3:2) is the form of the Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note>, how is it possible that the Octave plus a Major Third has its form from the Double Sesquialter, and not from the Double Sesquiquarta? GIOSEFFO: I understand from your words that you would prefer it if one said that the Double Sesquiquarta proportion was the form of the Octave plus a Major Third—since it is composed of the Octave and the Major Third—rather than the Double Sesquialter. You feel that by its name, the Double Sesquialter should instead name the Octave plus a Fifth, since "Double" is the form of the Octave and "Sesquialter" is that of the Fifth. Is it not as I say? ADRIAN: That is correct. GIOSEFFO: If it must be so, then we shall sum them together in the manner I demonstrated in Chapter 33 of the First Part of the* Institutions <note>Zarlino's "Istitutioni Harmoniche," his most famous work.</note>: *we will add the Double proportion (2:1) together with the Sesquiquarta (5:4). If the proportion you named results, then all is well. But we see that it works out differently: it results in a Double Sesquialter (5:2), as the Definition states; therefore, your naming does not hold. Furthermore, summing together the Double (2:1) with the Sesquialter (3:2) in the same way, the Double Sesquialter does not result; rather, the Triple (3:1) is born, which is the form of the Octave plus a Fifth. Thus, one sees that to say "Triple" and to say "Double Sesquialter" is not to say the same proportion, but different ones. We see this again: summing the proportion of the Octave (2:1) and that of the Fourth (4:3) <note>original: "Diateſſaron"</note>, the result is not the Double Sesquiterza, even though Double is the Octave and Sesquiterza is the Fourth; instead, it results in the Supertripartient fifth (8:3), which is the form of the Octave plus a Fourth, as I declared in its Definition. From this, it is manifest that the Ancients looked more to the universal than the particular, and toward removing confusion from the minds of men. They wished (as was right) to name the proportions in every Genus according to how many times the larger term contained the smaller entirely, or multiple times plus one or more parts of the smaller. They did this so that these names would serve not only musical proportions and intervals specifically, but also those used in other Sciences, so that there would be no confusion.*

<margin>Part 1, chapter 25.</margin>
*And though you might tell me that this word "Sesqui"—as I declared in the* Institutions—*means "the Whole," and "Altera" signifies one of two parts made of a thing, and that it would be better to say "Double and a Half" than "Double Sesquialter," I will respond that this would not be wrongly done if, in this and every other compound Genus, the word "Sesqui" were taken only as a syllabic addition (as some wished) and signified nothing else. But let us speak according to its true meaning: that "Double Sesquialter" means "Two times the Whole and one part." It is of little importance whether one adds or removes such a particle, since it is already accepted as such, and it is added beyond these terms like Double, Triple, and others. Similar names—like Sesquialter, Sesquiterza, and the others in order—are the names of the parts by which the larger term exceeds the smaller, which are found in the denominators of the proportions. This should suffice for you for now. ADRIAN: I am very well satisfied. GIOSEFFO: I shall proceed, then, and say that all these Definitions I have given are sufficient regarding those intervals that are Consonant and that pass beyond the limits of the Senario at least potentially, if not in act; and their limit is the Septuple propor-*

### DEFINITION XX.

->The Major Tone is that interval by which the perfect fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note> exceeds the perfect fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' at the beginning of the paragraph.</image-desc>
This interval was defined differently by the Ancients: for they said that the Tone was the "principle of Consonance," which is born, proceeding from sound to sound, from the Sesquioctave proportion <note>A ratio of 9:8.</note>. ADRIAN: For what reason, then, did you not state in your definition—as you did in the others—that this Tone is born from such a proportion, since you have said so many times in the *Institutions*? GIOSEFFO: If I had put in the Definition that it was born from the Sesquioctave proportion, I could not then demonstrate it to you, because Principles are not demonstrated <note>In classical logic, a definition is a starting point, not something to be proven.</note>. But because I intend to demonstrate this very thing to you, I refrained from saying it; I have told you only that it is the difference found between the perfect fourth and the perfect fifth. I want to make you aware, through these Definitions, that all those intervals that are smaller than the minor third <note>original: "Semiditono"</note> and are dissonant are nothing other than the differences found between a larger interval and a smaller one. CLAUDIO: This pleases me greatly; but tell us, I pray, what does this word "Tone" <note>original: "Tuono"</note> mean? GIOSEFFO: It is Greek, and is called Τόνος <note>original: "Τόνος" (Tonos)</note>, which implies Firmness or Stability. And because no consonant interval is found that does not contain this interval—or at least its proportion—the Ancients called it the Principle of Consonance. This was because they held the opinion that every interval larger than itself was, or ought to be, composed of it and their minor semitone. Hence, from this perceived firmness and stability they saw in it, they called it a Tone. ADRIAN: Are there not two kinds of Tones? GIOSEFFO: There certainly are, and it is recognized by this: that to this one I add the word "Major," which distinguishes it from the other that I will define for you right now, which will be the "Minor."

### DEFINITION XXI.

->The Minor Tone is that difference which falls between the perfect fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> and the minor third <note>original: "Semiditono"</note>.<-

But let us move a little further along, so as not to waste time.

The **Minor Semitone**, or **Major Enharmonic Diesis**, is that interval by which the major third <note>original: "Ditono"</note> exceeds the minor third <note>original: "Semiditono"</note>; or, by which the minor tone exceeds the major semitone.

It is quite true that when one wishes to treat these minutiae and demonstrate the place where they occur and are found in an order of sounds, it will not be impossible, though difficult; and I once reduced them to practice upon an instrument built for that purpose, for I wished to hear them.*

Thus, among those numbers smaller than this, one does not find the proportion of the Minor that you mean, but rather the "Minimum" which is this one, which I call "Minor." Because if I were to say "Minimum," it would be necessary for there to be a "Minor" before it, or at least after it, since "Minimum" is a relative of "Minor" in the degrees of comparison. Therefore, it did not seem appropriate to me to name a Minimum when there was no Minor; thus I named it Minor in respect to the Major. The other reason was that the Minor which you speak of does not serve our purpose.*

See, I pray you, what a beautiful order this is, born from Nature: that the Chromatic <term>Chromatic: a genus of music using semitones</term> makes use of the major semitone, which is common to the Diatonic; and the Enharmonic <term>Enharmonic: a genus using even smaller intervals, like quarter-tones</term> uses the minor [semitone], which is common to the Chromatic in such a way that you can understand how admirable Nature herself is as a mistress of all things. **CLAV.** *See also what a beautiful and regulated order this is: that the minor third <note>original: "Semiditono"</note>, which is found in the Diatonic between the first and third strings of its tetrachord, is found in the Chromatic between the third and fourth. And if they said at least that the minor third—which is found between the string E (speaking as a practitioner) and the string C marked with this sign # <note>The sharp sign was often referred to as a "Diesis" in this period.</note>, which we call Diesis—and this descending: one could almost, if not entirely, at least in part agree with them; but certainly not otherwise.* **FRAN.** *In what way, sir, would you wish to side with them in this matter?* **ADRI.** *In this: when the named consonance happened to be placed between a diatonic string, marked E, and a chromatic one, marked #, as I said above; because then it would not be found to be simply between diatonic strings, but between one marked Diatonic and one marked Chromatic. In that case, I could hold to their view. But that this interval is not found in the Diatonic between the strings ♮ and b <note>Referring to the natural and flat B strings, which create the semitone.</note>, and cannot be sung without interposing a middle string, and that it is not a Diatonic interval—this I will never grant them. For if the Fourth <note>original: "Diateſſaron"</note> is sung without being mediated by any other sound and as a single interval, and this does not create any variety of Genus <note>i.e., it doesn't force the music to change from Diatonic to Chromatic</note>, the same must also happen when the major third or the minor third is sung as a single interval. For I do not see, nor can I find, any greater reason why one should have more right than the other among these intervals, since they are all consonant. Indeed, if any respect should be shown to any of them—that as more consonant intervals they could be sung mediated or unmediated without creating a change of Genus—as perhaps these men might say of the Fourth (because it was held by the Ancients to be the primary consonance), much more should the major third and the minor third have this privilege. For among the moderns until now, the Fourth is not placed by many in the number of Consonances, as are the Octave <note>original: "Diapaſon"</note> and the Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note>, but certainly the major and minor thirds are. And that this is true, see these two consonant intervals, which interchangeably are placed in the low part of our compositions, one under the other, as much as in the high part. This is not done with the Fourth and the Fifth, because the latter is always placed under the Fourth, and the Fourth stays above it; or truly we are accustomed to place them under the major or minor third.* **CLAV.** *I want to say one word, sir, and then you shall continue. ### DEFINITION XXV.

## The Comma is an interval by which the major tone exceeds the minor tone.

*It is called a Comma <note>original: "Κόμμα"</note>: as if to say a "Cutting," or a "part," or whatever we wish to call it. **CLAV.** This Comma of ours does not resemble that of the Ancients, from what I have been able to see. **GIOS.** Not only does it not resemble it in its proportion, but not even in its origin. For the ancient Comma <note>The Pythagorean comma, the difference between twelve perfect fifths and seven octaves.</note> is that by which the tone of a nine-to-eight ratio <note>original: "sesquiottauo"</note> is greater than two of their minor semitones. Or, it is that difference found between the Apotome <note>original: "Ἀποτομὴ"; the major semitone in Pythagorean tuning</note> and the Limma <note>original: "Λεῖμμα"; the minor semitone in Pythagorean tuning</note>. It is contained by the proportion of 531,441 to 524,288 <note>original: "Super. 7153. partiente. 524288"</note>, as the nature of such a thing carries. But that which I have defined is contained by another proportion <note>The Syntonic Comma, with a ratio of 81:80.</note>, as I am to demonstrate to you in its proper place. And it is different by origin, as the definition reveals to us. **ADRI.** Will you tell us anything of their Schisma and Diaschisma? For I see that you proceed along a different path from that which the Ancients took. **GIOS.** I will truly tell you, and this is the place for it: for the Schisma is born from the Comma, and the Diaschisma from the minor semitone, as you shall hear. We shall say, then:*

### DEFINITION XXVI.

## The Schisma is the full half of the Comma.

***ADRI.** Which Comma do you mean: ours, or that of the Ancients? **GIOS.** Although it should be understood as that of the Ancients—since these terms and these divisions came from them—nevertheless, I do not want us to make any distinction between ours and theirs, even though that one is very different from this one in proportion; provided that I demonstrate to you what I intend to demonstrate in its place. **CLAV.** What does "Schisma" truly mean? **GIOS.** Schisma <note>original: "Σχίσμα"</note> is a Greek word and it means "Division." For, as you have heard in its definition, the Ancients made two equal parts, or rather they understood them as parts of the Comma, and each of these they called a Schisma. **ADRI.** That is well. But what then will the Diaschisma be? **GIOS.** That which I told you above, which we shall define in this way:*

### DEFINITION XXVII.

## The Diaschisma is the full half of the minor semitone.

***ADRI.** Of which semitone is this to be understood: the Ancient one, or ours? **GIOS.** You are very diligent, sir. This is because they cannot be named with determined and rational numbers, but with irrational and "deaf" numbers <term>Deaf numbers: a historical term for surds or irrational numbers that "cannot be heard" as a simple ratio</term>. But what I have said so far may be enough for you, for I want us to come to the Proposals. **DESI.** It will not be out of place, as there is nothing else to say upon these Principles; therefore, give a beginning to whatever is most convenient for you, and we shall listen to you attentively. **GIOS.** You say well. ### PROPOSITION IV.

## The Octave is born from the joining of the Fifth and the Fourth put together.

DESI. This proposes the opposite of what the First proposition proposed. ### PROPOSITION VIII.

## The Major Tone and the Minor Tone arise from the harmonic division of the Major Third.

*Desi.* **How does it happen that in all the divisions made harmonically until now, you have always taken the larger part of the preceding division and not the smaller?** *Gios.* **Because the smaller part does not produce those intervals that suit our purpose—neither consonances nor even useful dissonances. You can understand this from the following: if the Fourth <term>Diatessaron; the interval of a Perfect Fourth</term> is divided harmonically into two parts, let us say, two intervals result. The larger is contained by the Sesquiquarta ratio <term>5:4, a Major Third</term>, and the smaller by the Sesquiquintina ratio <term>6:5, a Minor Third</term>. Although these are Superparticular ratios <term>ratios where the numerator is one greater than the denominator</term>, they do not create any Consonance. This is because their terms are not contained within the ratios of the parts of the Senario <term>The "number six"; Zarlino's system where consonances are derived from the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6</term>, according to the Definition. Thus, they do not serve our Harmonies, as they are not intervals by which a larger consonant interval exceeds a smaller one, such as the intervals of Tones and Semitones and others we have defined.** *Desi.* **Why does this happen?** *Gios.* **It happens because such intervals, by their nature and property, are not suited to receive such a division that can produce consonant intervals—as occurs with the Fifth <term>original: "Diapete," likely a printer's error for "Diapente"</term>. Or, if they are not consonances, they should at least serve the melody of songs <term>cantilene</term>, such as those that arise (as I will show you) from the division of the Major Third <term>Ditono</term>; I say the same for the others.** *Desi.* **This reason is very general.** *Gios.* **For now, I cannot tell you anything else; but when you can provide a more specific and appropriate reason, mine will give way to it. But tell me, in good faith: for what reason can the number Three <term>Ternario</term> not be divided into two other numbers that are equal?** *Desi.* **For the same reason you gave for the named part. However, with your question, you have made me realize that the reason you provided is a good one, even if it is not "proper" <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "proper" reason is one that identifies the specific essence of the cause.</note>, since in truth nothing else can be said about this fact except that such properties come from their Nature. Continue, then, with what you have started, for I am satisfied with this.** *Gios.* **Let **a–b** be the Major Third <term>Ditono</term> divided by **c** harmonically into two parts, **a–c** and **c–b**. I say that from such a division, the Major Tone and the Minor Tone are produced.**

## PROPOSITION IX.

### The interval of the Major Tone is Sesquioctave: and that of the Minor is Sesquinonal.

*We have from today’s Twentieth definition: that the Major Tone is that interval by which the Fifth <term>Diapente</term> exceeds the Fourth <term>Diatessaron</term>. Wherefore, by the twenty-sixth proposition of the first book, since such an interval is Sesquioctave <term>9:8</term>—as was also said in the Preceding one—it also follows that the interval of the Major Tone is Sesquioctave. Similarly, by the Twenty-first Definition given in this reasoning: it is clearly seen and known that the Minor Tone is the difference found between the Fourth <term>Diatessaron</term> and the Minor Third <term>Semiditono</term>, by how much one exceeds the other. And it has already been demonstrated in the past reasoning, in the Twenty-seventh proposition and in its Corollary, that such a difference is a Sesquinonal <term>10:9</term>; therefore it necessarily follows that the interval of the Minor Tone is Sesquinonal. And this is what you requested that I should demonstrate to you. ADRI. I am satisfied. GIOS. Therefore I shall continue by demonstrating to you: that*

## PROPOSITION X.

### The interval of the Major Tone, and that of the Minor Tone, are Superparticular.

*DESI. This is an easy thing: because, if by the Definition, that interval is Superparticular which has its terms in such a manner that the greater contains the lesser plus one Aliquot part <note>An "aliquot part" is a part that divides the whole exactly; in superparticular ratios, this part is always 1 (e.g., in 9:8, 9 contains 8 plus 1/8th of 8).</note> of it: the interval of the Major Tone and that of the Minor are without doubt Superparticular. For, as you have demonstrated in the Preceding proposition: one is Sesquioctave and the other Sesquinonal, and in both of them the larger term contains the smaller and its named Aliquot part. Thus I can say, that this is what you were able to demonstrate. GIOS. The matter goes well; therefore we shall go one step further. But since we have finished demonstrating in what manner all those intervals that are simple arise from the harmonic division of the Octave <term>Diapason</term> made into its parts; I want us at present to demonstrate some things that will give you much contentment to have seen. For from these you will understand how Mother Nature, the instrument of the Supreme Creator, is most admirable in producing and ordering her things. And you will see that the things of Music are not made by Art, nor do they happen by chance; but by their nature they are necessarily such: and as such they must be [recognized] by the Musician...*

### PROPOSITION XII.

->Every arithmetic progression, which begins from whatever num-<-

**LAV.** First you must clarify the proposition for us: and then perform the demonstration at your pleasure. **GIO S.** *You are right. Note then, that I mean a number added to itself five times: when first there is added to it once another number equal to it; then twice; beyond this three times; also four; and ultimately five times: from which arises the Arithmetic Progression. From which I say, that every arithmetic progression which begins from whatever number you please added to itself in this way, contains the form of every musical consonance. And furthermore I say to you: that the two first simple major consonances, which are the <term>Octave; original: Diapason</term> and the <term>Fifth; original: Diapente</term>, each by itself, are found in such a progression divided, according to the likeness of harmonic proportionality, into two minor consonances.* **CLAV.** *Now we understand you very well: proceed to demonstrate this thing to us.* **GIO S.** *This is an easy thing: and you shall see that it is true. Let **a** be the number which we wish to add to itself five times, in such a way that it produces the arithmetic progression. I say that we must first double this **a**, and from it will come **b**. And because **b** is the double of **a**, therefore, by the eighth definition, **b** and **a** contain the form of the <term>Octave; original: Diapason</term>. Then we shall add **a** to **b**, and from it will come **c**. But because **c** contains **a** three times, and **b** once with its third part: therefore, by the definitions, **c** to **a** is Triple, and is the form of the <term>Twelfth; original: Diapason diapente</term>; and **c** to **b** is <term>Sesquialtera; the ratio 3:2</term>, and is the form of the <term>Fifth; original: Diapente</term>. Again we shall add **a** to **c**, and from it will result **d**. It is a manifest thing that **d** contains **a** four times, and **c** once with its third part; wherefore, by the definitions, **d** to **a** is Quadruple, and comes to contain the <term>Double Octave; original: Disdiapason</term>; and **c** to **d** is <term>Sesquitertia; the ratio 4:3</term>, and contains the <term>Fourth; original: Diatessaron</term>. To **d** we shall again add **a**, and from it will be born **e**: I say **e** contains **a** five times, and is Quintuple; and contains **d** one time and its fourth part; therefore **e** and **d** is <term>Sesquiquarta; the ratio 5:4</term>. Wherefore from the definitions given at the start of this reasoning, it is manifest that between **e** and **a** is found the form of the <term>Double Octave plus a Major Third; original: Disdiapason Ditono</term>; and between **e** and **d** that of the <term>Major Third; original: Ditono</term>. Beyond this: because **d** contains **b** two times: therefore **d** and **b** are in Double proportion: and such a proportion is the form of the <term>Octave; original: Diapason</term>; and it is divided (as the second part of the proposition says) into two parts: that is, into a Fifth, **c** and **b**, and into a Fourth, **d** and **c**. Similarly, because **f** contains **d** one time and its half: therefore I say, by the definition, **f** and **d** are <term>Sesquialtera; the ratio 3:2</term>, and are the form of the consonance of the <term>Fifth; original: Diapente</term>. Being then mediated by **e**, I say that it is divided into two parts: one of which is found between **e** and **d**, which is the <term>Major Third; original: Ditono</term>, and the other between **f** and **e**, which is the <term>Minor Third; original: Semiditono</term>, as was shown above. And to demonstrate this to you with some understanding: you must know that (as Boethius affirms) the Ancients held this opinion: that <margin>Boethius, *Arithmetic*, book 2, chapter 54.</margin> that was a Maximum & Perfect harmony which contained within itself four terms one after the other, ordered in such a manner that (just as I showed you a little while ago) among four other numbers one found the Harmonic and the Contra-harmonic proportionality, so among these four of theirs one would find the Geometric, the Arithmetic, and the Harmonic joined together. In such a way that between the Largest and the Smaller of the two middle terms, and between the Larger of the middle terms and the Smallest, one finds the Geometric; between the Largest, the Larger of the middle terms, and the Smallest, the Arithmetic; and the Harmonic between the Largest, the Smaller middle term, and the Smallest. And they intended that this, their Maximum & Perfect harmony, should have great power in Music, and in the speculations of natural things: and that nothing more perfect than this proportionality <note>original: "medietà"</note> could be found. Since it is contained between three intervals <note>In this context, Zarlino refers to the three spatial dimensions</note>, it had taken the nature of the Substance of a perfect Body, which similarly consists of three intervals: that is, length, width, and depth (or height). They were led to this by the harmony found among the qualities of the Cube <note>original: "corpo Cuba"</note>: which, being composed of Twelve edges, Eight angles, and Six surfaces—passing from length to width, and from this to depth (or height), increasing equally and making its progress from equal things and arriving at equal things—is equally proportioned to itself. Therefore, because of the suitability of all these things thus placed together, which is harmonic, they named it Geometric harmony. They called Harmonic Proportionality by no other name than this, except for the great suitability that this has with that. But to finish telling you: among this Maximum harmony of theirs, they said that all the consonances of Music are contained, as well as the Tone, which they affirmed to be the common measure of all musical sounds, because they intended it to be the smallest of all others. And although the Ancients have shown this Maximum harmony of theirs to be contained between Four terms, and that among them were found all the Consonances and also the Major Tone, nevertheless one does not find in it those consonances which are most pleasing to the ear and are greatly put into use by Musicians <note>Zarlino is likely referring to the Major and Minor Thirds (5:4 and 6:5), which weren't part of the ancient Pythagorean system</note>. Therefore, I want to show you this Maximum harmony among Five terms and four intervals, which will similarly contain not only the Geometric, the Arithmetic, and the Harmonic in their manner, but also the Contra-harmonic, and whatever consonance you wish, as well as the forms of the Major Tone and the Minor Tone. **ADRI.** This will be very dear to us: but before you pass further on: give us an example of this, their Maximum & perfect harmony, I pray you: because a doubt regarding it arises in my mind. **GIOS.** I am content, and I give you the example. All this is what they understand by Maximum harmony. **ADRI.** It is well. I see now that between 12, 9, 6 there is the Arithmetic proportionality; and between 12, 8, 6 one finds the Harmonic; or that which you named above as Geometric harmony; but...

<image-desc>A mathematical diagram illustrating geometric proportionality. Four points are labeled 12, 9, 8, and 6. Curved lines (arcs) connect 12 and 6 (the extremes) and 9 and 8 (the means). *...understand, for they knew very well that the <term>Tone</term> <note>original: "Tuono"; the interval of a major second (ratio 9:8)</note> is not a consonant interval. ## PROPOSITION. XIII.

->One can provide as many Maximal and Perfect harmonies as one wishes; each of which will contain, in itself, the Major and Minor Tone, along with all the consonances between its terms and their differences.<-

<margin>Part 1, Chapter 36.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative drop cap 'S' featuring a figure in classical dress standing amidst ornate scrolling foliage.</image-desc>
*Let there be then, according to the eleventh point of our discussion, c. f. e. d., the <term>Harmonic</term> and <term>Counter-harmonic</term> proportionality joined together. And let c-d be <term>Dupla</term> <note>2:1 ratio, an Octave</note>; c-e <term>Sesquialtera</term> <note>3:2 ratio, a Fifth</note>; c-f <term>Sesquiquinta</term> <note>6:5 ratio, a Minor Third</note>; f-d <term>Super-bipartient third</term> <note>5:3 ratio, a Major Sixth</note>; f-e <term>Sesquiquarta</term> <note>5:4 ratio, a Major Third</note>; and e-d <term>Sesquiterza</term> <note>4:3 ratio, a Fourth</note>. To these we must add the <term>Arithmetic</term> and the <term>Geometric</term>. To find the Arithmetic, I double—according to the method shown in the "Institutions"—c & d, resulting in g & h, which, by the Fifth Dignity, contain that same proportion found between c & d. Thus, c-d being Dupla, g-h similarly becomes Dupla. Now I take the mean of g & h added together, and I make "i". I now say g-i is <term>Sesquiterza</term> and i-h is <term>Sesquialtera</term>; for since "n" is the difference found between g & i, and g contains four "n" and i contains three, by definition g-i is Sesquiterza. Similarly, because i contains three "n" and h contains two, by definition i-h becomes Sesquialtera. Wherefore, I say g. i. h. <note>The text has "K" here, but the logic follows the terms g, i, h</note> by yesterday’s eleventh definition is the sought-after Arithmetic proportionality, since the differences found between the terms g, i, h are equal to each other and similar to the difference "n". Having done this, I similarly double f & e, resulting in K & l. Thus I say that between g, K, l, h are contained those same proportions placed between c, f, e, d by the named Fifth Dignity: namely g-h Dupla, g-l Sesquialtera, g-K Sesquiquinta, K-h Super-bipartient third, K-l Sesquiquarta, and l-h Sesquiterza. But because the proportion found between g & i is equal to that between l & h, and the two means i & l multiplied together yield the same as the extremes g & h multiplied—both giving 72—therefore, according to what I declared in the preceding [proposition], I say: that between g & i and between l & h, we have the Geometric proportionality. Having also shown that g-h is Dupla, by yesterday’s seventeenth [definition], g-l will be Sesquialtera and l-h Sesquiterza. It is certain, by what I have shown, that i & h is Sesquialtera; therefore, by that same seventeenth, g & i becomes Sesquiterza. If then from i-h, which is Sesquialtera, we take away g-i Sesquiterza, by the twenty-sixth [proposition] of the past discussion, there will remain i & l, which will be <term>Sesquiottava</term> <note>9:8 ratio, the Major Tone</note>. Similarly, if from g-i Sesquiterza we take away g-K Sesquiquinta, by yesterday’s twenty-seventh, there will result K & i <term>Sesquinona</term> <note>10:9 ratio, the Minor Tone</note>. Whence it is seen that between g, K, i, l, & h are contained the forms of all the consonant intervals, and also those of the Tone...*

## PROPOSITION XIIII.

**If a Square is divided into three equal Parallelograms, and the middle one is also divided in two: If we draw a straight line from a corner of that Square over the opposite side, so that it divides it into two equal parts; between the parts of the sides of the Parallelograms made by the segments of the line, such parts will arise that, compared to one another, will give us the forms of all the Musical consonances.**

<meta>This page continues the mathematical demonstration of how musical intervals are derived from the geometric proportions of a square. In the previous page, a table established the numerical ratios; here, those ratios are mapped onto specific line segments within a geometric figure.</meta>
