<header>Second Book.</header>

*Let the Square a.b.c.d. therefore be divided first into three equal parallelograms* <note>A parallelogram is a four-sided shape with opposite sides parallel; here it refers to the rectangular sections of the square.</note> *a.b.e.f, e.f.g.h, and g.h.c.d. Then let the middle one, e.f.g.h, be divided into two: e.f.q.k and q.k.g.h, in such a way that e-q is the sixth part of the whole a-c, and the same for q-g. This done, we shall draw from angle a the line a-l, so that it cuts c-d into two equal parts at point l; thus c-l will be the full half of c-d, and also of the side a-c; and the same for l-d. And let g-h be divided into g-o and o-h. Here g-o shall be the third part of a-c, and o-h shall be two-thirds. Likewise, q-k shall be divided into q-n and n-k, of which q-n contains the fourth part of a-c, and n-k three-fourths. Finally, let e-f be divided into e-m and m-f, such that e-m contains the sixth part, and m-f five-sixths of a-c. I say now, that among these parts of e-f, q-k, g-h, and c-d—created by the segments of the line a-l—and the side a-b, we will find the forms of all the musical Consonances.* <note>In this context, "form" refers to the mathematical ratio that defines the interval.</note> *Because a-b is to c-l as <term>Dupla (2:1)</term>; and since the Double ratio, by definition, is the form of the <term>Diapason (Octave)</term>, it follows that a-b and c-l are the form of the Diapason. But because a-b contains o-h plus its half, by definition, these are in <term>Sesquialtera (3:2)</term> proportion. And since the Sesquialtera, by definition, is the form of the <term>Diapente (Fifth)</term>, then a-b and o-h contain the Diapente. Furthermore, because a-b contains n-l once plus a third of it, a-b and n-l contain the <term>Sesquiterza (4:3)</term>; and this proportion being the form of the <term>Diatessaron (Fourth)</term>, it follows that a-b and n-l are the form of the Diatessaron. Moreover, m-f and o-h are in <term>Sesquiquarta (5:4)</term> proportion, because m-f contains o-h plus its fourth part; and since the Sesquiquarta is the form of the <term>Ditono (Major Third)</term>, it follows that m-f and o-h are the form of the Ditono. Beyond this, because a-b contains m-f plus a fifth part of it, I say by definition that a-b and m-f are <term>Sesquiquinta (6:5)</term>. Since this proportion is the form of the <term>Semiditono (Minor Third)</term>, consequently a-b and m-f come to be the form of this consonant interval. And because n-k contains o-h with an eighth part of it, I say that n-k and o-h are <term>Sesquiottava (9:8)</term>. Since, by the ninth [proposition] of this book, the Sesquiottava is the form of the <term>Major Tone</term>, we shall say that n-k and o-h contain the form of this Tone. Finally (as I do not wish to waste more time demonstrating everything that could be demonstrated), because m-f contains n-k with a ninth part of it, I say m-f and n-k are <term>Sesquinona (10:9)</term>. But the Sesquinona, by the same proposed ninth proposition, is the form of the <term>Minor Tone</term>; therefore m-f and n-k are the form of the Minor Tone. And this is all that, in short, I wished to say and demonstrate to you. This I could also easily demonstrate to you, but so as not to be long-winded, I will leave this task to the rest of you.*

...little: however, listen to the demonstration, which will proceed in this way. That interval, of which the greater term contains the lesser once plus one <term>Aliquot part</term> <note>An aliquot part is a portion of a number that divides it exactly without leaving a remainder; for example, 1 is an aliquot part of 15.</note>: by yesterday's fifth definition: is <term>Superparticular</term> <note>original: "Superparticolare"; a mathematical ratio where the numerator is exactly one more than the denominator (n+1)/n. These were considered the most "natural" ratios in Renaissance music theory.</note>. But the <term>Sesquiquintodecimal</term> <note>The ratio 16:15.</note> is subject to such a law: because the greater term, which is 16, contains the lesser, which is 15, one time, and furthermore its fifteenth part, which is called an Aliquot part. # PROPOSITION XVII.

->The interval of the Minor Semitone is contained by the ratio of twenty-five to twenty-four (Sesquiventesima quarta).<-

Wherefore I say: the interval of the <term>Ditone</term> <note>A Major Third, represented by the ratio 5:4.</note> is contained by the <term>sesquiquartal</term> ratio, and that of the <term>semiditone</term> <note>A Minor Third, represented by the ratio 6:5.</note> by the <term>Sesquiquintal</term> ratio. Similarly, that interval by which the Ditone exceeds the Semiditone is, by definition, the **Minor Semitone**. But the interval by which the sesquiquartal ratio [5:4] surpasses the sesquiquintal [6:5]—according to yesterday’s twenty-ninth proposition—is the difference found between these two ratios. Therefore, such an interval is the difference found between the Ditone and the Semiditone. And because such a difference is the <term>Sesquiventesima quarta</term> <note>The ratio 25:24; mathematically, (5/4) divided by (6/5) equals 25/24.</note> interval, we conclude that the Minor Semitone is contained by said ratio, as was required to be demonstrated. And to this I wish us to add, in order to maintain the order kept in the others, that:

# PROPOSITION XVIII.

->The interval of the Minor Semitone is placed among the Superparticulars.<-

To demonstrate this, I wish to tell you briefly: that by the fifth definition of the past day, that ratio is Superparticular which has its greater term in such a way that it contains the lesser plus one Aliquot part of it. And because the <term>Sesquiventesima quarta</term> is of such a nature—since its greater term, which is 25, contains the lesser, which is 24, one time and one twenty-fourth part of it—I say that the Sesquiventesima quarta is contained within the genus of ratios among the Superparticular intervals. But such a ratio, according to the preceding [proposition], is the form or interval of the **Minor Semitone**. Therefore, such an interval is placed among the Superparticulars. And this is what, briefly and succinctly—so as not to multiply words—I wished to demonstrate to you. ADRIANO: This matter is settled; now it is time for another. GIOSEFFO: So it shall be; therefore, listen.

## If the major semitone is added to the minor semitone: the result will be a minor tone.

## PROPOSITION XX.

### The Comma is contained by the sesquioctagesimal ratio among the superparticulars.

**Adrian:** This proposition has two parts, from what can be seen. First, you wish to demonstrate that the <term>Comma</term> <note>A very small musical interval representing the difference between two larger intervals, such as the Major and Minor Tone.</note> takes its form from the sesquioctagesimal ratio <note>The ratio 81:80.</note>; then you wish to demonstrate that this ratio is placed among the <term>Superparticulars</term> <note>A class of mathematical ratios where the larger number contains the smaller number exactly once, plus one part (e.g., 3:2, 9:8, 81:80).</note>. Therefore, I believe you will provide two demonstrations.

**Gioseffo:** That is exactly what I intend to do. To begin with the first part, I say: By the thirty-first proposition from yesterday, it was concluded that if one wishes to subtract a <term>sesquinonal</term> <note>The ratio 10:9, representing the Minor Tone.</note> ratio from a <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>The ratio 9:8, representing the Major Tone.</note> ratio, the result will be a <term>sesquioctagesimal</term> <note>The ratio 81:80.</note> ratio. And by the corollary of that same proposition, we have established that such an interval is the difference found between the sesquioctave and the sesquinonal. 

Now, the form of the **Major Tone**, according to the ninth proposition of this book, is the sesquioctave (9:8); and that of the **Minor Tone**, by the same proposition, is the sesquinonal (10:9). Since the Comma, by today’s twenty-fifth definition, is that interval by which the Major Tone exceeds the Minor Tone, it follows that because the sesquioctagesimal ratio (81:80) is the form of that difference, the Comma must be contained by the sesquioctagesimal ratio. 

Furthermore, because its larger term, which is 81, contains the smaller term, which is 80, one time plus one eightieth part (which is an <term>aliquot part</term> <note>A part that is contained an exact number of times in a whole; in this case, 1 is 1/80th of 80.</note>), it follows—by the definition of Superparticulars, which states that a superparticular interval is one in which the larger term contains the smaller once plus one aliquot part—that since the sesquioctagesimal interval fits these conditions, it is placed among the Superparticulars. And this is all that I needed to demonstrate to you according to the proposition.

**Francesco:** These things are so clear that no opposition can be found against them. But since we are discussing the Comma, tell me truly: is it possible to know the exact quantity of Commas contained within the Tones and Semitones you have shown us? And if it cannot be known, I pray you take the trouble to demonstrate the truth of this matter to us, if it can be done, so that you may remove all doubt from our minds.

**Gioseffo:** This can be demonstrated very well, and I wish to satisfy you, to show you that what I have said in my <margin>Part 2, chapter 4.</margin> *Institutions* <note>original: "Istitutioni"; Zarlino's own famous treatise, *Le Istitutioni harmoniche*.</note> regarding this subject is true. However, our Comma is very different from that of the Ancients, as I declared to you above in today’s twenty-sixth definition; just as all those intervals smaller than the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>A perfect fourth.</note> (except for the Major Tone) were considered dissonant by them. <header>Discourse</header>

## PROPOSAL XXI.

# The sesquioctave Tone is greater than nine Commas and less than ten.

---

<margin>
In the third book of *Music*, chapter 15. <note>original: "Musicæ libro. 3. cap 15." Referring to Boethius’s *De institutione musica*, the standard medieval music theory textbook.</note>
</margin>
**ADRIAN:** It seems to me, if I remember correctly, that <term>Boethius</term> <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works on music theory were foundational for the Renaissance.</note> wants this Tone to be less than nine Commas and more than eight. Thus, one can see that in this matter you disagree with him greatly; from where does this disagreement arise, if you please? **GIOSEFFO:** It arises because the Comma of Boethius is larger than ours. This is because the <term>sesquioctagesimal</term> <note>The ratio 81:80, also known as the Syntonic Comma.</note> ratio is smaller than the **super-7153-partient-524288** <note>The Pythagorean Comma, which is the ratio 531,441:524,288. It is mathematically larger than Zarlino's comma.</note>, which is the form of the true <term>Pythagorean Comma</term>. But coming to the demonstration, I say: Let **a** and **b** be the ratio of the Tone, proposed in its lowest and radical terms. And let **c** and **d** be the Comma, contained in its lowest terms or numbers. I first multiply **a** by **c** and by **d**: from which come **e** and **f**. Then I multiply **c** by **b**, and let the product be **g**. I say now that **e** and **f** represent the interval of the Comma: because every number (by the **Fifth Axiom**) <note>Referring to a common notion in Euclidean geometry: if equals are multiplied by equals, the results are equal; here applied to ratios where multiplying terms by the same number preserves the proportion.</note> multiplied by two others, whichever they may be, produces a ratio similar to that which was contained between the first two numbers. Therefore, since **c** and **d** were multiplied by **a**, there is no doubt that between **e** and **f** there is that same ratio found between **c** and **d**. I say the same for **e** and **g**: because **a** and **b** are multiplied by **c**; hence, just as between **a** and **b** one finds the ratio of the Tone, so that same ratio is found, by the said Common Opinion or Axiom, between **e** and **g**. Having done this, I multiply **c** by **e**, and **d** by **f**, and from this spring **h** and **i**. Similarly, I multiply **c** by **g**, and from it comes **K**. I say now that **h** and **i** represent the quantity of two Commas: that is, the one contained between **c** and **d**, and the one comprised between **e** and **f**; and **h** and **K** represent the Tone. Again, I multiply **c** by **h**, and **d** by **i**, and from this result **l** and **m**: which are three Commas added together; and I similarly multiply **c** by **K**, and from it comes **n**. Therefore I say, by the named Fifth Axiom, that **l** and **n** represent the interval of the Tone. I multiply again **c** by **l**, and **d** by **m**: and from this spring **o** and **p**, which for the reasons stated, contains four Commas; and **c** by **n**, and from it comes **q**, which with **o** makes, for the reasons adduced, the interval of the Tone. Once more I multiply **c** by **o**, and **d** by **p**, and from this result **r** and **s**, which contain five Commas; and **c** by **q**, and there is born **t**, which with **r** similarly contains the said Tone, as I could declare to you again; but, in order not to be long-winded, I leave that aside, as it is by now a manifest thing to you. Further on: I multiply **c** by **r**, and **d** by **s**, and also **c** by **t**, and there come **u**, **x**, and **y**, so that between **u** and **x** six Commas are added together, and between **u** and **y** the Tone is contained. Starting again, having done this, I multiply **c** by **u**, and **d** by **x**: and there come **Z** and **A**, which contain seven Commas; and I multiply **c** by **y**, and the product is **B**, which with **Z** contains the interval of the Tone. I keep this same order, multiplying once more **c** by **Z**, and **d** by **A**, and **c** by **B**: and there come **C**, **D**, and **E**. Therefore I say that **C** and **D** contain eight Commas, and **C** and **E** the Tone. Still in the same way, I multiply **c** by **C**, and **d** by **D**, and from it results **F** and **G**, which contain nine Commas; and again **c** by **E**, and there is born **H**, which together with **F** likewise contains the Tone. Up to here, you see clearly that the Tone is greater than nine Commas. For if one compares the number **F** to the number **G**, and again the same **F** to the number **H**, since **G** is a larger number than **H**, there is no doubt that (by the thirty-sixth rule of the first book) the ratio of **F** to **G** will be smaller than that of **F** to **H**. Therefore, since **F** to **G** is the interval containing nine Commas, and **F** to **H** is the interval of the sesquioctave Tone or Major Tone, it follows without any doubt that the Major Tone exceeds the number of nine Commas, as the proposal says. But to demonstrate to you that it is less than ten: I multiply again **c** by **F** and **d** by **G**, from which come **I** and **K**, which contain ten Commas. Therefore I also multiply **c** by **H**, and from it is born **L**, which with **I** similarly, for the reasons adduced other times, contains the named Tone. See now how the matter goes...

Therefore, the proportions of the Schisma and the Diaschisma are not known and rational, but rather unknown and irrational: as I was meant to demonstrate to you. From which is drawn this Corollary.

->COROLLARY.<-

From which it arises that of those proportions which do not have in their <term>Roots</term> <note>The lowest terms of a mathematical ratio (e.g., 3:2 is the root of 6:4).</note> a larger term that is a <term>Square number</term> and a smaller term that is <term>Unity</term> <note>The number 1.</note>: the proportions of its divisions are unknown and irrational.

### PROPOSITION XXVI.

## The Semiditone contains one Tone and one Semitone, both of which are Major.

*According to today's twentieth definition, the <term>Major Tone</term> <note>The interval of a 9:8 ratio.</note> is that interval by which the <term>Diapente</term> <note>The Perfect Fifth (ratio 3:2).</note> exceeds the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>The Perfect Fourth (ratio 4:3).</note>. Therefore, the Diapente is larger than the Diatessaron by one Major Tone. Furthermore, by the twenty-second definition: the <term>Major Semitone</term> <note>The interval of a 16:15 ratio.</note> is that interval by which the Diatessaron is larger than the <term>Ditone</term> <note>The Major Third (ratio 5:4), literally "two tones."</note>. Therefore, the Diatessaron exceeds the Ditone by one Major Semitone. But because the Diapente exceeds the Diatessaron by a Major Tone, and the Diatessaron exceeds the Ditone by a Major Semitone, therefore the Diapente is larger than the Ditone by one Major Tone and one Major Semitone. However, by the sixth proposition of this book, it has been demonstrated that the Ditone and the <term>Semiditone</term> <note>The Minor Third (ratio 6:5).</note> arise from the <term>Harmonic Division</term> <note>A mathematical method of dividing a string or ratio so that the resulting parts create harmonious intervals.</note> made of the Diapente. Since the Ditone is one part of such a division, it follows that the Major Tone and the Major Semitone are parts of the Semiditone, which is the other part of that division. And thus the Semiditone contains one Tone and one Semitone, both of which are Major, as the proposition says, and as I had to demonstrate to you. But let us pass on to demonstrate that which follows.*

### PROPOSITION XXVII.

## The Ditone contains two Tones, one Major and the other Minor.

<sig>FRANCESCO</sig>

### PROPOSITION XXVIII.

## The Fourth contains two Tones: that is, the Major and the Minor, along with the Major Semitone.

From the preceding it is manifest that the Major Third contains two Tones, one of which is the major and the other is the minor. ### PROPOSITION XXIX.

## Three Major Tones, or rather two Major and one Minor, surpass the Fourth.

Three Tones are the same as that interval which we call the <term>Tritone</term> <note>original: "Tritono"; an interval consisting of three whole tones, notorious in early music for its dissonance.</note>. And this can be understood from the name: whether they are all three Major, or two Major and one Minor; since between the former and the latter there is no difference other than that of a <term>Comma</term> <note>original: "Comma"; the tiny mathematical difference between two types of whole steps (9:8 and 10:9) in Just Intonation tuning.</note>, which matters little. And although this is manifest from the preceding [proposition]—given that one Major Tone and one Minor, with one <term>Major Semitone</term> <note>original: "maggior Semituono"; a half-step used in Renaissance tuning systems.</note> are equal to the <term>Fourth</term> <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>; and three Tones are larger than the three named intervals—nevertheless, I want us to demonstrate this in another way.

I say then first: By the thirty-fifth [proposition] of the first discourse, it was demonstrated that three <term>Sesquioctave</term> <note>original: "Sesquiottaui"; the ratio 9:8, representing a Major Tone.</note> intervals are more than one <term>Sesquitertial</term> <note>original: "Sesquiterzo"; the ratio 4:3, representing a Fourth.</note> interval. But, by the ninth [proposition] of today, three Sesquioctaves are three Major Tones; and by the tenth definition, the Sesquitertial interval is the form of the Fourth; therefore, three Major Tones, or the Tritone as you wish to call it, exceed the consonance of the Fourth, according to the purpose, as I first ought to have demonstrated to you.

Next: because the Major Tone exceeds the Minor by one Comma, according to the twenty-fifth definition reversed; therefore I say, two Major Tones and one Minor are smaller than three Major Tones by the interval of one Comma. This interval, however, is neither larger than a <term>Minor Semitone</term>, nor smaller than a Major one, nor even equal to it; as can be understood from the fifteenth, seventeenth, and nineteenth propositions of today, and also from the seventh <term>Axiom</term> <note>original: "Dignità"; used here in the Euclidean sense of a self-evident principle.</note> of yesterday. Therefore, two Major Tones and one Minor exceed the consonance of the Fourth, as I ought to have demonstrated to you.

Further still: by the preceding [proposition] I have shown that the Fourth contains two Tones—one Major and the other Minor—and one Major Semitone. And by the twenty-fifth definition of this [work] reversed, the Major Tone exceeds the Minor by one Comma; therefore two Tones, one Major and the other Minor, are smaller than two Major [Tones] by one Comma. Besides this: by the twenty-third proposition of today, the Major Semitone is less than six and more than five Commas; and by the twenty-first, the Major Tone is less than ten and more than nine; therefore the Tone exceeds the Semitone by four Commas. 

And because the second Tone of the three Major ones exceeds the second and Minor [Tone] of the Fourth by one Comma, and similarly, because the third of the three Major ones exceeds the Major Semitone of the Fourth by four Commas; therefore one Major Tone, one Minor Tone, and one Major Semitone are smaller than three Major Tones by the quantity of five Commas. Thus, three Major Tones exceed the Fourth, according to the purpose, as I secondly ought to have demonstrated to you.

CLAUDIO: These demonstrations have been very beautiful, but I especially liked this last one concerning the Commas. However, what will come after this?

The <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapente"; an interval spanning five notes of a scale, such as C to G.</note> contains two Major Tones, one Minor, and one Major Semitone. This can also be demonstrated by another means. The sixth [proposition] of this book shows that the <term>Major Third</term> <note>original: "Ditono"; literally "two tones."</note> and the <term>Minor Third</term> <note>original: "semiditono"; literally "half-two-tones."</note> arise from the harmonic division of the Fifth. Thus, the Major Third and the Minor Third, by way of their <term>Corollary</term> <note>a logical deduction that follows naturally from a proven proposition.</note>, are integral parts of that same Fifth. But according to the twenty-sixth [proposition], the Minor Third contains one Major Tone and one Major Semitone; and according to the twenty-seventh, the Major Third contains one Major Tone and one Minor Tone. Therefore, the Fifth contains two Major Tones and one Minor, along with one Major Semitone, according to the proposition. 

This can also be demonstrated in another way, by saying: if from a <term>Sesquialter</term> <note>the 3:2 ratio, representing the Fifth.</note> interval—as per yesterday's twenty-sixth proposition—one removes a <term>Sesquitertial</term> <note>the 4:3 ratio, representing the Fourth.</note>, the resulting interval will be a <term>Sesquioctave</term> <note>the 9:8 ratio, representing a Major Tone.</note>. But according to the definitions given above, the Sesquialter is the Fifth, the <term>Fourth</term> <note>original: "Diateffaron"</note> is the Sesquitertial, and the Sesquioctave is the form of the Major Tone (per the ninth proposition demonstrated to you above). Therefore, when the Fourth is removed from the Fifth, the remainder is the Major Tone. Furthermore: according to the twenty-eighth [proposition] of this book, the Fourth contains two Tones—one Major and the other Minor—along with a Major Semitone. But these three intervals, added to another Major Tone (by which the Fifth exceeds the Fourth), make two Major Tones and one Minor, with one Major Semitone. Thus, the Fifth comes to contain two Major Tones, one Minor, and also a Major Semitone, as the proposition states and as I was to demonstrate.

### COROLLARY I.

->Thus it follows that when the Major Tone is taken from the Fifth, the Fourth remains; and when the Fourth is taken from the Fifth, the Major Tone remains.<-

For if the Fifth contains two Major Tones, one Minor, and one Major Semitone (as we have demonstrated), there is no doubt that by taking away one Major Tone, the remainder is two Tones—one Major and the other Minor—with one Major Semitone. These, as we demonstrated in the twenty-eighth [proposition] above, are contained within the Fourth. Therefore, when the Major Tone is removed from the Fifth, the Fourth remains. But since this Fifth contains two Major Tones, one Minor, and the Major Semitone, once the Fourth (which contains the Major Tone, the Minor, and the Major Semitone) is removed from the Fifth, there remains—according to the second part of the Corollary—the Major Tone. And so you can see that everything placed in the Corollary proves to be true. 

ADRI. Everything is fine and good; I like it all, and you have satisfied me greatly; indeed, you have added the Corollary, which I was not expecting. 

FRAN. I now understand the utility gathered from these Corollaries—something I did not see before. But tell me, please: what does "Corollary" mean properly? 

GIO S. This is called <term>Porisma</term> <note>original Greek: "Πόρισμα"; a deduction or "gain."</note> by the Greeks, as if to say "acquired" or "thought of." This is because it arises (as Proclus says regarding the first Proposition of Euclid's *Elements* in the Third Book) like another theorem, even though we did not originally propose to demonstrate it. It is therefore added to a demonstration already made, which generates knowledge like a certain gain made beyond the original purpose. And although there are two types of such Corollaries, I do not wish to waste time explaining this to you, as it is not of great importance. 

FRAN. You do well; but from what I have understood, I believe this is also true: that

->From which it arises, that the Major Sixth exceeds the<-

*We come to the rest of the proposition. If we again take the lowest terms of the <term>Major Semitone</term> <note>ratio 16:15</note>, which are i and k, and multiply a by i, and b by k, we will have l and m. Therefore, when the Major Semitone is added to the Fifth, the Minor Sixth is born, as the proposition says. But if we again take I and K, the root terms of the <term>Minor Third</term> <note>original: "Semiditono"</note>, and multiply A by I and B by K, there will result without any doubt L and M, which will contain the <term>Sesquiterza</term> <note>4:3</note> and <term>Sesquiquinta</term> <note>6:5</note> proportions. Wherefore I say that L and M will similarly give us the Minor Sixth, as can be known from N and O, which are the root terms of L and M obtained by dividing L and M by three <note>original: "Ternario"</note>. Because they contain the Super-tripartient Fifth, which, by the named eighteenth definition, is the form of the said Sixth. These terms, since they can be mediated by Q (as seen between P, Q, and R), give us a manifest sign that all that has been said is true: because between P and Q is the form of the Fourth, and between Q and R that of the Minor Third. From the conjunction of the Minor Third, therefore, with the Fourth, the Minor Sixth is born, as the proposition says. And this is everything I had to demonstrate to you.*

### PROPOSITION XXXVI.

**The Minor Hexachord contains two Major Tones, one Minor, and two Major Semitones.**

<image-desc>Decorative square drop cap initial 'E' with foliage and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>*And this is manifested in such a way: The <term>Minor Hexachord</term> <note>A minor sixth interval.</note>, by the thirty-fourth [proposition] of today, is born from the conjunction of the Major Semitone with the Diapente. *Furthermore: the aforementioned thirty-fourth [proposition] demonstrates that from the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>The perfect fourth, ratio 4:3.</note> and from the <term>Semiditono</term> <note>The minor third, ratio 6:5.</note> placed together, the named Hexachord is made. Thus, the Minor Hexachord contains two Major Tones, one Minor, and two Major Semitones, as the proposal says, and as I had to demonstrate to you.*

**The Major Hexachord contains two Major Tones, two Minor, with one Major Semitone.**

*The <term>Major Hexachord</term> <note>The major sixth, which Zarlino defines here by its component parts.</note>, according to today's Thirty-fourth proposition, arises from the conjunction of the <term>Major Tone</term> <note>The ratio 9:8.</note> with the <term>Diapente</term> <note>The perfect fifth, ratio 3:2.</note>. Therefore, the Major Hexachord contains two Major Tones, two Minor Tones, and one Major Semitone. Similarly: according to the aforementioned Thirty-fourth proposition, the Major Hexachord arises from the addition of the <term>Ditono</term> <note>The major third, ratio 5:4.</note> to the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>The perfect fourth, ratio 4:3.</note>. But according to the Twenty-eighth proposition, the Diatessaron contains one Major Tone, one Minor Tone, and one Major Semitone. And the Ditono, according to the Twenty-seventh, contains one Major Tone and one Minor Tone. Thus, the Major Hexachord contains two Major Tones, two Minor Tones, along with one Major Semitone, just as the proposal states. And this is what I wished to demonstrate to you.* DESI. *This cannot be denied; therefore, you may be content to move further ahead.* GIOS. *Having now dispatched those intervals that are smaller than the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The octave, ratio 2:1.</note>, I shall now come to treat the Octave itself. And because many of the Ancients held that it contains six <term>Sesquioctave</term> <note>The ratio 9:8, which defines a Major Tone.</note> tones, I wish to demonstrate to you that this is impossible—even though this fact is not accepted as true by others. Whence I shall propose to demonstrate to you that:*

### PROPOSITION XXXVIII.

->The Diapason is smaller than six Major Tones, and larger than five.<-

*I will settle this in few words. You know that, by the penultimate proposition of yesterday’s discussion, five Sesquioctave intervals joined together are smaller than one <term>Duplo</term> <note>The "double" ratio 2:1, which forms the octave.</note> interval. And by the last proposition, six are even larger than that same Duplo. And you know very well that the Duplo is the form of the Diapason, and the Sesquioctave is the form of the Major Tone. Whence five Major Tones are less than a Diapason, and six surpass it. And because in fact it is so, the Diapason, according to the proposal, is smaller than six Major Tones and larger than five, as I had to demonstrate to you.* ADRI. *Demonstrate to us also, according to the truth, how many Tones and how many Semitones it contains.* GIOS. *This is very necessary; therefore I tell you that:*

### PROPOSITION XXXIX.

->The Diapason contains three Major Tones, two Minor Tones, and two Major Semitones.<-

*And because you know—if you remember—that the Diapente and the Diatessaron added together, by the fourth proposition of today, make the consonance of the Diapason. And I have demonstrated to you, by the Twenty-eighth proposition, that the Diatessaron contains one Major Tone and one Minor Tone, with one Major Semitone. And by the Thirtieth it was concluded that the Diapente contains two Major Tones, one Minor Tone, and one Major Semitone. All of these gathered together make three Major Tones, two Minor Tones, with two Major Semitones. Therefore, the Diapason contains three Major Tones, two Minor Tones, with two Major Semitones.*

sounds: according to what I had to demonstrate. Now I want to clarify a fine difficulty, and reconcile (if I can) two contrary opinions from two very distinguished factions in Music. Therefore listen to me, for I want to demonstrate to you together that:

---

### PROPOSAL XL.

## The <term>Diapason-diatessaron</term> <note>The interval of an octave plus a perfect fourth, equivalent to a compound eleventh.</note> is not a consonance Properly so-called: but is Commonly so-called.

<margin>
Ptolemy, *Harmonics*, Book 1, Ch. 6. 
Boethius, *Music*, Book 5, Ch. 8.
</margin>
DESI. Some have held that this interval is dissonant, and you want to prove the contrary, from what I see. Where does this disagreement arise? GIOS. You shall see. <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), an influential Greco-Roman mathematician and astronomer who wrote extensively on music theory.</note>—and after him many others—holds this conclusion to be true, against the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed musical intervals must be defined by simple mathematical ratios.</note>: that the Diapason-diatessaron is a consonance. And although it seems to some that Ptolemy has reason on his side because of what he adduces in his favor, nevertheless the Pythagoreans are not in the wrong either. Ptolemy offered this reason: When the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The octave (ratio 2:1).</note> consonance has its containing sounds well tuned, they are no different in virtue and power from a single sound. Whence, when it is applied to whatever simple interval smaller than itself, it preserves that species whole and inviolate, just as the <term>Denary</term> <note>The number ten.</note> preserves within itself the other numbers that are smaller than it. For this reason, just as when some sound is added to the Diapason from the lower or the higher part, a certain suitability and power to move the <term>ear</term> <note>Original: "V dito," a common early printing variation of "udito" (hearing/ear).</note> is found between it and that which is closest to it, so too does such suitability and power appear between it and the sound further away. Wherefore the <term>Diapente</term> <note>The perfect fifth (ratio 3:2).</note> and the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>The perfect fourth (ratio 4:3).</note> consonances have by themselves that sonority in that suitability from that part of the Diapason which is closest to them; hence the ear deservedly receives the <term>Diapason-diapente</term> <note>An octave plus a fifth (a twelfth).</note> or the Diapason-diatessaron in the same way that it receives the Diapente or the Diatessaron when placed alone and by themselves. Therefore, for this reason it follows infallibly: that since the Diapente is a consonance, and also the Diatessaron, then the Diapason-diapente and the Diapason-diatessaron must also be consonances, and each of these two is received by the ear in the same way as the Diapente and the Diatessaron are received when each is placed alone; as clearly appears through experience. Finally, he concludes that both of these named compound intervals are consonant. On the other side, the Pythagoreans adduced in their favor this reason, which they held to be true—even most true: that every consonance arises either from the <term>Multiple</term> <note>A ratio where the larger number is a multiple of the smaller, like 2:1 or 3:1.</note> or from the <term>Superparticular</term> <note>A ratio where the larger number is exactly one more than the smaller, like 3:2 or 4:3.</note> genus, and from no other category; and that since the Diapason-diatessaron is neither Multiple nor Superparticular, it could by no means be a consonance. But this would conclude excellently if it were simply true that no other consonances were found except those arising from the two named genera, and those "Properly so-called." We see, however, in fact that it is otherwise, just as we have been certified until now by experience and science. And although these two opinions are contrary, they can nevertheless be easily reconciled by considering what I said in the First and Second definitions today concerning Consonances Properly so-called and those commonly so-called, and also what I said yesterday regarding the locations or positions of consonances. For everything consists in these two things, if you remember them. ADRI. We remember them very well. GIOS. Therefore: even if some interval added to the extremes of the Diapason (as Ptolemy said) makes no variety of sound, in such a way that it is heard differently from the first sound of the added interval—as if the Diatessaron added to the Diapason does not vary the resulting sounds so much that they seem like another consonance, but rather similar to the Diatessaron which is added—nevertheless one cannot say that such a compound is that same simple interval that existed before it was accompanied by the Diapason. Just as one cannot say with truth that the number twelve is the same number as two, simply because the <term>Binary</term> <note>The number two.</note> is accompanied by the Denary;

<vocab>Tolomeo: Ptolemy. Pitagorici: Pythagoreans. Diapaſon diateſſaron: Octave plus a fourth. Diapente: Perfect fifth. conſonanza: consonance. Molteplice: Multiple ratio. Superparticolare: Superparticular ratio. Binario: Two. Denario: Ten.</vocab>

<meta>This page continues Gioseffo Zarlino's explanation of musical intervals, specifically focusing on the Diapason-diatessaron (the interval of an eleventh). He is addressing a historical dispute between the followers of Pythagoras and the theorist Ptolemy.</meta>

<page-num>142</page-num>
<header>Discussion</header>

Since even if both one and the other are even numbers, it cannot be said that the **number two** <note>original: *Binario*</note> is of the same nature as the **number twelve** <note>original: *Duodenario*</note>, nor that it has those same properties. Nor can one say without error that since the **Diapason-diatessaron** <note>The interval of an eleventh, composed of an octave (diapason) and a fourth (diatessaron).</note> is composed of the Diapason and the Diatessaron—both simple consonances—that such a compound interval is "simply consonant" or "simply dissonant." Rather, one can well say that it necessarily falls into the number of those intervals counted between the two named extremes: that is, among those intervals we have called **Commonly-called consonances**. For if we regard the ratio that arises from the joining of the two named intervals, we will find that it will be the **double superbipartient-third** <note>The ratio 8:3. In Zarlino's system, this is "double" because 8 contains 3 twice (6), with 2 left over—and 2 is two-thirds of 3 (superbipartient-third).</note>, contained between 8 and 3. This ratio is neither **Multiple** <note>A ratio like 2:1 or 3:1 where the larger number is a perfect multiple of the smaller.</note> nor **Superparticular** <note>A ratio like 3:2 or 4:3 where the larger number is the smaller number plus one part (e.g., 3 is 2+1).</note>. Therefore, it cannot be placed among those consonances contained in the first order—called **Properly-called**—because its mathematical form is not located among the parts of the **Senario** <note>The numbers 1 through 6. Zarlino argued that only ratios derived from these first six numbers were "proper" or "perfect" consonances.</note>, as was demonstrated in the First Definition. For this reason, it can by no means be a "Properly-called" consonance. And in this, one may agree with the **Pythagoreans**. 

But that it is not a consonance of the second kind—**Commonly-called**—this cannot and will never be denied if one pays attention to what was said in the Second Definition. Therefore, what **Ptolemy** has said and concluded will not have been said or concluded out of place. It is quite true that if one wanted to say Ptolemy's intention was that this compound interval is a "Properly-called" consonance, and the Pythagoreans' intention was that it is a "dissonant interval," this would be false; it would conflict with our principles that we established at the beginning of this discussion, and with truth itself. One must, therefore, hold with Ptolemy: that adding the fourth to the octave creates a consonance between the outer notes—though not a "Properly-called" one, but rather a "Commonly-called" one. And with the Pythagoreans: that the Diapason-diatessaron is not, and cannot be, a consonance of the first kind. In this way, we reconcile the different opinions of these most excellent musicians so that they are not discordant with one another regarding the sensory experience, even though in their words they seem contrary to each other. And by this path, both shall be found to have spoken well. You have now heard what you must hold to understand how these two opinions agree. And if you have anything to say to me on this, say it before I go any further.

**ADRIANO.** I do not wish to say anything else to you, except that you have now clarified a doubt for me without me even asking it—one which was giving me much trouble: that the Pythagoreans granted Ptolemy his premise but denied his conclusion. However, this distinction of yours that you have made, in placing these "middle intervals" between those "Properly-called consonances" and the "dissonances," settles everything. Thus, one can harmonize these flutes <note>An idiom meaning "reconcile these viewpoints."</note> very well and say: that the Pythagoreans, considering such an addition in terms of its proximity to dissonance, said it was dissonant; and that Ptolemy, considering it insofar as it was (so to speak) supported by the octave and approached consonance, said it was consonant—considering the whole matter both by the sense of hearing and by reason.

**GIOSEPFO.** That is exactly how the matter stands, as you see, Sir.

**ADRIANO.** I pray you then to continue, since from you I am learning many things worthy of great consideration, which I have never heard from others.

**GIOSEPFO.** Having understood, then, in what manner these two contrary opinions can be reconciled, I will proceed to demonstrate what the Proposal says, and I will speak in this way: Let **a** and **b** be the radical terms of the ratio of the **Diapason** <note>2:1</note>, and **c** with **d** be the lowest numbers containing the ratio of the **Diatessaron** <note>4:3</note>. I multiply these two ratios together, following the second rule of the discussion we had yesterday, and the result is **e**, **f**, and **g**; that is, **e** and **f** are a **Double ratio** <note>2:1</note>, and **f** with **g** is a **Sesquitertia ratio** <note>4:3</note>. Thus I say: that **e** and **g** come to be composed of the Double **e-f** and the Sesquitertia **f-g**, and contain the Diapason and Diatessaron consonances. But because **e** and **g** is neither Multiple nor Superparticular—since it contains **g** twice and two of its third parts (whence it is called a **Double superbipartient-third**, contained in the fifth genus of ratios called **Multiple superpartient**) <note>The ratio is 8:3. Since 3 goes into 8 twice with 2 left over, it is "Multiple" (2x) and "Superpartient" (the remainder is more than 1).</note>—therefore, by the First Definition of this, the Diapason-diatessaron is not a "Properly-called" consonance. But by the Second, it is indeed "Commonly-called," as the Proposal says, and as I had to demonstrate to you.

### PROPOSITION XLI.

### The Octave-plus-fifth <term>Diapason diapente<gloss>The interval of a twelfth.</gloss></term> arises from the Octave and the Fifth joined together, and it contains five major Tones, three minor [Tones], and three major Semitones.

### PROPOSITION XLII.

> **The Double Octave <term>Disdiapason<gloss>An interval spanning two octaves, or a fifteenth.</gloss></term> arises from the Octave doubled, or rather from two Octaves added together; and it contains six major Tones, four minor [Tones], and four major Semitones.**

Because by the twenty-third [proposition] of the first day: a doubled "Double" interval <note>original: *interuallo Duplo*</note> constitutes the Quadruple <note>original: *Quadruplo*</note>. But according to the Definitions: the Double is the form of the Octave <term>Diapason<gloss>The 2:1 ratio.</gloss></term>, and the Quadruple is that of the Double Octave <term>Disdiapason<gloss>The 4:1 ratio.</gloss></term>. Therefore, the Octave doubled—or one Octave added to another—creates the Double Octave. And this concerns the first part of the proposition. But coming to the second [part], I say: the Double Octave being, by the seventh definition, a composite Consonance <term>Consonanza composta<gloss>An interval larger than an octave, viewed as a combination of smaller intervals.</gloss></term>—as its name says—made of two Octaves, or the Octave doubled; and the simple Octave containing (by today’s thirty-ninth [proposition]) three major Tones, two minor [Tones], with two major Semitones: it is necessary that the doubled [Octave] contains six major Tones, four minor [Tones], and four major Semitones: as was to be demonstrated to you. *DESIDERIO.* This cannot be denied: and I very much like those reasons that you state in the *Instructions* <note>Referring to *Le Istitutioni harmoniche*.</note> regarding this: that the Ancients—and especially the followers of Pythagoras <note>The Pythagoreans believed numbers and ratios were the foundation of the universe and initially limited "perfect" harmony to ratios within the number 4 (the *Tetraktys*).</note>—forbade going beyond the Quadruple, or beyond the Double Octave; wherefore they established that this interval should be the limit of the Consonances. However, as you all know, one can go further: which each of you does in your compositions, according to what little light I have on this matter. And I believe that you too, *Master Gioseffo*, will want to observe this custom; and that you will not want to go any further in these Demonstrations, so as not to exceed the Quadruple proportion or the Double Octave consonance, where finally, with God's help, you have arrived. *GIOSEFFO.* I am truly of this opinion, and there is no need to go further; but one can stay with these Propositions demonstrated until now: for although one could proceed further almost to infinity, nonetheless other Demonstrations are not as necessary as these are. Therefore, whenever you wish to go further, from those Demonstrations that I have placed before you until now, you can conveniently know for yourselves what you seek. Especially having discussed with you not only simple Consonances but also composite ones. Thus, by your good grace, I will conclude for this time. Tomorrow you will return again to this place, for I am about to tell you things that will please you. *CLAUDIO.* You are very right to rest, since you have been speaking for a long time. Therefore it is proper that silence be now placed upon this discussion. *ADRIANO.* I thought you had demonstrated everything that can be demonstrated regarding this matter; but from what I see, there still remains a good part to be demonstrated. I will therefore wait with great desire for tomorrow to come, so that I may hear what you have to treat. *GIOSEFFO.* We have yet to treat the most beautiful part, Sir: so do not be troubled, for tomorrow will come all too soon; then you will see that I am not deceiving you. But to finish it for now, remain all in peace. *Master Francesco*, let us go with God. *FRANCESCO.* Sir, be cheerful, for tomorrow we will come to visit you. *ADRIANO.* Please do so. *GIOSEFFO.* We shall. *DESIDERIO.* I am coming too. *CLAUDIO.* Nor do I want to be left behind. Farewell then, Sir. *ADRIANO.* Farewell, farewell.

<image-desc>Large woodcut decorative initial 'C' depicting a man in robes and a hat (likely a scholar or philosopher) seated in an outdoor setting, looking up and gesturing towards a crescent moon in the sky.</image-desc>

I BELIEVE that not a single day has passed since I saw that beautiful and true sentiment of Boethius: *That it is the mark of a most wretched and poor mind always to use things found by others, and never those that can be found oneself:* that I have not held this matter in my memory.
<margin>Metaphysics, Book 1, Chapter 1.</margin>
Thus, moved first by the natural appetite that men commonly have for knowledge: knowing that what was said by that great Philosopher—who for his excellence was called "Thrice Great"—is most true: *The greatest part of what we know is the smallest part of what we do not know.* <note>The "Thrice Great" refers to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and the "Hermetic" sciences.</note> Then, moved by that which remained fixed in my mind after having seen it: I gave myself to searching and seeing if, beyond the things said and shown by the ancient musicians, anything remained that could be newly discovered, which might bring some use to students of this <term>Science<gloss>The formal study of musical theory, which in the Renaissance was considered a mathematical science of "ratio and proportion."</gloss></term>. How well I have succeeded in this—after many long labors and varied, lengthy studies—I shall leave, without saying a word, to the judgment of those who (having an understanding of the matters of <term>Music<gloss>Specifically *musica speculativa* or the theoretical side of music.</gloss></term>) will deign to look upon my labors. For beyond what I have taken from the Ancients for the arrangement of those things I had to demonstrate, I have demonstrated and declared so many things that, if all those who have devoted and still devote their work to <term>Music</term> had toiled—and were still to toil—in the manner that I have, I believe that not much time would pass before this most worthy <term>Science</term> would achieve as much growth as any other has done, whatever it may be, that is comprised under the title of <term>Mathematics</term>, or under any other title. For my part, I have done my share: and God grant that the will may come to some noble spirit to bring to perfection what I have thus far (so to speak) sketched out; for then perhaps one might see that which will be of great contentment to those who are curious to know perfectly, and according to the truth, the matters of this <term>Science</term>. Since until now I have placed so many things at the beginning <note>original: *incapò*</note> that anyone who wishes to follow further may have the subject and matter to reason upon at length. But no more of this; for it is necessary to return to our purpose. Therefore I say: that the sun had already passed the meridian line by a twelfth part of its circle <note>Given a 24-hour cycle, a twelfth part of the circle indicates it is two hours past noon, or roughly 2:00 PM.</note> when each of us, hearing the signal for Vespers, without delaying a moment,

## POSTULATE II.

### When two or more strings are stretched over the same equal space, and tuned together in perfect unison: let them be regarded as, or let them function as, a single string.

*GIOSEFFO. Do you grant me this, or do you deny it?* 

*ADRIAN. This too is only right to grant you; since (as you declare in the **Institutions**) the **Unison** does not create a larger interval, but rather adds voice to voice, or sound to sound.*

*DESIDERIO. Just as adding water to water of the same quality does not create a mixture, but only multiplies that water—that is, the quantity becomes greater—so adding one sound to another equal sound does not change the primary quality, but multiplies the sounds and the voices.* 

*GIOSEFFO. You speak well, by my faith, and the comparison fits perfectly regarding the quality. Therefore we shall come to the next Postulate, which shall be this:*

its ratio. **ADRIAN.** *Move now to the Demonstration, which will be the Fifth thing.* <note>Referring to the fifth of the six parts of a mathematical proof: the "Apodeixis" or logical proof itself.</note> **GIOSEFFO.** *I shall; for without it, I would have accomplished nothing. Therefore, I say first: That interval in which the greater of two quantities contains the lesser plus one-eighth part of it—according to the Fifth definition of the First Discourse—is a <term>Sesquioctave</term> <note>original: "Sesquiottauo"; a ratio of 9:8 (one plus one-eighth).</note>. Next, I add: The whole space of string **a b** contains the space **c b** once plus one-eighth part of it; since **a c** is equal to one of its eighth parts. Thus, the ratio of space **a b** to space **c b** is Sesquioctave. Hence, by the first Postulate proposed to us a little while ago, the same ratio will exist between the sound of the whole string **a b** and the string **c b** as is found between the space **a b** and the space **c b**. And further, by the final Postulate: the ratio found between **a b** and **c b** in terms of space will be the same as that found between number and number—namely, between 9 and 8. Therefore, to add the final part, which is the Conclusion, I say: Since the Sesquioctave is the form of the Whole Tone, it follows that the Tone is contained between the strings **a b** and **b c**. And thus, upon a given string, we have placed the Whole Tone according to its ratio, as proposed; and this is what I was to demonstrate to you.* **ADRIAN.** *I had need of you mentioning those Six things again; for having now applied them to this musical proposition, they are so well fixed in my memory that they will never leave me. But it seems to me that this proposition was universal; nonetheless, you have applied it to the Major Tone <note>The "Major Tone" (9:8) is slightly larger than the "Minor Tone" (10:9).</note>, even though it could also be understood as the Minor. This surely carries some importance.* **GIOSEFFO.** *Note this well, so I do not have to repeat the name "Major" so many times: when in the future I name "the Tone" without adding "Major" or "Minor," you should always understand it by way of excellence to mean the Major, and not the Minor. When I mean the latter, I will always add the term "Minor" to distinguish them from one another.* **CLAUDIO.** *Pray, if it does not weary you, demonstrate to us in what manner.*

### COROLLARY.

**From this it follows, that the more intervals are multiplied by joining one to another toward the high pitch: the more they contain narrowed and smaller physical spaces. And the more they are placed before one another in the low pitch: the more the spaces are larger and wider.**

---

*And this is made manifest by today's Fourth Demand: that the Whole, compared to the Part, sounds lower; and the Part, compared to the Whole, sounds higher. Wherefore, if to the <term>Tone</term> <note>The Whole Tone</note>—which is undoubtedly placed between a b and c b—another Tone is added: the one that is added will undoubtedly be higher by the same proportion as that contained in the first. Thus, if the space c b were to be divided into nine equal parts: each of them would be smaller than the space c d, which is its eighth part. Because each of them is the ninth part, and is named by a larger number than the eighth. Therefore, each of the nine parts will be smaller than the space a c: since a c and c d are equal. And what I have said of one Tone can also be said of every other that might be added toward the high pitch. I do not wish, however, for you to restrict yourselves to believing that this Proposition is true only for the interval or space of the Tone: but I want you to know: that it is common to any other interval whatsoever, of any kind: whether large or small: provided that the same proportion is observed. ADRIANO: This matter is clear and carries no doubt with it. GIOSEFFO: It is therefore manifest that the more a Tone (or indeed any other interval of the same proportion) is added to another toward the high pitch, the more it contains narrowed and smaller spaces. Gioseffo Zarlino is explaining why a Whole Tone—defined by the ratio 9:8—cannot be split into two musically equal semitones by simply dividing the physical space on the string into two equal halves. This touches on the historical problem that a "half-step" is not a simple mathematical half of a whole step's length.</meta>

### PROPOSITION VI.

->**If a Whole Tone is divided into two equal parts at the midpoint of its extremes, it is not thereby divided into two proportional parts.**<-

DESIDERIO. What is the *middle* of the extremes?
GIOSEFFO. Now I will tell you. Let *ab* and *cb* be the interval of the <term>Whole Tone</term> <note>original: "Tuono"; the musical interval defined by the ratio 9:8</note> adjusted to its proportion: and let *ab* be divided (as was done in the preceding page) by *c. d. e. f. g. h. i. k.* into nine equal parts. I say that the middle of the extremes of the Tone, which are *ab* and *cb*, is that space found between *a* and *c*: even if it is divided into two equal parts, the Tone is not thereby divided into two proportional parts <note>In music theory, for two intervals to be "proportional" or "equal," their ratios must be identical. Zarlino is arguing that a physical midpoint does not create a musical midpoint.</note>.
DESIDERIO. So, you mean to infer that if the space *ac* is divided into two equal parts:

<image-desc>The page features two technical diagrams representing the mathematical or geometric division of a musical interval (the Whole Tone). The first diagram shows a horizontal bar (representing a string) divided into segments by vertical lines, labeled with letters a, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, k, b across the top and numbered 9 through 1 within the segments. The second diagram, directly below, shows a similar bar further subdivided into smaller intervals, labeled with letters like l, m, n, o, p, q, r, s, t, and numbered from 18 down to 1, demonstrating the doubling of the terms to find a midpoint.</image-desc>

*the Tone will not be partitioned into two equal proportional intervals.*
GIOSEFFO. So I say.
DESIDERIO. How is this possible?
GIOSEFFO. You shall see soon. But take note, so that you do not fall into error: I am speaking of dividing the entire proportion of the Tone <term>geometrically</term> <note>Finding a mean proportional, which would create two equal musical ratios</note> into two equal parts, and not its difference, or its extremes. For by performing the division of the difference in such a way, such a division is <term>arithmetic</term> <note>Dividing the physical length into equal parts (like 10 being the midpoint of 8 and 12)</note>, and not geometric; and thus the parts of the divisions are unequal in proportion rather than equal.
DESIDERIO. I understand you very well now, and I was greatly wondering about such a thing. But please, continue to tell us more, for this matter is now clear to me.
GIOSEFFO. Rather, I wish to demonstrate this thing to you minutely, to keep the pact I made with you.
DESIDERIO. I do not say this to interrupt you: for the demonstration of easy things ought to be as dear to us as that of difficult ones, since by their means we come to know them. For even if we know them without such means, we know them only in a certain way that is not properly "knowing," especially since we do not know them by their causes.
GIOSEFFO. Therefore, the line *ab* being divided into nine equal parts, and the extremes of the Tone being *ab* and *cb*: I say that if the space *ac* (which is the mean of these two extremes) is divided into two equal parts at point *l*, the Tone will not be divided into two proportional and equal parts. And that the sound <note>The pitch produced by the string lengths</note> *ab* to *lb* will not be equal in proportion to the sound *lb* to *cb*, I shall prove. I divide each of the other parts, or spaces, similarly into two equal parts at points *m. n. o. p. q. r. s. t.* Now it is manifest that the whole space *ab* is divided into eighteen equal parts: which are *al, lc, cm, md, dn, ne, eo, of, fp, pg, gq, qh, hr, ri, is, sk, kt, tb.* Therefore, by the preceding [proposition]: the proportion *ab* to *lb* <note>18:17</note> is smaller than *lb* to *cb* <note>17:16</note>. And the Tone being divided in this manner, it is not divided into two equal or proportional parts. As*

<meta>catchword: says</meta>

<summary>Zarlino demonstrates that dividing the physical difference between the two lengths of a Whole Tone (9:8) into two equal halves (an arithmetic mean) results in two musically unequal intervals (18:17 and 17:16) rather than two equal semitones.</summary>

### PROPOSITION VII.

->**If the interval of the Whole Tone is divided into two equal parts at the midpoint of its extremes, it is partitioned into a <term>Sesquidecimoseptimal</term> and a <term>Sesquidecimosextal</term> interval.**<-

Let the interval *a-b* be divided, as in the preceding proposition, into eighteen equal parts, and let *a-b* and *c-b* be the interval of the <term>Whole Tone</term> <note>Original: "Tuono." In the Pythagorean system used here, the Whole Tone is the ratio 9:8, which Zarlino doubles to 18:16 to find a whole-number midpoint (17).</note> likewise divided in the middle of its extremes at point *l* into two equal parts. I say that the interval of the Tone *a-b* and *c-b* is divided into a Sesquidecimoseptimal *a-b* and *l-b*, and into a Sesquidecimosextal *l-b* and *c-b*. And

<image-desc>A horizontal diagram representing a monochord division. A single line is marked with four points. Above the points are labels: 'a', 'l', 'c', and 'b'. *because **a-b** contains eighteen parts, and **l-b** contains seventeen: therefore I say, according to the Fifth Definition of the First Discourse, that **a-b** and **l-b** are a <term>Sesquidecimoseptimal</term> interval <note>A ratio of 18:17</note>: because **a-b** contains the whole of the other plus one seventeenth part of it, called an <term>Aliquot part</term> <note>A part that divides the whole exactly, like a fraction with 1 in the numerator.</note>. Similarly, because **l-b** contains seventeen parts and **c-b** contains sixteen: therefore I say that **l-b** and **c-b**, by the aforementioned definition, are a <term>Sesquidecimosextal</term> interval <note>A ratio of 17:16. The original text uses "sesquiseftodecimo," a variation of the term for 17:16.</note>, given that **l-b** contains **c-b** and one sixteenth part of it, called an Aliquot part. Thus, the interval of the Tone being divided in the middle of its extremes into two equal parts: it is divided into a Sesquidecimoseptimal and a Sesquidecimosextal interval: which, according to the proposition, I had to demonstrate to you. ADRIANO: This is clearly seen, and even felt (as they say) with one’s own hand; hence it needs no further reply. GIOSEFFO: Listen then to what I wish to tell you as a consequence of what I have demonstrated.*

### PROPOSITION VIII.

->**When the space of the Whole Tone is divided into two equal parts at the midpoint of its extremes: the sound of the middle string of the entire division exceeds the sound of the greater extreme in height, and is exceeded by the lesser extreme in depth.**<-

*CLAUDIO <note>OCR reads "Slav.", likely referring to Claudio Merulo, a composer and organist participating in the dialogue.</note>: Although this cannot be denied by anyone with judgment, given the things you have demonstrated: nevertheless, by means of a demonstration, if it pleases you, you will make it clearer. ## PROPOSITION IX.

# The Whole Tone cannot be divided into two equal parts using certain and determined rational numbers.

<margin>Arithmetic, Book 1, Chapter 9.</margin>
DESIDERIO: How so? Did Michael Stifel <note>Michael Stifel (1487–1567) was a German monk and mathematician who pioneered the use of logarithms and early algebraic notation.</note> not labor to demonstrate, against those who held the contrary, that this can be done perfectly well? And he even demonstrated it with determined numbers; how can it be then that this cannot be done? GIOSEFFO: How does Stifel demonstrate it? Do you remember? DESIDERIO: Yes, indeed. GIOSEFFO: Please, demonstrate it, for I want to show you the error in this matter. DESIDERIO: Stifel multiplies the root terms of the <term>Sesquioctave</term> proportion <note>The ratio 9:8, which defines the musical interval of a Whole Tone.</note>—which is (as you have said many times) the form of the Whole Tone—by one another: and the product he places between the larger and smaller terms of the proportion, dividing it in this way with these symbols ♮ — and with two minor <term>semitones</term>, which are followed by the <term>schisma</term> <note>A very small musical interval, roughly the difference between a Pythagorean comma and a syntonic comma.</note>. <image-desc>A horizontal diagram showing the division of a musical interval. On the left, a bracket is labeled "Whole Tone" (Tuono). you clearly see that 9, ♮ 72, and 8 are certain and determined numbers. GIOSEFFO: Very well. But how do you intend to put such a division into practice? I remember Stifel’s division only too well; and 
<margin>Book 7, Chapter 13.</margin>
I also remember that Niccolò Tartaglia <note>A famous Italian mathematician (1499–1557) known for solving cubic equations.</note>, in the second part of his *General Treatise on Numbers and Measures*, followed right along with Stifel; for in that place he set down everything that this truly learned mathematician had written. But (as I have said before) in what way will you put such a division into practice? See that it is <term>Irrational</term>: because every time one multiplies the lowest terms of a proportion together, and one cannot extract the <term>square root</term> from the product, he places this symbol near it: ♮
<margin>Part 1, Chapter 37.</margin>
which signifies (as I showed in the *Institutions* <note>Referring to Zarlino's own "Le istitutioni harmoniche" (1558), a foundational text of music theory.</note>) that root which must be extracted from that number. Wherefore the 72 which Stifel posits—which is the product of multiplying 9 by 8—does not have a square root at all, and therefore he has placed the symbol ♮ next to it <note>In this context, Zarlino uses the natural sign ♮ as a radical symbol; ♮ 72 is equivalent to √72.</note>. Thus, such a division is called <term>Surd</term> <note>From the Latin "surdus" (deaf/mute); in mathematics, it refers to an irrational number that cannot be expressed as a simple fraction.</note> and Irrational. And therefore I say that the <term>Sesquioctave</term> proportion cannot be divided into two equal parts with certain and determined rational numbers.

...and the other: as are $d$ $e$ $h$, and $h$ $e$ $g$: equal to two right angles: those two straight lines are placed in a straight line with one another: as are $d$ $e$ and $e$ $g$: and they form a single line. **FRANCESCO.** I am satisfied with this one; go to the next. **GIOSEFFO.** The Eleventh [proposition] of the First [Book of Euclid] is also easy: for it demonstrates in what manner, from a marked point, such as $e$, in a straight line, as is $d$ $g$: a straight line can be raised, such as $e$ $h$: which makes two right angles: which are those already shown. And so that when you happen to need to raise such a line, you may do so quickly: I want to show you a beautiful and brief practical method. Let $d$ $g$ be a straight line, like the one shown in the example I have given you.

<image-desc>A geometric construction diagram showing how to draw a perpendicular line and its relation to a semicircle. A horizontal base line is marked with points d, k, e, l, and g. Point e is the center. Two arcs centered at k and l intersect at point m above the line. A vertical line rises from point e, passing through m to a point h. ...and let it be the point from which it is necessary to raise another perpendicular straight line: which from one side and the other makes two right angles. We will first mark two points on the line $d$ $g$, which are equidistant on either side from point $e$: and they will be $k$ and $l$. This being done, we will place the fixed foot of the Compass in one of the marked points: such as $k$: and with whatever opening pleases us most: provided that it is a short distance from the other point $l$: for greater convenience: we will describe the curved line <note>original: "piegata linea", referring to a circular arc</note> $k$ $m$. Now with that same compass opening we will place the fixed foot in point $l$: and we will describe the curved line $k$ $m$, according to the quantity of $l$ $m$. This being done, from point $e$ to point $m$, where $l$ $m$ and $k$ $m$ join, we will draw a straight line precisely: which will be $e$ $m$: and this I say will be the sought-after Perpendicular. **ADRIANO.** You have done me a singular favor by teaching us this beautiful and easy way to raise such a line. **CLAUDIO.** And I have held it very dear: because it is necessary to know it for one who works in matters of measurement. **FRANCESCO.** Continue then to the next, Master Gioseffo, if it pleases you. **GIOSEFFO.** The Thirty-first [proposition] of the Third [Book] demonstrates that all angles made of two straight lines: such as $d$ $h$ and $h$ $g$: in a Semicircle: such as $d$ $h$ $g$: are right [angles]: as is the angle $d$ $h$ $g$. **CLAUDIO.** This is manifest, beyond the example you have shown. But what does the Corollary of the Eighth [proposition] of the Sixth [Book] say? **GIOSEFFO.** That in every right triangle: such as $d$ $g$ $h$: if from the right angle $d$ $h$ $g$ to the base $d$ $g$ a perpendicular straight line is drawn, as is $h$ $e$: such a line will be the <term>mean proportional</term> <note>In geometry, the mean proportional (or geometric mean) of two segments is the length of the perpendicular dropped from the right angle of a triangle to the hypotenuse. Zarlino uses this to find the exact middle of a musical interval that cannot be divided by whole numbers.</note> between the two segments of the said base $d$ $e$ and $e$ $g$. And similarly both sides: that is $h$ $g$ and $h$ $d$, [will be mean proportionals] between the whole base $d$ $g$: and the part of the base shared by those sides. And this is said because the line $h$ $e$ divides the Triangle $d$ $h$ $g$ into two smaller triangles of the same species: for each, compared with the larger, has a right angle: and they are $h$ $e$ $d$ and $h$ $e$ $g$. And $e$ $g$ is called conterminal to side $g$ $h$: and $e$ $d$ to side $d$ $h$. See, I pray you, what beautiful and resonant harmony of its kind is found between the lines of these triangles: which are made by the said perpendicular. **ADRIANO.** Truly the matter of numbers is a marvelous thing: but above all else the miracle in nature is Man: who with his divine intellect goes investigating and finding things so subtle, difficult, and rare. **GIOSEFFO.** This is but a small thing, Sir, compared to what the Mathematician sees: for in truth he sees such things among Numbers and other Quantities: that he may deservedly esteem—

# PROPOSITION XI.

## We can divide any given Interval into several equal parts: and demonstrate the Points of these parts on the sounding strings.

**FRANCESCO.** I believe that here it will be necessary to use the <term>Mesolabe</term> <note>An ancient Greek mechanical instrument, often attributed to Eratosthenes, used for finding geometric mean proportionals between two lines.</note>; is that not so, Master Gioseffe? **GIOSEFFO.** It is so: because without its help I would not be able to demonstrate anything to you. **DESIDERIO.** It seems to me almost superfluous to want to repeat what you have demonstrated at other times. **GIOSEFFO.** I do not judge as superfluous that which needs to be recalled and demonstrated for the sake of the Demonstrations that must serve our current discussions. Especially since I already taught you, by means of this Instrument, how to find a single <term>mean proportional</term> <note>A value $x$ such that $a:x = x:b$. In music, this is used to find the exact geometric middle of an interval.</note> line between two given lines: and now I want to show you that not only one, but two and even more can be placed there, if you will lend me your ear. **ADRIANO.** We desire nothing else: so continue cheerfully to demonstrate what you have proposed to us. **GIOSEFFO.** So I shall do, Sir: nor do I wish to lose my way in any manner. Let there be, then, the string $a$ $b$, upon which any interval between $a$ $b$ and $c$ $b$ is accommodated.

It is necessary that, according to the method shown in the *Institutions* <note>Referring to Zarlino's own seminal work, *Le Istitutioni harmoniche* (1558).</note>, one finds two <term>mean proportional</term> strings between the string $a$ $b$ and $c$ $b$. Thus, I first take the Mesolabe instrument: and I arrange it in the appropriate manner: placing three Parallelograms $d$ $e$ $f$ $g$; $h$ $k$ $l$; and $m$ $n$ $o$ $p$: one under the other, as you see. So that $d$ $e$ $f$ $g$ stays above the others: and the side $d$ $e$ comes to be exactly equal to the quantity of the proposed string $a$ $b$. I then make the side $p$ $o$ of the third parallelogram $m$ $n$ $o$ $p$ equal to the string $c$ $b$, at point $f$. And I accommodate the others in such a way that their diagonals <note>Original: "diametri." In Renaissance geometry, this term was frequently used for the diagonal of a figure.</note> $k$ $h$ and $m$ $o$ meet with the sides $g$ $f$ and $l$ $k$ at points $q$ and $r$. From this, two mean lines arise, $q$ $f$ and $r$ $k$: which I say are proportional to $d$ $e$ and $f$ $o$: and which must be placed between the strings $a$ $b$ and $c$ $b$: because they will divide the interval between $a$ $b$ and $c$ $b$ of the given strings

# Discussion

...into three equal parts: according to the purpose. And that such lines are proportional: I demonstrate it in this way. Let us suppose that the lines created in the <term>Mesolabe</term> <note>An ancient Greek calculation tool used to find mean proportionals, essential for dividing musical intervals into equal parts like the halftone.</note> are $d e$, $q f$, $r K$, and $s o$; and let $q$ and $r$ be the points where the sides of the <term>Parallelograms</term> <note>Four-sided figures with opposite sides parallel.</note> meet the diameters. I extend the lines $d f$ and $e o$ so far that they meet together: which, by the **Fifth Postulate of Euclid**, will meet at point $t$. From this, Triangle $d t e$ will be born: which will have angle $e d t$ smaller than angle $d e t$; and by the Eleventh Definition, this is called an **Acute** angle. And $d e t$: which, by the Eighth, is called a **Right** angle. But because before the Parallelograms were moved, the angles $d e f$, $h i K$, and $m n o$ of the Parallelograms, and their sides opposite to these angles, were equal: the angles $e f d$, $i K h$, and $n o m$ will also be equal among themselves: as is determined and demonstrated by the **Sixth Proposition of the Sixth Book** <note>original: "Sesta del Sesto"</note>. And, by the **Twenty-eighth Proposition of the First Book**, the lines $d f$, $h K$, and $m o$ will also be **Parallel**. And because the Triangles $d e t$, $q f t$, $r K t$, and $s o t$ have the angle $d t e$ in common, and also share a right angle: therefore, by the **Second Common Notion**, and by the second part of the **Thirty-second Proposition of the First Book**, I say such Triangles consist of right angles. And by the **Fourth Proposition of the Sixth Book**—and similarly by the Second of the same—they have proportional sides: and just as $d e$ corresponds to $q f$, so $d t$ corresponds to $q t$. And just as $r K$ to $s o$, so $r t$ to $s t$. Then, because $h K$ was made parallel to the other side of the Triangle $d f t$: therefore, I say first separately, by the **Second Proposition of the Sixth Book**: just as one finds $d q$ with $q f$, so one finds $f K$ with $f t$. And then together, by the **Eighteenth Proposition of the Fifth Book**: as $d t$ corresponds with $q t$, so $f t$ corresponds with $K t$. And because the side $q f$ of Triangle $q t f$ is made parallel to $r K$: therefore, by the same Propositions, as $f t$ corresponds with $K t$, so $q t$ corresponds with $r t$. And by the **Eleventh Proposition of the Fifth Book**: so do $d t$ correspond with $q t$. And again, by the same Propositions: as $q t$ together correspond with $r t$, so $r t$ correspond with $s t$. Whence I say these four lines $d t$, $q t$, $r t$, and $s t$ are proportional. But we have demonstrated that just as one finds $d t$ with $q t$, so $q f$ corresponds with $r K$. Similarly, that correspondence found between $r t$ and $s t$ is also found between $r K$ and $s o$: therefore, by the **Eleventh Proposition of the Fifth Book**, these lines $d e$, $q f$, $r K$, and $s o$ will be proportional. And between $d e$ and $s o$, two <term>mean proportional</term> lines $q f$ and $r K$ will be found, which are proportional: as I had to demonstrate to you. Thus is the proposed interval $a b$ and $c b$ divided into three equal parts: as you have been able to see, and as I had to demonstrate to you.

**DESIDERIO.** You have demonstrated this proposition so well that it is impossible it could be otherwise. But you have not treated such a demonstration as a Musician, but as a Geometer.

**GIOSEFFO.** It is true, and it is not inappropriate: for I then apply this demonstration to our purpose, as you have seen.

**DESIDERIO.** It is a very convenient thing, and it sits very well.

**FRANCESCO.** In the preceding [discussions] you declared upon the Figure all the propositions that you alleged from Euclid, with which you demonstrated your purpose; therefore, if it does not displease you, please do so in this one as well.

**GIOSEFFO.** It is a fair request; therefore, I am at your service, even if things will take a little longer.

**FRANCESCO.** Leave out the **Sixth Proposition of the Sixth Book**, however, for it is manifest from what you have said; and explain to us the **Twenty-eighth Proposition of the First Book**, and thus you will be a bit more brief.

**GIOSEFFO.** This proposition says: If a straight line—as would be in the Figure I have made, line $d t$—falls upon two straight lines, such as $q f$ and $l K$, and the exterior angle caused by it, such as $d q f$, is equal to the opposite interior angle, such as $q r K$; or that the two interior angles, such as $f q r$ and $q r K$ on the same side, are equal to two right angles: those two lines will be equidistant <note>Parallel.</note>.

**FRANCESCO.** It is very well stated.

**CLAUDIO.** The **Second Common Notion** is manifest.

**GIOSEFFO.** It is true, and it says that if to equal things, such as $d e$, $q f$, and $r K$, one adds equal things, such as $e t$, $f t$, and $K t$, so that there results $d t e$, $q t f$, and $r t K$: all the sums will be equal.

**CLAUDIO.** Explain to us then the second part of the **Thirty-second Proposition of the First Book** with an example.

**GIOSEFFO.** This says: that all three interior angles of a Triangle, such as angles $d, t,$ and $e$ of Triangle $d t e$, must necessarily be equal to two right angles, which are $K o f$ and $s o t$.

**ADRIANO.** A great deal of labor goes into demonstrating these proportional lines, since one must pass through the middle of so many things. But tell us the Fourth, or the Second of the second.

**GIOSEFFO.** Rather, I want to show you that which demonstrates and concludes both one and the other.
