*...intersected. And starting from the Second [Proposition], this proposes: that if a straight line, such as $g f$, is placed parallel to one side of any triangle, such as $d e$ of the Triangle $d e t$, it will cut the sides of that triangle, which are $d t$ and $e t$, proportionally. And if, on the contrary, the sides of a Triangle are cut proportionally by a straight line, that straight line will be parallel to the other side of the Triangle.*

ADRI. *This is understood very well; therefore, follow with the Fourth.*

GIOS. *The Fourth proposition of the Sixth [Book of Euclid] <note>This proposition states that equiangular triangles have their sides about the equal angles proportional.</note>, which I cited to you, demonstrates: If two triangles, such as $d e t$ and $q f t$, have equal angles together, the sides which are around such angles are proportional; and those which are under these angles, such as $d e, e t : q f, f t$; and $r K, K t$, are of a similar ratio.*

FRAN. *This is clear enough from the example you have brought forward. However, continue by explaining the Eighth of the Fifth [Book] to us.*

GIOS. *This one will seem a little strange to you, because it seems to contain some contradiction within itself. But in truth it is so, according to what it demonstrates: which is that among unequal magnitudes, such as $d e, q f,$ and $r K$, the greater $d e$ has a greater proportion than the smaller $q f$ to the same [magnitude] $r K$. It then says: and the same $r K$ has a greater proportion to the smaller $q f$ than to the larger $d e$.* <note>This is a fundamental rule of ratios: if you compare two different sizes to a third size, the larger one creates a larger ratio. Conversely, the third size has a larger ratio when compared to the smaller of the two.</note>

DESI. *It would consume much time to want to demonstrate it in such a way that one would be left without any doubt. But hold it as true, because it is so in fact.*

ADRI. *We believe it so; but there is also the Eleventh, also of the Sixth, to be explained.*

GIOS. *In citing that proposition to you, I also gave you the examples; therefore, there is no difficulty in it.*

ADRI. *Since there is no other difficulty, it seems to me it would be vain to want to repeat things pointlessly. Therefore, if you have nothing else to say upon this demonstration, we being clear on everything, I would like you to pass on to demonstrating something else to us. But I must tell you, one must have a good memory to want to remember so many things: because in truth, by what you have shown, a great quantity of material and a great labor <note>original: "fattura"</note> goes into it.*

GIOS. *Many things indeed go into it, and much labor has been done; and should one wish to demonstrate all the Propositions I have cited, an entire day would not suffice.*

FRAN. *You have done quite enough; indeed, for some of us, more than was necessary, because these things are all accepted as true, being demonstrated in Geometry. Hence, all that has been asked was for no other purpose than to have a slightly greater understanding of it.*

GIOS. *You have therefore understood it all. If you have any doubt remaining, reveal it before I pass further on.*

CLAV. *Nothing remains for us to doubt. But tell me, please: if I wanted to divide the interval—which you have shown divided into three parts—into more than three parts, what method should I hold?*

GIOS. *The same method; but it will be necessary to add a <term>parallelogram</term> for every part you wish to make beyond the three already done, even if there were (so to speak) a thousand; and in such a way you will always have that which you seek. But let us now leave these Geometric things aside and return to the proper matters of Music.*

DESI. *By your faith, before you pass further on, let me say a few words.*

GIOS. *Speak them as it pleases you.*

DESI. *If it is not true that the <term>Tone</term> can be divided into two equal parts—as we are all certain by now from what you have demonstrated—it seems to me that the opinion held by that great ancient Musician **Aristoxenus** <note>Aristoxenus (4th century BCE) argued that musical intervals should be judged by the ear rather than mathematical ratios, suggesting a tone could be divided into two equal semitones.</note> should be embraced by few. He divided the Tone in another manner than what you demonstrated in the Ninth proposition; and he did not care that the parts of his Tones, divided into <term>Semitones</term>, were one narrower than the other, contrary to the Corollary of the Fifth. But according to what he called a Semitone, he wanted them to be understood as the exact half of the Tone.*

GIOS. *This opinion cannot be accepted with truth as either good or true; because, as you have seen in the Sixth proposition exactly: it is most false to say that, having divided the difference of the Tone on the string into two equal parts, the Tone is divided into two proportional parts. Hence the division of Aristoxenus was—to give you an example and place it before your eyes so you may more easily comprehend it—the aforementioned Sixth Proposition. For having divided the interval $a c$ into two equal parts $a l$ and $l c$, two proportions are born: one, <term>Sesquiseptendecima</term> <note>original: "Sesquidecima settima"; the ratio 18:17.</note> $a l$, and the other...*

...multiplied produces 9; and multiplied by 9 it produces 27, which is the second <term>Cube number</term> <note>A number resulting from multiplying a value by itself twice (3 x 3 x 3 = 27).</note> and the greater term of the proportion of the <term>Major Tone</term> <note>The musical interval 9:8.</note>. This is accompanied by 24, which arises from the multiplication of the <term>Ternary</term> <note>The number 3.</note> into the first Cube number, which is 8. This 24 is the lesser term of the aforementioned Tone proportion, which contains the <term>Sesquioctave</term> <note>original: "Sesquioctaua"; the ratio 9:8, where the larger number contains the smaller plus an eighth part of it.</note> proportion. This is found in its radical terms between the named first Cube number and the <term>Novenary</term> <note>original: "Nouenario"; the number 9.</note>, which is the second of the <term>Square numbers</term> <note>A number produced by multiplying a value by itself (3 x 3 = 9).</note>. Since 27 is distant from 24, it maintains the same difference of the Ternary; for the Ternary is the eighth part of 24, and when this Ternary is added to it, it likewise returns 27. Wherefore, this most excellent Philosopher and Musician of those times divided this entire sum into two parts in this manner: that is, into 14 and 13. He called the larger part <term>Apotome</term> <note>A Greek term for "a segment," referring here to a major semitone.</note> and the smaller <term>Diesis</term> <note>A small interval, here used to mean a minor semitone.</note>, which was afterward named by Musicians the <term>Minor Semitone</term>. And the difference between these two parts—14 and 13—which is <term>Unity</term> <note>The number 1.</note>, he named the <term>Comma</term>, as you see drawn in this figure. <header>Discussion</header>

### PROPOSITION XXXVII.

## The Minor Third can be placed at its proper proportion upon a given string.

*Let the string be **a b**, upon which we wish to place the <term>minor third</term><note>original: "semiditono"; literally "half-ditone," referring to the interval of a minor third.</note>. I first divide, according to the third requirement of today, **a b** into six equal parts: so that **c b** contains five of them, and **a c** is one of the six parts. I say that **a b** and **c b** contain the minor third, and that I have placed it at its proper proportion upon the given string. For the entire space of the string **a b** contains the space **c b**, and additionally a fifth part of it, which is equal to **a c**, one of the six parts. Therefore, according to the definition of <term>superparticulars</term><note>A ratio where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator, such as 3:2 or 6:5.</note>, the space **a b** is <term>sesquiquintal</term><note>The ratio 6:5.</note> to **c b**. Thus, by the first requirement of today, that same proportion is also found between the sound of the entire string **a b** and that of **c b**. But since the sesquiquintal ratio is the form of the minor third interval, I say that upon the given string **a b** we have, according to our purpose, placed the minor third between **a b** and **c b**, as I was meant to demonstrate to you. This demonstration is certainly easy, nor is there anything to doubt; therefore, I shall pass to the next, speaking a bit further regarding the minor third.* **DESIDERIO.** *You may do so.* **GIOSEFFO.** *Know then: that*

# Book Three

Before I go any further, I want to inform you: I do not want to arrange these consonances according to the order I previously showed you—starting from the <term>Minor Third</term><note>original: "Semiditono"; an interval of three semitones, having a 6:5 ratio.</note> and proceeding to the <term>Octave</term><note>original: "Diapason"; the interval where the frequency doubles (2:1 ratio), encompassing eight notes of a scale.</note>—but I wish to start first with that consonance whose form is found among the primary numbers and is simpler than any other. This will be the Octave; afterwards, we will come to the <term>Fifth</term><note>original: "Diapente"; an interval encompassing five notes of a scale, with a 3:2 ratio.</note>, to which the <term>Fourth</term><note>original: "Diatessaron"; an interval of four notes with a 4:3 ratio.</note> will be added, and step by step the <term>Major Third</term><note>original: "Ditono"; literally "two tones," an interval with a 5:4 ratio.</note> and finally the Minor Third. Thus, we will have arranged all the consonances I have discussed so far according to their proportions. Once this is done, you will be able to hear, besides the named consonances, the <term>Double Octave</term><note>original: "Disdiapason"; a 4:1 ratio.</note>, the <term>Octave-plus-Fifth</term><note>original: "Diapason diapente"; a 3:1 ratio.</note>, the <term>Double-Octave-plus-Major-Third</term><note>original: "Disdiapason ditono"; a 5:1 ratio.</note>, and the <term>Double-Octave-plus-Fifth</term><note>original: "Disdiapason diapente"; a 6:1 ratio.</note>; since being arranged in this manner, one will also be able to hear the <term>Octave-plus-Fourth</term><note>original: "Diapason diatessaron"; an 8:3 ratio.</note>, and whatever Harmony you wish.

ADRIANO. *That will be well done. But tell me, upon your faith: for what reason did you not begin these demonstrations according to this order, which seems to me more reasonable?*

GIOSEFFO. *Because I wanted to show you that the larger intervals are built up from the smaller ones, as if from their own parts. And although, as you know, in any "Whole" subject to Quantity, the Whole itself comes before its parts—and knowledge of them is gained through its measurement—nonetheless, wishing to show you how that Whole is made complete by those parts, I simultaneously show you their underlying logic. Therefore, do not be surprised. Now, having understood all these things, I say: Let there be the string **a b**, upon which we wish to arrange all the musical consonances I have demonstrated so far according to their proportions. # Third [Book].

### PROPOSAL XLIIII.

It is possible to describe with <term>rational numbers</term><note>Whole numbers or fractions used to express the relationship between string lengths.</note> the proportions of all the <term>consonances</term><note>Harmonious musical intervals.</note> arranged above according to their proportion on the given string: following the divisions made of the whole into its parts.

LET IT BE, then, that we wish to describe with rational numbers, according to the Proposal, the proportions of the divisions that arise from the division made of the string, in the fitting of the consonances to their proportions in the preceding [proposal]. It is first necessary to know the "radical" <term>greater terms</term><note>The largest numbers in the simplest whole-number ratio (e.g., in a 2:1 ratio, 2 is the greater term).</note> of all the ratios of the arranged consonances. And afterward, according to such terms, one must find a larger number that contains the parts named by these terms; once this is found, it will be an easy thing to do the rest. Let, then, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 be the greater terms of the radical ratios of the consonances already fitted upon the string *ab*, as in the Previous [proposal]. I first find, by the twenty-fifth [proposition] of the First Day, a larger number that contains the parts named by the numbers of such terms, to which all its ratios can be assigned: and such a number is 720, which can be divided by each of the five given terms.

But if we take away *ae* from *af*—that is, the <term>disdiapason</term><note>The interval of two octaves (4:1 ratio).</note> from the disdiapason ditone—there will remain, as is manifest, *ef*, the <term>ditone</term><note>A major third, formed by the ratio 5:4.</note>. By definition, the <term>sesquiquartal</term><note>The ratio 5:4.</note> is its form; therefore, *ef* will be sesquiquartal. Finally, I take the sixth part of *a*, and *g* results. I say now that *ag* contains the <term>sextuple</term><note>The ratio 6:1.</note> proportion, which is the form of the <term>disdiapason diapente</term><note>An interval of two octaves plus a perfect fifth.</note>; and that *fg* contains the <term>sesquiquintal</term><note>The ratio 6:5.</note> proportion, which is the form of the <term>semiditone</term><note>A minor third.</note>. For if from *ag* (the disdiapason diapente) we take away *af* (the disdiapason), without any doubt the <term>diapente</term><note>A perfect fifth.</note> *fg* will remain; but taking the ditone from the diapente, the semiditone will certainly remain. This is because, by the corollary of the sixth [proposition] of the second [book], the diapente is made whole by the ditone and the semiditone as its parts. Therefore, having taken the ditone *ef* from the diapente *eg*, the semiditone *fg* remains. And because, by the definition, the form of the semiditone is the sesquiquintal proportion, I say that *fg* contains the sesquiquintal proportion. Thus, the proportions of all the consonances arranged upon the given string are marked with rational numbers according to the proposal; in such a way that every part is marked according to the proportion it has to its Whole, as was to be demonstrated to you. But take note: the numbers, or terms, which contain the proportions in this order are not <term>radical</term><note>Numbers in their simplest, irreducible form.</note>, as they are composite among themselves and not <term>prime to each other</term><note>original: "Contra se primi"; numbers that share no common divisor other than 1.</note>. Hence, it cannot be said that such proportions are placed in order in their lowest terms.

<margin>Part 1, Chapter 43.</margin>
Therefore, wanting to reduce them, it will be necessary to find the greatest possible number that commonly measures each of them, and divide each of them by that number. The products, when placed in order below the original numbers, will make a radical sequence, because it will be contained by numbers prime to each other. Working in the manner I showed in the *Institutions* <note>Referring to Zarlino's own famous treatise, *Le Istitutioni Harmoniche*.</note>, we will find that it will be 12. By dividing the others—*a, c, d, e, f, g*—by 12, there will result *h, p, K, l, m, n*, which will be, by the ninth definition of the First Day, numbers prime to each other and, together, the root of all the named proportions. In this way, we will have our objective. **ADRI.** We have understood very well, and it seems to me that it is not a very difficult thing; so if you have anything else to say about this, continue. If not, pass to another proposal. But since you have shown all these things in a natural order of consonances, by your faith, let it not be a displeasure to you to demonstrate them in an order of intervals that are consonant one after another, but let such an order be of another kind. **GIOS.** I will do so very willingly. But first, I want to tell you and demonstrate some things to you before I come to what you request of me; therefore, listen.

# PROPOSAL LXV.

## If two simple and similar consonances are added together at a common middle string, and the Diapason is taken away, their extremes do not make any kind of harmony.

Because in the second proposal of the past Discussion I showed you the exception made regarding the <term>Diapason</term><note>The octave.</note>, wanting to demonstrate it here would be to repeat the same thing; therefore, I will not spend more words on it but will come to demonstrate the rest. Know, then, that adding together two simple and similar consonances means nothing else than doubling them, in the way I demonstrated in the aforementioned second proposal. Therefore, let *ab, cb,* and *db* be the two simple and similar consonances, so that *ab*

# Third.

And let *ab* be the first: *ab* and *db* the second: and let them be added together with the middle common string *cb*. I say that their extremes, *ab* and *db*, do not produce any kind of <term>Harmony</term><note>In this context, "Harmony" refers to a pleasing arrangement of consonant intervals.</note>. Because, according to the second named proposition: any simple <term>consonance</term><note>A combination of notes that sounds stable and pleasant.</note> when doubled does not produce any interval that is consonant. But *ab* and *db* is a simple consonance doubled: therefore, *ab* and *db* do not give any interval that is consonant. And because all those intervals, or consonances, that are divided into two other consonances by a middle string—according to the fourth and fifth definitions from yesterday—make one of the two types of Harmony: however, since such conditions are not found in these two similar consonances added to a middle term: it follows that they do not make any kind of Harmony. Therefore, when two simple and similar consonances are added together to a common middle string—subtracting the <term>Diapason</term><note>original: "Diapason"; the interval of an octave.</note>—their extremes do not make any kind of Harmony. And this is everything that, according to the proposition, I was to demonstrate to you.

<image-desc>A linear diagram of a monochord or string divided into segments. Vertical lines represent points labeled from left to right: a, c, d, and b. These points define various lengths on the string used to calculate ratios.</image-desc>

FRANCESCO. In truth, we see this thing in practice: that two <term>Diapente</term><note>original: "Diapente"; the interval of a perfect fifth.</note> added together make a ninth; two <term>Diatessaron</term><note>original: "Diatessaron"; the interval of a perfect fourth.</note> make a seventh; two <term>Major Thirds</term><note>original: "Ditoni".</note> make an augmented fifth; and two <term>Minor Thirds</term><note>original: "Semiditoni".</note> make a diminished fifth: so that even without the demonstration, one must confess this to be true. Because although each one is consonant by itself, nevertheless added together they do not make any Harmony: as you have excellently demonstrated.

GIOSEFFO. This is so evident that it needs no further comment; therefore, listen.

# PROPOSITION XLVI.

## Between the second, the third, and the fourth strings of those shown above, one finds Harmony simply so-called.

And let *cb* be the first of the three named, *db* the second, and *eb* the third. I say that between them is found Harmony simply so-called. By the forty-third [proposition] demonstrated a little while ago: *cb* and *db* is the <term>Diapente</term><note>A perfect fifth.</note>: *db* and *eb* the <term>Diatessaron</term><note>A perfect fourth.</note>: and *cb* and *eb* the <term>Diapason</term><note>An octave.</note>. And by the first proposition of yesterday, the *cb* and *eb* is divided by *db* into <term>Harmonic mediocrity</term><note>original: "Harmonica mediocrità"; the harmonic mean, a mathematical proportion used to define musical intervals.</note>: therefore, between *cb*, *db*, and *eb* the said Mean is found. But among the consonances placed in such an order: by the fourth definition of yesterday likewise: one finds Harmony simply so-called: therefore between *cb*, *db*, and *eb*—the second, third, and fourth strings shown above—the total Harmony is found: as I was to demonstrate to you.

CLAUDIO. This cannot be denied.

GIOSEFFO. Moving further.

## PROPOSITION XLVIIII.

->We can place all the Musical consonances at their proper proportions upon a given string, in such a way that said string is common to each of them: and we can hear them at our every pleasure.<-

FRANCESCO. For what reason have you said that there should be a low string common to each of them? GIOSEFFO. Because in the forty-third [proposition] that I showed you, the low string of the <term>Diapason</term><note>original: "Diapason"; the interval of an octave (ratio 2:1).</note> is not common with any of the <term>Diapente</term><note>original: "Diapente"; the interval of a perfect fifth (ratio 3:2).</note>: nor is the low string of this consonance common with any of the other consonances: and so on. But in this case, the low string of a smaller consonance will be common with the low string of a larger one; indeed, it is the very same string. DESIDERIO. What you have said has brought to my mind (even if it is off-topic) something I have many times heard you others say in your compositions: that when you fit two consonances together, an interval is not born that contains the total number of strings <note>In this context, "strings" or "chorde" refers to the notes or steps in a musical scale.</note> counted in the two consonances: but rather it contains a smaller number, that is, one string less. For example: when you fit together those two consonances that you call a Fifth and a Fourth: a Ninth is not born, but rather an Octave. Yet, when we add together five and four, nine is undoubtedly born. However, your mentioning of this "common string" has removed every doubt

that I had. Therefore, if I have interrupted your speaking, forgive me: because not having much experience in musical matters makes me wonder about such things, even though they are not of great importance. GIOSEFFO. Your interrupting me is not without my great pleasure. And doubting (as I have said before) is never without use. But to demonstrate what I have proposed, I say: Let a b be the given string, in which we wish, according to the proposition, to fit all the musical consonances at their proportion. First, I divide a b into six equal parts: of which I take one, and mark c. Then I divide the same a b again into five parts: and taking one I mark d. Again I divide it into four parts: and similarly I take one, and mark e. I also divide a b into three parts in the said manner, of which I take one and mark f. Lastly, I divide it into four, and I take three, and mark p. # Reasoning

First, I divide line $a-b$ into five parts: taking two of these, I mark them $k$. Secondly, I divide it into eight: and first I take three of them, marking them $l$; then I take five, and mark them $m$. Having done this, I say that all the Musical consonances are arranged in order according to their proportions, starting from the smaller and proceeding to the larger, upon a common string. For, by the thirty-seventh [proposition] of this reasoning, the strings $a-b$ and $c-b$ come to be a <term>Semiditono</term><note>A Minor Third (ratio 6:5).</note>; and by the fortieth, $a-b$ and $d-b$ are a <term>Ditono</term><note>A Major Third (ratio 5:4).</note>. Similarly, by the forty-second, $a-b$ and $e-b$ is the <term>Diatessaron</term><note>A Perfect Fourth (ratio 4:3).</note>; and by the same, $a-b$ and $f-b$ is the <term>Diapente</term><note>A Perfect Fifth (ratio 3:2).</note>. It also happens, by its definition, that $a-b$ and $l-b$ are a <term>Minor Hexachord</term><note>A Minor Sixth (ratio 8:5).</note>; since $a-b$ contains $l-b$ once and its three-eighth parts, which are $a-b$. But $a-b$ and $k-b$ contain the <term>Major Hexachord</term><note>A Major Sixth (ratio 5:3).</note>; because $a-b$ contains $k-b$ once, and two-fifth parts, which are $a-k$. But, by the forty-second again, $a-b$ and $g-b$ contain the <term>Diapason</term><note>An Octave (ratio 2:1).</note>, and $a-b$ and $m-b$ the <term>Diapason diatessaron</term><note>An Octave plus a Fourth (ratio 8:3).</note>: because $a-b$ contains $m-b$ two times, and two of its third parts: that is $a-e$. Therefore, such a proportion is called <term>Double super-bipartient third</term><note>original: "Dupla superbi partiente terza"; a ratio where the larger number is twice the smaller plus two-thirds of the smaller (8:3).</note>: which, as we saw in the fortieth proposition of yesterday, is the form of that same <term>Diapason diatessaron</term>, if you remember it. ADRIANO. We remember it. GIOSEFFO. Similarly $a-b$ and $h-b$, by the forty-first of yesterday as well, comes to be a <term>Diapasondiapente</term><note>An Octave plus a Fifth (ratio 3:1).</note>: since $a-b$ and $h-b$ contain the Triple proportion, as I also demonstrated in the forty-third of this [book]. Finally, $a-b$ and $p-b$ contain the <term>Disdiapason</term><note>A Double Octave (ratio 4:1).</note>: because $a-b$ contains $p-b$ four whole times. Thus arises the Quadruple proportion: which, by definition, is the form of that same <term>Disdiapason</term>. Now, by adding another string to string $a-b$ (which is stretched over the <term>Harmonic Ruler</term><note>The monochord, a scientific instrument used to measure musical intervals.</note>) and tuning it to be a perfect unison, and placing an <term>Hemisphere</term><note>original: "Hemispherio"; a moveable bridge used to divide the string at precise points.</note> beneath it, moving it over every point made in the divisions: all the ordered consonances will be heard sensibly, without a hint of error, by touching and striking $a-b$ marked with the addition. And this is all that I wished to demonstrate to you, according to what you requested of me. But this proposal made at your instance, Monsieur, has made me desire not to finish so soon as I had intended: because it has brought to my memory some things which, by its means, I will be able to demonstrate to you. And if you find it a burden, blame yourselves: because I do not want to leave the matter imperfect, nor do I want to have cause to repeat anything to you another time. ADRIANO. For my part, I will never be burdened when I see that I may gather fruit from something. FRANCESCO. Nor could I complain of a thing from which I might make some gain. CLAUDIO. Nor am I one to be inconvenienced. DESIDERIO. We are all then in agreement on this. But please, before you pass further, be content to show us in what manner.

<header>Book Three.</header>

By the second <term>Corollary</term><note>A logical conclusion follows from a previous proof.</note>, it exceeds by such a <term>Semitone</term>. Furthermore, according to the penultimate proposition, the points *a b* and *l b* form the <term>Major Hexachord</term><note>A Major Sixth.</note>. Therefore, by taking the *a b* and *k b* <term>Minor Hexachord</term><note>A Minor Sixth.</note> away from the *a b* and *l b* Major Hexachord, according to the aforementioned second Corollary, there remains *k b* and *l b*, which is a <term>Minor Semitone</term>. This is because, according to the named <term>Thirty-fourth</term><note>referring to Proposition 34 of Zarlino's work.</note> proposition, the <term>Minor Tone</term> is that interval added to the <term>Diapente</term><note>A Perfect Fifth.</note> to achieve the Major Hexachord; and the <term>Major Semitone</term> is what is likewise added to achieve the Minor Hexachord. Since the penultimate proposition also finds that the minor semitone is the difference by which the Minor Tone exceeds the Major Semitone, it follows that because *K b* and *l b* represent this difference, they must also be the Minor Semitone.

Similarly, because *ab* and *fb* is a <term>Diapente</term> and *ab* and *l b* is a <term>Major Hexachord</term>, by subtracting the *ab* and *fb* Diapente from the *ab* and *l b* Major Hexachord, the <term>Minor Tone</term> remains. This is because (as I said a moment ago) such a Tone is added to the Diapente to create the said Hexachord. According to the same penultimate proposition, *ab* and *gb* form the <term>Diapason</term><note>An Octave.</note>. Thus, if the *a b* and *k b* <term>Minor Hexachord</term> is subtracted from the *a b* and *gb* Diapason, there remains *k b* and *gb*, which is a <term>Ditone</term><note>A Major Third.</note>. 

This is because, according to yesterday's <term>Thirty-ninth</term> proposition, the Diapason contains three Major Tones, two Minor Tones, and two Major Semitones. Furthermore, by the <term>Thirtieth</term> proposition, the Diapente contains two Major Tones, one Minor Tone, and one Major Semitone. According to the <term>Thirty-sixth</term> proposition, the Minor Hexachord will contain a Major Semitone more than the Diapente, making it two Major Tones, one Minor Tone, and two Major Semitones. When these are subtracted from the Diapason, there will remain one Major Tone and one Minor Tone, which, by the <term>Twenty-seventh</term> proposition, make a <term>Ditone</term>. This matches our proposition. 

But if one subtracts the *a b* and *l b* Major Hexachord from the *a b* and *g b* Diapason once more, there will remain *l b* and *g b*, a <term>Semiditone</term><note>A Minor Third.</note>. This is because, by adding the Minor Tone to the Diapente (according to the same Thirty-fourth proposition), the resulting Major Hexachord will contain two Major Tones, two Minor Tones, and one Major Semitone. When these are subtracted from the Diapason, there will remain one Major Tone and one Major Semitone, which, by the <term>Twenty-sixth</term> proposition, are contained within the semiditone. Thus, the proposition is proven. 

It was also shown, by today's <term>Forty-ninth</term> proposition, that *d b* and *m b* form the <term>Diapason-diatessaron</term><note>An Eleventh (an octave plus a fourth).</note>. Therefore, by subtracting the *a b* and *g b* Diapason from the *a b* and *m b* Diapason-diatessaron, there remains *g b* and *m b*, a <term>Diatessaron</term><note>A Perfect Fourth.</note>, as is quite obvious from the fortieth proposition of the previous day. The aforementioned Forty-ninth proposition also showed us that *a b* and *h b* form a <term>Diapason-diapente</term><note>A Twelfth (an octave plus a fifth).</note>. Therefore, who would deny—as it is a clear thing—that by subtracting the *a b* and *m b* Diapason-diatessaron, there remains *m b* and *h b*, a <term>Major Tone</term>? To deny this would be an error, as this is known from the first Corollary of the Thirtieth proposition of the Second Book. 

But if from the *a b* and *h b* Diapason-diapente, by the same Forty-ninth proposition, we subtract the *a b* and *g b* Diapason, it is quite obvious that *g b* and *h b*, a <term>Diapente</term>, will remain. Now, to finish this demonstration for you: we know from the same penultimate proposition that *a b* and *p b* contain the <term>Disdiapason</term><note>A Double Octave or Fifteenth.</note>. Therefore, if we subtract the *a b* and *h b* Diapason-diapente from this, there will remain *h b* and *p b*, a <term>Diatessaron</term>. This is manifest in itself: for by subtracting one Diapason from a Disdiapason, another remains. But by subtracting a Diapente from a Diapason, according to the Corollary of the fourth proposition from yesterday, the Diatessaron results. And thus we have achieved the purpose of everything that I was to demonstrate to you according to the proposal. 

**ADRIANO.** If easy things can bring delight, this has been one of those that has pleased me immensely and has been most welcome; for you have demonstrated with great ease this proposition, which otherwise contains a long discourse. I thought you would have to dwell upon it for a great while. But since I see that the matter has proceeded in another way, and having nothing else to say, it will be good to move on to something else.

### PROPOSITION LII.

With these <term>consonances</term><note>Harmonious musical intervals.</note> arranged in this manner, the end of the <term>Ditone</term><note>A Major Third.</note> with the end of the <term>Diapente</term><note>A Perfect Fifth.</note> sounds the <term>Semiditone</term><note>A Minor Third.</note>; with the end of the <term>Major Hexachord</term><note>A Major Sixth.</note> it sounds the <term>Diatessaron</term><note>A Perfect Fourth.</note>; with the end of the <term>Diapason</term><note>An Octave.</note> it sounds the <term>Minor Hexachord</term><note>A Minor Sixth.</note>; with the end of the <term>Diapason-diapente</term><note>An Octave plus a Fifth, or a Twelfth.</note> it sounds the <term>Diapason-semiditone</term><note>An Octave plus a Minor Third, or a Minor Tenth.</note>; and with the end of the <term>Disdiapason</term><note>A Double Octave, or a Fifteenth.</note> it sounds the <term>Diapason</term> with the <term>Minor Hexachord</term><note>An Octave plus a Minor Sixth, or a Minor Thirteenth.</note>. Similarly, with the end of the <term>Minor Hexachord</term> and the end of the <term>Diapason-diatessaron</term><note>An Octave plus a Fourth, or an Eleventh.</note>, it is dissonant.

*I could have also placed the minor third in place of the major third, but this matters little, as from this one can find the way to demonstrate a similar thing, beginning from whichever consonance or interval one wishes. Let there be, then, in the manner newly shown, points a, c, d, e, f, l, K, g, m, h, p, b, with the consonances already arranged according to the forty-ninth proposition of this book. I say that the end of the Ditone (d b) and the end of the Diapente (f b) harmonize as a Semiditone. This is because, by the aforementioned forty-ninth proposition, a b and d b contain the Ditone, and a b and f b contain the Diapente. But because, by the sixth and also by the thirty-first proposition discussed yesterday, the Ditone and the Semiditone together make a Diapente, therefore, when the Ditone a b and d b is taken away from the Diapente a b and f b, there remains the end of the Ditone d b and the end of the Diapente f b, which together sound the Semiditone.*

*And because, by the named forty-ninth proposition, similarly a b and K b is the Major Hexachord, if the Ditone a b and d b is taken from it, there remains d b and K b as a Diatessaron. This is because, by the thirty-fourth proposition of the Second Book, adding—*

| a | c | d | e | f | l | K | g | m | h | p | b |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 120 | 100 | 96 | 90 | 80 | 75 | 72 | 60 | 45 | 40 | 30 | |

*—these two consonances together, they make the named Hexachord. Thus, when the Ditone is removed from the Major Hexachord, the Diatessaron remains; and so between d b and K b that Diatessaron resounds. The forty-ninth proposition also shows us that between a b and g b is the Diapason; therefore, if the Ditone a b and d b is taken from the Diapason a b and g b, the Minor Hexachord remains. For the Diapason, according to yesterday's thirty-ninth proposition, contains three major tones, two minor tones, and two major semitones; and by the twenty-seventh, the Ditone contains one minor tone and one major tone. But when two tones (one major and the other minor) are taken from three major tones, two minor tones, and two major semitones, there remain two major tones, one minor tone, and two major semitones. But two major tones, one minor tone, and two major semitones, by the thirty-sixth proposition of the Second Book, make the Minor Hexachord. Thus, when the Ditone a b and d b is removed from the Diapason a b and g b, the Minor Hexachord d b and g b remains.*

*Again, by the same forty-ninth proposition, a b and h b is the Diapason-diapente; therefore, when the Ditone a b and d b is taken from the Diapason-diapente a b and h b, the Diapason-semiditone remains. And because that which remains is d b and h b, I say that d b and h b is such an interval. This is because beyond the Diapason, when the Ditone is removed from the Diapente (by the <term>Corollary</term><note>A natural consequence of a proven proposition.</note> of the thirty-first of the Second Book), the Semiditone remains. But because beyond the semiditone there is not a full Diapason—*

*is complete: therefore, adding these two intervals together, they make the <term>Diapason-semiditone</term><note>An octave plus a minor third, also known as a minor tenth.</note>. Thus I say that d b and h b together sound the Diapason-semiditone. Lastly, it was demonstrated in the many-times-mentioned proposition that a b and p b form the <term>Disdiapason</term><note>A double octave, or a fifteenth.</note> consonance. Therefore, if from a b and p b we take away a b and d b, there will remain the <term>Diapason</term><note>An octave.</note> with the <term>Minor Hexachord</term><note>A minor sixth.</note>. This is because what remains is d b and p b; hence I say d b and p b are such an interval, and that d b and p b sound the Diapason with the Minor Hexachord. This is because, as we demonstrated a short while ago, when the <term>Ditone</term><note>A major third.</note> is removed from the Diapason, without any doubt the aforementioned Hexachord remains.*

*Since a b and l b are also a Minor Hexachord: if we wish to remove from it the Ditone a b and d b, a dissonant interval will remain. This is because this Hexachord is composed (according to the thirty-fourth proposition of the previous day) of a <term>Diatessaron</term><note>A perfect fourth.</note> and a <term>Semiditone</term><note>A minor third.</note>. These two together (by the twenty-sixth and twenty-eighth propositions) contain two major tones, one minor tone, and two major semitones. If from these we take away the Ditone—which, by the twenty-seventh proposition, contains one major tone and one minor tone—there will remain one major tone and two major semitones. These, when added together, do not form a consonance in any way, because no interval is found to be consonant that contains these three small intervals. Furthermore, the mathematical ratio of the outer points is contained by numbers that have no place among the parts of the <term>Senario</term><note>The numbers 1 through 6, which Zarlino believed were the "sonorous numbers" that produced all natural musical harmony.</note> or the <term>Ottonario</term><note>The number 8; Zarlino occasionally extends his mathematical proofs to include the number 8 to account for the octave.</note> number, as will be manifest when making a trial of it. And because d b and l b is the interval that remains, I say that a b and l b is a dissonant interval.*

*Similarly: because a b and m b is the <term>Diapason-diatessaron</term><note>An octave plus a fourth, or an eleventh.</note>, I say that by taking the Ditone a b and d b from the Diapason-diatessaron a b and m b, a dissonant interval remains. For by taking the Ditone from the Diatessaron, a major semitone remains, which is dissonant; and added to the Diapason (according to what I told you in the fortieth proposition of the previous day), it makes a dissonant interval. And because d b and n b is what is left, I say d b and n b is a dissonant interval. And thus you have everything contained in the proposition that I was meant to demonstrate to you.*

**FRANCESCO:** *These demonstrations are quite easy and beautiful: I would never grow weary of listening to you. However, if you have anything else to give us still, do not delay any longer; for the dinner hour approaches for the elderly, who are accustomed to going to rest early so they may rise at a good hour in the morning, seeing as they wake much earlier than young people do.*

**GIOSEPPO ZARLINO:** *I understand you very well. For now, there is nothing else of great importance I need to demonstrate. It is quite true that I wanted to show you another demonstration in almost the same manner, but we shall leave it be, as the hour is now late and it is not a matter of great moment; I would not want any of you to be inconvenienced.*

**ADRIANO:** *Do not stop on my account, I pray you, from saying what you have in your mind. You would do me a great displeasure, as this knowledge (I let you know) is my food this time—it will nourish me and give me life. Therefore, say what you wish and do not hide it from us.*

**GIOSEPPO ZARLINO:** *I am happy to do so, as I shall finish quickly. Listen then:*

### PROPOSITION LIII.

Arrange the Consonances also in this manner: from the end of the Diatessaron to the end of the Major Hexachord, the Ditone is measured; and from the end of the said Hexachord to the end of the Diapason, the Semiditone. Likewise, from the end of the Diapason to that of the Diapason-diatessaron, the Diatessaron is measured; but from the end of the Diapason-diatessaron to that of the <term>Diapason-diapente</term><note>An octave plus a fifth, or a twelfth.</note>, the major tone. Lastly, from the end of the Diapason-diapente to the extreme high string of the Disdiapason, the Diatessaron is measured.

*Let a b and e b, according to the forty-ninth proposition of this book, be the <term>Diatessaron</term><note original: "Diatessaron">A perfect fourth.</note>; likewise, let a b and K b be the <term>Major Hexachord</term><note original: "Hexachordo maggiore">A major sixth.</note>. I say that by taking a b and e b away from a b and K b, there remains a b and K b <note>This appears to be a typographical error in the original text; the mathematical logic and the following sentence indicate it should be "e b and K b."</note>, which is a <term>Ditone</term><note original: "Ditono">A major third.</note>. Since the aforementioned Hexachord is composed—according to the thirty-fourth proposition of yesterday—of the Diatessaron and the Ditone, there is no doubt that by removing the Diatessaron, the Ditone remains. This is because this Hexachord, by its first corollary, exceeds the Diatessaron by such an interval. And because that which remains, e b and K b, is the Ditone, I say that from the end of the Diatessaron to that of the Major Hexachord, one*

| a | c | d | e | f | l | K | g | m | h | p | b |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 120 | 100 | 96 | 90 | 80 | 75 | 72 | 60 | 45 | 40 | 30 | |

*sings the Ditone. But we have said that a b and K b is the Major Hexachord. Thus, as a b and g b is the <term>Diapason</term><note original: "Diapason">An octave.</note>, by taking a b and K b from a b and g b, there remains K b and g b, a <term>Semiditone</term><note original: "semiditono">A minor third.</note>. This is because if from a b and g b (which, by the aforementioned forty-ninth proposition, is the Diapason) we take away a b and e b, the Diatessaron, then by the corollary of the fourth proposition of the Second Book, the <term>Diapente</term><note original: "Diapente">A perfect fifth.</note> will remain. But we have proved e b and K b to be a Ditone; therefore, having taken the Ditone e b and K b from the Diapente e b and g b, by the corollary of the thirty-first proposition of yesterday, the Semiditone remains. And because K b and g b is what remains, I say that from K b to g b one sings the Semiditone. Now it is manifest that a b and g b is the Diapason, and a b and m b is the <term>Diapason-diatessaron</term><note original: "Diapason diatessaron">An octave plus a perfect fourth; an eleventh.</note>. Thus it is quite clear that by taking a b and g b from a b and m b, there remains g b and m b, a Diatessaron. This is because (as I demonstrated yesterday in the fortieth proposition) the Diapason-diatessaron is composed of the Diapason and the Diatessaron. And because that which remains is g b and m b, I say g b and m b is the melodic movement made from the end of the Diapason to the end of the Diapason-diatessaron, which is the Diatessaron. Then, since a b and m b is the Diapason-diatessaron and a b and h b is the <term>Diapason-diapente</term><note original: "Diapason diapente">An octave plus a perfect fifth; a twelfth.</note>, if one takes a b and m b from a b and h b, without any doubt there will remain m b and h b. I say this is the interval of the <term>Major Tone</term><note original: "Tuono maggiore">A whole step or major second.</note>. Since g b and h b is a Diapente and g b and m b is a Diatessaron, and a b and g b remains a Diapason common to both, if from g b and h b one takes g b and m b, by the first corollary of the thirtieth proposition of the Second Book, there will remain m b and h b, which makes a Major Tone. Therefore I say that from the end of the Diapason-diatessaron m b to the end of the Diapason-diapente h b, one sings the Major Tone. Finally, by what we have said and demonstrated until now, since a b and h b is the Diapason-diapente and a b and p b is the <term>Disdiapason</term><note original: "Disdiapason">A double octave; a fifteenth.</note>, there is no doubt that by taking the Diapason-diapente a b and h b from the Disdiapason a b and p b, there remains h b and p b, a Diatessaron. This is because, having taken the Diapente g b and h b from the Diapason g b and p b, and leaving the common Diapason a b and g b, there results (by the corollary of the fourth proposition of the Second Book) the Diatessaron. And because the remainder h b and p b is the Diatessaron, I conclude: that from the end of the Diapason-diapente to that of the Disdiapason, one modulates by a Diatessaron. And all this is what I wished to demonstrate to you according to the proposal. But what I have said until now can suffice quite well for today, for it has been a good measure compared to what was discussed yesterday. And being by now tired, I will leave you all with the peace of God; and after having taken a little fresh air, I will go to rest.*
ADRIAN. You are quite right; and if you wish to stay with me for dinner, you would do me a great favor.
GIOSEFFO. I thank you, Sir; stay in peace. FRANCESCO. We are coming too. DESIDERIO. Let us all go with God then.

### Fourth Reasoning.

<margin>1. Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, chapter 1.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'M' depicting two men in Renaissance clothing standing in a landscape with a tree, engaged in conversation.</image-desc>
*Many times I have wondered to myself not a little—since it is undoubtedly true that **Every man naturally desires to know**<note original: "Ogni huomo naturalmente desidera sapere">The opening line of Aristotle's Metaphysics.</note>—that if ever in any age there was an Art whose practitioners were deprived of those principles that serve the knowledge of what is done within it, Music is one of those. For few are those to be found who—beyond that small amount of practice, and even that not good, which they have in putting Consonances together—know how to give any reason for what they do. And I truly believe that this has proceeded from nothing else than meanness of spirit and their own laziness. Because, having only applied their study to an easy way of composing—aside from knowing how to recognize and discern Consonances from Dissonances, guided by a few of their Rules, though few indeed—they take no account of having any other knowledge. Since it seems to them a strange thing, requiring much effort, and also full of difficulty (as it truly is) to search for the reason and to investigate the Causes of things. It is quite true that they would dearly love to know them, provided no difficulty were involved in wanting to acquire them. But one cannot arrive at such a level without toil, as the ancient Poet Hesiod shows us:*

<margin>Hesiod, *Works and Days*, Book 1</margin>
> A long journey, tiresome and harsh,
> Is that which can lead us to Virtue;
> But once at the summit, the path then becomes easy,
> Which was so tiresome and harsh.
> Wherefore sweet fruits are then gathered
> From the labor: Because the Gods willed,
> That such rewards be acquired with sweat.*

<summary>This page serves as the title page and introduction to the "Fourth Reasoning" of Zarlino's work. He laments the lack of theoretical understanding among contemporary musicians and cites Aristotle and Hesiod to emphasize that true knowledge requires diligent study.</summary>
<keywords>Gioseffo Zarlino, Harmonic Demonstrations, Venice, Music Theory, Consonance, Dissonance, Aristotle, Hesiod, Virtue, Musical Education</keywords>

# Reasoning

Nor do I believe that this has proceeded from anything else than the fact that in our times the number of those who compose **Music** has grown beyond measure. This stems from the ease (as I have already said) they have in putting together **Consonances** <note>Harmonious intervals like thirds, fifths, and octaves.</note> using those few **Rules** which they employ, without a thought of knowing anything further, except that placing such-and-such a Consonance above or below another creates a chord. Wherefore we see that, whereas there was once a time when such a number was so small that if one or two had been found in one of the major cities—I will not say only of Italy, but even of another Province—they were held as a marvelous thing and admired as something divine; so in our times, there is no city or castle, however small it may be, that is not crowded with this sort of men. And not only the cities or the castles, but it may be believed that at present there is no village which does not have its **Composers**, of whatever quality they may be; for this matters little to those who do not understand the art.

Thus it seems to me that **Music** and **Poetry** in our days have reached almost the same condition. For just as Poetry is overflowing with **Versifiers** <note>Those who write verse mechanically without the inspiration or technical mastery of a true poet.</note> while the number of good and excellent **Poets** is small, so Music is filled with an almost infinite number of Composers, among whom few are found who truly deserve the name of a good and true **Musician**. And just as one cannot now find a **Mountebank** <term>Cantaimbanco: a street performer who literally "sings from a bench" to sell wares.</term> or a **Quack** <term>Cerettano: a traveling charlatan or seller of fake medicines.</term> (if I may say so) who does not profess to sing improvised stanzas, so there are very few singers and other professors of Music who do not claim to perform miracles spontaneously in their singing. 

But would to God that Music kept pace with Poetry, for then there would be a good number of learned men who would know how to give a detailed account of their works, and would not have **Ignorance** as such a close friend as they do now. This state of affairs has always greatly displeased me. Having seen and recognized this great abuse for many years now, and out of the love I bear for this so noble **Science**, driven by my natural delight in it, I took up the task—difficult as it was—of wanting to see if I could, if not entirely extinguish, at least remove a good part of this ignorance from the minds of the professors of this Science. I sought to lead them back to the right path and give them such method and light that they might know how to give a good reason for everything they do, so they would not be entirely blind and inferior to other craftsmen who know how to give a good account and the "why" of every operation in their craft. 

To this end, I worked to bring this thought of mine to its desired conclusion. Through the medium of the *Institutes* <note>Referring to Zarlino's famous 1558 work, *Le istitutioni harmoniche*.</note>, which I published many years ago, I strove to shed light on everything I could in this noble Science, as much in **Practice**—revealing many beautiful and admirable secrets not yet understood by a great number of Composers—as in **Theory** <note>original: "Speculatiua"</note>, clarifying many obscure and confused things and adding many beautiful and new concepts, which (as far as I have seen) have not only never been written about, but not even hinted at by others. 

And truly, I have recognized that I did not labor in vain, but have greatly helped the practitioners of this noble Art. Through these means, many have been restored to a good state and to the knowledge of many necessary and important things. Because I have seen that my labors were not unwelcome to noble and virtuous spirits, I took the strength and daring to go further. Thus, I worked on these present **Demonstrations**, so that the matters of Music might be known demonstratively <note>Based on mathematical proof rather than just ear or habit.</note> and in the manner they ought to be known. These, I hope, will be of great utility to the professors of this Science, as anyone will be able to see and recognize after they have studied them diligently. 

Beyond this, so that I might not fail to provide all the knowledge of musical matters that I am able to give, I formed—after the fashion of the perfect orator of **Marcus Tullius Cicero**—a **Perfect Musician**, in whom one can see everything necessary to be perfect in Music. And although I know it is impossible for one person to possess within themselves everything that belongs to the Perfect Musician as I describe him, it will at least not be impossible for a man to be called "perfect" in a certain way if he lacks only a few of those qualities. I have labored willingly, and I labor willingly still; nor will any effort ever cause me regret, because what I do, I do with delight. And that which has always moved me, and 
muoue <note>catchword: moves</note>

#### Fourth.

...is moved to act, it is for the praise and glory of the highest holy and blessed God: giver of all graces and of all good things. Nor do I seek any reward from the World for these labors of mine: but I leave the care to His divine Majesty: not only of this, but also of the punishment of the rivals and detractors of others' good works, who are never lacking. To these I protest that I have not taken up this enterprise to satisfy their whims—for that is an impossibility—but rather (if I am able) to satisfy the noble and virtuous minds of Students. And to return to our first purpose, I say that the hour destined for our discussions was already near when Viola <note>Likely Francesco Viola, a musician and student of Willaert.</note> came to find me at my house, so that we might go together to find Master Adriano <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), the influential Flemish composer and maestro di cappella at St. Mark's in Venice and Zarlino's teacher.</note>. Wherefore, having first questioned me about some things regarding the discussion of the previous day, we took the path toward the usual place. Once we arrived, we found, besides the usual company, many other gentlemen who had come to see Master Adriano. After they had entertained us for a good long while with discussions on matters of Music and finally departed, everyone remained nearly silent, and thus Master Adriano began to speak. <term>ADRI.</term> It would be a good thing, my Lords, if we gave a beginning to our discussions and followed what remains for us: because the earlier it seems to Master Gioseffo <note>Gioseffo Zarlino, the author, portraying himself as a character in the dialogue.</note> that he has finished, the more we might then be able to discourse a little upon whatever else we wish. Therefore, it is up to you, Master Gioseffo, to make the first move, if it pleases you. <term>GIOS.</term> So I wish to do, sir: and I am bound to obey you in a matter so honorable as this. And I want you to know: that having been my Preceptor in the matters of practice, and having given me a good part of my "well-being" (as they say), I hold no less obligation to you than I do to the Father who fathered me. But leaving words aside and coming to the facts: to begin, I want you to know that our discussion today is to be of nothing else but the **Making** <term>Fabrica</term> or **Construction** <term>Costruttione</term> of the **Monochord** <term>Monochordo</term> <note>A scientific instrument with a single string and a movable bridge, used to demonstrate the mathematical ratios of musical intervals.</note>, for all three Genera <note>The Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic systems of ancient Greek music theory.</note> of songs: and of those accidents that may occur in such constructions. Wherefore, for a greater understanding of what I have to tell you, it is necessary that you first have knowledge of some terms and principles; for not knowing them, you would not be capable of understanding. These terms, however, I will briefly make known to you through Definitions. And although some of them were declared and defined by me in the **Foundations** <term>Istitutioni</term> <note>Zarlino refers here to his famous work, *Le Istitutioni Harmoniche* (1558).</note>, and perhaps that might suffice for you, I nevertheless do not want to fail to repeat them in this place: because it could be that in hearing them mentioned again, some doubt regarding them might present itself to you, which I could then resolve. <term>FRAN.</term> It will be well done: because many times, even in hearing again a thing already heard, one comes (not without utility to the listener) to fix it in the memory in such a way that it never leaves. <term>ADRI.</term> This I know by experience: that things I hear from another are fixed more strongly in my memory than those I read by myself while studying. <term>DESI.</term> It is truly so: because the living voice, which sounds in the ears, has greater power from without than the eye has in matters of **Science** <term>Scienza</term>. I say this because the majority of those things studied by reading are skimmed with the eye; or truly, if they are read, they are read in such a manner that the voice is not heard. Therefore, it lacks that power found in the voice of one who sounds it into the ears. However, I truly like such repetitions: because they cannot be made without some gain. <term>GIOS.</term> This was one of the reasons that in past discussions I have sometimes repeated certain things which I explained in the **Foundations**. <term>ADRI.</term> Repeat as much as you like and according to what is convenient for you: for we are all content with such things, as we know very well that you do not repeat anything except what is necessary and to clarify what is not understood. <term>GIOS.</term> Therefore, wishing to come to the division of the **Monochord**: we shall see first what it is, and then those things which fall by accident within its division.

<margin>Part 2, ch. 27</margin>

<header>Discussion</header>

# D E F I N I T I O N

## F I R S T .

A <term>Monochord</term> <note>A fundamental tool for music theorists since antiquity, consisting of a single string stretched over a soundboard with a movable bridge to demonstrate the mathematical ratios of musical intervals.</note> is an instrument of only one string: upon which every consonance and every interval is arranged according to its proper degree and order, as required by the nature of the Genus in which they are placed.

*But take note that all instruments played with a single string can be called Monochords, according to their etymology; for this name derives from two Greek words joined together: one of which is Μόνος <note>original: Monos</note>, which means "Single" or "Alone," and the other is χορδὴ <note>original: chorde</note>, which means "String." Thus it is called a Monochord, as if to say an instrument of a single string. However, when an instrument contains more strings, the name varies: for when it has four strings, it is called a <term>Tetrachord</term>, or Quadrichord; and <term>Pentachord</term> when it has five; <term>Hexachord</term> when it has six; <term>Heptachord</term> when it has seven; and so on, according to the number of strings. Finally, when it contains many strings, it is called a <term>Polychord</term>. For this reason, we can say that a Tetrachord is an instrument containing four strings. But because in Music we do not only consider the instrument in terms of the aforementioned number, but also in terms of its order—since these strings are contained under a specific Genus of modulation—whenever I name the Tetrachord in the future, I want you to understand it according to its definition, which I am about to show you. I say the same for the Pentachord, or the Hexachord, and other such terms. But let us first see what "Genus" is, and then we shall see the rest. I say, then, that:*

---

## DEFINITION II.

<term>Genus</term> <note>In ancient Greek music theory, a "genus" (plural: genera) described the specific way the two inner notes of a four-note scale (tetrachord) were tuned.</note> is a certain and determined division, or melodic progression, which is created through the number of four strings.

*Hence, when Euclid defines it in his "Introduction," he speaks in this manner: "The Genus is a certain division of four sounds" <note>original Greek: Γένος δ' έςι ποιὰ τετΤάρων φθόγγων διαίρεσις; Zarlino refers to the 'Harmonic Introduction' traditionally attributed to the mathematician Euclid, though now often attributed to Cleonides.</note>. But because the Genera of melody are three—<term>Diatonic</term>, <term>Chromatic</term>, and <term>Enharmonic</term>—before we go any further, I want us to look separately at what each of them is. FRANCESCO: Do you perhaps wish to discuss all the species of these Genera, as you did in the "Institutions"? <note>Referring to Zarlino's own seminal 1558 work, "Le Istitutioni harmoniche."</note> GIOSEFFO: No, sir; for we would never reach the end. I only want to show you those species that are useful and can offer some help to harmonies. FRANCESCO: Very well; continue with what you wish to say. GIOSEFFO: That is what I intend to do.*

<meta>This page continues the technical dialogue between Adrian Willaert, Francesco Viola, and Gioseffo Zarlino. Following the definition of the Monochord on the previous page, Zarlino now moves into the specifics of the three musical genera, starting with the Diatonic.</meta>

<header>Fourth [Book]. DEFINITION III.</header>

The **Diatonic Genus** is that which proceeds through a series of four strings <note>A <term>Tetrachord</term>.</note> in such an order that, from the lowest to the highest, one moves by a major semitone, then by a major tone, and finally by a minor tone. Conversely, moving from the highest to the lowest, one proceeds by a minor tone, then a major tone, and lastly a major semitone.

*ADRIAN. These modern chromaticists <note>A group of 16th-century avant-garde composers, such as Nicola Vicentino, who attempted to revive ancient Greek musical practices.</note> of ours do not want anyone to be able to pass from the first string to the third by a leap when singing in this Genus, because that creates the interval of a <term>Semiditone</term> <note>A minor third.</note> or <term>Trihemitone</term>. Nor do they want one to leap from the second to the fourth string, as that creates a <term>Ditone</term> <note>A major third.</note> without any middle string. They claim these intervals do not belong to the Diatonic Genus, but rather that every time one sings in that manner, the other two Genera <note>The Chromatic and Enharmonic.</note> are being used. FRANCESCO. Oh, what a fine subtlety, Sir! Therefore, every time we wish to sing in this Diatonic Genus, must we always proceed by the steps named in the definition and never transgress this law? I believe these men think the steps of this order are like those of the ladders used by peasants when they harvest grapes or pick other fruits from trees. They seem to think that if one of the rungs were missing, or if one in the middle were skipped by chance—especially when they are a bit far apart—the climber would be in danger of falling and breaking his neck. But here there is no such danger, even if one were to skip two rungs.*

*GIOSEFFO. Is it not a ridiculous thing (by your faith) to say that we cannot pass by a leap from one string to another as it is most convenient, and sing the Ditone and the Semiditone without changing the Genus? For these two intervals are found in the Diatonic both in potential and in act. In potential, I say, because with the proper and natural diatonic strings, one can form the Ditone and the Semiditone between two voices in compositions. And in act, they are found in the melodies of every four-string grouping in this Genus. It is truly laughable that in their own compositions, which they call "Chromatic," they do not allow the melodic movement of a Ditone, but only that of a Semiditone; nonetheless, between the voice parts, one hears nothing but Ditones! Similarly, in the compositions they call "Enharmonic," they only allow the melody to move by a Ditone, and they would think they had committed a great error if a Semiditone were heard even once; yet, between the parts of their songs, one hears nothing but the Semiditone. They maintain this same observance in those they call "Diatonic," in which they want neither the Ditone nor the Semiditone to be sung; nevertheless, between the parts of the song, nothing else is heard but these two intervals. And they call these compositions made with such observances "Simple Diatonic," "Simple Chromatic," or "Simple Enharmonic." For when they use such intervals in the melodies, they call them "Mixed." See, I pray you, if you ever heard more beautiful or sweet chimeras than these. But if you were to ask them if the Ancients sang the Ditone and the Semiditone in the Diatonic before the latter two Genera were discovered, I do not know what they could answer you. FRANCESCO. I do not know either; but I well know that they say that the Tetrachord used for the Diatonic is not the one you call the "Syntonic Diatonic" in your* Institutions <note>Referring to Zarlino’s own treatise, *Le Istitutioni Harmoniche*.</note>. *Instead, it must be the one you call the "Diatone" <note>Referring to the older Pythagorean tuning where major thirds were considered dissonant.</note>.*

<margin>Part 2, Chapter 16</margin>
*GIOSEFFO. This is even worse: for the Ditone of that species is not consonant at its outer limits, while the one from the first species is. Yet they accept the former in their counterpoint and reject the latter in their melodies. But*

<header>Reasoning</header>

*What does it matter, Sir, if, regarding the logic of singing, one is more important than the other? For from what has been said, I do not see why one should have more respect for the <term>Diatonon</term> <note>The traditional Diatonic genus based on Pythagorean tuning (two 9:8 tones and a 256:243 limma).</note> than the <term>Syntonon</term> <note>The "Syntonic Diatonic" of Ptolemy, which Zarlino championed because it used the "just" 5:4 major third.</note>, or for any other. What then will they say of the <term>Ditone</term> <note>A major third.</note> and <term>Semiditone</term> <note>A minor third.</note> that they place in compositions—which are contained by the proportions that are the true forms of the Ditone and Semiditone intervals—if it were necessary to use those found in the Diatonon?* ADRIAN. *It seems to me they do not know what they are saying, and they move against all reason; all the more because the Enharmonic Ditone, being contained by two sesquioctave tones <note>A ratio of 9:8.</note>, cannot cause any consonance at its outer points (as you have already demonstrated). And the force of their reasoning consists in what Boethius <note>A 6th-century philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was the standard music theory textbook for a millennium.</note> argues in Chapter 23 of the First Book of Music. There, he names the Ditone composed in the Diatonic from two sesquioctave tones, and in the Enharmonic he calls it "incomposite" <note>Simple or undivided by a middle note.</note>.* GIOSEFFO ZARLINO. *Look, by your faith, if they are not out of their minds: they want to place in compositions those intervals found in the Diatonon, which do not tune at their extremes, as I have demonstrated in the Second Part of the <term>Institutions</term> <note>Zarlino's own "Le Istitutioni harmoniche" (1558).</note>. This cannot be denied. And then they want to say that this is not what serves the Diatonic and the* <margin>Chapter 31.</margin> *Enharmonic. But as for the authority of Boethius, which they allege in their favor, I do not wish to say more here; for in Chapter 75 of the Third Part of the Institutions, I have reasoned about it sufficiently. Therefore, by reading it again, you will be able to see how these men understand it. However, let us now leave them aside and return to our purpose.* ADRIAN. *That would be well done.* GIOSEFFO ZARLINO.

---

->DEFINITION IV.<-

The **Chromatic Genus** is that which is divided in such a manner that, from the low to the high, it proceeds through every four strings <note>A <term>Tetrachord</term>.</note> by a major semitone, then by a minor semitone, and then by a Semiditone or <term>Trihemitone</term> <note>An interval of three semitones, forming a minor third.</note>.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'E' at the start of the commentary paragraph, featuring stylized foliage and a dark background.</image-desc>
*And this interval is understood to be "Incomposite"—that is, without any middle sound that divides it into two parts. And what I have said of singing while ascending from the low to the high, you must also understand for the contrary: that is, singing from the high to the low, because then one sings by a Semiditone, by a minor semitone, and by a major semitone.* <margin>Part 1, Chapter 32.</margin> FRANCESCO. *I remember you said in the Institutions that this Genus has the first, the second, and the fourth strings of its tetrachords in common with the first, second, and fourth of the Diatonic.* GIOSEFFO ZARLINO. *That is true.* FRANCESCO. *And that the third of the Diatonic is specifically Diatonic, and does not serve any of the other Genera. And likewise, the third Chromatic string is specific and has nothing to do with the others of the different Genera.* GIOSEFFO ZARLINO. *That is indeed the fact.* FRANCESCO. *Therefore, the difference that arises between these two named Genera consists in a single string. Wherefore, by adding a string among those of the Diatonic, a <term>Pentachord</term> <note>A series of five notes.</note> is made. And two Genera are joined together—namely the Diatonic and the Chromatic—which are different from one another only in the third and fourth strings of this Pentachord.* GIOSEFFO ZARLINO. *You understand it. But do you know for what reason the Ancients made two Genera out of this Pentachord and not otherwise?* FRANCESCO. *I would be very glad to know this.* GIOSEFFO ZARLINO. *Because they did not consider any other collection of sounds except those contained between four strings, whose extremes were contained by the <term>Sesquitertial</term> proportion <note>The ratio 4:3, which produces the musical interval of a perfect fourth.</note>; for they intended that such extremes should contain the First Consonance. Therefore, seeing that among the five strings of the Pentachord another manner of modulation was found, which was different from the first, they wished to show the reason for such a thing, and they attended to the logic of the Tetrachord; and*

-> DEFINITION V. <-

The Enharmonic [genus] is that which, for every four strings <note>Referring to the four notes of a tetrachord.</note>, is divided in such a way: that one can move from the low to the high by a <term>Diesis</term> <note>In ancient theory, this is a quarter-tone; Zarlino explains the specific mathematical ratios below.</note>, then by another [Diesis], and then by a <term>Ditone</term> <note>A major third.</note>: and from the high to the low by a Ditone and by two Diesis, one after the other.

ADRIAN WILLAERT. *How are these Diesis positioned in these Tetrachords, and what ratio will they have?* GIOSEFFO ZARLINO. *The first one placed in the low position has a greater ratio than the second one placed immediately toward the high. This is because the first is the minor semitone of the Chromatic, which in the Enharmonic becomes the major Diesis and is contained by the <term>sesquivigesima-quarta</term> <note>original: "Sesquiuentesima quarta." This refers to the ratio 25:24.</note> ratio. The second, which becomes the minor Diesis, is contained by the <term>supertripartient 125</term> <note>original: "Supertripartiente 125." This refers to the ratio 128:125.</note> ratio, as I explained to you on the second day by means of their definitions. But take note:*

-> DEFINITION VI. <-

<header>Discourse</header>

ADRIAN. For what reason have you not used the names of the Voices and the Strings according to how the Moderns name them at present? Why have you named them according to the Ancients, with Greek names? GIOSEFFO. So as not to cause confusion in your mind; but I will do so when the time is right. Know, however, that:

### DEFINITION VII.

**The Proslambanomenos** <note>original: "Προσλαμβανόμενος"</note> is the lowest String, added to the low string of the first Tetrachord of each Genus; it is distant by the interval of a Whole Tone from the **Hypate hypaton** <note>The "lowest of the lows," the first note of the ancient Greek Greater Perfect System.</note>.

LAVINIO. I remember that in the *Institutions* <note>Referring to Zarlino's *Le Istitutioni harmoniche* (1558).</note> you observed: that in every division of any Genus, you placed such a string at the lowest part, distant by such an interval as you have said. And I also remember the number of Tetrachords for each division, which are Five. GIOSEFFO. It is true. But take note, before we go further: that in proceeding by the number of four strings in each order of these three Genera—as I said in their definitions—I mean proceeding in each of their Tetrachords, and not by every number of four strings absolutely. CLAUDIO. I was just about to tell you: that when we walk (speaking as a practitioner) from **F, G, a, and ♮** <note>B natural; the text uses the square symbol for B-natural common in Renaissance notation.</note> toward the high by the number of these four strings, or returning from **♮, a, G, and F** toward the low, one does not find those intervals you named; nonetheless, one still proceeds through a count of four strings. GIOSEFFO. That is so. Therefore, so that you are not misled in the future, you shall understand such a number to be that found in the Tetrachord, which we shall define in this way so that you may know it.

### DEFINITION VIII.

A **Tetrachord** is an arrangement of four strings, contained within the outer limits of the <term>Sesquiterza</term> <note>The ratio 4:3, which produces the interval of a perfect fourth.</note> proportion; in which one can modulate through three intervals according to a certain and determined manner contained between those strings.

Just as the **Pentachord** <note>A five-note scale segment.</note> can be modulated or sung according to the spaces contained in the number of five strings. The same can also be said of the **Hexachord** <note>A six-note scale segment.</note> and the others, which I will not name so as not to be long-winded. DESIDERIO. Tell me, please, Master Gioseffo: what was the reason that the Ancients, in their demonstrations of the Genera, relied more on the division of the Tetrachord than on any other number or order of strings? GIOSEFFO. I want to tell you two things about this briefly. First: because they held the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>The Greek term for the interval of a perfect fourth.</note>, which this Tetrachord contains, to be the first Consonance, as I declared to you on the first day. Second: because within the number of four strings are found all the varieties that the diverse musical intervals can make in melodies. And this is the true reason why they divided or composed their Monochords by Tetrachords and not by Pentachords or other such things. And even if this were more convenient for them, it was also better done—even though our modern Latins <note>Referring to Western European musicians since the Middle Ages.</note> have composed or divided them by Hexachords, and not without purpose, as we shall see. DESIDERIO. I am satisfied; continue with whatever pleases you most. GIOSEFFO. Take note, furthermore, that

### DEFINITION IX.

The **First tetrachord** is that which, placed in the first and lowest position of each order, contains the strings **Hypate hypaton**, **Parhypate hypaton**, **Lichanos hypaton**, and **Hypate meson**; and it is called the **Hypaton** <note>Meaning "of the highest" (strings), though they were the lowest in pitch; named for their physical position at the top of the lyre.</note>. The **Second** contains, in the second position toward the high range, the **Hypate meson**, **Parhypate meson**, **Lichanos meson**, and **Mese**; and it is named the **Meson** <note>Meaning "of the middle."</note>. The **Third**, in the third position, contains the **Paramese**, **Trite diezeugmenon**, **Paranete diezeugmenon**, and **Nete diezeugmenon**; and it is called the **Diezeugmenon** <note>Meaning "disjunct" or "separated."</note>. The **Fourth**, in the last and highest position, contains the **Nete diezeugmenon**, **Trite hyperboleon**, **Paranete hyperboleon**, and **Nete hyperboleon**; and it is called the **Hyperboleon** <note>Meaning "extreme" or "highest."</note>. The **Fifth**, placed next to the **Meson** and joined to it, contains the **Mese**, **Trite synemmenon**, **Paranete synemmenon**, and **Nete synemmenon**; and it is called the **Synemmenon** <note>Meaning "conjoined."</note>.

*But take note that every Tetrachord is either conjoined to another, or it is separated. I will therefore provide their definitions so that you may recognize them and know how to distinguish one from the other.*

---

### DEFINITION X.

A **Conjoined Tetrachord** <note>original: "Tetrachordo Congiunto"</note> is one where the end of one is the beginning of another; or conversely, the beginning of one is the end of another.

<margin>Part 2, chapter 28</margin>
*FRANCESCO. I remember having seen this in the Institutions <note>Zarlino's "Le Istitutioni harmoniche" (1558).</note>, where you place the string **Hypate meson**, which is the end of the **Hypaton** tetrachord and the beginning of the **Meson**. Similarly, the **Mese** string is the beginning of the **Synemmenon** tetrachord and is the end of the **Meson**. GIOSEFFO. From this, you can understand why we call the **Synemmenon** "conjoined," as I stated in the definition, because it joins with the **Meson**. This conjunction is made all the more manifest when one sees in that same place that the **Diezeugmenon** is separated from the said **Meson**. Thus, from such a separation, it acquired its name.
