<header>Reasoning</header>

### DEFINITION XI.

A **Disjunct Tetrachord** <note>original: "Tetrachordo Separato"</note> is one in which the first, lowest string in any genus of melody is separated from the last, highest string of the preceding tetrachord by a **Whole Tone**.

SUCH is the **Diezeugmenon** <note>Meaning "disjunct" or "separated" in Greek.</note>: which is separated from the **Meson** <note>The "middle" tetrachord.</note> by a whole tone. It is called **Disjunct** because it shares no common string with the Meson, unlike the **Synemmenon** <note>The "conjoined" tetrachord, which shares a note with the middle tetrachord.</note>. However, I wish for you to know once more that among all the strings I have named, some are **Fixed**, some are **Movable**, and some are **Neutral**. Thus:

### DEFINITION XII.

**Fixed Strings** <note>original: "Chorde Stabili"</note> are those which, in each of the three musical genera <note>The Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic systems of tuning.</note>, change neither their position nor their name, but remain the same. And

### DEFINITION XIII.

**Movable Strings** <note>original: "Le Mobili"</note> are those which change both their position and their name according to each of the three genera. But

### DEFINITION XIV.

**Neutral Strings** <note>original: "Le Neutrali"</note> are those which remain permanent and do not change their position in only two of the three named genera.

AND these are the definitions which serve our purpose for the understanding of what I wish to discuss with you today. Therefore, having no other principles to propose to you than these, I shall come to the Demonstrations; and this shall be the text of the First.

# PROPOSITION
# ONE.

We can demonstrate the composition of the **regular Monochord** <note>A scientific instrument with a single string used to measure the mathematical intervals of the scale.</note> within the **Diatonic Genus**.

ADRI. *For what reason did you say the "Regular Monochord" <note>original: "Monochordo regolare"</note>, and not simply, without any addition, the "Monochord"?* GIOS. *For this reason, Sir: because with a single string stretched over the **Harmonic Rule** <term>Regola Harmonica: a calibrated straightedge used to mark the mathematical divisions of a string to produce specific musical pitches</term>, we go about investigating musical consonances with reason and rule. Or rather, because of the regulated order of the intervals that are placed upon it; or perhaps because the order it contains is regulated by those **tetrachords** <note>Four-note scales used as the building blocks of ancient music.</note> placed within it.* FRAN. *This is very well said; please continue.* GIOS. *I wanted to have this instrument brought here, made in this manner, which is our Harmonic Rule; it shall also be the Monochord, for it contains, as you see, a single string. This is so even though some wish—as I said yesterday regarding the First Definition—that the Harmonic Rule be a small strip of wood with a line drawn from one end to the other, placed underneath the string. But this matters little, since this instrument contains everything: not just the Line, which is **a** and **b**, as you see, reaching from one end to the other, but also the String. And this instrument was made for me by our Master Vincenzo Colombi—an excellent organ builder—through his courtesy. And to begin: let **a b** be the line, or string, as you prefer to call it, upon which we must demonstrate the composition of the **Regular Diatonic Monochord**. Before anything else, according to the First [Chapter] of the Third [Part], we shall place the **Major Tone** <note>original: "Tuono maggiore"; a whole step based on the ratio 9:8.</note> between **a b** and **c b**. Once this is done, according to the Forty-second [Chapter], we shall place the consonance of the **Diatessaron** <note>original: "Diatessaron"; the interval of a perfect fourth.</note> between **c b** and **d b**. Beyond this, according to the Nineteenth [Chapter], we shall place the **Major Semitone** <note>original: "semituono maggiore"; a half step based on the ratio 16:15.</note> between **c b** and **e b**, placing it before the Major Tone **e b** and **f b**, and the **Minor Tone** <note>original: "Tuo mi." or "Tuono minore"; a whole step based on the ratio 10:9.</note> **f b** and **d b**, so that the Major Tone immediately follows the Semitone. Thus, **a** shall be placed for the **Proslambanomenos** <note>The lowest note of the ancient Greek musical system, literally meaning "the acquired note."</note>. Having done this, we shall again place the Diatessaron at its proper ratio upon the string **d b**, and we shall have **d b** and **g b**. Now, upon **d b**, we shall place the Major Semitone, positioning it before the Major Tone and the Minor Tone, just as we did above according to the aforementioned Nineteenth [Chapter] proposal; thus **d b** and **h b** will be the Semitone, **h b** and **i b** the Major Tone, and **i b** and **g b** the Minor Tone. But upon **g b**, by that same First [Chapter] of the Third [Part], we shall place the Major Tone **d b** <note>likely a typo for g b</note> and **k b**. This done, we shall place the Diatessaron for a third time between **k b** and **l b**, within whose boundaries we shall place, in order, the Major Semitone **k b** and **m b**, the Major Tone **m b** and **n b**, and thus the Minor Tone **n b** and **l b**. Finally, upon **l b**, we shall place the Diatessaron **l b** and **o b**, within which we shall place the Major Semitone **l b** and **p b** in the lower part, followed by the Major Tone **p b** and **q b**, and **q b** and **o b** shall be the Minor Tone. And so, in this composition or division, it will happen that after the tone located in the lowest part of the string, the Proslambanomenos, an order will follow where one immediately finds the Major Semit...

*consonances, and many others besides, you had many strings doubled: among which*

*doubling. But if an instrument could be made that contained every interval*
*in its true and natural form without these doublings, it would be a most*
*perfect thing.*

## PROPOSAL II.

### We can demonstrate the regular construction of the Monochord in the Chromatic Genus.

*But before I come to demonstrate anything, I will bring to your memory some things which you already know through the reading of the* Institutions <note>Zarlino refers to his own seminal work, *Le Istitutioni harmoniche* (1558), which laid the foundation for modern music theory.</note>: *and they will ensure that in every regularly divided Monochord, the eighth string (as we have seen in the Preceding Proposal) corresponds to the first in the low register by a Diapason <note>Diapason: the Greek term for an Octave.</note>; and to the fifteenth in the high register by a similar consonance. Similarly, you must take note of what I said: that in the lowest part of every composition, the Tone is accommodated; and it is also accommodated immediately after the eighth string, in such a way that between the second string and the ninth, the named Diapason consonance is found. You must also note that the first, second, fourth, eighth, ninth, twelfth, and fifteenth strings in every composition of the regular Monochord are stable; and the strings which contain the Major Semitone of the shown Monochord are even common to the Chromatic and the Enharmonic <note>The three "Genera" of Greek music theory: Diatonic (standard steps), Chromatic (using semitones), and Enharmonic (using quarter-tones).</note>. And the third with the fifth, the sixth with the eighth, the tenth with the twelfth, and the thirteenth with the fifteenth contain the Ditone <note>Ditone: an interval of two whole tones, known today as a Major Third.</note>; and these are common with the Enharmonic. Wherefore, leaving aside the fourth, the seventh, the eleventh, and the fourteenth, we can make use of the rest in the composition of the Chromatic Monochord. And this you must keep in memory, because it will make what I have to tell you pass more briefly.* CLAV. *None of these things need a reply, because we remember them, and they are also easy; therefore, please pass further along, for we are ready to listen to you.* GIOS. *Since you remember them...*

## PROPOSITION III.

### We can demonstrate the regular division of the Monochord in the Enharmonic Genus.

AND because I have told you that the first, second, third, fifth, sixth, eighth, ninth, tenth, twelfth, thirteenth, & fifteenth strings of the Diatonic also serve the Enharmonic: and that between the second & the fifth: the sixth & the eighth: the tenth & the twelfth: and between the thirteenth & the fifteenth the Ditone is found: therefore it will suffice only to take the shown Diatonic Monochord with the named strings: and between the second & the third: the sixth & the seventh: the ninth & the tenth: and between the twelfth & the thirteenth place a middle string, which divides these intervals into two parts: one of which—that is, the lower <note>Original: *graue*, meaning lower in pitch</note>—contains the first Diesis <note>The Enharmonic Diesis is a tiny interval, roughly a quarter-tone</note>, or minor semitone: and the other contains the second, placed in the higher register <note>Original: *acuto*</note>: and in such a way we shall have our intent. Let there be, then, as in the first proposition, the string **a b** in the example below: and the others as well: that is **c b**, **e b**, **d b**, **h b**, **g b**, **K b**, **m b**, **l b**, **p b**, & **o b**. I now divide, by the thirty-third [proposition] of the third [book], each of the strings **c b**, **d b**, **K b**, & **l b** into twenty-five parts: and leaving one part of each division in the lower register, I mark the strings **x b**, **y b**, **z b**, & **& b**: and in such a manner the major semitone contained between **c b** & **e b**: **d b** & **h b**: **K b** & **m b**: **l b** & **p b**, comes to be divided into two Diesis: that is, into a major one placed in the lower register, **c b** & **x b**: **d b** & **y b**: **K b** & **z b**: & **l b** with **& b**: and into a minor one placed in the higher register **x b** & **e b**: **y b** & **h b**: **z b** & **m b**: and **& b** with **p b**. And that this is true, I prove it: Because if from the major semitone **c b** & **e b** one takes away the minor: which is the lower Diesis: without any doubt **x b** & **e b** remains. And because **x b** & **e b** is the difference by which the major semitone exceeds the minor...

Therefore, I praise you for holding this good opinion.* **ADRIANO.** *It certainly must be done. For even if the Greeks did not discover all the principles of things—and indeed the principles of Music may have originated from other peoples, as can be said with truth—nevertheless, they labored so much around it and illustrated it so well that one may truly say it was their own offspring. And this is all that, according to the proposal, I was meant to demonstrate to you.

*DESIDERIO.* From what I see, the **Ancients** added the **Proslambanomenos**—which contains a **Tone** with the **Hypate hypaton**—to the first tetrachord, so that with the string called the **Mese** <note>original: "Mese"; the "middle" note and the most important pitch in the Greek scale</note> they would have the consonance of an **Octave** <term>Diapason: An interval of a perfect octave</term>. Because of this effect, they named this string "**Acquired**" <note>original: "Acquistata"</note>. That is well; I understand it. But for what reason did our modern musicians not content themselves with this string, but added yet another one to it? <margin>Part 2, chapter 28.</margin>

*GIOSEFFO.* I have stated in the **Institutions** <note>original: "Istitutioni"; referring to Zarlino's definitive work, "Le Istitutioni Harmoniche"</note> that the **Ancients** proceeded in the division or construction of their **Monochords** by **Tetrachords**, and not by any other number of strings. Therefore, after joining two tetrachords together, they had arrived at the number of **seven strings**, which at their extremes created a dissonance. Thus, wishing to acquire a consonance which is the principal and the Queen of all others—which is the **Octave**—they added the **Proslambanomenos** at the distance of a **Major Tone** from the **Hypate hypaton**. But our musicians, who did not consider the division or composition of their monochord as being made of many tetrachords, but rather of **Hexachords** <term>Hexachord: A scale of six notes, popularized by Guido d'Arezzo</term>, added—

ADRIANO: You have not yet made any mention of the **Synemennon** <note>original: "Synemennon"; the "conjunct" tetrachord used to create the B-flat</note> tetrachord; which, if I remember correctly, you said is joined to the **Mese** string. And for what reason did you not mention it before the **Diezeugmenon**?

GIOSEFFO: For two reasons: one, to simply show you the order of the fifteen strings divided into tetrachords, in which there is a correspondence for each of those located between the **Mese** and the **Nete hyperboleon** with one of those contained between the **Proslambanomenos** and the **Mese**, sounding the **Diapason** <note>Octave</note> consonance. The other is so that you may know that although the **Synemennon** is added with such beautiful order among the fifteen strings, it is not, however, nor can it be called, "natural"—but rather "accidental." This is because the **Trite** string of this tetrachord <note>the B-flat</note> has no corresponding string in the lower part at the distance of an **Octave**, as all the others do; nor does the **Nete** string. For this reason, then, I did not want to add it so soon, but instead added the **Diezeugmenon**. After the **Hyperboleon**, I will then add it to the **Meson**, so that you may have everything in a distinct and orderly way.

ADRIANO: I understand you perfectly; please continue your reasoning.

GIOSEFFO: I will therefore set forth the proposal in this manner.

# PROPOSAL VII.

## We can add to the demonstrated Tetrachords the Hyperboleon tetrachord in the Diatonic Genus: and demonstrate its strings: and that among the strings of the Pentadecachordo the Disdiapason consonance is found.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring a figure in a landscape with a building in the background.</image-desc>
Let the twelve demonstrated strings be *a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, K, l,* and *m*, which contain the **Octave plus a Fifth**. I add to these the strings *n, o,* and *p*, in such a way that *m* and *n*—that is, the **Nete diezeugmenon** and the **Trite hyperboleon**—are in a **Sesquitertia** <term>Sesquitertia: the 4:3 ratio, which defines a Perfect Fourth</term> proportion, so that the **Diatessaron** <note>Perfect Fourth</note> can be sung; and let *p* and *o* be a **Minor Tone**, and *o* with *n* be a **Major Tone**. Therefore, by the twenty-eighth [proposition] of the second day, *m* and *n* will be a **Major Semitone**. Thus *m, n, o,* and *p* is, according to our purpose, the **Hyperboleon Tetrachord** <note>the "highest" tetrachord</note> measured in the **Diatonic Genus** by one major semitone, one major tone, and one minor tone, added to the **Diezeugmenon**. Of this tetrachord, according to the definition, the **Nete diezeugmenon**, **Trite hyperboleon**, **Paranete hyperboleon**, and **Nete hyperboleon** are its strings.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion between Gioseffo Zarlino (GIO S.) and Claudio Merulo (CLAV.) regarding the mathematical division of the monochord. <header>Discussion</header>

*...and between K and s there is the **minor tone**; between s and l is the interval of the **comma**; and between l and m is the **minor tone**. Because, according to today’s first proposition, K and l are a **major tone**, and according to the preceding one, K and s are a **minor tone**, I say that if we subtract K and s from K and l, the remainder will undoubtedly be the **comma**. By its definition, the comma is the amount by which the major tone exceeds the minor tone. Similarly, from the preceding discussion, we have that q and K contain the **major tone**, and i and K contain (by the first part of this section) the **major semitone**. Therefore, if we subtract the major semitone i and K from the major tone q and K, according to the corollary of the thirty-fifth part of the third discussion, there will remain an interval. This interval will be larger in proportion than the minor semitone; it will be q and i, which is not singable in the **Diatonic genus** <note>The standard musical scale consisting of tones and semitones.</note>. And this is what I had to demonstrate regarding the matters in the proposal.*

*CLAV. It would not be out of place if you also showed the method used to mark these strings along with the others using their numbers, so that one could see the proportion found between one and the other. You said in the Istitutioni <note>Zarlino's 1558 work, "Le Istitutioni Harmoniche."</note> that **Numbers** are the images of sounds.*

*GIO S. I want to satisfy you in this as well. Listen then to the proposal.*

# PROPOSITION 10

<margin>Part 1, Chapter 41</margin>

### We can find the Numbers, or Proportions, of the Strings contained / in the Diatonic Monochord.

*You must first know that the strings h, i, K, l, m, n, o, and p of the second **Diapason** <term>Octave; the interval of an eighth</term> (h and p) correspond to the strings a, b, c, d, e, f, g, and h of the first octave (a and h) in such a way that h corresponds to a, i to b, K to c, l to d, m to e, n to f, o to g, and p to h. Since each of the strings of the first octave corresponds to the strings of the second in order in a **double proportion** <note>A 2:1 ratio, which mathematically defines an octave.</note>, it will be an easy thing—once the numbers for the proportions of one are found—to find those of the other, which correspond in double proportion. But it is necessary first to see and consider which of these two octaves has greater difficulty within itself. We will find it to be h and p, because besides the intervals it contains—which are similar to the intervals in the first octave (a and h)—it contains more, as we saw in the previous section: the interval of the proportion **super 7-part 128** <note>original: "super. 7. partiente. 128." A complex ratio (135:128) representing a major semitone.</note>, which is larger than the minor semitone. It also contains the interval of the **comma**. Thus, if one started from a and h and found all the numbers for its intervals, they would not all correspond to the number of strings held by h and p. This is because strings q and r, placed in the octave h and p, have no corresponding string in the octave a and h that corresponds by a similar interval. Therefore, even if the numbers of the second octave were found corresponding to the numbers of the strings of the first, those two named strings would still be without numbers. It would then be necessary to find them later by multiplying all the prime numbers containing the proportions of all fifteen strings. This would result in a series of much larger numbers, as the first ones would be multiplied by whichever part one wished to take of any number—as demonstrated in the fifteenth part of our first discussion—to accommodate the proportions in this order. Therefore, for greater brevity and ease of work, we will first find the numbers and proportions of the intervals contained in the second octave (h and p). Once found, it will be easy, by doubling those that correspond to the strings of the first*

# Discourse

*...octave <note>original: "diapason"</note> from a to h, to achieve the objective.* DESIDERIO. *This was a helpful observation; and I am pleased that you strive for brevity and ease of understanding.* GIOSEFFO. *Let the strings then be a. b. c. d. e. f. g. h. q. i. k. r. l. m. n. o. & p: containing the five four-note scales <note>original: "Tetrachordi"</note>, the Lowest <note>original: "Hypaton"</note>, the Middle <note>original: "Meson"</note>, the Disjunct <note>original: "Diezeugmenon"</note>, the Highest <note>original: "Hyperboleon"</note>, and the Conjunct <note>original: "Synemennon"</note>. And let the First Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note> be between a & h, and the second between h & p. I see first what interval is found between the first and second low strings of the second octave, h & p: which is the Major Semitone. Its ratio <note>original: "pportione"</note> is contained in its lowest terms <note>original: "termini radicali"</note> between 16 & 15: these I write in the First Order: and they are h & q. I then see the interval found between the Second and Third strings: that is, between q & i: and I find that it is of a greater ratio than that of the Minor Semitone; its ratio, by the Corollary of the Thirty-fifth proposition of the Third book, is the "super-seven-part-128" <note>This is a technical way of describing the ratio 135:128 (where 135 is 128 plus 7).</note>, contained in the radical terms of these two numbers: 135 & 128. Now it is necessary to add this ratio to the ratio of h & q, in such a way that q is the greater term of the named ratio. But because q does not have a 135th part, I multiply the q placed in the First Order by 135: and there results the q placed in the second order, which contains such a part. I also multiply the h placed in the First Order by 135: and there is born the h placed in the second: which, by the Fifth Axiom <note>original: "Dignità, ò Parer commune"</note>, together with q placed likewise in the second, contains the 16:15 ratio <note>original: "Sesquiquintadecima"</note>: that is, the Major Semitone. Now, by the Fifteenth proposition of the First Day, I subtract from q the non-aliquot part of the named ratio: that is, I subtract seven times the 135th part, because between 135 & 128 there is a difference of seven: and what results is i: which with q contains the ratio of this interval, which is larger than the interval of the minor semitone. To this I add in order the ratio of the Major Semitone, which is contained between i & k: which is done by subtracting from i the sixteenth part; and between i & k placed in the second order, we have our objective. And because between k & r one finds the Minor Tone, the ratio of which is found between 10 & 9: therefore by subtracting from m the tenth part: between the product, which will be r: & p placed in the second order, we will have our intent. But between r & l one finds the <term>Comma</term> <note>A very small musical interval resulting from the difference between other intervals, specifically the ratio 81:80.</note> of the 81:80 ratio <note>original: "Sesquiottantesima"</note>: whence by subtracting from r the eighty-first part, there will remain in the second order l: which with r will contain the ratio of the named Comma. Then follows the interval of the Minor Tone: therefore if we subtract the tenth part: the remainder m with the said l will contain the ratio of the said Tone. But to this we will add the major semitone: therefore by subtracting from m the sixteenth part: there will result n: which with m will contain the ratio of the named Semitone. Then by subtracting from n the ninth part, there will result o: which with n will contain the ratio of the Major Tone: to which, wanting to add that of the minor tone which follows: by subtracting from o the tenth part: the remainder will be p: and thus between o & p we will have the ratio of this Tone. And in this way we will have all the Numbers & Ratios of the intervals contained in the second octave h & p. Now to have those of the First, a & h: we will double the Numbers h. i. k. l. m. n. o: and we will have the Numbers a. b. c. d. e. f. & g. I say now, that the Numbers placed in the Second order are the numbers found for the ratios contained between the seventeen shown strings, within two octaves. It is indeed true that such numbers are not the Lowest Terms <note>original: "Radicali"</note> of such an order. Therefore, wanting to reduce them to their root, one must observe the method held in the *Institutions*: finding the largest number that numbers and measures each of them entirely: which will be 5. Whence there will result the Third order of numbers, which will be found by the ninth definition of our First reasoning to be in their roots. And such numbers will be those found similarly, according to our purpose. And that this is true, one can...*

...of the minor semitone; and *l* with *r* contains the Comma <note>A tiny interval, the mathematical "remainder" that occurs in tuning systems when stacking perfect fifths against octaves.</note>; but because in the previous section I have demonstrated the whole, I do not wish to repeat anything to you now. I only want to tell you: since *m* & *p* are a Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>; *n* & *o* are a major Tone; and *o* with *p* are a minor Tone; that *m* & *n* is a major Semitone. Therefore, in conclusion, I say: that a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, k, r, l, m, n, o, & p are the discovered numbers for the named octaves <note>original: "Diapason"</note> in the Diatonic Genere. For the number of the *lowest note* <note>original: "Proslambanomenos"</note> with that of the *lowest of the low* <note>original: "Hypate hypaton"</note> contains the ratio of the major Tone; from the *lowest of the low* to the *next-lowest of the low* <note>original: "Parhypate hypaton"</note> that of the major Semitone; from the *next-lowest of the low* to the *index of the low* <note>original: "Lychanos hypaton"; named after the "licking" or index finger used to play it.</note> the form of the major Tone; and from the *index of the low* to the *lowest of the middle* <note>original: "Hypate meson"</note> that of the minor Tone. Similarly, from the number of the *lowest of the middle* to that of the *next-lowest of the middle* <note>original: "Parhypate meson"</note> is the major Semitone; from the *next-lowest of the middle* to the *middle index* <note>original: "Lychanos meson"</note> the major Tone; and from the *middle index* to the *middle* <note>original: "Mese"</note> the minor Tone. Beyond this, the number of the *middle* with that of the *next-to-middle* <note>original: "Paramese"</note> suits the ratio of the major Tone; that of the *next-to-middle* with that of the *third of the disjunct* <note>original: "Trite diezeugmenon"</note> that of the larger Semitone; the number of the *third of the disjunct* with that of its *next-to-last* <note>original: "Paranete diezeugmenon"</note> contains the ratio of the major Tone; and that of the *next-to-last of the disjunct* with that of the *last of the disjunct* <note>original: "Nete diezeugmenon"</note> contains the minor Tone. But from the number of the *last of the disjunct* to that of the *third of the highest* <note>original: "Trite hyperboleon"</note> is found the ratio of the major Semitone; from that of the *third of the highest* to that of its *next-to-last* <note>original: "Paranete hyperboleon"</note> the major Tone; and from that to the *last of the highest* <note>original: "Nete hyperboleon"</note> the minor Tone. Again, from the number of the *middle* and from the number of the *third of the conjunct* <note>original: "Trite synemmenon"</note> the ratio of the larger Semitone is comprised; from that of the *third* and from that of the *next-to-last of the conjunct* <note>original: "Paranete synnemmenon"</note> that of the major Tone; and to finally finish it, from that of the *next-to-last of the conjunct* to its *last* <note>original: "Nete synemmenon"</note> the ratio of the minor Tone is contained. But I want to repeat one word to you: that from the *third of the conjunct* and from the *next-to-middle* <note>original: "Paramese"</note> we have the ratio of that interval which is larger than the minor semitone; and from the number of the *last of the conjunct* and from that of the *next-to-last of the disjunct* <note>original: "Paranete diezeugmenon"</note> we have the ratio of the Comma. Wherefore I say: that this is all that, according to the proposal, I had to demonstrate to you. And if you have any doubt regarding this division or construction, step forward; for I have nothing more to say to you of this Genere for now. <term>ADRIANO.</term> For my part, I have no doubt at all. <term>FRANCESCO.</term> Nor I. <term>DESIDERIO.</term> We give you permission, then, to proceed further. <term>CLAUDIO.</term> So you shall do. <term>GIOSEFFO.</term> Coming then to what I wish to demonstrate to you, I say that:

## PROPOSITION XI.

### In the Chromatic Genere, we can add the *Lowest* <note>original: "Hypaton"</note> four-note scale <note>original: "Tetrachordo"</note> to the *lowest string* <note>original: "Proslambanomenos"</note>.

<term>ADRIANO.</term> This Genere has given, and still gives, work to some who pick at it <note>original: "se la beccano"; an idiom meaning they struggle with the complexity or are obsessed with it.</note>. Because of the light—I will not say little, but much—that you have given regarding it in the *Institutions* <note>Referring to Zarlino's own famous work, *Istitutioni harmoniche*.</note>, and by the instrument that Master Domenico of Pesaro <note>Domenico di Lorenzo da Pesaro, a renowned keyboard builder who constructed a "polychord" for Zarlino to demonstrate different tunings.</note>, your friend and excellent in his art, made for you for this purpose in the year 1548 and which you showed me: I seem to know it: if not definitively, at least by negation. <term>FRANCESCO.</term> How do you say, Monsieur, "by negation"? <term>ADRIANO.</term> It seems strange to you that I say I know such a thing by negation. # Discussion

<meta>catchword: re la</meta>

*Idea or Intellect: that which one might not know or cannot explain well, for lack of having at hand those distinctions and those fitting terms that would serve for the explanation of the thing. Wherefore, seeing or hearing someone represent the thing that he knows—by that which he has in his mind—and truly knowing that it is not only not that thing, but does not even resemble it: even if he does not know how to give the reason or say in what manner the thing stands, he will at least deny that it is what the other claims it to be. Wherefore such a negation will proceed because he will not have any distinct reason for such a thing, but only a confused one, for lack of those terms that essentially express the thing. But if by chance something were represented that was similar to it: even if it were not the thing itself, he would nevertheless have to examine such a thing and see if it contains within itself all those parts that the thing he has in his intellect seems to have. And this I call, for my part, "Knowledge by negation" <gloss>per negatione</gloss>.*

*FRANCESCO.* I understand you. Do you believe then that those Songs <note>original: "Canzoni"</note> which these modern composers compose as "Chromatic" are indeed Chromatic?
*ADRIANO.* I believe they are not.
*FRANCESCO.* Would you have the heart to give some reason for it?
*ADRIANO.* Yes, certainly.
*FRANCESCO.* Please, tell it.
*ADRIANO.* I am happy to. First: it does not seem to me that they are Chromatic for this reason: because the Ancients in their <term>Tetrachords</term> <note>The basic four-note scales that formed the building blocks of Ancient Greek music.</note>—as we have learned—had only four diatonic strings and one particular Chromatic one, which fell between the second and third Diatonic notes; and with the sharp Fourth it made the minor third, which they call the <term>Trihemituono</term> <note>Literally "three half-tones," the interval of a minor third.</note>. And these moderns not only use such a string in a Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> or Tetrachord, but they add to it as many more as they wish, so that in their Songs one sees nothing but <term>Sharps</term> <term>♯</term> <note>original: "Diesis"</note> and <term>Flats</term> <term>♭</term> <note>original: "b molli"</note>. Furthermore: it does not seem to me that they are Chromatic because the ancient strings had their own proper names—such as <term>Hypate</term>, <term>Lychanos</term>, <term>Trite</term>, and the others—yet the strings that these men put in their melodies cannot be named with any of the said names, or even with others similar to them. This is a manifest sign that they are not, nor can they ever be, what these men preach. Beyond this, they do not observe any <term>Mode</term> or <term>Tone</term> in their composing, such that one could say: "this melody is composed in the <term>Dorian</term>, <term>Ionian</term>, or <term>Phrygian</term> mode," or under another Mode, as the Ancients said. Instead, they are composed of confusion and with a certain mixture of things that greatly offend the refined hearing of the judicious, as one finds in them little order, nor can any stable mode of Harmony be discerned.

*FRANCESCO.* These reasons are good, and to tell the truth, whoever wants to compose a Chromatic melody must imitate the Ancients in this. One must not distance oneself much from their way, and one must also observe the Tones or Modes, of which the Ancients were great observers and held in high esteem—unless one wants to make things up out of one's own head; but then they will not be the things they claim they are. For just as when one wishes to make a Garment, it is necessary to have the material and the form suited to making such a Garment—otherwise it would not be a Garment, but another thing, and perhaps a strange one—so to want to compose a Chromatic melody, it is necessary that all those things concur which give being to such a melody. Wherefore, when in their compositions they use intervals other than Chromatic ones, in my opinion this is not Chromatic composing, but a way that has neither the one nor the other. Therefore, it seems to me they ought to use only those strings and intervals contained in the Chromatic Tetrachord, if they wish to compose Chromatically as they say, and not other foreign strings as they do.
*ADRIANO.* It is true. And although the things I have said are sufficient to demonstrate the contrary of what they feel, I will nonetheless add this other point, which is of no small importance: they use in singing certain intervals so ungainly, such as <term>diminished fourths</term> <note>original: "semidiatessaron"</note>, <term>Tritones</term> <note>An unstable interval of three whole tones.</note>, <term>diminished fifths</term> <note>original: "Semidiapente"</note>, <term>augmented fifths</term> <note>original: "Diapente superflui"</note>, and even <term>false octaves</term> <note>original: "Diapason false"</note>, with other similar intervals that bring little pleasure to the ear. Nevertheless, they count them among the good ones, even though the good and learned Ancients greatly avoided and abhorred them, because they never held these intervals to be consonant in their Melodies, nor capable of making good harmony, unless they were contained in their proportions of the <term>Superparticular Genus</term> <note>A mathematical ratio where the numerator is exactly one more than the denominator (e.g., 3/2, 4/3), which the Greeks believed defined perfect musical intervals.</note>. 
*CLAUDIO.* I know what to tell you, for I observe this law. You, Master, have labored much along with many other good musicians more ancient than you, in reducing the...

#### Fourth Book.

*...to render Music in a certain manner or form: that would have some gravity and majesty together: but with those men your design was almost in vain: because besides the fact that they do not observe the good precepts of the Art: they also teach and exhort others to spoil that which is good and well-ordered: and to do the worst they know how. And when they do something that is outside the good and beautiful of Music: they cover themselves with the shield of ignorance: and say that they are things done in the Chromatic Genus: even if they do not know, nor do they understand what it truly is. See, please, how much these men are not only worthy of blame: but even of punishment.* ADRIANO.

<margin>Boethius, Book 1, Chapter 1, On Music. <note>original Latin: "Musifices"</note></margin>
*Know that if the Ancient Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans, known for their strict discipline.</note> drove out and banished from their City that great Musician Timotheus, the inventor of the Chromatic: for having only added a single string to the usual instrument: just think, if they were judges of these men in our times: what they would do. I am certain they would drive them from the world: so that they would not infect men with so many of their strange things: that they make heard. Which arise, not indeed from a single string that they add to the usual and used number: but from many and many additions without any purpose, and without judgment. These men can be likened to that most insolent and ambitious Herostratus: who burned the ancient and most celebrated Temple of Diana of Ephesus: not out of hatred for her: but to leave a memory of himself to posterity with such a wickedness: since he had little grace to do it with illustrious deeds that he had performed. Whence, because these men have not been able to acquire the name of excellent Musicians with their works: they have toiled and still toil to do the worst they know: to acquire a name, and become famous. But the thought goes failed: because it is seen that the world holds little account of such men.* GIOSEFFO. *Sir: let it suffice you to have spoken of these men until now: and let them go, for your faith: for with all the worst they will do: I do not believe they will ever be as highly esteemed as brave in Music as you are esteemed: and many others, who do not go after these so strange things. However, since you have mentioned a single string added by Timotheus: we will come to demonstrate the proposal: finding this string alone: to be brief: which will be Third in every <term>Tetrachord</term> <note>A four-note scale segment.</note>: and will make the variety of the Genus. But because I said in the Second proposal, that the First, the Second, and the Fourth string of every diatonic Tetrachord, are also common to the First, Second, and Fourth of every Chromatic Tetrachord: therefore we will only seek to accommodate the Third among the named Diatonics: which should be distant from the high Fourth of every Tetrachord by a <term>semiditone</term> <note>A minor third.</note>, or <term>Trihemituono</term> <note>An interval of three semitones.</note>. One must however notice what I have said several times: that the string <term>Proslambanomenos</term> <note>The lowest note of the Greek system.</note> and the <term>Mese</term> <note>The middle note.</note> are distant from the tetrachords <term>Hypaton</term> and <term>Diezeugmenon</term> by a major Tone—the former from <term>Hypate hypaton</term>: and the latter from <term>Paramese</term>.*
<margin>Jean Ravisius Textor in "The Workshop" <note>original: "Io. Ra. Text. in Officina"</note></margin>

FRANCESCO. *This we remember: you having said it also before. But why is this string of the Chromatic Tetrachord placed distant from the Fourth string by a Semiditone: if no one has ever mentioned this interval in such a Genus?*

<margin>Book 1, Chapter 15</margin>
GIOSEFFO. *On the contrary, <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century mathematician and music theorist.</note> speaking of the "soft" Chromatic Genus, places this interval, which is the Third of his Tetrachord, under the <term>Sesquiquinta</term> <note>The ratio 6:5, which produces the modern minor third.</note> proportion. But the reason I also told you in the "Institutions" <note>Refers to Zarlino's 1558 work, *Le Istitutioni harmoniche*.</note>: and at present I am about to repeat it. For although the Ancients marked other intervals or proportions for the Trihemituono than that of our Semiditone: nevertheless, as I have also said: it seems to me that a string is added uselessly to any instrument whatsoever: when it does not make any consonance with another. And because the other strings that are added do not make any consonance with the Fourth string of the Tetrachords: therefore I say: that such strings are placed in instruments vainly and without any utility. Wherefore I judged, and am also of the opinion: that the Semiditone of the diatonic, placed by Ptolemy in the Sesquiquinta proportion: which I mentioned to you a little while ago: and serves also for the Trihemituono of the soft Chromatic, should be that one: which we should use in the Chromatic: and no other interval: which is entirely without consonance.* CLAUDIO. *It truly seems to me that you are right. Nor can I see anything that could be contrary to you. Wherefore you will begin to demonstrate what you have proposed: if you have nothing else to say to us.* GIOSEFFO. *Without placing any time in between, I will begin, saying. Let the diatonic strings be a. b. c. &*

...and let **a** be the *Proslambanomenos* <term>The "added note" at the bottom of the Greek scale, serving as the foundation.</term>: and **b** the first string, lower than the others of the following diatonic *Hypaton* tetrachord <term>The "lowest" of the four-string groupings in ancient music theory.</term>: **c** the second: and **e** the fourth. And let **a** and **b** be distant by a **major Tone**: **b** and **c** by the **major Semitone**: and let **b** and **e** be the *Diateffaron* <note>The interval of a perfect fourth.</note>: and **a** with **e** the *Diapente* <note>The interval of a perfect fifth.</note>. And because, by the First Corollary of the Thirtieth, also of the second day: having removed the **a-b** major Tone from the **a-e** *Diapente*: the **b-e** *Diateffaron* remains. Similarly: because, by the Twenty-seventh of the same day: two Tones—one major and the other minor—with a major Semitone following make the *Diateffaron*: and being **b-c** and **c-d** together: by the Nineteenth also of the second day, a **minor Tone**: it therefore follows: that **d** and **e** contains the major Tone and the major Semitone: which, by the Twenty-sixth of the second [day] make the *Semiditono* <note>A "half-ditone," or minor third.</note>, or *Trihemituono*. ...[by] a minor third <note>original: "Semiditono"</note>; and we will have our goal among **b, q, f,** and **r**. For since **b** and **r** form a Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>: if we take from it the major semitone **b** and **q**, and from **q** and **r** the minor third, without any doubt the minor semitone **f** and **q** will remain. And because the melody found in these strings proceeds by a major semitone, a minor semitone, and a Trihemitone <term>Trihemitone: An interval consisting of three semitones, equivalent to a minor third.</term>; therefore, by definition, **b, q, f,** and **r** become the Chromatic Conjunct Tetrachord <note>original: "Tetrachordo synemennon Chromatico"</note>, because it is joined to string **b**, which is the Middle string <note>original: "Meson"</note>. **ADRIAN:** You will perhaps want to keep the same order you held for the Diatonic: marking each string with its numbers, so that one can understand how much proportion is found between one string and another. **GIOSEFFO:** Yes, I wish to; and to make you certain of this desire of mine, I propose this:

### PROPOSITION XV.

# One Can Assign the Numbers of the Shown Division or Composition 
# of the Chromatic Monochord.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring floral motifs at the beginning of the paragraph.</image-desc>

And here I will also dispatch the matter briefly. You already know, as I have shown you, that many diatonic strings are shared with the Chromatic ones; where the strings are shared, their intervals also become shared. Therefore, we shall take only the First, Second, and Fourth strings of every diatonic tetrachord with their marked numbers; and by adding to every Fourth string toward the bass the numbers of a string distant by a *Sesquiquinta* <term>Sesquiquinta: A mathematical ratio of 6:5, used here to define the interval of the Trihemitone or minor third.</term>, we will achieve our purpose. We shall take then **a, b, c, e, f, h, q, i, K, r, m, n,** and **p** with their numbers placed in the Second order of the Tenth Proposition of today; and we will make **d, g, r, l,** and **o** distant from **e, h, f, m,** and **p** by a *Sesquiquinta*, which is the proportion containing the Trihemitone, adding to each of them its fifth part; and we will have the result. 

And because **e, h, m, p,** and **f** are numbers that have a fifth part, starting from **e** (placed in the second order), we will take its fifth part and add it to **e** itself. This will give us **d** (likewise placed in the named Second order), which with **e** will contain the Trihemitone; for it will come to contain **e** one time plus its fifth part. Wherefore, by definition, **d** and **e** come to contain the *Sesquiquinta* proportion, which is the form of this Trihemitone. In this way, we will have marked the Third highest string of the Lowest Tetrachord <note>original: "Tetrachordo Hypaton"</note> with its numbers. 

This will also occur when one subtracts from **c** its twenty-fifth part; for **d** will likewise be born, which with **c** will contain the ratio of 25:24 <note>original: "sesquiuentesima quarta"</note>, or the minor semitone, as we wish to call it; and between **d** and **e**, the aforementioned Trihemitone, as I have shown you. Now, adding to **h, m, p,** and **f** their fifth part—or rather, subtracting the twenty-fifth part from **f, K, n,** and **q**—there will result **g, l, o,** and **r**. These will be the Third strings of the other tetrachords, marked with their numbers, according to the proposal I was to demonstrate to you. 

But because this order of numbers is not contained in its Root <note>In this context, Zarlino refers to the lowest possible whole numbers for these ratios.</note>, because they are composite numbers—wherefore they can be numbered and divided by a number other than Unity, according to the Tenth definition of the First Day—wishing to reduce them to their Root (that is, to numbers that are relatively prime <note>original: "Contra se primi"</note>), we will find a number, according to the method given in the penultimate chapter of the First Part of the *Institutions* <note>Referring to Zarlino's own famous work, *Le Istitutioni harmoniche*.</note>, which numbers and measures each of those contained in the named order (the Second), which will be the *Ternario* <note>The number three.</note>. From this will arise a Third order, which will contain those same proportions contained in the Second, by the Fifth Dignity; and all those intervals that are contained in the construction or manufacture of the Monochord of the Chromatic Genus. We have therefore found the numbers of the strings of the chromatic monochord, according to the proposal.

<meta>catchword: proposal [posta].</meta>

<summary>Zarlino explains how to calculate the mathematical ratios for the Chromatic scale by building upon the existing Diatonic system, specifically by adding a string at a 6:5 ratio (the Trihemitone) to each tetrachord. He describes the process of reducing these large string-length numbers to their simplest "root" forms using the number three as a common divisor.</summary>

### PROPOSITION XVI.

**The Hypates, the Parhypates, the Mese, the Paramese, the Trites, and the Paranetes of the modes of the Diatonic correspond to the Hypates, the Parhypates, the Mese, the Paramese, the Trites, and the Paranetes of the modes of the Chromatic.**

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting a person in a rural or pastoral landscape with a building in the background, enclosed within a square border.</image-desc>

Inasmuch as in both of these two Genera, the interval of the Major Semitone is found from the Hypate <note>The lowest note of a tetrachord.</note> to the Parhypate <note>The note second from the bottom of a tetrachord.</note>; similarly from the Mese <note>The central "middle" note.</note> to the Trite synemmenon <note>The third note of the conjunct tetrachord.</note>; from the Paramese <note>The "side-middle" note.</note> to the Trite diezeugmenon <note>The third note of the disjunct tetrachord.</note>; and from the Nete diezeugmenon <note>The highest note of the disjunct tetrachord.</note> to the Trite hyperboleon <note>The third note of the highest tetrachord.</note>. Just as one also finds the Major Tone from the Mese to the Paramese, and also from the Proslambanomenos <note>The lowest added note of the scale.</note> to the Hypate hypaton. In such a way, each of us can recognize that in the Diatonic and in the Chromatic, those voices <note>The pitches or notes.</note> contained in one of the named strings <note>The Greek term "chord" literally means string.</note> are contained in the other, and that really there is no difference at all from one to the other. Wherefore it follows that you not only understand this by yourselves, but also know perfectly, as good musicians, that the Proslambanomenos, the Hypates, the Parhypates, the Mese, the Paramese, the Trites, the Paranetes, and the Netes of one of the named Genera correspond interchangeably to the Proslambanomenos, the Hypates, the Parhypates, the Mese, the Paramese, the Trites, the Paranetes, and the Netes of the other. 

**ADRIAN.** This is true: because in both of the two Genera (as you have said), from the Proslambanomenos to the neighboring Hypate, there is the interval of the Major Tone; and to the Hypate meson, the Perfect Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note>.

*Similarly, according to the twenty-eighth [proposition] of the Second [Book], the Perfect Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> contains a major tone, a minor tone, and a major semitone; and notes **b** and **c** combined with **c** and **d** form a major semitone. CLAUDIO: This demonstration is so evident that anyone who wished to argue otherwise would have to be considered lacking in intellect. Pray continue with the rest, if it pleases you.*

*...and **m**, the Highest note of the Disjoined tetrachord <note>original: "Nete dieZeugmenon"</note> at the interval of a Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note>; likewise **p**, the Highest note of the Highest tetrachord <note>original: "Nete hyperboleon"</note> at the interval of an Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note>. ### PROPOSITION XX.

#### We can gather together the numbers of the strings of the Enharmonic 
#### Monochord, contained in their root terms.

<image-desc>An ornamental drop-cap letter 'O' depicting a leafy design inside a square frame.</image-desc>

To shorten the matter, as you know, the numbers of the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note> placed in the low range must correspond in double proportion to the numbers of the Octave in the high range. Therefore, by first finding those in the high Octave—as it is somewhat more difficult—it will be very easy to find those of the low Octave, since its numbers correspond to the high ones in a 2:1 ratio <note>original: "Dupla pportione"</note>. Let **h** and **q** be the lowest terms of the Major Diesis placed in the low part of the Octave **h** and **p**. To the smaller of these, **q**, we need to add the high Minor Diesis. I first multiply **h** and **q** (placed in the First order) by the larger term of the Minor Diesis, which is 128. Following the eighth proposition of the First Day, I set this as the difference between **h** and **q**, so that I may find the 128th part <note>original: "Centesima uetesima ottaua parte"</note>. Since **q** is a number that does not contain such a part, **h** and **q** move into the Second order; by the fifth dignity <note>an axiom or rule of proportions</note>, they contain the same proportion as **h** and **q** in the First: that is, the 513:512 ratio <note>original: "Sesquiquentesima quarta"</note>. Now, because **q** in the second order contains that part, I take from it (by the fifteenth proposition of the First Day) three times the 128th part, which results in **r**. This **r**, with **q**, contains the proportion of the Minor Diesis placed in the high range. And because, according to the corollary of the thirty-second proposition of our first discussion, the Major Semitone (the 16:15 interval <note>original: "Sesquiquintodecimo"</note>) is reconstituted from the 513:512 proportion and the 128:125 ratio <note>original: "supertripartiente 25"</note>—or rather, from the Major and Minor Diesis—we shall say **h** and **r** form the Major Semitone. In the Enharmonic Genus, this is divided into two parts according to its nature. We then take from the fourth part, and **l** will result, which with **r** contains...

*will be the Sesquiquarta <note>a ratio of 5:4</note>: and consequently the Ditone <note>a Major Third</note>. And in this manner we will have found the numbers **h. q. r.** and **l** in the second order of the Conjoined Tetrachord <note>original: "Tetrachordo Synemennon"</note>. These numbers are not radical <note>meaning they are not in their lowest possible terms</note>: because they are composite numbers. Therefore, so that one can find the others with more brevity and ease, we will reduce this order to its Root <note>the simplest form of the ratio</note>: by finding a number that measures each of them, in the manner that I showed in the penultimate chapter of the First Book of the Institutions. And we will have **8**, which will divide each of the named numbers of the Second order: and we will have **h. q. r.** and **l** in the Third order: which will be Relatively Prime <note>original: "Contra se primi," meaning they share no common divisor other than 1</note> and in their root.*

*But to find those of the Disjoined Tetrachord <note>original: "Diezeugmenon"</note>: we will see if the Ninth part can be taken from **h** of the Third order, so that we can add the Sesquioctave proportion <note>the 9:8 ratio that forms a Major Tone</note> to the number **h**. And because it truly does not have a ninth part, we will multiply **h. q. r.** and **l** of this last order: and **h. q. r.** and **l** will be placed in the Fourth and last order: which, by the Fifth Axiom <note>original: "dignità"</note>, will contain the same proportions contained between the terms of the Third order. Now from these Numbers we will have everything: because if we take the Ninth part from **h**, **i** will result: which with **h** will contain the Sesquioctave proportion: which is the form of the Major Tone.*

*From **i** we will also take the Twenty-fifth part: and we will have **k**: which with **i** will contain the numbers of the Major Diesis <note>the larger of the two small intervals in the Enharmonic genus</note>. But to find those that contain the minor one: we will take three times the One-hundred-and-twenty-eighth part of **k**: and what results will be **l**: which will contain with **k** the proportion of the named Diesis. But taking the Fourth part from **l**, **m** will be born: which with **l** will contain the proportion of the Ditone: that is, the sesquiquarta. In the same way, taking the Twenty-fifth part from **m**, **n** will be born: which with the said **m** will contain the proportion of the Major Diesis. Therefore, taking three times the One-hundred-and-twenty-eighth from **n**, **o** will result: which with **n** will contain the proportion of the minor one. But if from **o** we take the Fifth part, **p** will result: which with **o** will contain the Sesquiquarta proportion, and also the Ditone.*

*And in such a manner we will have gathered together all the numbers of the Second high Octave <note>original: "Diapason acuta"</note>: which will contain three Tetrachords: namely **h. q. r.** and **s** <note>referring to the Conjoined tetrachord</note> Conjoined; **i. k. l.** and **m** Disjoined: and **m. n. o.** and **p** Highest <note>original: "Hyperbolen"</note>. But to have those of the Low Octave <note>original: "Diapason graue"</note>: it will be enough only to double **h. i. k. l. m. n.** and **o**: and **a. b. c. d. e. f.** and **g** will result: which with **h** will contain all those of the said Octave, divided into two Tetrachords: namely **b. c. d.** and **e** Lowest <note>original: "Hypaton"</note>: and **e. f. g.** and **h** Middle <note>original: "Meson"</note>. And in such a way we will have the gathered Numbers of all five Enharmonic tetrachords: according to our purpose: placed by the Ninth definition of the First Day: in their Root.*

*Therefore, since **a** and **b** are a Major Tone: and **b** with **c** is a Minor Semitone, or Major Diesis: and **c** with **d** is a Minor Diesis. Similarly, since **a** with **e** becomes a Sesquialter <note>a 3:2 ratio, or a Fifth</note>: and **a** with **o** are the numbers of the Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note>: and **a** with **b** the numbers of the Major Tone: then, having taken the Tone **a** and **b** from the Fifth **a** and **e**: by the first Corollary of the Thirtieth [chapter] of the Second [book]: there remains **b** and **e** as a Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>: and **b c** with **c d** together: by the Corollary of the Thirty-second [definition] of the First Day: they make the Major Semitone. Therefore, by the Twenty-second definition of the Second [book], **d** with **e** contain the Ditone. And **a** with **h** is the Octave: therefore, by the Corollary of the Fourth proposal of the named second book, **e** with **h** is the Fourth. And because **e f** and **f g** are the two Diesis: namely the major and the minor: then **g** and **h** results in being the Ditone. In this same way one could demonstrate **h** and **i** to be a Major Tone: **i k** and **k l** two Diesis: **l** and **m** the Ditone: and thus the other intervals as well: just as **m n** and **n o** are two Diesis: and **o p** the Ditone: and also **h q** and **q r** being similarly two Diesis: and **l** with **r** being a Ditone. But so as not to weary you, since what I have said is clear: I will make an end.*

ADRIANO. *I have indeed observed one thing while you made these demonstrations: and it seems to me that I have not been deceived: and it is this: that*

## PROPOSITION XXI.

### The *Parhypate* of the Diatonic and Chromatic systems become the *Lychanos* of the Enharmonic modulations; and the *Trite* become *Paranete*.

FRANCESCO: This is clear, and can be seen plainly in both the Diatonic division (or construction) and the Chromatic. In each of these two, the interval from the <term>Proslambanomenos</term> <note>The "Acquired Note," the lowest pitch in the ancient Greek system.</note> to the <term>Hypate hypaton</term> <note>The "Principal of the Low" notes.</note> is a Major Tone; this also occurs in the Enharmonic division. But from the *Hypate hypaton* to the <term>Parhypate hypaton</term> <note>The "Next-to-principal of the Low" notes.</note> there is the interval of a Major Semitone, which is the same interval found in the Enharmonic system from the *Hypate hypaton* to the <term>Lychanos hypaton</term> <note>The "Index-finger note," which changed pitch depending on the musical genus.</note>. Therefore, the Diatonic and Chromatic *Parhypate* is changed, and in the Enharmonic system, it undoubtedly becomes the *Lychanos*. The same can also be said of the others—that is, the <term>Trite</term> <note>The "Third note" of a tetrachord.</note> becoming the <term>Paranete</term> <note>The "Next-to-highest" note.</note>.

GIOSEFFO: It is true.

CLAUDIO: In effect, musical instruments teach much more than one might believe, for there one sees everything in action. It is truly the physical realization of everything the theoretical mind has constructed.

ADRIANO: This can be easily understood and grasped through the senses in the musical instruments mentioned: especially in the keyboard layout of <term>Organs</term>, <term>Harpsichords</term>, <term>Virginals</term>, <term>Monochords</term>, and others like them. If, in the three mentioned genera <note>The Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic systems of tuning.</note>, the *Proslambanomenos* and the *Hypate* are tuned in unison, then we will clearly see that the *Lychanos* of the Enharmonic is in unison with the *Parhypate* of the others. And we can also see that the *Paranete* of the Enharmonic will be in unison with the *Trite* of the Diatonic and Chromatic.

GIOSEFFO: This is all true, Sir; but add to this as well that...

## PROPOSITION XXIII.

### One can investigate which strings are Stable, which are Mobile, and which are Neutral in each division of the named Genera.

YOU know that, by the preceding [Proposition], the <term>Proslambanomenos</term>, the <term>Hypate</term>, the <term>Mese</term>, the <term>Paramese</term>, and the <term>Nete</term> <note>These are the fixed structural notes of the Greek Great Perfect System, roughly corresponding to the "anchors" of the scale.</note> are common to each of the three named genera. <header>Discussion</header>

## PROPOSITION XXIII.

In the Diatonic division from the <term>Added Note <note>original: *Proslambanomenos*; the lowest note of the scale</note></term> as the first term of the consonances up to the <term>Highest of the extremes <note>original: *Nete hyperboleon*; the highest note of the scale</note></term>, the <term>Octave <note>original: *Diapason*</note></term> is found eight times: four times among the Stable strings; twice among the Neutral; and twice among the Mobile. The <term>Fifth <note>original: *Diapente*</note></term> is found seven times: three in the Stable; two between the Neutral and Mobile; once among the Neutral; and once among the Mobile. Similarly, the <term>Fourth <note>original: *Diatessaron*</note></term> is found eight times: four times among the Stable strings; twice in the Neutral; and twice in the Mobile.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter A featuring a landscape with a building, trees, and water.</image-desc>

ADRIANO. What do you call the "First term of the consonances"? GIOSEFFO. The first string of the division, which is the <term>Added Note <note>original: *Proslambanomenos*</note></term>, as the proposition states. CLAUDIO. For what reason do you name it the First term? GIOSEFFO. Because that is where one begins to form the consonances, following them one by one. FRANCESCO. When you say, "Up to the <term>Highest of the extremes <note>original: *Nete hyperboleon*</note></term>," do you mean for that note to be counted? GIOSEFFO. Yes, sir. FRANCESCO. Very well; continue then. GIOSEFFO. I shall do so. Let the strings then be **a. b. c. d. e. f. g. h. i. k. l. m. n. o. & p.** which contain the four <term>Tetrachords <note>groups of four notes</note></term>: the <term>Principal <note>original: *Hypaton*</note></term>, the <term>Middle <note>original: *Meson*</note></term>, the <term>Disjunct <note>original: *Diezeugmenon*</note></term>, and the <term>Extreme <note>original: *Hyperboleon*</note></term>. I say first that from **a** (the Added Note) to **p** (the Highest of the extremes), eight <term>Octaves <note>original: *Diapason*</note></term> are contained. And this occurs four times in the Stable strings; twice in the Neutral; and another two times in the Mobile. 

Because **a** with **h**, by the fifth proposition of this book, contains within itself three major Tones, two minor [Tones], and two major Semitones: Therefore, by the thirty-ninth [proposition] of the Second Book, **a** with **h** contains the Octave consonance. Thus, **a** with **h** will be the first Octave. Similarly: because **b** with **i**, **c** with **k**, and **d** with **l** each contain the five named Tones and the two Semitones; which is also done by **f** with **n**, **g** with **o**, and **h** with **p**. However, I say that **a** with **h** is the <note>The text here seems to mistakenly say 'fifth' (Quinta) but the logic suggests 'first' (Prima)</note> first Octave, **f** with **n** the sixth, **g** with **o** the seventh, and **h** with **p** the eighth. Therefore, from the Added Note **a** to the Highest of the extremes **p**, eight Octaves are contained, according to our purpose. 

But the Added Note and the <term>Middle Note <note>original: *Mese*</note></term> give us the first; the second comes from the <term>Lowest of the principals <note>original: *Hypate hypaton*</note></term> and the <term>Next to the middle <note>original: *Paramese*</note></term>; and from the <term>Lowest of the middle <note>original: *Hypate meson*</note></term> and the <term>Highest of the disjunct <note>original: *Nete diezeugmenon*</note></term> comes the fifth; similarly from the Middle Note and the Highest of the extremes arises the eighth. Because a different order is found in voices than that which is found in artificial instruments. Wherefore in the former, because they can bend in every direction and are not fixed, one can always form whatever interval one wishes, reducing it to its true and natural form: but in the latter <note>instruments</note> one cannot do this, except as much as the order contained in their strings allows: which, after having been stretched according to those proportions found in a specific order, can no longer be altered without ruining that order. ### PROPOSITION XXV.

**Among the fifteen Chromatic strings, the <term>Octave <note>original: *Diapason*</note></term> consonance is found eight times: four times among the Stable strings; twice among the Neutral; and twice among the Mobile. Beyond this: the <term>Fifth <note>original: *Diapente*</note></term> is found three times among the Stable strings: and the <term>Fourth <note>original: *Diatessaron*</note></term> is found eight times: four among the Stable; twice among the Neutral; and twice among the Mobile.**

*Since **a** and **e** are a Fifth (according to today’s eleventh proposal) and, by the twelfth, **e** and **h** are a Fourth: by the fourth [proposal] of the Second Book: **a** and **h** will be the Octave. Thus **a** and **h** will be the first instance, and **b** with **i** the second: because **b** and **e** are found to be a Fourth, given that **b** and **c** happens to be a major semitone and **c** and **d** a minor one. These two semitones combined (by the nineteenth proposal of the second discussion) make a minor tone, and **d** with **e** make the <term>minor third <note>original: *Trihemituono*, literally "three semitones"</note></term>. Because **e** and **i** are also a Fifth—since it contains the Fourth **e** and **h**, and the major tone **h** with **i**—it necessarily follows that **b** and **i** contain the Octave. And because, by today’s twelfth proposal, **e** and **h** contains the Fourth, and **h** with **i** is a major tone—and similarly because **i** and **m** is a Fourth—by adding the major tone **h** and **i** to the Fourth (according to the second corollary of the thirtieth proposal of the Second Book), the Fifth is produced. When this Fifth is added to the Fourth (by the fourth proposal of the second day), the Octave **e** and **m** is produced, which is the fifth instance. Similarly: because **h** and **m** is a Fifth and **m** with **p** is a Fourth, **h** and **p** will be the eighth Octave. But because the first Octave is contained by the <term>Added Note <note>original: *Proslambanomenos*</note></term> and the <term>Middle string <note>original: *Mese*</note></term>; the second by the <term>Lowest of the lowest <note>original: *Hypatehypaton*</note></term> and the <term>Next to the middle <note>original: *Paramese*</note></term>; the fifth between the <term>Lowest of the middle <note>original: *Hypatemeson*</note></term> and the <term>Highest of the disjunct <note>original: *Netediezeugmenon*</note></term>; and the eighth between the <term>Middle string <note>original: *Mese*</note></term> and the <term>Highest of the extreme <note>original: *Netehyperboleon*</note></term>—all of which are <term>Stable strings <note>Strings that do not change their tuning between the different Greek genera (Diatonic, Chromatic, Enharmonic)</note></term> by the twenty-third proposal of this book—we shall therefore say that among the fifteen chromatic strings, four Octaves are found located among the stable strings. Beyond this: because **f** and **g** is a minor semitone, and **g** with **h** is a <term>minor third <note>original: *semiditono* or *Trihemituono*</note></term>, therefore **f** and **h** will be a <term>Major Third <note>original: *Ditono*</note></term>. This is because (by the twenty-third Definition of the second day) the minor semitone is the interval by which the Major Third exceeds the named minor third. But **h** and **i** is a major tone, and similarly **i** and **k** is a major semitone, which (by the twenty-sixth proposal of the aforementioned Second Book) make a minor third. Therefore **f** with **k** (by the thirtieth and thirty-first of the Second again) is a Fifth. And **c** with **f** is a Fourth, which when combined with the Fifth (by the fourth of the Second) makes an Octave; therefore from **c** to **k** the third Octave is found. And in the same way we can speak of the sixth, which is contained between **e** and **m**. <header>Part Four.</header>

*...<term>Octave <note>original: *Diapason*</note></term> of the eight contained among the fifteen strings: which are the fourth and the seventh. Thus, among the fifteen chromatic strings, the octave consonance is found eight times: four times among the Fixed strings, twice among the Neutral, and twice among the Movable. Desi. This is understood perfectly.*

*Gios. I will proceed, then, to demonstrate to you that among the named fifteen strings, the <term>Fifth <note>original: *Diapente*</note></term> is found only three times, and this occurs among the fixed strings. And because it is clearly seen that b and e, and e with h, and similarly i and m form a <term>Fourth <note>original: *Diatessaron*</note></term>, and a with b—and also h with [the next string]—form a Major Tone; therefore, by the second corollary of the thirtieth [proposition] of the second day: a and e will make the first Fifth, e with i the second, and h with m the third. This is because this last pairing corresponds in a double ratio <note>A 2:1 mathematical ratio, which defines the octave.</note> with a and e. Wherefore, for the sake of brevity, I will leave off saying more of it, as the matter is clear and manifest in itself. But since the first Fifth is contained between the <term>Added Note <note>original: *Proslambanomenos*</note></term> and the <term>Lowest of the Middle <note>original: *Hypate meson*</note></term>; the second between the <term>Lowest of the Middle</term> and the <term>Middle-adjacent <note>original: *Paramese*</note></term>; and the third between the <term>Middle <note>original: *Mese*</note></term> and the <term>Third of the Highest <note>original: *Tritehyperboleon*</note></term>—which are, by today's Twenty-third proposition, all Fixed strings—one can therefore say that the Fifth is found placed three times in the fixed strings, as the proposal states. Fran. This is well put; but show us how many times the Fourth is found among these fifteen strings. Gios. The Fourth is contained only four times among the first eight strings of the fifteen shown, and four times in the others corresponding to those in double ratio. Therefore, it is found four times among the Fixed, twice among the Neutral, and twice among the Movable. Because, by the Eleventh [proposition] of this book, b and e make the Fourth; thus b and e will be the first. And because, by that same Eleventh, c and d [form] a Minor Semitone, and between d and e is found the <term>Trihemitone <note>An interval of three semitones, characteristic of the chromatic genus.</note></term>, therefore c and e contain one Major Tone and one Minor Tone. And, by the Twelfth of this book, e and f is a Major Semitone. Therefore c and f are two Tones—one major and the other minor—with a Major Semitone; and they will form, by the Twenty-seventh of the second book, the Fourth. Thus c and f will be the second Fourth. And because also, by today's Twelfth proposal, e with f is a Trihemitone, therefore d and g contains one Major Tone and one Minor, with a Major Semitone. Thus d and g is the third Fourth. But, by the same Twelfth, e and h contain the Fourth; therefore e and h will be the fourth. And in this way we will have, within the first Octave from a to h, four instances of the Fourth, to which four others correspond placed between the Octave from h to p: that is, i and m corresponding to b and e; k and n to c and f; l and o to d and g; and m with p to e and h. And because the first, b and e, is found between the <term>Lowest of the Low <note>original: *Hypate hypatōn*</note></term> and the <term>Lowest of the Middle</term>; the fourth, e and h, between the <term>Lowest of the Middle</term> and the <term>Middle</term>; the fifth, between i and m, between the <term>Next-to-the-highest of the Disjunct <note>original: *Paranete diezeugmenon*</note></term> and the <term>Highest of the Disjunct <note>original: *Nete diezeugmenon*</note></term>; and the eighth, m and p, between the <term>Highest of the Disjunct</term> and the <term>Highest of the Highest <note>original: *Netehyperboleon*</note></term>—all these strings being, by today's Twenty-third, Fixed—it follows that these four Fourths are placed among the Fixed strings. Then, since c and f are contained between the <term>Next-to-the-lowest of the Low <note>original: *Parhypate hypatōn*</note></term> and the <term>Next-to-the-lowest of the Middle <note>original: *Parhypatemeſon*</note></term>, and k with n are placed between the <term>Third of the Disjunct <note>original: *Tritediezeugmenon*</note></term> and the <term>Third of the Highest</term>—which are Neutral strings—it follows that among the eight Fourths contained within the fifteen chromatic strings, two are found placed among the Neutral strings. Furthermore, because d and g is placed between the <term>Indicator of the Low <note>original: *Lychanos hypaton*</note></term> and the <term>Indicator of the Middle <note>original: *Lychanos meſon*</note></term>, and l with o is placed between the <term>Next-to-the-highest of the Disjunct</term> and the <term>Next-to-the-highest of the Highest <note>original: *Paranete hyperboleon*</note></term>—the <term>Indicators</term> and the <term>Next-to-the-highest</term> being, by the mentioned Twenty-third, Movable strings—it follows that these two Fourths are placed among the Movable strings. And this is all that, according to the proposal, I was to demonstrate to you. Clav. This is something that cannot be denied; therefore continue with the rest, if you please. Gios. It pleases me; and I wish to demonstrate only one other proposal to you, and then make an end; and it shall be this.*

### PROPOSAL XXVI.

Among the assigned limits of the fifteen Enharmonic strings, the Octave consonance is found eight times, the Fifth three times, and the Fourth eight times, under the same conditions shown in the preceding [proposition].
