<header># Fourth Reasoning</header>

*...bounded at its extremes by a <term>Lowest Note <note>original: Hypate; the name for the lowest notes in the Greek tetrachord system</note></term>, or a <term>Middle Note <note>original: Mese; the central note of the Greek scale</note></term>: or indeed by a <term>Note Next-to-the-Middle <note>original: Paramese</note></term>, or a <term>Highest Note <note>original: Nete</note></term>: which, according to the twenty-third proposition of this book, are all **Fixed** strings: therefore we say the <term>Fifth <note>original: Diapente</note></term> is found three times among the fixed strings within the fifteen proposed enharmonic strings. But without doubt, it is impossible that between **a** & **d**: and between **h** & **l** there should fall a <term>Fourth <note>original: Diateſſaron</note></term>. Because **a** & **b**, and **h** with **i** are two Major Tones: and **b** with **c**, or **i** with **k**, is a <term>Major Diesis <note>A microtonal interval used in the Enharmonic genus, roughly a quarter-tone</note></term>, which Diesis with **c** & **d**: or with **k** & **l** (a <term>Minor Diesis</term>) contains the Major Semitone. Hence, in each of these two Fourths, a Minor Tone would be missing: since, according to the twenty-seventh proposition of the Second Book: the Fourth contains one Major Tone and one Minor Tone, with a Major Semitone: and **a** with **d** would contain, according to the eighteenth and twenty-sixth [propositions] of the same Second Book, only a <term>Ditone <note>A Major Third</note></term>. This impossibility is also found between **f** & **i**: and between **g** & **k**: which exceed the Fourth: since the Fourth contains (as I have said) a Major Tone, with a Minor Tone, and the Minor Semitone: but **f** & **i** contains a Minor Diesis, a Ditone, and a Major Tone: and **g** with **k** contains a Ditone, a Major Tone, and a Major Diesis: as is manifest. Hence, except for these: for every four continuous strings a perfect Fourth is found: such as **b** & **e**: **e** & **h**: **i** & **m**: and **m** & **p**: with their middle strings: which are located among the **Fixed** strings. I say the same of **c** & **f**: and of **k** & **n**: which are bounded among the **Neutral** strings: and of **d** & **g**: and of **l** & **o**: which are placed among the **Movable** strings. Therefore, having considered and demonstrated all these Fourths: according to what we have done in the preceding [demonstration]: we have achieved the purpose of everything contained in the proposal. And forgive me if I do not specifically address all the demonstrations that could be made in this proposal, demonstrating each thing one by one: which I do for several reasons. First, because by now I am tired from so much reasoning: secondly, because by remembering the demonstrations made above, the whole can be manifest to you. Be content then, I pray you, to have had from me today all this that I have told you: and I await you tomorrow at the usual hour: because I want to finish demonstrating and reasoning that which will lead to the perfection of these our discussions. And if you have anything else to say to me at present: I am prepared to satisfy you, as far as I am permitted.*

**ADRIANO.** *It is right that you finish: because it is a good while that you have been speaking. Nor does anything remain for me to doubt. Therefore, if it were to your liking: you would do me a signal favor by staying all together to dine with me: and it is something that could be done easily and without your inconvenience.*

**GIOSEFFO.** *I cannot serve you this time, Sir: because I have some duties remaining which I wish to have finished before I dine. Therefore I will leave you with the peace of God.*

**DESIDERIO.** *All of us thank you, Master Adriano, for your courteous and loving invitation: nor does any of us intend to stay: because we all have some business to do before dinner: therefore remain in peace.*

**CLAUDIO.** *I will do so as well, thanking you and leaving you with a good evening.*

**FRANCESCO.** *Nor can I stay here: therefore, to God, Sir.*

**ADRIANO.** *Go all of you in pleasure: and remember to return tomorrow at the usual hour: for I shall be waiting for you with great desire: so that I may take a little restoration and consolation.*

**FRANCESCO.** *So we shall do.*

*Antigenidas of Thebes, a most ancient and expert player of the <term>Pipe <note>original: Piffero; in this classical context, Zarlino refers to the aulos, a double-reed instrument of ancient Greece</note></term>, had a disciple named Ismenias. After Ismenias had made excellent progress in the matters of Music, he once performed very well in singing at the Theater; yet, by his misfortune (as sometimes happens), he was not well-received by the people. While he remained unhappy, Antigenidas noticed this and said to him in such a way that everyone heard: "Do not concern yourself with the people, Ismenias; for it is enough that you please me and the <term>Muses <note>The nine Greek goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences</note></term>." He wished to demonstrate that one must place little value on the judgment of the unskilled multitude, who almost always know not how to discern or recognize good things from bad. For the greater part of them are men of low, vile, coarse, and abject intellect, given more to vice than to virtue. And he spoke well; for it seems to me a great and abundant reward for an Art and a Science: first to know that one knows, and then to be judged, praised, and esteemed by expert and judicious men.* <margin>Lucian in *Harmonides*</margin> *To this second point, that great musician Timotheus exhorted his disciple Harmonides: to this, I say: that he should seek to please those who are experts and of some authority, and place little value on the judgment of the common multitude. This advice is fitting not only for Harmonides, but for any other who wishes to appear in the theater of this mad world. For no matter what good thing one might do, when ignorance or malice—and sometimes both of these joined together—set themselves against it, it becomes impossible to satisfy not only the common people, but even those who make a profession of knowing. But to apply this story to my own case, I say that I had not yet written half of these Demonstrations when some professors of the Art of Music—though they may understand little of the science—doubting perhaps that I might reveal their ignorance by this means (as will indeed happen), almost rebuking me, exhorted me with many words that I ought to leave this*

# Reasoning

this undertaking: saying, that I could be content to have published the *Istitutioni* <note>Zarlino’s *Le Istitutioni harmoniche* (1558), his most famous work on the foundations of music</note>: which had been a good means for me to acquire a good reputation in the eyes of the world. Because it is a work that treats various matters, it is also very delightful and of no small utility to all those who delight in the art of composing **Music**: and the *Dimostrationi* <note>The current work, *Dimostrationi harmoniche* (1571)</note> being difficult material—dealing with Numbers and Proportions, which bring more tedium to the mind than delight—they would perhaps not be as pleasing to the professors of this art as the former were. Therefore, it would be better for me to turn my mind to spending time writing other things, such as matters belonging to the study of Holy Scripture. 

They do not know that although I apply myself to the study of Music—having the charge and obligation that I hold with my Most Illustrious Lords <note>Zarlino was the *Maestro di Cappella* at St. Mark's Basilica in Venice, answerable to the Venetian government</note>—I do not fail in those duties to which every man of my station is bound. For besides the *Trattato della Patienza* <note>*Treatise on Patience*, a devotional work Zarlino published in 1561</note> published by me many years ago, I have others as well, through which it can be seen that I do not fail in those things that can benefit others, and also myself. Therefore, having not yet even come out to show myself in this Theater—let alone be heard—and having hardly imagined coming here, among these foolish and ignorant people, without them hearing or seeing anything of what I had to recite, I was not only failing to receive honor or reward for my long labors, but I began to receive blame for them. 

Now that I have finally come out, and am heard by everyone who wishes to see and hear me, I do not know what they will want to say. I know all too well that these <term>Aesop’s Cocks <note>A reference to Aesop’s fable where a rooster finds a precious pearl but prefers a worthless grain of barley; it signifies an ignorant person who cannot recognize true value</note></term> will not be pleased: for it will go a long way in revealing (as they fear) their ignorance, and manifesting to the world how little they understand of the matters of Music. Indeed, so little that, upon considering it, they might greatly blush (if they have any shame for their own incompetence); for from these writings they will understand by how much ignorance their intellect is clouded, and how worthy they are to be numbered among Musicians. 

And if by chance they blame this new labor of mine, I wish to hold to what the aforementioned Master <note>Antigenidas, mentioned on the previous page</note> said to his disciple: to please all those who are students of good Music and desire to know the sound foundations of this Art—as to an Antigenidas—and even more so the Muses: that is, to men learned and skilled in the fine arts, dedicated to good character, caring little for those who delight more in blaming than in imitating the good works of others. And it will be enough for me, as a reward for my labors, to report that if they are not praised by these noble spirits, at least they are not blamed. 

But let us leave these things aside and return to our purpose. I say that on the following day, a great deal of time had already passed since the hour of Vespers. I had already gathered before everyone else with the good old **Master Adriano** <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), the influential Flemish composer and Zarlino's predecessor at St. Mark's</note>, and we had discussed many things regarding the previous day’s discourse, when the rest of our usual company appeared together, apologizing for their lateness, having been with the Lord Duke <note>Likely referring to a high-ranking Venetian official or a visiting noble</note> to see the marvelous building of the **Arsenal** <note>The Venetian Arsenal, the massive complex of shipyards and armories that was the center of Venice's naval power</note>. Whereupon, they having recounted with great wonder the infinite things they had seen there—all of which are for the preparations made for wars on Land and Sea—Master Adriano, seeing that a good part of the time had passed beyond the usual hour of other days, began to exhort us that we should give a beginning to the remainder of those things that were to be said in these our reasonings. Therefore, desiring to satisfy his will, I began to speak thus:

**GIOSEPPO**. To bring an end to this reasoning of ours, Monsieur, and to finish that which I have begun to demonstrate to you, I wish first—according to the promise I made you—to demonstrate a **Temperament** or **Participation** (as you prefer to name it) of artificial instruments, such as **Organs**, **Harpsichords**, **Lutes**, **Monochords**, and other similar ones that have a keyboard of the same manner.

This being done, having first added one string in the low register to the number of fifteen, and having divided them...

# Fifth Reasoning

...into five <term>Hexachords</term> <note>original: "Hexachordi"; six-note scales that were the foundation of Renaissance music theory</note>: to keep the order that our modern Musicians follow. I will then come to reason about the Species of the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: "Diapason"</note>; those of the <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapente"</note>; and those of the <term>Fourth</term> <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>. And finally, to conclude our reasoning, I will demonstrate a great part of those things that can occur regarding all the <term>Twelve Modes</term>, or Tones—whichever you wish to call them—and then I will make an end, God willing. But before I come to reason on anything, I want, according to our custom, for you to know certain Principles; for if these were not known to you, our work could not be brought to its desired end. **DESI.** Tell me, please, Master Gioseffo, before you proceed any further: what utility does it bring to know this <term>Temperament</term> <note>The adjustment of intervals to allow keyboard instruments to play in different keys</note> mentioned by you, or <term>Participation</term>, in the matters of Music? **GIOS.** To this I want our Master Claudio <note>Claudio Merulo (1533–1604), the famed organist of St. Mark's and a participant in this dialogue</note> to answer you: so that you may recognize that all those who practice on these sorts of instruments know the great utility derived from it. Therefore, Master Claudio, satisfy, I pray you, the request of this Gentleman. **CLAV.** To obey, I will do what pleases you; and I will say everything that comes to my memory regarding this matter. I will say first: that this was one of the beautiful inventions that could ever be found in Music. Which (according to what I have heard from others) has never been—not only touched upon, but not even hinted at—by any Greek, Latin, or Barbarian writer. Whence, to tell you of its utility, I say it is such: that by means of it, one can know infallibly by what amount every interval found in the instruments—which were named a short while ago—has been increased or diminished outside of its true and natural proportion. And it is something that is not only useful to know for the perfection of the Science, but is also necessary for the Art of building such instruments with reason. For it helps much to know the reason for such temperament, and perhaps more than anyone could imagine. Since in the measurement of the sounding bodies that go into such instruments—which are the Pipes and the Strings—one sees that when such bodies are regulated, and the places where the strings rest upon the bridges (that is, the interval that contains the string) and other things besides are made with measure and proportion, a very great utility follows. From this results a great and excellent quality in such instruments, provided one has also well-regulated their bodies. And so great is the difference between an interval that is not proportioned and one that is made with proportion, that it is (I will say it thus) as light is to darkness. Because when strings are stretched over those places that are not proportioned, the sounds that arise from them are also disproportionate among themselves; so that, one being longer or shorter than it should be and out of measure, in tuning them, one becomes tighter or slacker than the other. Thus one hears one having greater vehemence, or being weaker than the other, being disproportionate between them. But when such places are proportioned, everything becomes convenient, and the whole stands well. And this is not only useful in regulating the extensions and the places where the strings are placed, but also for the size of the bodies of the pipes of Organs, as I have said. For by such means, they come to be regulated not only as to their length, but also as to their diameters, as those who are skilled in the art of making such instruments know all too well. These are the things I can tell you that have come to my mind, but there are many others which would take a long time if one wanted to recount them one by one. **DESI.** These few are enough for me; for from them I understand the utility that this matter brings to Music. Therefore it is your turn now, Master Gioseffo, to follow by saying what you wished to say. **FRAN.** I also want to ask you one thing before you proceed further. **GIOS.** Say it, I am listening to you. **FRAN.** For what reason do you not first demonstrate the Species of the consonances you named, and also the Modes, and then do the Participation or Temperament of which you speak? **GIOS.** Many reasons move me to do this, of which I will tell you only one: and it is this. It matters little to me whether such demonstrations are done before or after the demonstration of the named Temperament, were it not that (as I have already said) many difficulties are avoided; because after the Participation or Temperament is made, everything is demonstrated more conveniently and with fewer entanglements than it would be otherwise. **ADRI.** What are these en...

# Reasoning

...diatonic? **GIOS.** The doubling of the string 'd': speaking according to our practical method—
<margin>Part 2, chapter 40.</margin>
as I have shown in the *Institutions* <note>original: "Istitutioni"; Zarlino’s "Istitutioni harmoniche", his most famous work</note>—which is found between the string <term>Nete synemmenon</term> <note>original: "Netesynemennon"; the highest note of the "connected" tetrachord in the Ancient Greek system</note> and the <term>Paranete diezeugmenon</term> <note>original: "Paranetediezeugmenon"; the second-highest note of the "disjunct" or separated tetrachord</note>. These contain the interval of the <term>Comma</term> <note>A tiny musical interval, the small "leftover" difference resulting from tuning pure intervals</note>, just as I showed you yesterday in the eighth, ninth, and tenth propositions. This is done to gain a <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapente"</note> and a <term>Fourth</term> <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> that would otherwise be lost if the named string *Nete* were not added. This string creates such a doubling by the addition of the <term>Synemmenon tetrachord</term> <note>The four-note scale segment that allowed for "B-flat" in ancient theory</note> to the other four, and also to compensate for the loss of many imperfect consonances <note>Intervals like thirds and sixths</note> which are regained by means of such a <term>Temperament</term> <note>The intentional "mistuning" of certain intervals so that all keys sound acceptable on a keyboard</note>. By this means, everything is made easy and clear; otherwise, it would be a long and difficult task to show how they are acquired by adding the interval of the Comma, now in the low range and now in the high. **ADRI.** I have understood very well, and I like it when difficulties are removed from these matters; thus, I remain satisfied. But tell me: in the <term>Participation</term> <note>Another term for temperament, where the "pure" mathematical intervals "participate" in a shared adjustment</note> or Temperament that you are about to create, will there be Major and Minor Tones, just as they are found in the divisions of the <term>Monochords</term> <note>An ancient scientific instrument with a single string used to measure musical intervals</note> we have already seen? 
<margin>Part 2, chapters 43 & 44.</margin>
Similarly, will those same intervals be found that you demonstrated in the participation made in the *Institutions*? **GIOS.** I already said yesterday that this Participation or Temperament will be of another sort, and different from that one. It will keep the <term>Major Third</term> <note>original: "Ditono"</note> and the <term>Minor Sixth</term> <note>original: "Hexachordo minore"</note> in their true and natural form <note>Meaning they are tuned to "pure" whole-number ratios like 5:4 and 8:5</note>, but the other intervals will be comprised of another form, and their proportions will be dull and irrational <note>original: "sorde & irrationali"; mathematical ratios that cannot be expressed as simple fractions, often involving square roots</note>, as you shall see. And the Tones—although they cannot be named in their forms with certain and rational numbers—will nonetheless be equal in proportion, just as those used in the <term>Diatonic Ditone</term> <note>A tuning system where every whole step is an identical 9:8 ratio</note> are found to be equal in proportion, where each one in every tetrachord is of a <term>Sesquioctave</term> proportion <note>The 9:8 ratio, the standard "Major Tone"</note>. And because those in the Participation made in the *Institutions* differ from each other by a seventh part of a Comma—and the Major Third and Minor Sixth are contained together with every other interval by an irrational proportion—this system will be very different from that one. **CLAV.** So you wish to make a new Temperament and demonstrate a new Participation. **GIOS.** That is what I wish to do. **CLAV.** This pleases me greatly; therefore, the sooner you begin to demonstrate this thing to us, the more we shall cherish it. **GIOS.** To return, then, to where I left off, I say: you must first know the form of those intervals that increase or decrease, so that we do not proceed without knowledge of what we ought to know first. Therefore, we shall come to their Definitions, so that from them you may come to such knowledge. But take note: I do not wish to define for you any intervals except those that undergo an alteration of their proper form. As for those that are not subject to such change and remain in their pure essence, you are already capable of understanding them. And because the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: "Diapason"</note> cannot be altered by increasing or decreasing it more or less than its natural form—which is the <term>Double Proportion</term> <note>The 2:1 ratio</note>—without offending the ear, regardless of the tuning, temperament, or participation one chooses; and similarly, because the Major Third and the Minor Sixth remain in this temperament in their true and natural form and proportion; therefore, whenever I name these three intervals, you are always to understand them in every place as being in their perfection. But when I mean to speak of any other interval that is altered and outside of its form, I will always add a word to alert you as to which interval should be understood. Beginning, then, with the <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapente"</note>, which is closest to the form of the Octave in its proportion and is greater than any other simple interval, whatever it may be, I shall speak in this manner:

# DEFINITION
## THE FIRST.

->The <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapente"</note> is a consonance which, in its temperament, remains diminished and reduced from its true form by one whole quarter part of a <term>Comma</term> <note>A tiny interval representing the small mathematical "gap" between pure musical ratios; here, it refers to the fractional adjustment needed for keyboard tuning</note>.<-

**ADRI.** Which is a larger quantity: two-seventh parts, or a quarter part of a thing? **FRAN.** I would believe that two-seventh parts are larger than a quarter part. **GIOS.** That is so: because a quarter part is smaller than two-sevenths by a twenty-eighth part of a thing. **ADRI.** Therefore, the Fifth gains in this <term>participation</term> <note>original: "partecipatione"; a 16th-century term for temperament or the distribution of the tuning "error"</note> that you wish to make, a twenty-eighth part of a Comma; a part of which it was deprived in the temperament described in the *Institutions* <note>original: "Istitutioni"; referring to Zarlino’s seminal 1558 work, *Le Istitutioni harmoniche*</note>. Thus, it is closer to its perfection when reduced by a quarter than when it is made imperfect by two-sevenths. **GIOS.** It is true. **ADRI.** By my faith, I like this gain! For the <term>Major Third</term> <note>original: "Ditono"</note> and the <term>minor Sixth</term> <note>original: "Hexachordo minore"</note> remain in their natural perfection, and the Fifth approaches its perfect state; as does the <term>Fourth</term> <note>original: "Diateſſaron"</note> by logic. **GIOS.** This is true: for whatever is taken from the Fifth is given to the Fourth, and whatever is added to the former is taken from the latter. And it cannot be otherwise: for since the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: "Diapaſon"</note> remains in its true form (as I have told you), and being composed of these two intervals—as I demonstrated in the Fourth Proposition of our second discussion—it must necessarily follow this way: that what is taken from one is restored to the other, so that things proceed justly. Therefore, we shall say that:

## DEFINITION II.

->The Fourth is a consonance which remains in its temperament increased beyond its true form by one whole quarter part of a Comma.<-

**LAV.** Therefore, this consonance will become smaller by a twenty-eighth part of a Comma compared to that which is set down in the temperament of the *Institutions*. **GIOS.** That is how the matter stands. **ADRI.** Can this difference cause any ill effect? **GIOS.** No, sir; for such a quantity is so small that you could hardly imagine it. **ADRI.** Pray, tell it to us. **GIOS.** I am happy to. The Comma is an eighty-first part of a sounding body <note>referring to the length of a musical string</note>. If you divide this Comma into seven parts (as was done in the temperament of the *Institutions*), one-seventh part comes to be 1/567th of the whole aforementioned body; for if you multiply all these parts by the number seven, they make 567. But because the difference between two-sevenths and one-quarter is one twenty-eighth, this difference comes to be the 1/2268th part of such a body, given that 81 multiplied by 28 results in 2268. **DESI.** This part, which is the aforementioned difference, is so small that it is almost beyond the reach of the senses, as I believe. **GIOS.** You believe correctly: because

### DEFINITION V.

**The <term>minor Tone</term> <note>original: "Tuono minore"</note> is an interval which, after being tempered, is increased by two full quarter-parts of the Comma.**

*That is, by a full half. ADRI. I remember that in the Twenty-sixth Definition of our Second discussion, you said that the Comma is the interval by which the Major Tone exceeds the minor; therefore, the Comma is the difference found between the Major Tone and the minor. GIOS. So it seems to me. ADRI. This gives me such content that I would never tire of speaking with you on this subject. But let us move forward.*

Therefore, I am not surprised if Aristotle, that great Philosopher, in the <note>original: "Problemi"</note> *Problems* <note>The "Problemata," a series of questions on science and music attributed to Aristotle.</note> calls only the Octave, and no other interval, a perfect consonance. This interval does not wish to give nor receive anything beyond what it holds; thus it seems to me that the other intervals are better companions: for they agree among themselves and allow themselves (when done with skill) to be handled as one wishes. From this we gather that the interval of the Octave will always be <term>rational</term> <note>In music theory, "rational" refers to intervals that can be expressed as simple fractions or whole-number ratios.</note>, and can be described with rational numbers wherever it is found. ### DEFINITION VIII.

The **First species** of the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: "Diapason"</note> is that which contains the <term>Major Semitone</term> between the third and fourth strings, and between the seventh and eighth strings. The **Second** is that which contains it between the second and third, and between the sixth and seventh strings. *CLAUDIO: I now wish to ask you two things, Master Gioseffo. But as for the second question, I want you to know: that what I do, I do not do without reason, and the causes that move me are many. In the first of these, which is the lowest, the Major Tone is found; in the second, the Minor; and in the third, the Major Semitone. Similarly, the Major Tone is placed again in the fourth, and the Minor in the fifth...*

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Gioseffo Zarlino justifies his controversial decision to renumber the musical modes, moving the "First Mode" from the traditional starting note of A (the Dorian on A) to C (the Ionian). <header>Book Five.</header>

*...in the sixth place also the <term>Major Tone</term>; and in the seventh and last place in the high register is found the <term>Major Semitone</term>: I clearly understood that such an <term>Octave</term> <note>original: "Diapason"</note>, divided according to the nature of the <term>Harmonic Number</term> <note>Zarlino's mathematical theory of proportions that defines musical intervals</note>, is located between our modern strings C, D, E, F, G, a, ♮, and c: and this was also the first Octave that was naturally considered in Music.*
*Wherefore I was forced by every reason to believe: that being the first—among the others which (by the addition of the strings Γ, A, and ♮ in the low register, and d, e, f, g, and a with many others in the high register) are born after this one—that it should also hold the first place among all the others: and that being in this <term>Genus</term> <note>The "diatonic" genus of scales</note> more natural than any other, it should also hold the name of **First Species**: and that the others, which followed this one one by one, should hold their places according to how they were positioned in order: and that they should have their beginnings on the strings signified and noted by the first seven letters that I have shown you. This, then, was the first reason that moved me to do this.* CLAV. *What do you say to this, Sir? It seems to me that this cannot be contradicted in any way.* ADRI. *In truth, it cannot; and it seems to me that Master Gioseffo has a great reason. And to tell you the truth: there was nothing in Music that seemed stranger to me than this. For since we have this order of syllables <term>Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, and La</term> <note>The six syllables of the hexachord system, the basis of sight-singing in the Renaissance</note>, it was surely against what is right that the First Species of all the primary consonances had to begin on the second syllable, and not on the first of such an order. Therefore, I am highly pleased that Master Gioseffo wishes to discuss this thing, and that he has entered into this good opinion of ordering this disordered order.* GIOS. *Sir: I am very happy that this thought of mine pleases you. Since I have always known you to be a man of intellect and judgment, I could not imagine in my mind that things done with reason would displease you. Therefore, I wish to cheerfully follow with the **Second reason**: which is the very same that moved you. Because our ancestors, having reduced the order of musical strings into <term>Hexachords</term> <note>original: "Hexachordi"; six-note scales</note>, and having attributed to them that order of Syllables that you named: it was rather necessary to give the beginning to these Species on the first syllable, Ut, rather than on Re, which is the second: so that when one arrives at the Fourth species in their manner, one would not have to turn back and begin in the fourth place of such an order from the syllable Ut: which, by every right, should hold the first and not the last place, as you see done in their Fourth species of all the primary Consonances. This, then, was the second reason.* FRAN. *This is a reasonable reason.* GIOS. *The **Third reason** was: that besides what I have said, which is all done with reason, I saw that by placing as the foundation of these Species the first string of the named divided Octave, and applying to them (to speak to you in a practical way) the syllables Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, and La: let us set aside for a moment that these syllables serve the memory to remember that the First is the foundation of the First species of each of the named consonances, and the Second that of the Second, and so the others in order: we would also have gathered in this First species all the Species of the other named consonances, which would orderly have their beginning and foundation on C, the first string of the said Octave, and on Ut, the first syllable of our Hexachord: which would turn out extremely well, and better than what our Ancients did; who, having first placed the First species on the string A and on the syllable Re, although they followed after and everything turned out convenient for them, yet they could not place the species of the <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapente"</note> in such a way one after another: because the Second species could not fall between the string ♮ and F <note>This interval is a diminished fifth, which Zarlino considers unusable as a "species" of a perfect fifth</note>. Wherefore they were forced to begin on the string D and follow one by one. But they could not yet give a beginning to the species of their <term>Fourth</term> <note>original: "Diateffaron"</note> on such a string: because the Third species can in no way fall between the string F and ♮: since it is (as you know, and as you call it) a <term>Tritone</term> <note>original: "Tritono"</note>, which is a most dissonant interval in Music.* ADRI. *This is only too true, and truly I tell you that this order is very necessary: first to regulate and direct the matters of Music well, and then it is useful for the memory of things, as you have said; therefore, I highly praise this thing. And even if to some at first sight this thing will perhaps seem difficult and bitter, do not doubt that use will make it easy and sweeten the whole.* GIOS. *I believe so...*

Sir. *But the Fourth reason that has moved me is this: because I saw that I could arrange the Modes, or <term>Tones</term> <note>The Renaissance terms for musical scales</note>, which are (as you may remember) Twelve: one after the other in a natural and uninterrupted order, unlike what has been done until now. For by arranging or attributing the First Mode to the first <term>Octave</term> <note>original: "Diapason"</note> C to c, and to the first syllable **Ut** <note>The predecessor to the modern "Do"</note>, following the other syllables or voices and the other Modes in order, their final strings came naturally to be C, D, E, F, G, and a. Their melodies, with a beautiful and regulated order, came to end on the syllables Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, and La, as you will be able to see in the proper places. And the Sixteen strings—<term>Gamma</term> <note>original: "Γ"</note>, A, B-natural <note>original: "♮"</note>, C, D, E, F, G, a, b-natural, c, d, e, f, g, and aa—will come to contain all these Modes, both the <term>Authentic</term> and the <term>Plagal</term> <note>Authentic modes range upward from their starting note; Plagal modes range both above and below it</note>, without any string being left over beyond those of the said Modes. Therefore, the utility and convenience that this order brings—as it seems to me—made me enter into this thought many days ago. These things invited and persuaded me; reason gave me heart and encouraged me; and the very nature of the matter constrained me and did me violence. You will perceive this from what I am about to demonstrate to you. So, if ever in the past I held another opinion on this, and intended to follow the Ancients, now in everything and for everything I move away from it.* **FRAN.** *Many times I have been greatly marveled within myself by these orders of species, and I did not know how to find any other reason for them except that our predecessors had wished it so. But I am much pleased by the reasons you have stated, which (even if they brought nothing else) I will carry with me to Ferrara as beautiful and new things; and I promise you that we will put them into practice with all our power.* **GIOS.** *I do not want you to believe, however, that I wish to be a destroyer of the works of the Ancients, for I never had such a wicked thought. Rather, I want you to think that, while leaving their works in their own being, I will come to change them only according to certain <term>accidents</term> <note>In Renaissance logic, an "accident" is a property (like a name) that can change without changing the "substance" or essence of the thing</note>, such as "First" and "Second," without any other alteration of their substance; and I will always seek to make the matters of this science easier. Nor should you think that I could do otherwise, since any species of consonance is always immutable and invariable regarding its form. But as for the accidents, which are also extrinsic—such as being first or second, or being low or high—they can be varied without any alteration regarding the name. And if you wish to see that this is so, take any Octave you like and give it the name of First or Second, as you best please; such an accident will not have the power to make it vary in form. For if you attributed a thousand and then another thousand names to it, and moved it or gave it a thousand varied places, it would never change its form and substance, but would always remain the same. The name of "First" or "Second" arises from pure <term>Relation</term>, which among other accidents is the weakest and most extrinsic to things reduced into an order. Hence, such a relation can be changed at our every pleasure without any variety in the Form or Substance of things. But if one tone or semitone is removed from it, transporting it toward the high or toward the low, there is no doubt that such an Octave will not be as it was before, but will change the first form into another, because it will be changed in its intrinsic and essential things. Therefore, to return to saying something on the point: I say that if I have given the Second place to the Octave D to d in the order of its species, and the first to C to c, for this reason I have changed neither the one nor the other in form and essence, but they remain in their first being. And if the Ancients attributed the first species of the Octave to the one placed between the <term>Proslambanomenos</term> <note>The lowest note of the Greek system, usually A</note> and the <term>Mese</term> <note>The middle note of the Greek system, an octave higher than the Proslambanomenos</note>, they did so because the Proslambanomenos was the first string of the order of their sounds; wherefore it was right that on such a string, as the first of all others, they should give a beginning to their Species. This is especially true because they never took into consideration whether the named Octave was divided by <term>harmonic division</term> or not, as we have; and this was not without purpose. Since we have added another string in the low register to their order, which you call <term>Gamma Ut</term> <note>The low G added in the medieval system</note>, and considering the said Octave C to c divided in the named manner, it is necessary that we have another consideration of it.* **DESI.** *In truth, it is a very reasonable and laudable thing that you have entered into this honored thought, worthy to be embraced by everyone, because it seems to me that you have arranged the matters of Music very elegantly.* **GIOS.** *I want to add yet another reason to the others that pushed me to want to hold this order, which has just now occurred to me: and*

### DEFINITION IX.

The First species of the <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapente"</note> is that which contains the <term>Major Semitone</term> between the third and the fourth string. The Second is that which contains it between the second and the third. The Third is that which contains it between the first and the second. And the Fourth is that which contains it between the fourth and the last: always moving from the <term>low to the high</term> <note>original: "dal graue allo acuto"</note>.

The <term>Octave</term> is said to be arithmetically divided into two parts when it is split by a middle string in such a manner that the <term>Fourth</term> occupies the low position and the <term>Fifth</term> the high position within it, in such a division.

*ADRI. These things are manifest also from what you have demonstrated: because the seventeenth proposal of our First Discourse (if I remember correctly) demonstrates that the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: Duplo</note> interval arises from the conjunction of the two major <term>superparticulars</term> <note>A ratio where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator (e.g., 3:2 or 4:3).</note>: the <term>Sesquialtera</term> <note>The ratio 3:2, which produces the musical Fifth.</note> and the <term>Sesquiterza</term> <note>The ratio 4:3, which produces the musical Fourth.</note>; and the eighteenth demonstrates that when these two are added together, they constitute <term>Harmonic Proportionality</term>. Thus, since the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: Duplo</note> interval is the form of the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: Diapason</note>, the Sesquialtera is that of the <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: Diapente</note>, and the Sesquiterza is that of the <term>Fourth</term> <note>original: Diatessaron</note>, adding these last two together necessarily constitutes this proportionality. This also follows when the Octave is divided in the manner stated in the definition into the two named parts by a middle string. This is a thing that no one of sound judgment would deny. FRAN. Nor can this be denied, sir, speaking of the Octave arithmetically divided, as the definition says: because from the twelfth proposal of the Second Discourse one sees it demonstrated that within this <term>Arithmetic progression</term> 4, 3, 2, one finds the ratio 4 and 2 (which is the form of the Octave), divided by the 3 into two parts: that is, into 4 and 3, which is the Sesquiterza (the form of the Fourth), and into 3 and 2, the Sesquialtera (the form of the Fifth). And because (as I have said many times) the larger number of any order of musical proportions represents the lower part, or the larger string of any division, one cannot deny that the Fourth—placed between the terms 4 and 3—occupies the lower part; and that the Fifth—placed between 3 and 2—holds the higher part in an Octave divided in such a manner, and that it is divided in <term>Arithmetic proportionality</term> <note>In an arithmetic division of the octave, the smaller interval (the Fourth) is on the bottom, whereas in a harmonic division, the larger interval (the Fifth) is on the bottom.</note>. ADRI. This is true. GIOS. But to come to the definition of all those Modes which are in the first part of the two mentioned: we will first define all the Modes together; then we will define all those contained by an odd number, such as the First, Third, Fifth, Seventh, Ninth, and Eleventh. Having done that, we will define those of an even number, such as the Second, Fourth, Sixth, Eighth, Tenth, and Twelfth. Hence, we shall name the first group (as they are called by practitioners) Principal or <term>Authentic</term>; but the others we shall call Non-principal, Lateral, or <term>Plagal</term>, because they are placed at the side of the first. Let us then define all the first ones together with all the second ones in this manner.*

LAV. *I do not believe there is anything in Music more obscure and difficult to understand than the matter of the Modes according to the use of the Ancients. This is because not a single musical example of theirs remains in the world. With other things, we have at least some small trace, as we see in ancient buildings which belong to the science of Architecture; even if some of them are not seen in their perfection, at least their floor plan is found, from which one can draw some knowledge of their form. But regarding what is found on this subject of the Modes, it generates confusion rather than knowledge.*

GIOS. *Truly, it is just as you say. Please look, since we are on this subject, at what you can make of reading Boethius on this matter: <margin>On Music, Book 4, Chapter 14.</margin> what distinction can you make between these Modes, one from another, based on what he writes? For he maintains that by making the entire order of the <term>Hypodorian</term> <note>A low-pitched ancient Greek scale.</note> higher by a Tone—while keeping those same original intervals exactly as they were, without leaving any out—the <term>Hypophrygian</term> mode is generated. And by making this order higher again by a Tone, similarly without moving any of the first intervals, the <term>Hypolydian</term> mode is made; and so on with the others, making them higher or lower than one another by a Tone or a Semitone, without any alteration of the first arrangement.*

DESI. *It seems a very strange thing to me that Boethius would make such an error.*

GIOS. *This is made clear by his words and the examples he provides, and it cannot be denied. But it is not to be wondered at, because anyone can be mistaken in things in which they are not very practiced, as perhaps Boethius was. Yet, that the Modes were distant from each other by a Tone or a Semitone is not an error at all, because it conforms to what Ptolemy writes in Chapter 10 of Book 2 of his Music. From this, we see that our predecessors have erred in naming "Dorian" that mode which they call the First; "Phrygian" the one they call the Third; and "Lydian" the one they call the Fifth. This is because the First is distant from the Third by a Tone, and the Third from the Fifth by a semitone, as is known to all who practice Music. Therefore, if we wish to align ourselves with the Ancients—at least in names—we must call "Dorian" what I call the First in this discussion, which is contained in the first species of the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: Diapason</note> harmonically divided, which I defined above. We must call "Phrygian" what I call the Second, which is contained in the second species; and "Lydian" what I call the Third, which is contained within the third species. Being understood this way, they will be placed in order according to the minds of those two most celebrated authors named. And this will truly be the natural order, because to every note of our <term>Hexachord</term> <note>The six-note scale (ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la) used in medieval and Renaissance music pedagogy.</note>, without any interruption, one can conveniently attribute the end of two Modes: one <term>Even</term> <note>Plagal modes, which sit lower relative to their final note.</note> and the other <term>Odd</term> <note>Authentic modes, which sit higher.</note>. In this way, the First will be distant from the Third by a Tone, the Third from the Fifth by another Tone, and the Fifth from the Seventh by a Semitone. And perhaps it would not be wrong to say in this new order that the First is the Dorian, the Third the Phrygian, the Fifth the Lydian, the Seventh the Mixolydian (or Locrian), the Ninth the Ionian, and the Eleventh the Aeolian, as an order more conforming to the minds of the two named authors and many others besides.*

DESI. *In truth, the first three Modes are a Tone apart from each other. Thus, I cannot see on what foundation our predecessors called their "First" mode Dorian, which would actually be your Third; and their "Third" Phrygian, which corresponds to your Fifth; and so on. But be that as it may, we must not focus on names now, but on the things themselves. Therefore, I greatly like the order you have proposed to follow; but please take care that we do not become confused.*

GIOS. *There will be no confusion at all, as long as you keep this in memory: that when...*

### DEFINITION XVII.

-> **The true final <term>string</term> <note>original: "chorda"; here meaning the specific note or pitch.</note> of any Mode, whether Principal or Non-Principal: is the lowest note of its <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapente".</note>.** <-

*DESIDERIO. It is necessary that every thing has its end: thus it is necessary that the Modes also have a note in which each one must regularly conclude. GIOSEFFO. ### DEFINITION XIX.

*ADRIAN. Give us an example: so that you may be more easily understood. GIOSEFFO. I will. You know all too well what <term>Rational and Irrational Quantity</term><note>In Renaissance music theory, a "rational" quantity is a ratio of whole numbers (like 2:1 for an octave). Therefore, Sir: if you had before you a mountain of a thousand florins, and another person came and added five hundred to them, would you not know the quantity and sum of all that money? ADRIAN. Yes, indeed. GIOSEFFO. Similarly: if four hundred were taken away from this sum, would you not also know the sum that would remain before you? ADRIAN. Without doubt: for eleven hundred would remain. GIOSEFFO. You see then, that by knowing what is added and what is taken away, you also know the increase and decrease of your florins? So, regarding our subject, I say: that by knowing the proportion you wish to add to or take away from another (be it greater or smaller than itself), you also easily know what results from that addition or subtraction. And this happens because all these quantities are rational, and can be described with numbers. But it will not happen so when one of them is rational and the other irrational; or indeed when both were irrational. For that which would be born from them would be entirely irrational. And take the example of the florins, since we are discussing them: if you had many before you, of which you knew the number, I say that if you added to them, or took away from them, a quantity of which you did not know the amount, the quantity that remained would also be unknown and irrational to you. ADRIAN. I now understand very well everything you have said to me; though you are teasing me with the business of the florins. GIOSEFFO. I am not teasing you at all, Sir, because you are not a man to be teased. But I have given you the example of them because I know that you know what they are, having earned plenty of them by means of your own merit; and you have honorably distributed them, giving to each of your closest kin their share, and you have also saved a good portion for yourself, which will allow you to live happily, if you wish to spend it. <image-desc>Two technical diagrams related to music theory. FRANCESCO. *Here you wish to demonstrate Participation <note>Italian: *Partecipatione*; a Renaissance term for musical temperament, describing how intervals "participate" in a shared adjustment of pitch to make a scale more playable.</note>: from what I see: is it not so?* GIOVANNI. *It is so. Therefore, following the First proposition of the past day, let there be the <term>Diatonic Monochord</term><note>A scientific instrument with a single string and a movable bridge, used to measure the exact physical lengths required to produce specific musical notes.</note>: which, for its Twenty-fourth [proposition], similarly contains among the number of fifteen strings: considered however as marked in this manner: hb, Kb, Cb, lb, Eb, mb, nb, ob, pb, cb, qb, eb, rb, sb, & tb. Eight times the <term>Octave</term><note>original: *Diapason*</note>: Seven times the <term>Fifth</term><note>original: *Diapente*</note>: & eight times the <term>Fourth</term><note>original: *Diatessaron*</note>. And we wish to reduce such a number to a <term>Temperament</term><note>The process of slightly shifting the pitch of certain notes so that all keys sound acceptable on a fixed-pitch instrument like a harpsichord.</note>, or proportion: so that we acquire two Fifths, which between the Fourth & the Eighth string: & between the Eleventh & the Fifteenth: that is, between l b and o b: & between q b & t b have no place: & two Fourths, which are missing between the First & the Fourth: & between the Eighth & the Eleventh string: that is, between hb & lb: & between ob & qb: leaving the <term>Ditone</term><note>The Major Third (ratio 81:64 in Pythagorean tuning, but usually 5:4 in meantone temperament).</note> & the <term>Minor Sixth</term><note>original: *Hexachordo minore*</note> in their true & natural forms, or proportions. I first accommodate upon the string h n the interval of the <term>Comma</term><note>The Syntonic Comma (ratio 81:80) is a tiny pitch discrepancy between four pure fifths and two octaves plus a major third. It is the "error" that must be distributed during the tuning process.</note>: by the Thirty-sixth proposition of the Third day: at its proportion toward h: in such a way that n b comes to be its acute <note>higher pitch</note> extreme. Which Comma, by the Eleventh also of the said day, I divide into four parts: whence taking the three parts, more grave <note>lower pitch</note> at point G: by the Twenty-sixth definition of today: I come to make the interval C & n smaller by a fourth part of the said Comma: & increase the interval n & c by such an amount. But because*

# Fifth Part.

...that C and *n* contain, according to the First [proposition] of yesterday: two major Tones, one minor, and one minor Semitone: therefore C and *n*, according to the Thirtieth of the Second [book], will result in being a <term>Diapente</term><note>A perfect fifth, an interval encompassing five notes of the scale.</note> contained in its true form. But C and *n* remain lacking and diminished by a fourth part of the <term>Comma</term><note>A very small musical interval, specifically the difference between a major and minor tone (the syntonic comma) or other small discrepancies in tuning.</note>: which is G and *n*: thus, by the First definition of today: the Diapente C and *n* remains diminished by the fourth part of a Comma, and <term>tempered</term><note>Adjusted away from a pure mathematical ratio to allow for better harmony across different keys.</note> between C and G, according to our purpose. Likewise: because *n* and *c* contain one major Tone, with one minor, and one major Semitone: therefore, by the Twenty-eighth of the Second reasoning: *n* and *c* is a <term>Diateffaron</term><note>A perfect fourth, an interval encompassing four notes of the scale.</note> in its true form: which, being increased by a fourth part of the said Comma—which is G and *n*—I say that G and *c*, by the second Definition of today, contains the Diateffaron increased by a fourth part of the said Comma, and tempered according to our intention.

I now add, by the aforementioned Thirty-sixth [proposition], the Comma to the string *mb* toward *b*: in such a way that *mb* is the low extreme: and I divide it, by the named Eleventh [proposition], into four parts: then, leaving one part closest to *m*, between F and *c* one will have a tempered Diapente: because it contains, by the Thirtieth [proposition] mentioned above: Three tones and one major Semitone: diminished, however, by a fourth part of the Comma, which is *m* and F. But between C and F we will have a Diateffaron, which by the said Twenty-eighth [proposition] contains two Tones and one major Semitone: increased, however, by the part *m* and F of the said Comma. And so these two consonances will be reduced to their temperament: *mb* and *cb* being a Diapente, and *Cb* and *mb* a Diateffaron. Wherefore *Fb* and *cb* remain imperfect by a fourth part of the Comma: which, by the Definition, is a tempered Diapente: and *Cb* and *Fb* come to be increased by such a quantity: Therefore *Cb* and *Fb* become, according to the Definition, a Diateffaron similarly increased by such a quantity.

Further on: by the fourth Definition: *Fb* and *Gb* come to be a tempered Tone: given that *mb* and *nb* (a major Tone) is found diminished by two fourth parts of the Comma—that is, by one fourth part *mF*, and by one fourth part *Gn*—as can be seen. But because C and E is a <term>Ditono</term><note>A major third, literally "two tones."</note>: and these two terms remaining in their natural proportion: I say *Eb* and *pb*, by the Thirtieth of the Second day, is a Diapente: because it contains three Tones and one major Semitone: which we will accommodate to its temperament: adding, by the Thirty-sixth of the Third [book], the Comma to the string *pb* toward the lower part: and dividing it, as we did the others, into four equal parts: taking only the three lower ones: and between *Eb* and *♮b* we will have the Diapente tempered: and diminished, by the Twenty-sixth definition, by one fourth part of a Comma: which is *♮* and *p*. Wherefore between *Gb* and *♮b* we will also have a Ditono contained in its true proportion: because having been found first between *nb* and *pb* in its true form: it is made lower, by the Twenty-seventh Definition of today, by as much quantity as that of *Gn* and of *♮p*.

And because *Eb* and *ob* contain one major Tone, one minor, and one major Semitone: therefore *Eb* and *ob*, by the Twenty-eighth of the Second [book], is a Diateffaron. Wherefore to reduce it to its temperament: we will add the Comma to the string marked *o*, toward the high side: which, divided in the said manner into four parts, and the fourth part *o* and *a* being added to *Eb* and *ob*: between *Eb* and *ab* we will have the Diateffaron increased by a fourth part of the Comma: which will be reduced, according to its Definition, to its temperament. We will also say, by the fifth Definition, that *Gb* and *ab* is a Tone reduced to its temperament: because *nb* and *ob* being a minor Tone: it becomes increased between *Gb* and *ab* by two fourth parts of a Comma: which are *Gn* and *oa*: as is manifest. Which is also done by the major *ob* and *pb*: because *ob* is made higher at *ab* by a fourth part of a Comma: and *pb* is made lower at *♮b* by another fourth part. Wherefore it comes to be diminished by an entire half of a Comma. Therefore, by the Fourth definition: this Tone comes to be contained between *ab* and *♮b* made smaller by half a Comma.

Furthermore, because *ob* and *cb* contains a major Tone and a major Semitone: therefore by the Twenty-sixth of the Second [book], *ob* and *cb* comes to be the interval of the Semitone: contained in its true form. And because such an interval is made smaller by a fourth part of the Comma *o*: which is *o* and *a*: therefore, by the third Definition: *ab* and *cb* is the interval of the <term>Semiditono</term><note>A minor third.</note>, reduced to its temperament. Again: because *pb* and *cb* is a major Semitone: and from the string *♮b* it is increased by a fourth of a Comma, which is *♮* and *p*: therefore according to the Sixth definition given above: *♮b* and *cb* is the interval of the major Semitone increased by a fourth part of the Comma: and reduced to its temperament. Which can also be said of the Semitone *Eb* and *mb*: which is increased by such quantity from the Comma...

->Reasoning<-

*...but m: which is m & F: as is clearly seen. Now, to acquire a <term>Fifth (Diapente)</term><note>A perfect fifth.</note> that is not found between string lb & ob—because this interval contains only two minor Tones and one major Semitone, and according to the Thirty-seventh [proposition] of the Second [book], it should contain two major Tones, one minor, and one major Semitone—it remains diminished by an entire <term>Comma</term>.* This comma, according to the Twenty-fifth definition likewise of the Second day, is the difference found between a major Tone and a minor one. Therefore, I add the Comma *l* to the string *lb* toward the bass; thus, between the whole of this Comma added to *lb* and the string *ob*, the Fifth is contained in its true and natural proportion. I now divide the said Comma, by the Eleventh [proposition] of the Third [book], into four equal parts. Because the entire interval of Comma *l* joined to the string *lb* creates a Fifth with *ab* that is larger than a fourth part of a Comma (which is *o* and *a*), I first leave aside the lower fourth part of the named Comma, equal to *o* and *a*, and the Fifth results in its true form. But for the sake of the <term>temperament</term><note>The adjustment of musical intervals from their pure mathematical ratios to make them usable in all keys.</note>, I then leave another following fourth part; and thus between *Db* and *ab*, by the Definition, the Fifth becomes tempered according to our purpose. Furthermore, the major Tone found between *cb* and *lb* is found to be diminished and reduced by two-fourth parts (or we might say by an entire half of the Comma) by virtue of string *Db*, which are *D* and *l*. And the minor Tone found between *lb* and *Eb* is increased by that same quantity, according to their definitions. I also say that the <term>Fourth (Diatessaron)</term>, which is found between *lb* and *nb* in its true and natural form, is found to be increased by a fourth part of the Comma; for if string *nb* becomes lower by a fourth part at string *Gb*, and string *lb* extends further toward the bass by two fourth parts at string *Db*, there is no doubt that between *Db* and *Gb* one finds the Fourth increased by the fourth part of a Comma, according to the Twenty-sixth Definition. In this way, we have tempered the strings *Cb, lb, Eb, mb, nb, ob, pb, & cb* of the proposed <term>Monochord</term><note>An ancient musical and scientific instrument with a single string and a movable bridge, used to demonstrate mathematical relationships between pitches.</note> among the strings *Cb, Db, Eb, Fb, Gb, ab, ♮b, and cb*. In this manner, while the <term>Major Third (Ditono)</term> *Cb & Eb* and the minor <term>Sixth (Hexachordo)</term> *Eb & cb* remain in their true forms and proportions, the other intervals are reduced to such a temperament that if one places the <term>bridges</term><note>original: "Hemisperij", literally hemispheres or small movable bridges used on a monochord.</note> under the tempered strings according to the logic shown, one may hear whatever consonance one wishes, and the hearing will be greatly satisfied. But to reduce the *♮b* and *Kb* placed in the bass together with the others to such a temperament—in order to acquire a Fourth that is not found between the first and fourth strings *hb* and *lb*—it will suffice only to ensure that *Ab* and *♮b* correspond with *ab* and *♮b* as an <term>Octave (Diapason)</term> in <term>double proportion</term><note>The 2:1 mathematical ratio that defines an octave.</note>. This is done by making *Aa* equal to *ab*, and *♮♮* equal to *♮b*. In this case, both string *Ab* and *♮b* will be divided into two equal parts at points *a* and *♮*. Thus, the proportion of *Ab* and *ab*, and of *♮b* and *♮b*, will be the same from sound to sound (by the First and Fifth demands of the Third reasoning) as it is from number to number. Therefore, since *Ab* and *ab* (and similarly *♮b* and *♮b*) are in double proportion, by the Eighth definition of the Second [book], *Ab* and *ab* (and similarly *♮b* and *♮b*) will create the Octave consonance. And the Tone *Ab* and *♮b* will be equal to the Tone *ab* and *♮b*; likewise, the Semitone *♮b* and *Cb* will be equal to the Semitone *♮b* and *cb*. This is because the proportion found between *hb* and *Ab* and between *♮b* and *Kb* is the same as that found between *ob* and *ab* and between *♮b* and *pb*. For the Octave *hb* and *ob*, by the Twenty-seventh definition of today, is made higher by the quantity *ob* and *ab* (which is the fourth part of the Comma), and *Kb* and *pb* are lower by that same quantity: the former in strings *Ab* and *ab*, and the latter in *♮b* and *♮b*. But because *Ab* and *ab* contain the Octave, and *Db* and *ab* is a Fifth, *Ab* and *Db* will result in being a Fourth, by the <term>Corollary of the Fourth proposition</term><note>original: "Corrolario della Quarta proposta"</note> of the Second day. And just as it has been demonstrated that *Db* and *ab* is a Fifth reduced to its temperament, so *Ab* and *Db* will be a Fourth reduced to such a quality. In this way, we will have acquired a Fourth between the First and Fourth strings, which did not previously exist; and this is according to our purpose. Furthermore, if we divide the string *Db* into two equal parts and mark the midpoint as *d*, we will have, by the Forty-second [proposition] of the Third [book], a double proportion between string *Db* and *db*, and by the Eighth Definition named above, the Octave consonance. ### Fifth Book

The interval *c b* & *d b* is equal to *C b* & *D b*: which is the <term>Tone</term><note>A whole step.</note>: and the *d b* and *e b* is likewise equal to *D b* & *E b*, a Tone, while the strings *E b* and *e b* remain immobile; these, with *C b* and *c b*, contain the <term>Major Third (Ditono)</term><note>Literally "two tones."</note> in its true and natural form and proportion. But to find the corresponding <term>Octave (Diapason)</term><note>The interval of an eighth.</note> for *F b*: we shall divide, according to the forty-second proposition mentioned earlier, this *F b* into two equal parts: and between this *F b*, which will contain two parts, and *f b*: which will contain one: we will have the Octave consonance in its true form: and the <term>Major Semitone</term><note>A half step.</note> between *e b* and *f b* will be increased by one-fourth part of a <term>Comma</term><note>A tiny musical interval used in tuning theory to account for mathematical discrepancies.</note>. We will also find the corresponding Octave for *G b*, dividing it into two equal parts according to the proposal mentioned just now: and taking one part at point *g*: between *G b* and *g b* we will have what was intended, and between *f b* and *g b* we will have the Tone: which will be of equal proportion to the Tone *F b* and *G b*. We shall do the same for string *a b*: because by dividing it into two parts: and taking one part of it at point *aa*: between *a b* and *aa b* we will have an Octave: which will be equal to *Ab* and *a b*: and it will be higher in pitch (according to today’s twenty-seventh Definition) than *ob* and *t b*, by one-fourth part of a Comma: just as *Ab* and *ab* is also compared to *hb* and *ob*. But the Tone *g b* and *ab* will be equal to *G b* and *a b*: because it is increased by two-fourth parts of the Comma: which are *g s* & *t aa*, just as *G b* & *a b* is increased by *G n* and *o a*. And just as the strings *a b* & *d b* correspond to *Ab* & *D b* in a double proportion: and between the first two the tempered <term>Fourth (Diatessaron)</term> is found: so it is also found between the other two: because, according to the twenty-eighth [proposition] of the second day: both contain two Tones and one Major Semitone. Thus we have acquired two Fourths: one *Ab* & *Db* placed in the low register, and the other *a b* & *d b* placed in the high register, which were missing between the first and the fourth: and between the eighth and the eleventh of the proposed fifteen strings: as the proposition states. And just as *Db* & *ab* correspond to *d b* and *aa b* likewise in double proportion: and between the first two the tempered <term>Fifth (Diapente)</term> is found: so it is also found between the following two. Thus we have two acquired Fifths: which were missing between the fourth and the eighth string: and between the eleventh and the fifteenth of the fifteen proposed strings, one is between *Db* and *ab*: the other between *d b* and *aa b*: according to the goal. But having tested with our senses that the harmony produced by these strings: *Ab, ♮b, Cb, Db, Eb, Fb, Gb, ab, ♮b, cb, db, eb, fb, gb,* and *aa b*: is pleasing and sweet to the ear: therefore we shall say: that all these intervals, reduced to such a <term>temperament</term><note>The adjustment of intervals to make them usable in harmony.</note>, are consonant, without any contradiction. And this is all that, according to the proposal, I had to demonstrate to you.

DESIDERIO. This has been a long stretch: and truly it is a beautiful thing to know: especially for those of you who make a profession of the matters of Music. And I believe that those who are ignorant of this matter lack a great perfection: I mean those who make a profession of building musical instruments: as I can understand from the words spoken a little while ago by Master Claudio.

CLAUDIO. It is truly so: and no one can truthfully deny it.

ADRIANO. Oh, how arrogant are those who are simple composers of Music, who though they are ignorant of the things of Science: nevertheless wish to hold the leadership in this Art: and it seems to them that they are the most learned and wisest men in the world. But take them away from that little bit of composing they do with little practice: they remain naked, without knowing anything at all: therefore it is a good thing to learn: so as not to enter into the number of those: who live among men only to make up the numbers. Continue then, Master Gioseffo, your reasoning: because we all listen to you willingly, all the more since we see that every so often you propose to us something new, beautiful, and ingenious.

GIOSEFFO. Listen to me then: for you shall have pleasure.

### PROPOSAL II.

# The proportions of the Fifth, the Fourth: that of the Minor Third, the Tone, & that of the Major Semitone: are <term>surds</term><note>original: "sordi." In mathematics, a "surd" or "deaf" number refers to an irrational number that cannot be expressed as a simple fraction.</note>, & irrational.

<margin>Part 1, Chapter 2</margin>
ADRIANO: I believe you mean that a <term>Surd</term><note>In Renaissance mathematics, a "surd" (sorda) refers to an irrational number—one that cannot be expressed as a ratio of whole numbers.</note> and irrational quantity is one that cannot be described or named with rational numbers: as you have said in the *Institutions* and in the twenty-fifth proposal of these discussions.
GIOSEPPO: It is so, sir: although one might say that the <term>Fifth (Diapente)</term><note>An interval of five scale degrees.</note> is larger or smaller than an entire fourth part of a <term>Sesquiottantesima proportion</term><note>The ratio 81:80, which defines the "comma."</note>—which is the form of the <term>Comma</term><note>A tiny musical interval used as a unit of measure in tuning theory.</note>—and such a part might be considered rational in a certain way. This is because, as was said and demonstrated in the Ninth Proposal of our first discussion: a <term>Superparticular</term><note>A ratio where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator (e.g., 3:2, 4:3).</note> interval, such as the one named, does not admit one or more rational middle terms that would divide it into two or more proportional parts. Therefore, returning to our subject, I say: That quantity, according to today’s last definition, is said to be irrational when it arises from adding or taking away a rational from an irrational, or conversely, an irrational from a rational. Consequently, since in the temperament made in the preceding section we have taken away from or added to the quantities of the Fifth, the <term>Fourth (Diatessaron)</term>, the <term>Minor Third (Semiditono)</term>, the <term>Tone</term>, and the <term>Major Semitone</term>—which are all rational—such an irrational quantity, it follows that all these named intervals, when tempered, are contained by surd and irrational proportions. For the proportion of the Fifth, as is manifest from the preceding, remains diminished in its temperament (as its definition also says) by one-fourth part of a comma; this part cannot be described or named with certain and determined numbers, according to the Ninth Proposal of the First Book recently mentioned. Thus, when such a part is taken away from the <term>Sesquialtera</term><note>The 3:2 ratio, the mathematical "true" form of the Fifth.</note>—which is the true form of the Fifth and is rational—by the last definition already named, there undoubtedly results a surd and irrational proportion. I say the same of the Fourth: because it is increased by such a part. Therefore, the fourth part of the comma, which is irrational, being added to the <term>Sesquiterza</term><note>The 4:3 ratio, the mathematical "true" form of the Fourth.</note>—which is rational and the form of the said Fourth—there results an irrational interval and quantity. We say the same of the Minor Third, which becomes smaller by a fourth part; and of the Major Tone, which likewise becomes smaller by two-fourth parts; and of the Minor Tone, which is increased by that same amount. And finally, of the Major Semitone, which is increased in the same way by a fourth part of the named comma. Therefore, I say that the proportions of the Fifth and the Fourth, those of the Minor Third and the Tone, along with those of the Major Semitone, are surds and irrational: as I was to demonstrate to you according to the proposal.
CLAUDIO: These are things that cannot be denied, for the truth is seen in the principles and means by which they are demonstrated and proven.
FRANCESCO: Truly, there is no contradiction here; since there is nothing else to say on this matter, it would be well to move further.
GIOSEPPO: That would certainly be good. However, note that

### PROPOSAL III.

->We can add the <term>Proslambanomenos</term><note>original: "τωωπροσλαμβανόμενος" — the lowest note of the ancient Greek musical system (A).</note> to the fifteen strings reduced to the shown temperament.<-

DESIDERIO: What necessity is there to place this string among the number of the others?
GIOSEPPO: I wish to tell you only two things for your understanding. The first is because from this string, which I wish to add, the first and lowest <term>Hexachord of the Hypatōn</term><note>The lowest six-note scale in the medieval system.</note> begins. The second is because, by its means, I come to arrange the <term>Modes</term><note>The melodic scales or "keys" of Renaissance music.</note> in order one after another among sixteen strings, without anything lacking and without anything being superfluous, as you will see. Without this string, our entire design would be broken.
DESIDERIO: These are two important reasons; please continue.
GIOSEPPO: Let the fifteen strings Ab, ♮b, Cb, Db, Eb, Fb, Gb, ab, ♮b, cb, db, eb, fb, gb, & aa b be marked according to the First Proposal of this [book] above the string h & b; and let Ab be the Proslambanomenos, to which we have to propose the <term>Gamma-Ut</term><note>original: "τωωπροσλαμβανόμενος : ouer Gamaut" — the lowest note G of the Guidonian Hand.</note>. # Fifth [Day]

...ne: and the **major Tone** <note>original: "Tuono maggiore"</note> in its proportion above the string $\natural b$: in such a way that $A b$ becomes its acute extremity. Therefore, I divide this $A b$ into eight equal parts, for the minor term of the <term>Sesquiottava</term><note>The ratio 9:8, which defines a major whole tone in Pythagorean tuning.</note>, which is its proportion: and I add to these parts the ninth at point $l$: and between $l b$ and $A b$ we have the objective, having proposed it to the Tone $A b$ and $\natural b$.

But because it is necessary to reduce this interval to the temperament of the other Tones: so that the grave [low] string of this accommodated Tone corresponds exactly with the $G b$ in <term>Dupla proportion</term><note>The 2:1 ratio, which creates the interval of an octave.</note>: and the <term>Diapason</term><note>The interval of an octave.</note> sounds in consonance with it: therefore, by the thirty-sixth [rule] of the Third day: we will accommodate the <term>Comma</term><note>A tiny interval (81:80) representing the difference between a major and minor tone; here it is being used to "temper" or adjust the tuning for harmony.</note> above the string $l b$: which will be $l b$ and $m b$: and we will divide it, by the tenth [rule] of the said Third day: into two equal parts. Thus, leaving the graver part, and the one closest to the $l$ on one side: between $\Gamma b$ and $A b$ we will have placed the proposed Tone in its proportion: and we will have also placed it before the Tone $A b$ and $\natural b$. But because $l b$ and $A b$ is the major Tone, contained in its natural proportion: and by the string $\Gamma b$ it is made smaller by half of a Comma: which is $l b$ and $m b$: therefore I say, by its definition, $\Gamma b$ and $A b$ is the major Tone tempered as was necessary. And because $A b$, by the eighth definition of the Fourth [day]: is the <term>Proslambanomenos</term><note>The lowest note of the ancient Greek musical system, equivalent to the note A.</note>: and the $\Gamma b$ is distant from it by a Tone, and is placed in the grave: therefore I say, by today’s nineteenth definition likewise: $\Gamma b$ is the string <term>Hypoproslambanomenos</term><note>Literally "the note below the Proslambanomenos." This note was added to the Greek system later and is represented by the Greek letter Gamma (Γ).</note>, placed before the Proslambanomenos: and before the fifteen proposed strings: as I had to demonstrate to you according to the proposal.

FRANCESCO: Here no doubt falls at all.

GIOSEPPO: I want to tell you one more thing before we go further: that the named string **Hypoproslambanomenos** can be added by another means. Because if we double the string $G b$, which will be doubled at point $\Gamma$: we will have the string $\Gamma b$, which by the Fourth Definition of the First day: will contain the **Dupla proportion** with that $G b$: because $\Gamma b$ contains $G b$ exactly two times. Whence, by the Eighth Definition of the Second discussion: they come to contain the **Diapason consonance**. And because this consonance contains within itself (by the thirty-ninth [rule] of the Second [day]) five Tones and two major Semitones: and the interval $A b$ and $G b$ contains only four Tones and the two named Semitones: therefore the interval $\Gamma b$ and $A b$ will come to contain the Tone: which, placed together with the other four and the two Semitones, will make a Diapason consonance. Being then $\Gamma b$ and $A b$ a Tone: and being $\Gamma b$ distant from $A b$ (the Proslambanomenos) by a Tone: it follows, by the named nineteenth definition: that $\Gamma b$ is the Hypoproslambanomenos: just as it was necessary to demonstrate.

CLAUDIO: In truth, nothing can be said to the contrary, and this which you have now demonstrated by means of the Dupla, or Diapason, is so manifest: that, not disagreeing at all with the given definition, one must perforce confess that such an added string is the Hypoproslambanomenos that you have said: or the <term>Gammaut</term><note>The traditional name for the lowest note of the medieval musical scale (Gamma-ut).</note>: as it is called by practitioners. Follow on then with the rest, if it pleases you.

GIOSEPPO: I will continue then to tell you that:

# PROPOSAL IIII.
