### PROPOSITION V.

## The fifth Hexachord, called the ***Synemennon***, can be added to the first four.

Let the strings Γ, A, ♮ <note>This symbol represents B-natural, also known as "hard B."</note>, C, D, E, F, G, a, ♮, c, d, e, f, g, and aa be arranged as in the penultimate [proposition]: above the noted strings *h* and *k*: which, as in the preceding [page], contain the first four **Hexachords** <term>Hexachord: A six-note musical scale used in the Middle Ages and Renaissance for sight-singing.</term>: ***Hypaton***, ***Meson***, ***Diezeugmenon***, and ***Hyperboleon*** <note>These terms are borrowed from Ancient Greek music theory, meaning Lowest, Middle, Disjunct, and Highest.</note>. To these, it is necessary to add the fifth, called the ***Synemennon*** <note>Greek: "conjunct" or "connected." This hexachord is unique because it introduces the B-flat to the system.</note>. First, I arrange the major Semitone in its true and natural proportion above the string *a K*, following the nineteenth [proposition] of the Third Day <note>A reference to a previous section of the author's mathematical demonstrations.</note>: from which come *a K* and *l K*. But because *a K* and *l K* is a major Semitone and is contained in its natural form, it must—according to its definition—be larger by one-quarter of a **Comma** <term>Comma: A very small musical interval resulting from the difference between two other intervals (like six whole tones vs. an octave).</term>. Therefore, I first arrange this Comma according to its proportion, by the thirtieth [proposition] of the Third Argument, so that the string *l K* is the low end of this interval and *m K* the high end. Then, I divide it similarly into four equal parts using the eleventh [proposition] of the same Third Argument. By adding *l b* with *a l*, we will have the major Semitone between *a K* and *b K* according to its definition. However, this is increased—following today's twenty-sixth definition—by one-quarter part of the Comma *l K* and *m K*, as is manifest to the senses.

*Therefore, note that: according to today’s Eleventh definition: a <term>Mode: A specific arrangement of intervals forming a musical scale.</term> is that which contains within itself a form, or quality of harmony: which is found in one of the Seven species of the <term>Octave: (Diapason) An interval spanning eight scale degrees.</term>: modulated by those species of the <term>Fifth: (Diapente) An interval spanning five scale degrees.</term>, and of the <term>Fourth: (Diatessaron) An interval spanning four scale degrees.</term>, which are suitable to its form. But because such Species cannot be modulated except in Twelve manners: because: according to today’s Eleventh proposition: the Octave is found harmonically divided <note>Harmonic division places the larger interval (the Fifth) at the bottom.</note> into six modes: and according to the Twelfth proposition: into six other modes arithmetically <note>Arithmetic division places the smaller interval (the Fourth) at the bottom.</note>: so that all these manners amount to the number of Twelve: I say therefore, that the Modes can be neither more nor less than Twelve. And because: according to the Fifteenth definition: from the first division arise six principal and <term>Authentic: Modes where the melody primarily moves above the final note.</term> Modes: and from the second; according to the Sixteenth: come the Six non-principal and <term>Plagal: Modes where the melody moves around the final note, often going a Fourth below it.</term>: therefore there are Six principal and Authentic Modes: and also Six Non-principal and Plagal: as I had to demonstrate to you. ADRIANO. This point cannot be denied: for it is too manifest. GIOSEPPE. Therefore I will follow with the next: so as not to lose time: which shall be this.*

# PROPOSITION XV.

## The final Strings of the Six principal Modes are common with those of their Collaterals.

*ADRIANO. This is a true conclusion in practice: therefore it will not displease me if you demonstrate it to us. GIOSEPPE. That is exactly what I wish to do. But all the First of the named Modes are Principal: and the Second are the <term>Collaterals: Another name for Plagal modes, which share a final note with an Authentic mode.</term>: therefore the final strings of the Six principal modes are common with those of their six collateral modes: as I had to demonstrate to you. FRANCESCO. This demonstration is easy and clear: and if one did not already know this conclusion by virtue of the principles, it would not be necessary to do it otherwise. But let us come to another. GIOSEPPE. I want you to know also; that*

GIOS. <note>Gioseffo Zarlino, the author.</note> This is the proper place, sir: so please pay attention.

## PROPOSITION XIX.

The notes of the Third mode are higher <note>original: *piu acute*, literally "sharper" or higher in pitch.</note> than those of the First by one Whole Tone: those of the Fifth are higher than those of the Third likewise by one Whole Tone: those of the Seventh are higher than those of the Fifth by a Major Semitone: those of the Ninth are higher than those of the Seventh by one Whole Tone: and those of the Eleventh are even higher than those of the Ninth by—

by a <term>Tone: A whole step interval in music.</term>. Similarly, the strings of the Fourth mode are higher than those of the Second by a Tone; those of the Sixth higher than those of the Fourth by a Tone; those of the Eighth higher than those of the Sixth by a <term>major Semitone: A larger half-step, often found between E-F or B-C in historical tuning.</term>; and those of the Tenth are higher than those of the Eighth by a Tone. FRANCESCO. *This is a long discourse.* <note>The speaker Francesco finds the technical explanation of intervals somewhat tedious.</note> GIOSUÈ. *We will make it short, God willing. There is no doubt that, according to today’s First Proposition, the string D is higher than C; E than D; G than F; and 'a' than G—each by itself—by one Tone. Similarly, F is higher than E, and also C higher than <term>B-natural: Notated as ♮ or "B-quadro" in the original text.</term> by a major Semitone. Therefore, since C is the lowest string of the First mode; D that of the Third; E that of the Fifth; F that of the Seventh; G that of the Ninth; and 'a' that of the Eleventh. Furthermore, since <term>Gamma: Γ, the lowest note in the medieval musical system (the "Gamut").</term> is the lowest string of the Second mode; A that of the Fourth; B-natural that of the Sixth; C that of the Eighth; D that of the Tenth; and E that of the Twelfth: the others follow in order, according to the nature of their <term>Octave: (Diapason) The range of eight notes.</term>. Thus, the strings of the Third mode are higher than those of the First; and those of the Fifth higher than those of the Third; those of the Ninth higher than those of the Seventh; and those of the Eleventh higher than those of the Ninth, by a Tone. And those of the Seventh are higher than those of the Fifth by a major Semitone, as the first part of the proposition states. And for the second part, I say: that by the aforementioned First Proposition, the string A is higher than Gamma; B-natural than A; also D than C; E than D by a Tone. And C is higher than B-natural by a major Semitone. But Gamma is the lowest string of the Second mode; A that of the Fourth; B-natural that of the Sixth; C that of the Eighth; D that of the Tenth; and E that of the Twelfth. Therefore, the strings of the Fourth mode are higher than those of the Second; those of the Sixth than those of the Fourth; those of the Tenth than those of the Eighth; and those of the Twelfth than those of the Tenth, by a Tone. Likewise, those of the Eighth are truly higher than those of the Sixth by a major Semitone. And this is all that is contained in the second part of the proposition, and together everything that I was to demonstrate to you according to that proposition.* DESIDERIO. *When things are easy and known to the senses, yet one wishes to understand them through their principles and causes, it cannot be done otherwise. <note>Desiderio acknowledges that while these pitch differences are obvious to the ear, proving them through theory requires this detailed "long discourse."</note> However, we may move further, since this needs no further explanation.* GIOSUÈ. *It is exactly as you say, in fact; it cannot be done otherwise. Listen then to what I wish to tell you:*

---

## PROPOSITION XX.

The strings of the melodies of the Principal Modes contained within their Octaves are higher than those of their Non-principal modes; and conversely: those of the Non-principal are lower than those of their Principal Modes by a <term>Fourth: (Diatessaron) An interval of four notes.</term>

*WE HAVE, by today’s fifteenth definition, that the First, Third, Fifth, Seventh, Ninth, and Eleventh modes are Principal modes; and by the sixteenth, that the Second, Fourth, Sixth, Eighth, Tenth, and Twelfth are Non-principal modes. But by the fourteenth definition, the First mode is contained by the first species of the <term>Diapason: An octave, the interval of an eighth.</term>: C.D.E.F.G.a.♮.c; and the Second by the fifth [species]: <term>Γ: Gamma, the lowest note in the medieval system, equivalent to a low G.</term>.A.♮.C.D.E.F. & G. The Third by the second species: D.E.F.G.a.♮.c. & d; the Fourth by the sixth [species]: A.♮.C.D.E.F.G. & a; the Fifth by the third [species]: E.F.G.a.♮.c.d. & e; the Sixth by the seventh [species]: ♮.C.D.E.F.G.a. & ♮; the Seventh by the fourth [species]: F.G.a.♮.c.d.e. & f; the Eighth by the first [species]: C.D.E.F.G.a.♮. & c; the Ninth by the fifth [species]: G.a.♮.c.d.e.f. & g; the Tenth by the second [species]: D.E.F.G.a.♮.c. & d; the Eleventh by the sixth [species]: a.♮.c.d.e.f.g. & aa; and the Twelfth by the third [species]: E.F.G.a.♮.c.d. & e.*

*However, the lowest string of the First mode, which is C, is higher than the lowest string of the Second, which is Γ—or to put it the other way: this [Γ] is lower than that [C] by a <term>Diatessaron: An interval of a perfect fourth.</term>. That of the Third, D, is higher than that of the Fourth, A; that of the Fifth, E, is higher than that of the Sixth, ♮; that of the Seventh, F, is higher than that of the Eighth, C; that of the Ninth, G, is higher than that of the Tenth, D; and that of the Eleventh, 'a', is higher than that of the Twelfth, E. In other words, all the second-named notes are lower than the first-named ones by a fourth. Therefore, the strings of the melodies of the Principal Modes are higher than those of the Non-principal ones; or rather, the strings of the latter are lower than the strings of the former by a fourth, as was to be demonstrated. To this we shall add:*

## PROPOSITION XXI.

### We can reduce the Principal modes and the Non-principal modes into a single order, pairing them together according to their number and degrees.

*FRANCESCO: It seemed to me that this part was missing; well then, proceed. GIOSUÈ: Let C.D.E.F.G.a.♮.c be the strings of the first species of the Octave, in the first and eighth order; those of the fifth [species], Γ.A.♮.C.D.E.F. & G, in the second; those of the second [species], D.E.F.G.a.♮.c. & d, in the third and tenth; those of the sixth [species], A.♮.C.D.E.F.G. & a, in the fourth; those of the third [species], E.F.G.a.♮.c.d. & e, in the fifth and twelfth order; those of the seventh [species], ♮.C.D.E.F.G.a. & ♮, in the sixth; those of the fourth [species], F.G.a.♮.c.d.e. & f, in the seventh; those of the fifth [species] again, G.a.♮.c.d.e.f. & g, in the ninth; and similarly those of the sixth [species], a.♮.c.d.e.f.g. & aa, in the eleventh.*

*I say that the Principal modes (or <term>Authentic: Modes where the melody primarily moves above the final note.</term>) are reduced and paired together with the Non-principal (or <term>Plagal: Modes that share a final note with an Authentic mode but sit a fourth lower.</term>) modes, according to their number and degrees. This is because the first species of the Octave is found in the first order, and the fifth species in the second. Since the First mode is contained within the first [species], <term>harmonically mediated: Divided such that a perfect fifth is at the bottom and a fourth at the top.</term> by the string G, and the second mode is contained in the fifth [species], arithmetically mediated <note>An arithmetic division places the smaller interval (the fourth) at the bottom, which is characteristic of Plagal modes.</note>; and since string Γ of the Octave placed in the second order is lower than string C of the Octave placed in the first, it follows that the first order contains the first Authentic mode, and the second order contains the second Plagal mode. Thus, after the first Principal mode, we have placed the second Non-principal mode and paired it with the first, according to the number and degrees of each. There is no doubt that the Second in any ordered series must immediately follow the First.*

*After the Second follows the Third. According to the nineteenth [proposition] of this book, the Third is higher than the First by a <term>Tone: A whole step.</term>. Therefore, since the Octave D.E.F.G.a.♮.c. & d of the third order is higher than that of the first by a Tone—given that C is distant from D by such an interval, as I have demonstrated many times—and [since it is] divided harmonically by the string 'a' into a <term>Diapente: An interval of a perfect fifth.</term> and a fourth, it follows that this Octave contains...*

->THE NATURAL ORDER OF ALL THE MODES.<-

Γ. <term>Hypoproslambanomenos: The "lowest added note," equivalent to the low G at the bottom of the medieval gamut.</term>
---
A. <term>Proslambanomenos: The "added note" that begins the formal Greek scale, equivalent to A.</term>
---
♮. <term>Hypate hypaton: The "principal of the principals," equivalent to B.</term>
---
C. <term>Parhypate hypaton: The note "next to the principal of principals," equivalent to C.</term>
---
D. <term>Lichanos hypaton: The "index finger" note of the principal group, equivalent to D.</term>
---
E. <term>Hypate meson: The "principal" of the middle group of notes, equivalent to E.</term>
---
F. <term>Parhypate meson: The note "next to the principal" of the middle group, equivalent to F.</term>
---
G. <term>Lichanos meson: The "index finger" note of the middle group, equivalent to G.</term>
---
a. <term>Mese: The "middle" note of the entire system, equivalent to A.</term>
---
♮. <term>Paramese: The note "next to the middle," equivalent to B natural.</term>
---
c. <term>Trite diezeugmenon: The "third" note of the disjunct (separated) group, equivalent to C.</term>
---
d. <term>Paranete diezeugmenon: The "next-to-last" note of the disjunct group, equivalent to D.</term>
---
e. <term>Nete diezeugmenon: The "last" or highest note of the disjunct group, equivalent to E.</term>
---
f. <term>Trite hyperboleon: The "third" note of the extreme high group, equivalent to F.</term>
---
g. <term>Paranete hyperboleon: The "next-to-last" note of the extreme high group, equivalent to G.</term>
---
aa. <term>Nete hyperboleon: The "last" or highest note of the entire system, equivalent to a high A.</term>

# Fifth.

*The Third mode is <term>authentic</term> <note>a "principal" mode where the melody typically ranges from the final note to the octave above</note>: placed according to its number and degree after the Second and <term>plagal</term> <note>a "side" mode that shares the same final note as its authentic counterpart but sits at a lower pitch range</note> [mode]. To this follows the Fourth, placed in the fourth order according to the fourteenth definition, within the sixth species of the <term>Diapason</term> <note>original: "Diapason", meaning an octave</note> A, B, C, D, E, F, G, and a: <term>arithmetically</term> <note>divided such that the smaller musical interval, the fourth, is on the bottom</note> divided. This mode is distant from the Second mode by a <term>Tone</term>, as established by the nineteenth proposition of this work. Since we have demonstrated that the octave from D to d, with its middle notes, contains the Third mode, it follows that without any gap—and according to its number and degree—we have placed the Fourth mode after the Third. After the Fourth, the Fifth immediately follows; for the octave E, F, G, a, B, c, d, and e, contained in the fifth order and divided by the note B into two <term>harmonized</term> <note>original: "harmonicate", referring to a harmonic division where the larger interval, the fifth, is on the bottom</note> parts according to the cited fourteenth definition, contains this Fifth mode. And by the aforementioned nineteenth proposition, the Fifth mode is distant from the Third by a Tone, because—by that same tenth [definition]—it happens to be higher than D by such an interval. Therefore, since E, F, G, a, B, c, d, and e is the Fifth mode, and A, B, C, D, E, F, G, and a is the Fourth, I say that the Fifth is a principal mode and is arranged after the Fourth and plagal mode, just as their order and degrees require. After the Fifth follows the Sixth, within the octave of the sixth order B, C, D, E, F, G, a, and B; because, by the cited definition, it contains the Sixth mode, mediated <term>arithmetically</term> by the note E. And because, by the nineteenth proposition, the Sixth is higher than the Fourth by a Tone—with B to B and its middle notes being the Sixth mode, and E to e with its middle notes being the Fifth—it follows that the Sixth mode is placed after the Fifth, according to their number and degrees. After this follows the Seventh: for in the seventh order is contained the octave F, G, a, B, c, d, e, and f, which contains (by the said fifteenth definition) this Seventh and principal mode. This mode, by the cited nineteenth proposition, is distant from the Fifth by a <term>major Semitone</term>; for between E and F, as has been shown many times and especially in that nineteenth proposition, such a distance is found. Therefore, since B to B with its middle notes is the Sixth mode, and F to f with its middle notes is the Seventh, it follows that we have placed the Seventh after the Sixth mode according to their number and degrees. Now comes the Eighth after the Seventh, which I say is C, D, E, F, G, a, B, and c, divided arithmetically by the F; given that, according to the cited nineteenth proposition, it is distant from the Sixth by a major semitone. And because this follows immediately after the Seventh, I therefore say that the Eighth is arranged after the Seventh mode, according to their number and degrees. I say further that the octave G, a, B, c, d, e, f, and g contains the Ninth mode: because, by the eleventh proposition, it is the fifth species divided harmonically into two parts by the note d. Being higher than the F to f contained in the seventh place by a Tone, it follows that G to g with its middle notes contains the Ninth mode, and that the Ninth mode should be arranged after the Eighth, as their order and degrees dictate. Similarly, I say that within the octave D, E, F, G, a, B, c, and d—which immediately succeeds the G to g in the tenth order—the Tenth mode (which is not a principal mode) is placed. This is because the D to d is divided arithmetically into two parts by the note G, as we demonstrated in today’s thirteenth proposition; and by the nineteenth proposition, it is lower than the G to g by a <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>original: "Diatessaron", meaning a perfect fourth</note>. Wherefore, by the Definition and according to the numerical order and degrees of the Modes, the Tenth and plagal is accompanied by and arranged after the Ninth, which is its principal. To this succeeds the Eleventh, placed within the octave a, B, c, d, e, f, g, and aa, located in the eleventh order. Because it is arithmetically divided into two parts by the e, it comes to contain the Eleventh mode, being higher than the G to g by a Tone. Therefore, since D to d with its middle notes is the Tenth mode, we have demonstrated, according to our purpose, that the Eleventh is arranged after it, according to the order and degrees of the Modes. Lastly, I say that we have arranged the Twelfth after the Eleventh within the octave E, F, G, a, B, c, d, and e: because it is divided arithmetically into two parts by the note a. Such a mode is lower than the Eleventh by a Fourth, and lower than the Tenth by a Tone. Wherefore, by the Definition, the octave E to e with its middle notes comes to contain the Twelfth mode. And because it succeeds immediately after the Eleventh, according to the order and the degrees of the modes, I therefore say that after the eleventh mode*

## PROPOSITION XXII.

### We can demonstrate that all the principal Modes are placed among the thirteen highest of the sixteen notes shown above.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'L' with floral and geometric patterns in a square frame.</image-desc>

*LAURO. I believe this will be easily proven, from what I can see.*

*GIOSEFFO. I believe you are not mistaken; therefore, we shall speak. According to the fifteenth definition that I gave you today: a <term>Principal Mode</term> <note>also called an Authentic mode; its range extends upward from its final or "home" note</note> is that which is contained between the notes of one of the seven species of the <term>Diapason</term> <note>an octave</note>, divided <term>harmonically</term> <note>divided so the larger interval (the fifth) is on the bottom and the smaller (the fourth) is on top</note> by a middle note into a <term>Diapente</term> <note>a perfect fifth</note> and a <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>a perfect fourth</note>. But, according to the eleventh proposition, the notes of the octaves C & c, D & d, F & f, G & g, and similarly of a & aa, are divided in such a manner: because the notes of the first species of the octave C & c are divided by the note G into a fifth C & G and a fourth G & c. Those of the second species D & d [are divided] by the note a into a fifth D & a and a fourth a & d. Those of the third species E & e [are divided] by the ♮ <note>original: "♮", meaning B-natural</note> into a fifth E & ♮ and a fourth ♮ & e. Likewise, those of the fourth F & f are mediated and divided by the note c into a fifth F & c and a fourth c & f. Those of the fifth species G & g [are divided] into a fifth G & d and a fourth d & g by the note d. Finally, those of the sixth species a & aa [are divided] by the note e into a fifth a & e and a fourth e & aa. Thus the octaves C-G-c, D-a-d, E-♮-e, F-c-f, G-d-g, along with a-e-aa, each contain one of the Principal and Authentic Modes. Now, the lowest note <note>original: "chorda grauissima"</note> of the first species is C, and the highest <note>original: "acutissima"</note> of the last is aa. And from C to aa, including the intermediate notes, they reach the number of thirteen notes <note>original: "Tredici chorde"</note>; and these are the highest of all the sixteen notes given above in the order already shown. Therefore, all the principal and Authentic Modes are placed among the thirteen highest notes of the sixteen already shown: as I was meant to demonstrate to you.*

*ADRIANO. Very well; continue then with the others, if it pleases you.*

*GIOSEFFO. I certainly intend to; so listen.*

Now, the note is the *middle* note, which divides this <term>Diapason</term> <note>octave</note> arithmetically: just as the note $c$ divides the first <term>Diapason</term> into two parts: that is, into a <term>Diateffaron</term> <note>perfect fourth</note> $G$ and $c$ placed in the lower range, and into a <term>Diapente</term> <note>perfect fifth</note> $c$ and $g$ placed in the high range. We will have the same melody of the first species of <term>Diateffaron</term> between the notes $G$, $a$, $natural$, and $c$ of this octave as we have between the notes $\Gamma$, $A$, $natural$, and $C$ of the other. And there is just as much of the melody of the first species of <term>Diapente</term> between the notes $c$, $d$, $e$, $f$, and $g$ of this second <term>Diapason</term> as there is between the notes $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$, and $G$ of the first. This is because in one of these <term>Diateffarons</term>, one moves from the low to the high range by two whole tones and one major semitone, just as one does in the other. And likewise, one moves from low to high by tone, tone, one major semitone, and tone in one of these <term>Diapentes</term>, just as one moves in the other. Hence, the <term>Diapason</term> $\Gamma$ and $G$ of the fifth species will be exactly the same as the $G$ and $g$ species: because, by the Seventh Axiom, those intervals are called similar when they are contained by similar boundaries and proportions. Therefore, since the boundaries of the first <term>Diapason</term> shown are similar to those of the second, there is no doubt that no difference can fall between them, except that of being lower or higher.

However, since $G$ and $g$ are divided arithmetically <note>An "arithmetic" division of the octave places the smaller interval, the fourth, below the larger interval, the fifth. This creates what theorists call a "Plagal" mode.</note> by $c$, just as $\Gamma$ and $G$ are divided by $C$, and since both are <term>Diapasons</term> of the fifth species, it follows also—by today’s Fourteenth Definition—that both contain the Second Mode. But because the <term>Diapason</term> $G$ and $g$ is distant from the <term>Diapason</term> $\Gamma$ and $G$ by an entire octave, and what is played in one can also be played in the other, I say that the melody of the Second Mode can be transposed higher, or lower (if the transposition were done in reverse) by an octave. And this reasoning can also serve to demonstrate that the aforementioned <term>Diapason</term> $\Gamma$ and $G$ divided harmonically <note>A "harmonic" division places the fifth below the fourth, creating an "Authentic" mode.</note> by the note $D$ will contain the same mode as that contained between the <term>Diapason</term> $G$ and $g$ divided in the same way—changing, however, in the demonstration those terms which are necessary to change. And this will create the Ninth Mode, as has been demonstrated by the Eleventh Proposition. 

And because in this manner every Mode, whichever it may be (as can be clearly seen by making a test of it), can be transposed from the low to the high and from the high to the low by an octave, I say that the melody of each of the Twelve Modes can be transposed higher or lower by a <term>Diapason</term>, as I first had to demonstrate to you. But to show you that such melodies can be transposed by a <term>Diateffaron</term> toward the high range, or by a <term>Diapente</term> toward the low range: let the notes $C, D, E, F, G, a, natural, \text{and } c$ be those which contain the melody of the First Mode. Since these notes are divided harmonically by the note $G$, I say that even from the <term>Diapason</term> $F, G, a, b, c, d, e, \text{and } f$ divided by the note $c$ in such a way, we can have the same melody. This is because one moves in the <term>Diapente</term> $F, G, a, b, \text{and } c$ of this <term>Diapason</term> by tone, tone, major semitone, and tone—as is manifest—just as in the <term>Diapente</term> $C, D, E, F, \text{and } G$ of that one. And one proceeds by tone, tone, and major semitone in the <term>Diateffaron</term> $c, d, e, \text{and } f$ of the <term>Diapason</term> $F$ and $f$ just as in the <term>Diateffaron</term> $G, a, natural, \text{and } c$—that is, in the <term>Diapason</term> $C$ and $c$.

And because the <term>Diapason</term> $F$ and $f$, by today’s Twentieth [Proposition], is higher than the $C$ and $c$ by a <term>Diateffaron</term>, and that melody found in the <term>Diapason</term> $C$ and $c$ is also found in $F$ and $f$, I say that the melody of the <term>Diapason</term> $C$ and $c$ can be transposed higher by a <term>Diateffaron</term> into the <term>Diapason</term> $F$ and $f$. <meta>This page concludes the "Fifth Reasoning" or dialogue. It follows the mathematical and musical proof that any of the twelve modes can be transposed to different pitch levels—specifically by an octave, a fourth, or a fifth—without losing their essential melodic character (their "species"). This discussion serves as the finale to the series of dialogues presented in the book.</meta>

->### Fifth Reasoning<-

...those same intervals will modulate the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>original: "Diatessaron"; a perfect fourth</note> **e. f. g. & aa**, just as one would also modulate the <term>Diatessaron</term> **a. b. c. & d.** But because, by the Eighth definition and the Sixth proposition of today, the <term>Diapason</term> <note>original: "Diapason"; an octave</note> **a & aa** is of the sixth species, and the **D & d** is also of the sixth species; and both, divided harmonically, contain the Eleventh mode; and since, by the Seventh and Twenty-first propositions, **D & d** is lower than **a & aa** by a <term>Diapente</term> <note>original: "Diapente"; a perfect fifth</note>; I therefore say: that the melody of the Eleventh mode is transposed lower by a fifth. But because any melody of any mode one wishes can be transposed in this way—as can always be clearly known through the proof—I say: that the melody of each of the Twelve modes can ultimately be made lower by a fifth. The melody, then, of any of the Twelve modes can be transposed higher or lower by an octave; or it can be made higher by a fourth; or lower by a fifth. And this is everything that, according to the proposition, I was meant to demonstrate to you.

**CLAV.** <note>Claudio Merulo (1533–1604), a famous organist and composer</note> We organists know well how useful these transpositions are and how they can be performed. And although practice teaches us this—for I truly knew it through that means—it did not displease me to see such a demonstration depending on the proofs made previously.

**FRAN.** <note>Francesco Viola (d. 1568), Kapellmeister at the court of Ferrara</note> You have by now, Master Gioseffo, demonstrated so many things that I think little more can remain to be said on this matter. Since the hour is late and I have some business to attend to—because we wish to depart early tomorrow morning—if anything remains for you to say, let us not waste time, but come to the end of the matter.

**GIOS.** <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), the author and famous music theorist</note> Although one could discuss and demonstrate many other things beyond those already shown, nevertheless, having proposed (in my opinion) what seemed most necessary, and having touched upon all those things I thought useful to demonstrate in this Science, I do not wish to add anything more. Indeed, I have shown you that this proposition will serve as the conclusion to all these discussions of ours. If I have satisfied you, give thanks to the Blessed Lord God, the giver of all good and excellent things. If, by chance, it has happened otherwise (which could be the case), attribute it to my little knowledge; for I have told you everything I could provide on this matter, without dissimulation or keeping anything hidden. And if by chance I have failed in explaining anything to you for the sake of brevity, or have not satisfied you as fully as you desired, I do not doubt that you will keep in memory those things which I have written in the *Harmonic Foundations* <note>original: "Istitutioni harmoniche"; Zarlino's most famous work, published in 1558</note>. And if you see what I have dictated in the book which I have titled *THE PERFECT MUSICIAN* <note>original: "IL PERFETTO MVSICO"</note> and in the *MUSICAL SUPPLEMENTS* <note>original: "SVPPLIMENTI MVSICALI"</note>, you will be excellently instructed in every doubt that may occur to you. For it is impossible to be able to explain things perfectly all at once. Therefore, being now tired, I will bring my speaking to an end.

**DESI.** <note>Desiderio, likely a fictional or real student/interlocutor in the dialogue</note> It is very right to do so. But if I remember well, Master Gioseffo, I was the one who prompted you to this undertaking; and you have spoken so well and scientifically with such an abundance of musical matters that, besides satisfying me in particular, all of us generally declare ourselves content. And I promise you to keep a perpetual memory of it and to remain forever in your debt, since you have touched upon and resolved so well all those things which gave me trouble and annoyance, so that I have no further reason to doubt. And if a time comes in which I can show you with deeds how grateful this has been to me, I will let you see it. Therefore, at present, I can do nothing else but thank you.

**GIOS.** I am a debtor to all noble and virtuous spirits, such as that of your Lordship; therefore I do not wish there to be any obligation between us other than love. For as I love you, I desire in return that you love me.

**DESI.** In this, I will always be the debtor.

**CLAV.** I too am your debtor in this regard, and I do not know how I can ever—I do not say pay—but even diminish this debt.

**GIOS.** By that same means I mentioned to Signor Desiderio, you will be able to do everything; I wish for nothing else from you.

**FRAN.** Now we have entered into ceremonies and words, and God knows when it will end. Therefore, I too wish briefly to thank you, Master Gioseffo, for your courtesy. And because tomorrow morning we are all to board the boat and return to Ferrara with our Lord Duke, I wish to pray you that, wherever you see that I am able to be of service to you, you [will let me know] without any hesitation...

### Reasoning

*...whatever you may wish to command. And to you, Sir, I will say, exhorting you to live cheerfully; praying you to hold and keep me in your memory.*

**ADRIA.** <note>Likely Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), the influential Venetian chapelmaster and teacher of the author.</note> *I shall do so, my Master Francesco; but I pray you, kiss the hand of His Excellency on my behalf, and I ask you again to keep me alive in the memory of this Lord. And so, may you have a good journey.*

*After these and other sweet and affectionate words were exchanged on both sides, each of us departed and took the road that would most easily and quickly lead us to attend to our own particular business <term>before dinner</term> <note>original: "inanti cena"; a common literary trope in Renaissance dialogues to signal the end of a day's debate.</note>. And so it ended here.*

# Register.

->* A B C D E F G H I K L M N O P Q R S T V X Y Z<-

<note>These terms—Terni, Duerni, and Quaderno—are instructions for the bookbinder. They indicate how many folded sheets of paper make up each section (gathering) of the book. A "Ternion" (Terni) means three sheets were folded together to make six leaves (12 pages).</note>
